courses.title: Design Patterns in C++
courses.subtitle: Dr. Charles Dorner
courses.description: Understand the problem. Recall the pattern. Trace the C++. Study every chapter, then combine the lessons in the capstone.
courses.provenance: Study companion to Design Patterns in C++ by Dr. Charles Dorner. Lessons retain the supplied editable textbook’s chapter sections, example contracts, traces, focused explanations, exercises, lab instructions, and answers. Flashcards use those chapter explanations. Multiple-choice scenarios are original teaching questions. UML views render the supplied diagram definitions and exact focused source excerpts. This is a study companion, with the full runnable source in the C++ view and download package.

topics.title: Teach the pattern, then test the design
topics.summary: A student should finish a lesson able to identify the problem that needs a pattern, point to each role in code and UML, trace how those roles work together, and explain when the pattern is unnecessary. Recognizing a class diagram by its shape is not enough. The design must solve a stated problem.

blocks.text: Start each chapter with its concrete problem and the simplest reasonable approach. Let the limitation become visible before introducing the new arrangement. Then name the pattern and connect its roles to the program. The role table maps the standard role, the attached sample's name, and the name used in this chapter. This is the bridge between the supplied reading and the original teaching example.

Use the attached-example trace to revisit the provided code. Follow calls or ownership changes in their actual order. Then compare the new program. Ask which relationships stay the same and which language or application choices changed. The section on adaptations distinguishes the pattern's essential mechanism from optional features of one sample.

For a classroom demonstration, show the problem first, sketch the roles next, predict the call sequence, and run the complete example. Pause at each focused diagram page. Its code, line reading, and adjacent theory explain one important block. Finish by changing a requirement and asking whether the same design still fits. Each chapter supplies a specific teaching sequence and pattern questions.

Use the independent exercises in order: make a guided change, trace unfamiliar behavior, diagnose a defect, compare designs, extend while keeping earlier checks, and justify a decision. The implementation lab is a larger change with a runnable starting point and an explained solution. Pattern-check answers and exercise answers are kept in the separate answer section.

Read the short primer before the first pattern if objects, interfaces, ownership, or SOLID are unfamiliar. It defines the language needed for the pattern lessons. The course itself begins with Factory Method and continues through all 22 named patterns. The capstone then asks students to select and combine techniques rather than force every pattern into one program.

topics.title: Build the demonstrations and read the diagrams
topics.summary: Extract the companion ZIP and run the commands below from its top-level directory. Each examples/chNN/main.cpp is a complete independent program. Its expected.txt file contains exactly what it should print. The program also checks its own behavior. The exercises and solutions directories contain the corresponding lab versions.

blocks.text: The -std=c++17 option selects the language version. The warning options ask the compiler to flag suspicious code, and -Werror makes those warnings stop the build. The -pthread option supports standard-library threading used by the Singleton lesson. The -o option names the executable. Python 3.9 or later runs the test driver without extra Python packages.

A class diagram shows types and their relationships. A hollow triangle points from a derived class to its base interface. A filled diamond sits at the exclusive owner. A hollow diamond labeled shared ownership marks shared ownership; the last strong owner controls release. A dashed dependency arrow means uses or borrows, not owns. Each diagram has a numbered relationship key.

Activity diagrams follow actions and decisions. Sequence diagrams read from top to bottom as calls occur. State diagrams show states and permitted changes between them. The diagram type is chosen to explain the lesson's central mechanism. Pattern roles are named alongside the actual types or participants where appropriate.

The blue dotted connector on a focused page is a teaching annotation. It links the exact C++ excerpt to the adjacent theory panel; it is not a UML relationship. The line-by-line reading explains every selected nonblank source line. Paths and inclusive line ranges match the delivered files and are recalculated when the book is rebuilt.

A passing program supports the cases it actually checks. The release verifies the new teaching code, not every platform, every possible execution, or every supplied archive variant. Source-sample limitations are discussed where they affect understanding. Full verification details and untested conditions are recorded in the rebuild kit.

topics.title: Start with the pressure, then name the pattern
topics.summary: This book teaches the patterns in the supplied reading and C++ examples. Its central question is "What change is hard, and which design makes it safer?" A design pattern is a named way to arrange program parts to solve a recurring problem. Its name helps a team discuss the problem, roles, and tradeoffs.

blocks.text: An algorithm is a set of steps that computes a result, such as finding the largest number. A pattern describes how responsibilities fit together, such as letting a caller choose among several algorithms. A library supplies usable code. A pattern supplies an idea that you must adapt. Two programs may use Strategy even though their class names, data, and algorithms differ.

Begin with a concrete requirement. A monitor must report one estimate from a list of readings. If the only rule is an average, one small function is enough. Now users need the highest reading too, and must switch rules during a run. A growing branch in the monitor mixes input checks with each rule. Strategy becomes useful when we want those rules to change independently. The extra objects have a cost, so two stable branches may still be the better choice.

Each chapter states a requirement, exposes the limit of a simple design, introduces the named pattern, traces and tests the solution, and judges an alternative. A pattern succeeds when it makes a real change easier while preserving required behavior. More classes or a familiar diagram do not prove better design.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/primer.json → Start with the pressure, then name the pattern

topics.title: The object words used by the patterns
topics.summary: A type tells C++ what kind of value something holds and which operations are allowed. A class defines a type that can hold data and provide functions. An object is a particular instance with its own identity and lifetime. Two monitor objects can use the same class while holding different rules. A member is a variable or function declared in a class; a member function is also called a method.

blocks.text: An interface is the set of operations a caller can use, together with their promises. It is more than a list of function names. For an estimate, the promise might require a nonempty list and return a value inside a stated range. An abstraction keeps the facts a caller needs and leaves out details it does not need. The monitor needs "estimate these readings," not the exact steps for finding an average.

Encapsulation puts related data and behavior behind a controlled boundary. Private members stop ordinary outside code from changing them directly. A monitor can reject a missing rule before replacing its current rule. Its invariant, a rule that must remain true at its public boundary, is that it has a usable rule. Merely making a field private does not protect it if a public operation still allows a bad value.

Inheritance defines one class in terms of a base class. Public inheritance says that a derived object can be used through the base type. This is a promise about behavior, not just a way to reuse lines. Polymorphism lets the same interface call reach different implementations. Through an Estimate reference, value() can run the Average or Highest implementation. C++ also supports other forms of polymorphism; these chapters mainly use virtual member functions.

Composition builds behavior by connecting objects. A monitor has a rule instead of inheriting every possible rule. In UML, strict composition also shows a strong whole-part lifetime relationship: the whole is responsible for its parts. In broader design advice, "favor composition" includes collaboration with borrowed objects too. Ownership means responsibility for an object or resource and its eventual release; access alone does not imply ownership.

A dependency means that changing one part can force another part to change. Passing a report type to a function creates a dependency on that type. An association is a lasting link between objects, such as a controller retaining access to a screen. Aggregation describes a whole-part grouping whose parts may live independently, such as a view grouping existing sensors. Its hollow diamond does not specify who deletes a C++ object. State ownership separately and check the actual code.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/primer.json → The object words used by the patterns

topics.title: Three design habits that give patterns a purpose
topics.summary: Good design makes required behavior clear and likely changes manageable. Cohesion means keeping closely related work together. Coupling means how strongly one part relies on another. A useful design often raises cohesion and limits unnecessary coupling. There is no useful rule that all coupling must disappear: cooperating parts must agree on something. Aim for a small, stable agreement that a reader can explain and a test can check.

blocks.text: Encapsulate what varies. If new output styles keep changing a report calculation, separate formatting from calculation. The stable calculation can produce a result while a formatter chooses its presentation. First identify evidence of change: repeated edits, duplicated branches, or different user needs. Do not build a framework for a variation nobody needs. A function parameter may isolate the variation before a family of classes is worth its cost.

Program to an interface. A job that needs to store a result should ask for the storage behavior it needs, rather than reach into one particular file writer. The caller depends on a promise; implementations fulfill that promise. This permits a test implementation that keeps results in memory. It does not mean every class needs a separate interface. If there is one small, stable implementation, calling it directly can be clearer.

Favor composition over inheritance when separate choices must vary independently. With two report types and three delivery methods, making a subclass for every pair leads to six combinations. Connecting a report object to a delivery object keeps the choices separate. Inheritance still fits a true substitution relationship and a stable shared workflow. The question is which arrangement matches the change, not which language feature sounds more advanced.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/primer.json → Three design habits that give patterns a purpose

topics.title: SOLID: five questions to ask about a design
topics.summary: Single Responsibility Principle: keep a module responsible to one coherent source of change. A module is a part of a program that we can discuss as a unit, often a class or file. Suppose one class both decides which readings count as alerts and writes a color report. New alert policy and new report styling come from different needs. Separating those jobs lets each change without disturbing the other. This principle does not mean one function per class or one method per object.

blocks.text: Open/Closed Principle: allow a planned kind of extension without repeatedly editing the stable code that uses it. Suppose the monitor validates readings and then asks an Estimate for a result. Adding a Median implementation can preserve that monitor code. The program still needs code or configuration that selects Median. "Closed" does not mean never fixing a bug or never changing a requirement. It means protecting a useful boundary from a known direction of change. A small fixed set of choices may need no extension boundary.

Liskov Substitution Principle: a derived type must keep the promises callers rely on from its base type. If Estimate accepts every nonempty list of values from 0 through 1000, an implementation that secretly requires at least ten values breaks that promise. It has strengthened a precondition, a condition required before a call. Returning a value outside a promised range weakens a postcondition, a guarantee after the call. Derived types must also preserve the base invariants. Test every implementation against the same contract, including small and boundary inputs.

Liskov substitution concerns behavior as well as legal C++ syntax. A method can compile with override and still return the wrong units or reject a valid request. Replacing a base parameter type with a different type normally does not override the function in C++; matching the required signature matters. Do not confuse the broad idea of accepting more cases with permission to change a C++ override signature. The compiler checks part of the contract; tests and review check the rest.

Interface Segregation Principle: a caller should not have to depend on operations it does not use. Suppose a small archive reader needs only load(), but its interface also requires save(), erase(), and network setup. A read-only implementation then needs fake operations or surprising failures. Split the meaningful capabilities so a reader depends on reading. One implementation may support several capabilities. Do not split every method into its own interface: the goal is a useful contract for each caller, not the largest possible number of types.

Dependency Inversion Principle: high-level policy and low-level detail should depend on suitable abstractions; the abstraction should not depend on the detail. High-level policy is the rule that says what the program must achieve. Low-level detail is how a device, file, or service carries it out. Let an alert policy depend on an AlertSink promise. A file sink and a test sink implement that promise. Changing the file format then need not change the alert decision.

Dependency injection means supplying a needed collaborator from outside, often through a constructor. It can help implement dependency inversion, but the ideas are different. Passing a concrete file writer into a constructor is injection; policy can still depend directly on that writer. For inversion, inspect the types and their promises. SOLID principles help you ask questions. They are not five gates that force every small program to grow more classes.

topics.title: Read the C++ used by the pattern roles
topics.summary: The next excerpt becomes useful when an archive job must format records in different ways while keeping one workflow. Record names the common promise. TextRecord and BracketRecord provide choices in Chapter 1. A class body is inside braces, and the final semicolon ends the class declaration. public: marks members that callers may use. C++ has no separate interface keyword; an abstract class can express an interface.

blocks.text: Line by line: class Record begins the type. public: opens its public part. virtual ~Record() = default declares a virtual destructor and asks the compiler to supply its normal implementation. A destructor performs cleanup when an object is destroyed; the tilde marks its name. Virtual destruction makes deleting a derived record through the base pointer used by its owner safe. The format declaration returns a std::string, the standard library text type, and receives text as its input. The closing brace and semicolon finish the type.

In const std::string& text, the ampersand declares a reference: another name for an existing string, rather than a new string copy. const prevents changing that string through this reference. It does not promise that no other alias can change the same object. A value parameter would instead hold its own parameter object. The const after format(...) limits ordinary changes to the receiving object through that call. These two uses of const apply to different things.

virtual enables selection of an implementation through a base pointer or reference at run time. The = 0 marks a pure virtual function: this class leaves the operation to a derived implementation and cannot itself be instantiated. In a derived class, override asks the compiler to check that a function really overrides a base virtual function. final can prevent further derivation or overriding. Neither word proves the behavior is correct.

In Record* p, the star declares a pointer that holds an address and may be null. In *p, it follows the pointer to the object; a bad pointer makes that unsafe. p->format(text) calls a member through a pointer; a direct object uses a dot. A raw pointer does not state ownership. std::unique_ptr<Record> is an owning handle whose destructor releases its object. It permits one owner and cannot be copied. std::make_unique<TextRecord>() creates an object and returns its owner.

std::move(x) allows a move operation to be chosen; it does not itself move any object. Moving a unique_ptr into another owner transfers its object and leaves that particular source pointer empty. Do not assume all moved-from library objects are empty. The angle brackets in std::vector<int> or std::unique_ptr<Record> supply types to a library template, a reusable type recipe. You need to read these uses before you need to write templates.

In for (const auto& child : children), the colon means "take each element from children." auto asks the compiler to infer the element type; & borrows each element; const prevents changing that element through child. For a const unique_ptr this does not make the pointed-to object const. In a constructor, : member(value) instead starts member initialization. Context decides what the colon means. #include brings declarations from a header, std:: names the standard namespace, return supplies a result, and // starts a comment to the end of the line.

topics.title: Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime
topics.summary: A UML class diagram shows types and their relationships. A solid line ending in a hollow triangle points from a derived class toward its base. A dashed line with an ordinary arrow shows a dependency. An association uses a solid line; an arrow, when present, shows navigable access. A filled diamond sits at the whole end of composition; a hollow diamond marks aggregation. A realization of an interface may use a dashed line with a hollow triangle. Read each page legend because line styles carry different meanings.

blocks.text: An activity diagram follows actions and decisions. Its arrows show possible execution flow, not inheritance. A sequence diagram places participants across the page and calls downward through time. A state diagram shows states and permitted transitions caused by events. An ownership view names owners, borrowed links, and the events that end lifetimes. Teaching links connect notes to code blocks; they are labeled annotations and are not UML relationships.

Compilation checks source syntax and many type rules, then produces code that the linker combines into a program. Missing definitions may fail at link time. Execution creates objects, selects branches, calls functions, and destroys objects. override errors can be caught during compilation. Choosing a valid but wrong strategy is an execution problem. Virtual calls preserve the required behavior of selecting the final override; a compiler may optimize how it achieves that behavior.

Trace four paths separately. Data moves as arguments and results. Control moves through calls and returns. Ownership moves only when the code transfers responsibility. Lifetime begins with successful object construction and ends with destruction. A borrowed reference does not keep an object alive. A retained pointer can outlive its target unless the design prevents that. In each chapter, ask who creates each object, who may call it, who releases it, and which tests cover those promises.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/primer.json → Read diagrams as claims about code and lifetime

topics.title: Choose a chapter by the problem; teach it through a change
topics.summary: The catalog follows the supplied material: five creational patterns, seven structural patterns, and ten behavioral patterns. Creational patterns organize object creation. Structural patterns organize how parts fit together. Behavioral patterns organize decisions and cooperation. The table is a starting point, not an automatic selector. Several patterns can fit one program; compare their intent before comparing their box shapes.

blocks.text: For a class session, spend ten minutes on the simple design, ten on a new need that breaks it, fifteen tracing the solution and diagram, and fifteen making and testing one change. Use ten minutes to compare alternatives. Adjust the time to the class; require learners to predict behavior before running code.

Follow the exercises: guided change, code trace, bug repair, design choice, tested extension, and plain-English justification. In the capstone, name each pattern role in the source and state one invariant per boundary. Correct output is necessary; explain why the design stays correct under change.

topics.title: Foundations recall
topics.summary: Review the words and decisions used across every pattern.

cards.question: What is a design pattern?
cards.answer: A named arrangement of responsibilities that solves a recurring design problem. Identify the actual change pressure before choosing it.

cards.question: How does a pattern differ from an algorithm?
cards.answer: An algorithm supplies computational steps. A pattern describes how responsibilities collaborate and vary.

cards.question: What is an invariant?
cards.answer: A rule that must remain true at a stated program boundary, including after permitted operations.

cards.question: What does ownership mean in C++?
cards.answer: Responsibility for an object or resource and its eventual release. Merely holding a pointer or reference does not establish ownership.

cards.question: What does override check?
cards.answer: It asks the compiler to verify that the declaration overrides a base virtual function. It does not prove all behavioral promises.

cards.question: What does const T& express?
cards.answer: A reference borrowing an existing T object, preventing mutation through that reference. Another alias may still change the object.

cards.question: When is a simpler design enough?
cards.answer: When direct functions, a small branch, or a value type meet the requirements without needing the variation boundary a pattern introduces.

cards.question: What must agree in a useful UML lesson?
cards.answer: The relationship legend, diagram blocks, source code, call trace, and lifetime rules must describe the same implementation.

topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Factory Method lets a stable operation request an object while a subclass chooses its concrete type. The attached chapter begins with transport choices and later uses dialog buttons. Those settings lead to the same design question: how can a workflow use a product without fixing its concrete class?

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Identify the workflow that benefits from a creation hook.
Follow product ownership across a factory return.
Distinguish Factory Method from an ordinary factory function.

blocks.text: The creator declares a virtual creation operation returning the product interface. Its ordinary workflow calls that operation and then uses the returned product. A concrete creator overrides the creation operation. The important change is the path of the call: existing workflow code reaches the subclass through virtual dispatch. Moving new into a helper with no overridable creation step does not establish this relationship.

cards.question: What problem does Factory Method address?
cards.answer: Factory Method lets a stable operation request an object while a subclass chooses its concrete type. The attached chapter begins with transport choices and later uses dialog buttons. Those settings lead to the same design question: how can a workflow use a product without fixing its concrete class?

cards.question: What is Factory Method?
cards.answer: A virtual creation operation called by a creator’s inherited workflow, with concrete creation supplied by derived creators.

cards.question: What is Product?
cards.answer: An object created for another operation to use.

cards.question: What is Simple factory?
cards.answer: A function that selects and constructs a product without requiring an overridable creation hook in a creator hierarchy.

cards.question: If BracketJob overrides make but run directly constructs TextRecord, what prints for sample?
cards.answer: stored text:sample. The workflow bypasses the hook, so the override cannot select BracketRecord.

cards.question: Does returning unique_ptr<Record> from each override remove Factory Method?
cards.answer: No. It changes the ownership contract. Creator inheritance, virtual creation, and product-interface use still define the pattern.

topics.title: The archive workflow already knows too much
topics.summary: An archive tool accepts a nonempty text label of at most 20 bytes. It produces a demonstration receipt, either stored text:sample or stored [sample]. No file is written: stored is a message describing the workflow result. This boundary keeps the example deterministic and avoids pretending that a string return is a durable archive transaction.

blocks.text: The first version constructs TextRecord directly inside the job. That is the simplest sensible design for one format. Validation and the receipt prefix belong to the job. Formatting belongs to the record. These are already separate duties, but the job still names the one concrete record it can create.

blocks.title: Excerpt — simplest approach before the redesign
blocks.code:
TextRecord record;
return "stored " + record.format(text);

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch01.json → The archive workflow already knows too much

topics.title: The change should affect construction, not the workflow
topics.summary: A second integration needs bracketed records. Copying the whole job would copy validation and the stored prefix too. Adding a format switch works for a small closed choice set, but an extensible job family already uses derived types for integration-specific behavior. We want the common job to request a record without deciding its concrete class.

blocks.text: A product is simply an object made for another part of the program to use. A creator is the object that asks for or makes that product. The Factory Method pattern gives the creator a virtual creation operation. A derived creator decides which concrete product to return. Here ArchiveJob is the creator, Record is the product interface, and make is the creation hook. run still performs useful work; it is not merely a renamed constructor.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch01.json → The change should affect construction, not the workflow

topics.title: Two connected type families, one clear handoff
topics.summary: TextJob and BracketJob derive from ArchiveJob. TextRecord and BracketRecord derive from Record. These are separate relationships. A TextJob is a kind of ArchiveJob; it is not a kind of TextRecord. The job creates the record and then uses it through the Record interface. Confusing those relationships leads to misleading class diagrams and often to bad code.

blocks.text: The protected make declaration returns unique_ptr<Record>. Each override keeps that return type and constructs its concrete class with make_unique. A unique_ptr<TextRecord> can transfer into unique_ptr<Record> when the pointer conversion and deleter requirements are met. This is ownership conversion, not virtual return-type covariance. C++ covariant overrides apply to certain raw pointer and reference return types, not to arbitrary smart-pointer templates.

run receives the owning handle in a local variable. It checks the non-null postcondition, calls format, builds its result string, and leaves scope. The local handle then destroys the product. Returning the string does not extend the product lifetime because the string owns its own characters. If format throws, cleanup still releases the record. The virtual Record destructor is essential for complete destruction through a base owning handle.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch01.json → Two connected type families, one clear handoff

topics.title: Compilation fixes the request; execution chooses the maker
topics.summary: The compiler checks that ArchiveJob declares make and that each override matches it. At execution, the object on which run was called determines which make override runs. Calling run through const ArchiveJob& selected still reaches BracketJob::make when selected refers to the bracket job. A reference changes what operations the caller can name; it does not erase the actual object type.

blocks.text: The call to make happens after label validation. An empty or oversized label therefore creates no product. Once a product exists, its format method is another virtual call. The sequence is shared validation, virtual creation, virtual formatting, then shared receipt assembly. Factory Method is often one specialized step inside a Template Method-style workflow, but the terms describe different decisions: one concerns object creation; the other concerns algorithm order.

A null result is a broken creator contract, so the job throws logic_error. EmptyJob exists only to verify that guard. An allocation failure can also occur inside make_unique and propagate as an exception; no successfully constructed handle exists to leak. For a real file-backed product, document whether creation opens a file, delays opening, or can reuse a resource. The pattern alone says nothing about those effects.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch01.json → Compilation fixes the request; execution chooses the maker

topics.title: What does not make a Factory Method
topics.summary: A free function make_record(format) with a switch is commonly called a simple factory. It centralizes construction and may be exactly what a program needs. It is not this pattern’s defining mechanism because no inherited workflow calls an overridable creation hook. A static member named create is not automatically Factory Method either. Names do not decide a design pattern; relationships and control flow do.

blocks.text: If the caller can supply a ready-made Record, dependency injection is often simpler than subclassing ArchiveJob. If the workflow needs a fresh record for every run, it can accept a callable factory. Factory Method fits best when creator inheritance already has a clear role and subclasses should choose products. Avoid introducing two class hierarchies solely to hide one constructor.

New product behavior still needs interface-level tests. A new format that silently truncates labels could satisfy the C++ signature and still violate requirements. Likewise, switching the product does not make the stored prefix truthful about persistent storage. Keep the workflow’s externally promised behavior explicit, and test it through the base creator interface so extensions exercise the same path clients will use.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch01.json → What does not make a Factory Method

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Accept label lengths from 1 through 20 bytes.
Preserve the common stored prefix and validation across product formats.
Release each created product on success and on exceptions.

blocks.text: ArchiveJob owns a useful stable workflow and exposes one protected virtual creation hook. Concrete jobs select products; the workflow sees only Record.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: run validates before it calls make.

topics.title: A writer and reader must agree
topics.summary: A small teaching protocol transmits one decimal digit, from 0 through 9. A plain connection sends 7 as the string 7. A framed connection sends the same value as [7]. Each connection needs two objects: an encoder that writes a digit and a decoder that reads the resulting string. Every accepted digit must survive the trip unchanged. Invalid numbers and malformed strings must be rejected.

blocks.text: Constructing a PlainEncoder and PlainDecoder directly is enough for the first version. They have separate jobs, and their relationship is easy to see. The excerpt is a complete sequence of statements inside a caller, assuming the two types are available. It does not need a factory for its own sake.

blocks.title: Excerpt — simplest approach before the redesign

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → A writer and reader must agree

topics.title: The failure is a mismatched pair
topics.summary: When framed connections arrive, setup code selects both products independently. A copied branch can create FramedEncoder with PlainDecoder. Both objects implement the right C++ interfaces, so the compiler accepts the code. The encoder produces [7], but the plain decoder rejects its length. A more permissive decoder might silently misread the data instead. The problem is agreement between products, not merely selecting one product.

blocks.text: A family is a set of objects meant to work together. The Abstract Factory pattern gives the caller one object that creates all needed members of the selected family. CodecFactory offers encoder and decoder. PlainFactory creates the plain pair; FramedFactory creates the framed pair. The client chooses one factory, then asks that factory for both products. This reduces the number of places where incompatible choices can enter.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → The failure is a mismatched pair

topics.title: Two product roles are not one inheritance tree
topics.summary: Encoder and Decoder have different operations, so they remain different interfaces. PlainEncoder and FramedEncoder implement Encoder. PlainDecoder and FramedDecoder implement Decoder. Each concrete factory creates one of each. Abstract Factory does not require these two products to inherit from each other, share a common catch-all interface, or own one another. Their useful relationship is a protocol contract: decoder.read(encoder.write(value)) equals value for every valid value.

blocks.text: The factory itself is borrowed as const CodecFactory&. The client does not delete it and does not save its address. Each returned unique_ptr owns a fresh product. The products contain no reference back to the factory, so this implementation does not require them to die before the factory. In round_trip they are local and are destroyed when the call ends. A different implementation with shared factory state would need a documented lifetime rule instead of assuming this one applies.

The compiler checks product method signatures and factory overrides. During execution, the actual factory type chooses the concrete products. Calling through Encoder and Decoder then chooses their actual method implementations. The client contains no switch on wire format. It still knows the abstract protocol duties: one writer, one reader, a valid integer, and a round-trip invariant.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → Two product roles are not one inheritance tree

topics.title: Parsing is part of the contract
topics.summary: PlainDecoder checks that wire has exactly one character before testing its content. The || operator stops as soon as an operand is true. This short-circuit rule skips unnecessary content tests after a bad length. FramedDecoder uses the same ordering for a stronger safety reason: front() and back() require a nonempty string. Its size check rejects empty input before either operation can run. C++17 permits reading string[string.size()] as a zero character, so PlainDecoder’s wire[0] on an empty string is not the same invalid-access case as front() or back().

blocks.text: The character tests compare the input with '0' and '9'. C++ guarantees the decimal digit characters form a consecutive sequence, so subtracting '0' from a checked digit yields its numeric value. The framed reader first checks a three-character shape with opening and closing brackets. Only then does it take the one-character substring and reuse PlainDecoder. That reuse is a local parsing dependency, not membership in the plain factory family.

The encoder checks numeric range before making a string. The framed decoder rejects [x] even though its outer brackets are correct. Structural validity and content validity are different rules. These deliberately tiny formats let the tests cover all ten accepted numeric values. They are teaching protocols, not general-purpose serialization formats with escaping, byte-order rules, versioning, or checksums.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch02.json → Parsing is part of the contract

topics.title: A factory encourages compatibility; it does not prove it
topics.summary: Nothing in the return types prevents a faulty FramedFactory from returning PlainDecoder. The family rule is a design contract backed by tests. round_trip checks the value after decoding. That catches mismatches or broken decoding for the tested values. It cannot certify all future protocol extensions by itself. If a family has many configuration values, test representative boundaries and generated cases, and consider carrying a shared immutable configuration object into both products.

blocks.text: A factory is most useful when clients need several related product roles and whole families change together. Adding a new family is local: provide its products and a factory implementing the existing creation operations. Adding a new product role is less local: a new creation method affects every factory and every family. This is the pattern’s main change-direction tradeoff. Choose it when new families are more likely than new roles.

For one encoder-decoder pair with no planned variants, direct construction is clearer. A function returning a struct containing both owning handles can also preserve pairing with less inheritance. Compile-time family types or a single codec object can enforce stronger relationships when runtime variation is unnecessary. Do not split one naturally cohesive codec into separate products solely to make an Abstract Factory diagram. Here separate send and receive components are the stated need; the factory coordinates their creation.

topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Builder separates the steps that assemble a product from the completed product itself. The attached chapter motivates this with many house options and later shows vehicle/manual representations. The problem is a growing construction process, rather than choosing a single class with one call.

blocks.text: A builder retains work between construction steps. A director can package a repeatable sequence of those steps, while the client obtains the finished result from the builder. Different builders can interpret the same steps to produce different representations; their products need not share a base class. A chain of calls is optional syntax. The lasting design distinction is the separate construction process and product.

cards.answer: Builder separates the steps that assemble a product from the completed product itself. cards.question: What is Builder?
cards.answer: An object that collects construction choices in steps and produces a completed product.

cards.question: What is Director?

A valid plan can be handed to a presenter. An unfinished draft cannot. The title and durations arrive in separate setup steps, perhaps from a form or a configuration reader.

blocks.text: The simplest implementation is a struct with a title and a vector of minutes. Fill the fields and then call validate before using it. That can be enough in a short local function. The difficulty appears when the draft escapes to other code before validation or when one caller forgets the check. The same type then means both “possibly incomplete” and “safe to present.”

topics.title: Separate the draft from the finished product
topics.summary: A builder is an object that gathers construction choices in steps and produces a usable product when those choices are complete. This is the Builder pattern. PlanBuilder can be incomplete. Plan cannot be created through the public interface until build succeeds. The design makes the boundary visible: collecting settings is different from possessing a valid plan.

blocks.text: named sets a nonempty title. add accepts one valid activity while respecting the three-activity limit. build checks rules that need the whole draft: a title exists, at least one activity exists, and the sum is at most 90. A draft with two 60-minute activities can exist, but build rejects it. That is deliberate; intermediate choices are not claimed to be a finished plan. A form could let a user edit such a draft before trying again.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch03.json → Separate the draft from the finished product

topics.title: Why friendship is narrow here
topics.summary: Plan has a private constructor and private data. friend class PlanBuilder grants this one named class access to the private constructor. Friendship is permission, not inheritance, ownership, or automatic trust in every caller. It is not symmetric or transitive. The builder is responsible for checking its draft before using that permission. No other public function in this example can create an invalid Plan by filling fields afterward.

blocks.text: The finished Plan exposes a title reference for reading and a computed total. Its public interface has no setters. Calling title returns a borrowed const string reference, valid only while that Plan remains alive and unchanged by assignment or movement. Returning a copy would provide a simpler lifetime contract at the cost of copying the title. Do not retain the borrowed reference after the plan dies.

build returns Plan by value. The constructor receives a string and vector by value and moves those parameters into its members. Because build itself is const and passes its own members as lvalues, the constructor parameters are copies of the draft. The resulting plan therefore owns independent data. Later builder changes cannot alter earlier products. Plan explicitly defaults its copy constructor. This suppresses implicit move operations, so constructing or assigning it from an rvalue uses copying instead and leaves the source valid. Moving the builder’s temporary constructor parameters into the new product is still safe: those parameters are ordinary local values, not previously published plans. C++17 can construct the returned product directly in its destination; correctness must not depend on counting visible copy calls.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch03.json → Why friendship is narrow here

topics.title: Chaining steps does not create magic
topics.summary: named and add return PlanBuilder&, a reference to the same builder. return *this dereferences the implicit this pointer to refer to the current object. This supports builder.named("Practice").add(30).add(30): each call returns the object on which the next call operates. Chaining is an optional convenience. It is not what makes the design Builder; staged construction and the valid-product boundary are the important parts.

blocks.text: The member functions check invalid values before changing their vectors or titles. A rejected add(0) leaves the existing draft unchanged. A fourth activity is rejected even if it would fit the time total, because count and total are separate rules. The maximum sum of a draft is 180, so this example’s int arithmetic cannot overflow on the required compiler platform. A production planner with unbounded counts needs a different bound or checked accumulation.

The program demonstrates two snapshots from one builder. After 30 and 30, first totals 60. Adding another 30 produces second at 90. first still totals 60 because it owns its own copied durations. build does not reset the builder in this design. That policy is part of its contract, not a universal rule. A consuming builder might move data out and require a reset; a reusable builder might return snapshots, as ours does.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch03.json → Chaining steps does not create magic

topics.title: A director is just a reusable recipe
topics.summary: introduction records a repeated sequence of builder calls. Such a recipe is called a director in the classic Builder vocabulary. A director does not have to be a class. Here an ordinary function creates a builder, names the plan, adds two activities, and returns the result. The caller receives a Plan without knowing every construction step. If no recipe repeats, callers can drive the builder directly.

blocks.text: The broader Builder pattern can use one recipe with different builders to produce different representations, such as an executable session plan and a printed outline. Those products need not share a base type. A common step interface can express named and add, while each concrete builder exposes its own finished result. A function template can also apply one recipe to builders with matching operations. Introduce that machinery only when the second representation exists; one valid-plan builder does not need an abstract builder hierarchy.

For a small object with two required values available at once, a checked constructor or a named factory function is simpler. A builder becomes valuable when many optional choices accumulate, validation spans choices, or setup order and product readiness need clear separation. A fluent chain of trivial setters on a publicly mutable product does not provide the same guarantee. Ask what invalid state the design prevents, not how attractive the chained syntax looks.

topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Prototype copies an already configured object without requiring its caller to know the object's concrete class. The attached chapter distinguishes this active copying role from a rough early product model. Its object-copying problem is the same one our cue collection faces: the caller has a base interface, yet the copy must preserve the actual kind of object.

blocks.text: The base interface declares a virtual clone operation. Each concrete implementation creates its own concrete type using the current object as the source of values. The caller invokes clone through the base interface and receives a new object. A registry can hold named prototypes for reuse, but the registry is optional. The copy policy must say which data becomes independent and which resources, if any, remain shared.

cards.question: What problem does Prototype address?
cards.answer: Prototype copies an already configured object without requiring its caller to know the object's concrete class. The attached chapter distinguishes this active copying role from a rough early product model. Its object-copying problem is the same one our cue collection faces: the caller has a base interface, yet the copy must preserve the actual kind of object.

cards.question: What is Prototype?
cards.answer: A pattern in which an existing object creates a new object by copying its own state through a common operation.

cards.question: What is Object slicing?
cards.answer: Losing the derived part when a derived object is copied into a base value.

cards.question: What is Deep copy?
cards.answer: A copy that duplicates owned contents to the independence depth required by the application.

cards.question: What is Shallow copy?
cards.answer: A copy that duplicates handles while retaining some shared underlying objects.

cards.question: Why is copying the unique_ptr address into another owning handle not cloning?
cards.answer: Both handles would own the same object, leading to double deletion. clone must create a distinct object with the promised copied state.

cards.question: Is a prototype registry required for the cue example?
cards.answer: No. The collection already supplies each source object. A registry becomes useful when callers need to look up configured prototypes by a key.

topics.title: Duplicate cues without knowing their kinds
topics.summary: A presentation tool keeps a list of cues. A text cue has one name, such as Start. A list cue contains several names, such as Check and Begin. The user duplicates a group of cues and edits the first name in the copied list. The original group must remain unchanged. A cue name may not be empty, and a list must contain at least one name.

blocks.text: For a known TextCue, an ordinary copy is the simplest reasonable solution. C++ already knows how to copy a string member. No design pattern is needed for that case. The difficulty begins when a container stores owning handles to Cue and the duplication code cannot name each concrete type. The excerpt can copy a known object but does not solve copying an unknown derived object through its base interface.

blocks.title: Excerpt — simplest approach before the redesign

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch04.json → Duplicate cues without knowing their kinds

topics.title: The limitation is lost concrete type information
topics.summary: A unique_ptr cannot be copied because copying the sole owner would give two owners responsibility for deleting one object. Copying Cue itself would not solve the problem either. Cue is abstract here, so it cannot be constructed. In a nonabstract hierarchy, copying only the base part can discard derived data and behavior, a problem called object slicing. Neither copying the handle nor copying only the base subobject means “make an independent object of the same actual kind.”

blocks.text: The Prototype pattern asks the existing object to create that copy. Cue declares a virtual clone operation returning a new owning Cue handle. TextCue and ListCue each know their own concrete type, so each can call its own copy constructor. The caller asks for a clone without deciding which constructor to invoke. Prototype is therefore about construction from an existing object’s state, not simply about any function named copy.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch04.json → The limitation is lost concrete type information

topics.title: What clone preserves
topics.summary: ListCue::clone calls make_unique<ListCue>(*this). this points at the current ListCue; *this refers to the whole current ListCue object. Inside a const member, that expression is a const reference suitable for copying. The explicitly defaulted copy constructor copies the vector member. Both concrete cue types declare their copy constructors this way, suppressing implicit object moves. Constructing from an rvalue therefore copies instead of emptying the source; moves of unique_ptr handles still transfer ownership without moving the cue object itself. Copying a vector of strings copies each string value, so the clone owns independent character data in the normal observable sense. Editing one list’s first name does not edit the other list’s name.

blocks.text: The clone’s type is still ListCue even though its returned owner is unique_ptr<Cue>. Later virtual calls to text and rename reach ListCue behavior. The new object has a different address but starts with the same public value. Equal value and shared identity are different ideas: two clocks can display the same time without being the same clock. The program checks both equal initial text and distinct object addresses.

During compilation, the compiler generates the appropriate memberwise copy constructor and checks the clone override signature. During execution, the actual cue chooses which clone override runs. Allocation creates new storage, construction copies the concrete object into it, and ownership returns to the caller. If copying fails, make_unique cleans up the allocated storage; the original remains owned by its existing handle.

topics.title: Copy depth is a design decision
topics.summary: A shallow copy copies a handle or address while keeping the same underlying resource. A deep copy makes an independent copy of owned contents, to the depth promised by the application. The words need a boundary. A vector of strings gives independent string values. A vector of shared_ptr<Image> would copy handles and share images unless the clone explicitly copied them. That may be correct if images are immutable and expensive, but it would not be correct for an independently editable image promise.

blocks.text: A unique_ptr member normally makes the containing type noncopyable until a copy operation is explicitly defined. The lab adds BoxCue with a unique_ptr<string>. Its copy constructor allocates a new string initialized from the original string. Simply returning make_unique<BoxCue>(*this) without that copy constructor would fail to compile. Replacing unique_ptr with shared_ptr just to silence the error would change ownership meaning and make edits visible through both handles.

Some resources should not be cloned at all. A live socket, open transaction, mutex, or hardware session has an identity that copying bytes cannot duplicate. A clone may copy configuration while opening a fresh session, share a documented immutable resource, or reject duplication. Cyclic object graphs need additional rules: a map from old objects to new objects can preserve internal relationships without infinite recursion. Do not promise a universal deep copy without defining where the copy stops.

topics.title: Keep the generic loop simple and the copy rules local
topics.summary: The loop over originals uses const auto& because each vector element is a unique_ptr and must not be copied. The reference borrows the owning handle; const prevents reseating that handle through this reference. It does not by itself make the pointed-to object const. clone is separately declared const to promise that cloning does not mutate the cue’s ordinary members. The arrow calls the operation on the object reached through the handle.

blocks.text: Each new owner goes into copies. push_back accepts the returned temporary owning handle by move. After the loop, originals and copies are separate owning collections. Destruction of either collection destroys only its own objects. The program renames the first entry of the copied ListCue and checks that the original text is still list:Check;Begin; while the copied text becomes list:Inspect;Begin;.

Prototype is useful for user duplication, reusable configured objects, and heterogeneous snapshots when copying has a clear domain meaning. A registry may keep named prototypes and return clones, but the registry is optional. If the concrete type is already known and ordinary value copying works, use it. If objects should have unique noncopyable identities, omit clone instead of adding a misleading operation. Maintaining a clone requires adding new fields to its copy policy as the type evolves, especially when members change from values to owning or shared handles.

topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Singleton controls access to one instance while offering a shared way to obtain it. The attached chapter explicitly presents these as two linked decisions. A program may need one shared service while still benefiting from passing that service openly through parameters. Teaching this pattern includes recognizing its costs, not recommending it for every shared object.

cards.question: What is Singleton?
cards.answer: A design that controls access to one instance through a shared accessor.

cards.question: What is Mutex?
cards.answer: A synchronization object used to allow one participating thread at a time into a protected region.

cards.question: What is Critical section?
cards.answer: Code that accesses shared state while holding the required lock.

cards.question: What is Data race?
cards.answer: Unsynchronized conflicting accesses to memory by different threads, with at least one write; in C++ this causes undefined behavior.

cards.question: What is Dependency injection?
cards.answer: Supplying an object a component needs through an explicit parameter or constructor instead of locating it globally.

cards.question: Does a function-local static make next_++ thread-safe?
cards.answer: No. It protects initial construction, not later state changes. take must lock its exhaustion check and increment together.

cards.question: Why must a test not insist that the safe attached sample always prints FOO twice?
cards.answer: Either thread can initialize first. Both values must agree, but the language does not guarantee which input wins the race to acquire the lock.

topics.title: One dispenser, not one counter per caller
topics.summary: A small demonstration process issues tickets numbered 1, 2, and 3. Different callers must draw from the same sequence. After the third ticket, every request is rejected. Restarting the process starts a new sequence; the program does not store tickets on disk. This is a deliberately small model of a shared service, not a distributed ticket system.

blocks.text: The simplest good solution is often to create one ordinary dispenser in main and pass a reference to every user. That gives one instance by application arrangement. The excerpt shows a local counter’s core idea, assuming requests are sequential. If separate components each create their own counter, they can both issue ticket 1. Sharing one object is necessary for this requirement; global access is a separate design choice.

topics.title: What Singleton adds, and what it combines
topics.summary: The Singleton pattern controls construction so callers reach one instance through a shared access operation. TicketDispenser has a private constructor and destructor, deleted copy operations, and a static instance function returning a reference. Ordinary callers cannot create another object or copy the existing one. The function returns a reference because it lends the service; callers must not delete it.

blocks.text: Singleton combines two ideas: restricting instance count and providing global access. You may need the first without needing the second. Passing one ordinary object from main often expresses sharing more clearly, because function parameters reveal who depends on the service. We implement Singleton here to understand its exact mechanism and costs, then use the lab to remove hidden access from a consumer.

static on instance means the member function is called on the class rather than on an existing object. There is no this pointer for that call. The local static variable inside it has a different meaning: its storage lasts beyond one function call. It is initialized when execution first reaches its declaration and is reused on later calls. The returned references therefore all name the same completed dispenser in this program.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch05.json → What Singleton adds, and what it combines

topics.title: Once-only initialization is not method synchronization
topics.summary: Since C++11, initialization of a function-local static is guarded so concurrent first callers do not each construct the object. One performs initialization while other callers wait for it to complete. If initialization throws, a later call can try again. Re-entering that same local static initialization recursively is not a safe way to resolve dependencies; avoid service constructors that cycle back through one another.

blocks.text: That guarantee concerns construction only. It does not protect later reads and writes to next_. Two threads incrementing an ordinary shared int without synchronization cause a data race and undefined behavior. It is not accurate to promise merely “one lost ticket”: the C++ program has no defined result for that race. Making the constructor private or the object global does not repair it.

The take operation uses a mutex, a lock that allows only one participating thread at a time into the protected region. lock_guard acquires gate_ when the guard is constructed and releases it when the guard leaves scope. Both the exhaustion check and the increment occur under that same lock. If the exception is thrown, stack cleanup still releases the lock. The local static guard and this method lock solve different problems and neither replaces the other.

The expression next_++ returns the old value and then increments the stored integer. The first three successful calls return 1, 2, and 3, leaving next_ equal to 4. Later calls test next_ > 3 and throw before incrementing again. The bounded sequence avoids overflow. Each whole take operation appears indivisible to other calls that use the same mutex. The standard does not promise fairness or which waiting caller gets a particular number.

topics.title: Lifetime and tests reveal the hidden coupling
topics.summary: The instance is destroyed during normal program shutdown if it was successfully initialized. Its private destructor prevents ordinary callers from explicitly destroying the borrowed object. In this single executable the accessor identifies one service. Separate processes have separate address spaces and separate instances; dynamic-library boundaries can also require careful linkage and deployment rules. Singleton is not a machine-wide lock, a distributed coordinator, or a persistence mechanism.

blocks.text: Shutdown dependencies deserve care. Another static object’s destructor must not use a service whose lifetime has already ended. A main-owned service with explicit lifetime often makes this ordering easier to see. Deliberately leaking a service to avoid shutdown ordering changes resource cleanup behavior and should never be an unexamined default.

Tests in one process share singleton state. A test that consumes ticket 1 changes what another test sees. Running the second test alone may pass while running the whole suite fails. A reset-for-tests method can hide the problem and may create races if used while work is active. This chapter’s main is a fresh-process demonstration with a known initial state. Its sequential checks verify identity, numbering, and repeated exhaustion; they are not a concurrency stress test.

The lab introduces TicketSource as the operation a consumer needs. admit accepts TicketSource& rather than finding the singleton itself. The production boundary can pass TicketDispenser::instance(), while each test can create a fresh LocalTickets. That technique is dependency injection: supplying a needed object explicitly. It preserves the option of one production instance while making tests independent.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch05.json → Lifetime and tests reveal the hidden coupling

topics.title: Choosing a shared service deliberately
topics.summary: A singleton can suit a truly process-wide service with a clear lifetime and little need for alternate instances. It is a poor fit when the program may run two independent sessions, load different configurations in tests, or need controlled startup and shutdown. Global access can make dependencies look smaller than they are because every function can silently acquire the service.

blocks.text: Do not replace every injected reference with a global accessor just to shorten parameter lists. Those parameters explain what the operation needs. Likewise, do not introduce an interface for every tiny value. TicketSource is justified in the lab by a concrete testing requirement: a consumer should work with independent counters as well as the shared production service.

For concurrency, one mutex protects only the state consistently accessed under it. If a future peek method reads next_ without locking, take’s lock does not make that new read safe. If two operations must form one transaction, locking each separately may still allow interleaving between them. Define the operation boundary first, then choose locking or an atomic design that preserves that boundary. Singleton answers where the object comes from; it does not answer every question about its correct use.

topics.title: The problem: one program, two meanings of weight
topics.summary: A parcel station decides whether a sample weighs at most two grams. Its application already asks a Scale for grams. A replacement device is not available. The old device returns an integer count of milligrams through milligrams(), and a negative value means the device failed. We must reuse that device without teaching every parcel rule its old spelling, units, and error convention. The answer must preserve fractions: 1,250 milligrams means 1.25 grams.

blocks.text: For one caller, the simplest reasonable answer is a direct conversion. Read the integer, reject negative results, and divide by 1000.0. A helper function could keep that operation in one place. If every caller can use that helper, stop there. A class does not improve a problem that is already solved clearly. Our added constraint is different: existing rules accept a Scale reference and may receive several kinds of scales at run time.

blocks.title: Excerpt — simplest starting point

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch06.json → The problem: one program, two meanings of weight

topics.title: The failure that calls for a translator
topics.summary: Passing LegacyScale straight to light_enough does not compile. It is not a Scale, and it has no grams member. Merely renaming milligrams would still leave the wrong unit and would treat a failure signal as a very light parcel. Changing every rule would mix device concerns with parcel rules. Each new device would repeat that work.

blocks.text: An adapter is an object that makes an existing service meet another interface. An interface is the set of operations and promises callers may use. ScaleAdapter meets Scale by implementing grams. Inside that method it calls the old device, checks its result, and translates the unit. The caller sees grams throughout. The old device does not know that an adapter exists. This is useful at a boundary where two independently developed pieces already disagree.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch06.json → The failure that calls for a translator

topics.title: What the C++ mechanism does
topics.summary: The colon in class ScaleAdapter final : public Scale declares public inheritance: the adapter may be used wherever a Scale is required. This is a type relationship, not a statement that the adapter owns a Scale object. The inherited pure virtual function, marked = 0 in Scale, demands an implementation. The override word asks the compiler to check that grams matches it, including its final const. A misspelled name or missing const produces a compile error instead of a hidden new method. final prevents further derivation; this example does not need another layer of subclasses.

blocks.text: At compilation, the compiler checks that light_enough may call grams through const Scale&. At execution, virtual dispatch selects ScaleAdapter::grams for our actual object. The ampersand makes scale a reference, so the function borrows the existing object rather than copying it. const prevents that call from modifying the object through this interface. It does not prove the physical sensor never changes. Here the simulated device stores one fixed reading, making our printed results repeatable.

ScaleAdapter also contains a reference, device_. Its constructor stores a connection to a LegacyScale that already exists. No device copy is made; no allocation is needed. The caller must keep that device alive for every adapter call. main creates device first and scale second. Local objects are destroyed in reverse order, so the adapter goes away before the device. Destroying the adapter does not destroy the borrowed device. Scale has a virtual destructor so a future owner holding a base-class pointer can destroy a derived adapter correctly.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch06.json → What the C++ mechanism does

topics.title: Units and errors are part of the contract
topics.summary: A boundary must translate meanings, not just names. In grams(), raw is checked before conversion. The value -1 is an error marker, not negative physical weight. Throwing std::runtime_error ends the normal call, so light_enough cannot accidentally accept the parcel. The error reaches the test's matching catch block. The adapter leaves both itself and its device unchanged when the call fails.

blocks.text: Dividing two integers discards the fractional part. Writing 1000.0 makes the divisor a double; the integer is converted for floating-point division. The returned double represents grams. This does not make floating-point arithmetic exact for every fraction. The test therefore uses a small tolerance when checking 1.25. The exact boundary values used here, two and zero, are represented exactly. A measurement system with strict legal or scientific rounding rules would need an explicit rule and perhaps an integer base unit throughout.

The contract assumes nonnegative integer milligrams are valid readings and all negatives signal failure. Real devices may distinguish timeout, overload, and calibration errors. An adapter should preserve distinctions the application needs instead of flattening every failure into zero. It should also avoid inventing precision: dividing an integer milligram count does not create a more precise measurement.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch06.json → Units and errors are part of the contract

topics.title: Composition and multiple inheritance
topics.summary: C++ also permits a class to inherit from two bases. A class adapter could inherit from Scale and LegacyScale, then use the inherited milligrams member. That approach may fit a legacy class designed for derivation, especially when overriding its virtual behavior is necessary. However, the adapter then contains its own legacy base subobject. It cannot automatically wrap the device instance that the application already owns. Public inheritance from the legacy type can also expose operations the new interface was meant to hide.

blocks.text: Our object adapter uses composition in the broad design sense of holding a connection to another object. The connection is borrowing, so the diagram uses a dependency arrow rather than an ownership diamond. It keeps lifetime policy with main and permits several adapters to view one device when that is intended. If the adapter should control the device's lifetime, a value member or unique_ptr would state a different ownership rule. Choose that rule from the actual device lifecycle, not from the pattern's name.

When debugging an adapter, write down three things before changing code: the input unit and error range, the target unit and error contract, and the lifetime owner. A wrong answer can come from any of them. When replacing a device library, keep the parcel tests unchanged and add device-specific adapter tests. That small boundary limits how far vendor changes travel through the program.

topics.title: Two useful reports, two useful formats
topics.summary: A small inspection tool prints a count and also classifies that count. One screen wants count=6. Another wants [count:6]. The classification report calls counts above five high and all others normal. It must work in either format. Negative counts are invalid. Requirements now vary in two directions: what the report means, and how its fields are written.

blocks.text: The simplest first version returns a string directly from a function. That is a good solution when there is one meaning and one format. A second function can serve a second fixed report. The difficulty appears when both dimensions grow. If each combination has its own class, two report types and two formats need four combinations. Three types and four formats need twelve. The count is the product of the choices, not automatically an exponential function of one choice. What hurts is repeated policy and repeated formatting.

topics.title: Locate the two decisions before drawing classes
topics.summary: Suppose the warning boundary changes from five to ten. In the combined design, each warning-format class must change. Suppose the bracket screen changes its separator. Every bracket-report class must change. That gives a concrete reason to separate the decisions. The boundary rule belongs with the report; punctuation belongs with the writer. Neither side should inspect the exact type on the other side.

blocks.text: A bridge is a stable connection between a high-level operation and a lower-level implementation that can vary independently. Here Report supplies the high-level render operation and borrows a Writer. CountReport and WarningReport decide which field name to send. Plain and Brackets implement Writer::field. The bridge is the writer_ reference. The two families can now grow without adding one class for every cross-product combination.

The pattern's traditional word abstraction means the high-level view offered to the caller. It does not require every high-level class to be an abstract C++ base class. Our Report is abstract because two report meanings already exist and both must be usable through the same contract. A single concrete report with a Writer member would still separate format from meaning when only one report is needed.

topics.title: Trace data and control across the bridge
topics.summary: In main, plain and brackets are created before the report objects that borrow them. cp stores a reference to plain; cb stores a reference to brackets. Calling cb.render(6) enters CountReport. validate first rejects a negative value. The report then sends the label count and integer 6 to writer_.field. Virtual dispatch selects Brackets::field. It creates [count:6] and returns that string by value through the report to main.

blocks.text: WarningReport follows the same route but chooses its label first. The conditional expression n > 5 ? "high" : "normal" evaluates the condition, selects exactly one of the two strings, and initializes label. The question mark introduces the true result, and the colon separates it from the false result. This colon is different from the colon that begins a constructor initializer list or a range loop. Syntax takes its meaning from its surrounding statement.

The returned strings own their character storage. The label passed to field is a const reference, so field borrows the argument during the call. Neither writer keeps that reference afterward. writer_ is a longer-lived borrow stored inside Report. Those are different lifetime obligations: a call parameter need only stay valid for the call, while a stored reference must stay valid for later calls too.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → Trace data and control across the bridge

topics.title: What compilation guarantees and what it cannot
topics.summary: The compiler checks public inheritance, virtual signatures, and whether each concrete class implements the required operation. override catches a mismatch. protected makes writer_ and validate available to the derived reports while keeping them out of ordinary client code. The helper is static because it depends only on its argument and needs no Report object. Constructors initialize the reference before any render call can occur.

blocks.text: The compiler does not verify that a new Writer preserves the label and value faithfully. A writer could accidentally swap field names or drop a minus sign. That would still compile. The shared semantic contract is therefore essential: format the supplied name and integer without changing their meaning. The report checks the domain rule that counts cannot be negative. The generic writer is capable of formatting any integer, which makes it usable in other domains.

At execution the same report can use either writer selected during construction. Our design does not provide a setter to switch writer_ later; C++ references cannot be rebound. To change format, construct a new report borrowing another writer. This keeps ownership and configuration simple. An application needing live format changes could instead hold a non-owning pointer with an explicit non-null rule or own an interchangeable writer. That requirement has not appeared here, so its extra states are unnecessary.

topics.sourceRef: manuscript/ch07.json → What compilation guarantees and what it cannot

topics.title: When the split helps, and when it does not
topics.summary: A bridge gives independence only when the interface is stable and truthful. If field lacks data one format needs, reports may begin checking for special writers. That is a warning that the boundary is too narrow or the supposedly independent dimensions are actually linked. Improve the contract using a real use case, or accept a smaller set of supported combinations. Do not promise that every conceivable report will work with every renderer.

blocks.text: An enum and one formatting function may be smaller when the set of formats is fixed and tiny. A template can select a writer at compilation and may remove virtual calls, but it exposes more implementation to callers and moves the choice from runtime to build time. Neither alternative is inherently inferior. The reason for this bridge is the already demonstrated independent growth in report policy and presentation.

Bridge and Adapter can produce similar shapes in a diagram. Their motivations differ. An adapter repairs an existing disagreement between interfaces. A bridge deliberately separates dimensions that should evolve independently. When reviewing a change, ask what boundary is being protected. Add tests for each report's meaning and each format's text, plus a few combinations. That protects the separation more effectively than checking only class names.

topics.summary: Treat a whole tree and an individual item through the same operation. The attached EPUB motivates nested containers whose contents contribute to a combined result. Composite is needed when a child can itself contain children; a plain list with one fixed item type does not establish the same recursive relationship.
