topics.summary: This branch turns Fahrenheit into the internal Celsius scale and rejects any tag outside the two supported units. It changes only a local number, so no monitor history is at risk here.

Why: A comparison cannot be meaningful until both numbers use the same unit. Keeping that conversion at the boundary prevents every future rule and formatter from having its own conversion policy.

Invariant: After the full converter returns, celsius is finite, in the accepted range, and carries the same positive identifier as the input. Unsupported tags must never be silently treated as Celsius.
Risk: Integer 5 / 9 would become zero. Omitting the unknown-unit branch would accept values with an unexplained scale. This excerpt is only the conversion branch, not the full validation contract.

topics.summary: These private fields are the monitor's long-lived state. The owning pointer controls one rule lifetime, the vector owns stored values, and the enum names the current operating state.

Invariant: A usable monitor has one nonnull owned rule, a valid state, and at most eight valid records in increasing order. The constructor and public methods jointly establish and preserve this contract.

Risk: A raw borrowed rule pointer could outlive its rule. Exposing a mutable records vector would let callers bypass capacity and conversion checks. Raising capacity affects the cost of each staged copy.

Invariant: Only an idle monitor may enter running through start. A stopped object cannot restart, and a running object cannot be started twice.

Invariant: Before each iteration, staged contains valid increasing records. Before the final swap, records_ still holds exactly the original history, even if conversion or ordering rejects a later item.
Risk: Replacing staged with a reference to records_ would destroy isolation. Reading staged.back() without first testing empty would be invalid for the first reading in an empty session.

topics.summary: The chosen rule produces a boolean, a proposed record stores it, and one vector swap makes the completed batch visible. The flag becomes historical data at this point.

blocks.text: Where: This block is the end of ingest. The loop repeats classification and append for each valid sample; swap runs once after the loop ends successfully.

Invariant: Every staged record has been normalized, ordered, and classified. The live vector changes exactly once on success and never changes on an ordinary pre-commit exception.

Risk: Moving swap into the loop produces partial commits. Re-evaluating flags during reporting changes the meaning of history. Side effects inside alert would lie outside the vector rollback guarantee.

topics.title: Exercise 23.3: Diagnose a bug
topics.summary: A developer changes the adapter formula to c = (c - 32.0) * (5 / 9);. The monitor accepts identifier 1 with 212 F under AtLeast(80.0). What wrong row is printed, why, and how should the bug be repaired and checked?

Tests should accept 20 c as 20 C, accept 176 f as 80 C, reject 20 k, and reject a late bad lowercase-unit item without a partial commit. The main report and all current checks must still pass. A local explicit two-case mapping is clearer here than locale-sensitive character conversion.

topics.chapterTitle: Capstone: combine patterns in a complete system
topics.title: Exercise 23.6: Justify a decision
topics.summary: A reviewer wants Observer notifications, command objects for all button actions, and a different subclass for every state. Give a reasoned response for this program, and identify one concrete future requirement that would justify each addition.

blocks.title: Hint
blocks.text: An abstraction should buy a needed change boundary, not merely a pattern name.

blocks.title: Explained answer
blocks.text: Keep the current direct calls and enum because there is one report consumer, no queued action history, and short state gates. Observer becomes useful when multiple independent consumers must react to committed batches; define notification failure after commit explicitly. Command objects become useful for a queue or replayable operator actions; do not promise undo of external sensor effects. State subclasses become useful when states acquire substantial separate behavior or data. A sound justification names both the new requirement and the new contracts it creates.

topics.summary: Add OutsideBand as another AlertRule with finite low and high Celsius limits satisfying -40 <= low <= high <= 125. It must alert only below low or above high; both endpoints are acceptable. Preserve Monitor, adapter, state rules, original run_checks, and the exact original demonstration report. Add extension checks for invalid construction, both endpoints and adjacent outside values, a late invalid batch with rollback, replacement back to AtLeast while paused, and preservation of old OutsideBand flags. Add one extra final line: "extension checks: passed". The starter already runs and verifies the original system; implement the extension without weakening those checks.

items: OutsideBand(20,60) classifies 19,20,60,61 C as alert, ok, ok, alert.

After four accepted band records, reject {5,21,C},{6,9,K} without changing the entire report.
While paused, replace the band with AtLeast(100); admit 61 C afterward as ok while the old 61 C record remains alert.

blocks.text:
Starter: exercises/ch23/main.cpp
Solution: solutions/ch23/main.cpp

blocks.title: Solution reasoning
blocks.text: The reference solution stores two validated limits and implements alert as s.celsius < low_ || s.celsius > high_. Strict comparisons make the band endpoints acceptable. A new check_extension function tests the new behavior and its interaction with rollback and replacement, then main runs both old and new suites. No Monitor changes are needed because the existing interface already describes the varying decision. The solution briefly retains a reference to the vector object, which remains alive, but never retains a reference to an element across a commit. A function-based rule wrapper could also satisfy the behavior; explain its ownership and error contract if choosing that design.

topics.title: Book glossary
topics.summary: Search the terms used in the textbook and recall their meaning in context.

cards.question: Factory Method — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A virtual creation operation called by a creator’s inherited workflow, with concrete creation supplied by derived creators.

cards.question: Product — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object created for another operation to use.

cards.question: Simple factory — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A function that selects and constructs a product without requiring an overridable creation hook in a creator hierarchy.

cards.question: Abstract Factory — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An interface for creating the different product roles in one compatible family.

cards.question: Round trip — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Writing a value and then reading it back to verify that its meaning is preserved.

cards.question: Short-circuit evaluation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Skipping the remaining part of a logical expression when the result is already decided.

cards.question: Builder — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object that collects construction choices in steps and produces a completed product.

cards.question: Director — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A reusable recipe that calls builder steps in a chosen sequence.

cards.question: Snapshot — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An independent value representing data at one point in time.

cards.question: Friend declaration — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A C++ declaration granting a named class or function access to private and protected members.

cards.question: Prototype — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A pattern in which an existing object creates a new object by copying its own state through a common operation.

cards.question: Object slicing — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Losing the derived part when a derived object is copied into a base value.

cards.question: Deep copy — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A copy that duplicates owned contents to the independence depth required by the application.

cards.question: Shallow copy — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A copy that duplicates handles while retaining some shared underlying objects.

cards.question: Singleton — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A design that controls access to one instance through a shared accessor.

cards.question: Mutex — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A synchronization object used to allow one participating thread at a time into a protected region.

cards.question: Critical section — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Code that accesses shared state while holding the required lock.

cards.question: Data race — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Unsynchronized conflicting accesses to memory by different threads, with at least one write; in C++ this causes undefined behavior.

cards.question: Dependency injection — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Supplying an object a component needs through an explicit parameter or constructor instead of locating it globally.

cards.question: Adapter — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A boundary object that translates an existing service into a contract another caller needs.

cards.question: Adaptee — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The existing service whose interface or meaning must be translated.

cards.question: Class adapter — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An adapter implemented by inheriting from a target interface and a legacy class.

cards.question: Unit contract — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The agreement about what physical unit a number represents.

cards.question: Bridge — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A connection that lets a high-level operation and its implementation vary independently.

cards.question: Variation dimension — what does it mean?
cards.answer: One independent kind of change, such as report meaning or output format.

cards.question: Cross-product — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The set of every pairing from two sets of choices.

cards.question: Composite — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A design in which leaves and containers support the same useful operation over a tree.

cards.question: Leaf — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A tree node with no children.

cards.question: Recursion — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Solving a problem by calling the same operation on smaller parts until a stopping case is reached.

cards.question: Acyclic — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Having no path that leads back to an earlier node.

cards.question: Decorator — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object that adds behavior around another object while keeping the same interface.

cards.question: Noncommutative — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Describes operations whose result can change when their order is swapped.

cards.question: Idempotent — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Describes an operation whose repeated application has the same effect as applying it once.

cards.question: Facade — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A simpler public operation or interface over a related set of subsystem operations.

cards.question: Precondition — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule a caller must establish before invoking an operation.

cards.question: Token — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A small input unit, such as one whitespace-separated number.

cards.question: Closed range — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A range that includes both stated endpoints.

cards.question: Flyweight — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A design that shares repeated state while keeping per-use state separate.

cards.question: Intrinsic state — what does it mean?
cards.answer: State that belongs to the shared object identity and can be reused across contexts.

cards.question: Extrinsic state — what does it mean?
cards.answer: State that belongs to one use of a shared object.

cards.question: Interning — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Reusing one stored object for repeated requests with an equal identity key.

cards.question: Immutable — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Not changing after construction.

cards.question: Proxy — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A substitute service object that controls access, location, or lifecycle while keeping the service interface.

cards.question: Lazy initialization — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Creating an object only when it is first needed.

cards.question: Cache hit — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A request answered from an already stored result.

cards.question: Cache invalidation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Declaring a remembered result unusable so a later request must fetch again.

cards.question: Stale data — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Remembered data that is no longer known to match the current source.

cards.question: Handler — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A callable that decides whether it is responsible for a request.

cards.question: Chain of Responsibility — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Ordered handlers with an explicit rule for passing or stopping requests.

cards.question: Optional — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A value wrapper that may contain one value or no value.

cards.question: Pipeline — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Stages that may each contribute work before a later stage runs.

cards.question: Command — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object that stores a request and provides an operation to perform it.

cards.question: Receiver — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The object whose real state or service a command uses.

cards.question: Commit point — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The point after which an operation is recorded as successfully applied.

cards.question: Compensation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A later action intended to offset an effect that cannot literally be undone.

cards.question: Iterator — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object that represents a position and a way to traverse a collection.

cards.question: End position — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A valid traversal position after the last element, with no element to read.

cards.question: Invalidation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An event that ends the permission to use an existing cursor or reference.

cards.question: Generation — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A value used to distinguish one collection version from another.

cards.question: Mediator — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object that owns rules for how other components work together.

cards.question: Callback — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A function call made back to code supplied or represented by another object.

cards.question: Silent update — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A state change that deliberately sends no new change event.

cards.question: Feedback loop — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A chain of events that returns to its starting point and may repeat.

cards.question: Memento — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A saved record of object state whose details are controlled by the state owner.

cards.question: Originator — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The object that creates and interprets its own snapshots.

cards.question: Caretaker — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An object that keeps snapshots without managing their internal representation.

cards.question: Snapshot boundary — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The set of state restored together by one snapshot.

cards.question: Observer — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A listener registered to receive notifications about an event or change.

cards.question: Weak pointer — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A non-owning observer of an object managed by shared ownership.

cards.question: Reentrancy — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Entering an operation again before a previous call to it has finished.

cards.question: Fail-fast delivery — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A policy that stops notifying remaining listeners when a callback fails.

cards.question: State — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A current mode whose rules affect an object behavior.

cards.question: Transition — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A permitted change from one state to another in response to an event.

cards.question: Context — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The object that owns current state and delegates state-dependent work.

cards.question: Transition proposal — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A next-state value prepared before the context commits a change.

cards.question: Strategy — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A replaceable object or callable that supplies one way to perform a task.

cards.question: Context — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The object that keeps stable work and calls a selected strategy.

cards.question: Precondition — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule that must already hold when an operation begins.

cards.question: Template Method — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A base-class operation that fixes a sequence while letting derived classes replace selected steps.

cards.question: Hook — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An optional extension point with a useful default or an empty default action.

cards.question: Postcondition — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A rule that must be true when an operation successfully returns.

cards.question: Name hiding — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A derived declaration prevents ordinary lookup from finding a same-named base declaration; it is not necessarily an override.

cards.question: Visitor — what does it mean?
cards.answer: An operation object with a separate entry point for each supported element type.

cards.question: Overload resolution — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The compiler choosing a same-name function from its parameter types.

cards.question: Double dispatch — what does it mean?
cards.answer: Selecting behavior using both the actual element kind and actual operation kind.

cards.question: Closed type set — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A design that names all allowed element alternatives in one known interface or value type.

cards.question: Commit point — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The operation that makes a fully prepared change visible as the new accepted state.

cards.question: Strong exception guarantee — what does it mean?
cards.answer: For the stated objects and ordinary exception flow, a failed operation leaves their observable state unchanged.

cards.question: Normalized value — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A value converted into the one representation the internal program agrees to use.

cards.question: Intake decision — what does it mean?
cards.answer: The decision stored when data is admitted, preserved even if later policy changes.

cards.question: Finite-state machine — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A fixed set of named states with explicit rules for permitted changes between them.

cards.question: Regression check — what does it mean?
cards.answer: A check that old required behavior still works after a change.

lab.task: Add a public reset() operation that clears all draft choices without changing published plans. Preserve every existing check. Verify incomplete state after reset, successful reuse, independent old snapshots, and safe repeated reset.
checks: build immediately after reset throws logic_error.

lab.answer: The reference implementation calls clear on the draft string and vector. It does not need to touch any Plan because products own their own copies. A reset that only cleared durations would leave a stale title and violate the requested all-choices-cleared behavior. The added test supplies a duration without a new title and requires build to reject, so it catches that specific faulty reset.

lab.answer: The custom copy constructor copies the pointed-to string into a new allocation. The unique_ptr member then cleans up normally, so no custom destructor is needed. overview.explanation: Inheritance arrows point from concrete classes toward their bases. Dependency arrows show parameter knowledge and calls, not ownership. The actual part vector owns elements, and the caller owns Price. The focused trace explains the two dispatch steps that a class diagram alone cannot show.

focus.where: Virtual dispatch selects it when the actual Part object is Bolts.
focus.why: Inside this member, the compiler knows the element is Bolts.

overview.explanation: Ownership points from the responsible owner to what it keeps alive. Inheritance points from AtLeast toward the interface it implements. Comments inside blocks are teaching annotations, not extra UML relationships.

extra_overviews.title: Only these state changes are permitted
extra_overviews.explanation: Each arrow is a permitted state transition caused by its named public operation. The absence of an outgoing stopped arrow is intentional. Intake and reports do not change state, so they are not drawn as transitions. Replacement is permitted in idle or paused and also leaves state unchanged. These states are enum values in one class, not subclasses.

extra_overviews.title: One accepted item inside an all-or-nothing batch
extra_overviews.explanation: Numbered call arrows show execution order for each item. Return values are described in the blocks rather than drawn as additional arrows. A conversion or identifier failure prevents later steps for that item. After every item succeeds, the monitor commits with records_.swap(staged). The diagram shows one iteration, not a separate transaction for each record.

focus.title: Normalize the unit before any policy decision
focus.what: This branch turns Fahrenheit into the internal Celsius scale and rejects any tag outside the two supported units. It changes only a local number, so no monitor history is at risk here.
focus.where: SampleAdapter::convert runs inside ingest before the order check and rule call. Identifier and finite-input checks occur immediately before this focused block; finite-result and physical-range checks follow it.
focus.why: A comparison cannot be meaningful until both numbers use the same unit. Keeping that conversion at the boundary prevents every future rule and formatter from having its own conversion policy.
focus.invariant: After the full converter returns, celsius is finite, in the accepted range, and carries the same positive identifier as the input. Unsupported tags must never be silently treated as Celsius.
focus.risk: Integer 5 / 9 would become zero. Omitting the unknown-unit branch would accept values with an unexplained scale. This excerpt is only the conversion branch, not the full validation contract.

Copy the input number into a local double named c.
Compare the unit character with uppercase F and open that branch.
Subtract the Fahrenheit offset and apply the floating-point scale conversion.
If the unit was not F, test whether it is also not C.
Begin constructing and throwing an invalid_argument exception.
Provide the exception message and finish the throw statement.

focus.title: The replaceable decision contract
focus.what: The interface states the one decision that a rule must supply. It also makes deleting a derived rule through the base owning pointer safe. No specific threshold is stored in this base.
focus.where: Monitor stores an owning pointer to AlertRule. AtLeast derives from it, and the lab adds OutsideBand. Ingest calls this operation after conversion and ordering have succeeded.
focus.why: Changing the alert decision should not change unit conversion, state transitions, or commit behavior. A shared interface gives the monitor one stable call while the concrete decision varies.
focus.invariant: Each implementation must answer using the supplied valid sample without throwing or outside side effects. The virtual destructor must remain so ownership cleanup reaches the concrete type.
focus.risk: A missing override can leave a derived class abstract or select the wrong function signature. Noexcept is a promise, not a catch block; throwing from an implementation terminates the program.
explain: Declare the base class and open its definition.
Make the following interface members public.
The comment explains that cleanup must use the concrete object type.
Declare a virtual destructor and ask C++ to generate its usual behavior.
The comment documents the rule operation's exception promise.
Begin the virtual operation declaration, which returns a bool.
Borrow a constant Sample, keep the rule logically const, promise no escaping exceptions, and make this operation abstract.

focus.title: Ownership and state live in one authority
focus.start: // Own the rule and the record values.
focus.what: These private fields are the monitor's long-lived state. The owning pointer controls one rule lifetime, the vector owns stored values, and the enum names the current operating state.
focus.where: They are at the start of Monitor, before public operations. Constructors establish them; checked methods read or replace them. ReportFacade reaches history through a const accessor.
focus.why: Keeping the invariant-bearing fields private prevents callers from appending unchecked records or forcing an illegal state. One authority is easier to audit than unrelated globals or shared writable containers.
focus.invariant: A usable monitor has one nonnull owned rule, a valid state, and at most eight valid records in increasing order. The constructor and public methods jointly establish and preserve this contract.
focus.risk: A raw borrowed rule pointer could outlive its rule. Exposing a mutable records vector would let callers bypass capacity and conversion checks. Raising capacity affects the cost of each staged copy.
explain: The comment identifies which resources the monitor is responsible for keeping alive.
Declare the exclusive owning pointer to a rule through the base interface.
Declare a vector that owns Record values and its own storage.
Initialize the state field to idle when a monitor is constructed.
Define a compile-time size limit shared by all monitor objects.

focus.title: Guard a transition before changing state
focus.what: Start has one legal source state. The check rejects any other source before the state field changes, so a failed request leaves the machine where it was.
focus.where: This is a public Monitor member. Main calls it after construction, and run_checks also calls it from illegal states to verify rejection.
focus.why: A named operation keeps state rules beside the mutation they protect. Callers request an action rather than manufacturing a new enum value themselves.
focus.invariant: Only an idle monitor may enter running through start. A stopped object cannot restart, and a running object cannot be started twice.
focus.risk: Assigning running before checking idle destroys the evidence needed by the guard. Removing the guard would allow a stopped session to restart while retaining old history.
explain: Declare the start member with no parameters and open its body.
The comment states that the precondition must pass before any state change.
Check whether the current state differs from idle.
Begin throwing a logic_error to reject the action.
Provide the message explaining the missing precondition.
Close the rejection branch.
Enter running only after the check has passed.

focus.title: Prepare a candidate without altering accepted history
focus.what: A copy becomes the candidate history. Each new sample is normalized and checked against the most recent candidate record, so the same ordering rule covers both old and new items.
focus.where: This block follows state and capacity validation in ingest. Classification and staged append follow it; the final swap is outside the loop.
focus.why: Checking only records_.back() would miss a duplicate within the new batch. Checking staged.back() sees the accepted past plus every earlier proposed item without committing any of them.
focus.invariant: Before each iteration, staged contains valid increasing records. Before the final swap, records_ still holds exactly the original history, even if conversion or ordering rejects a later item.
focus.risk: Replacing staged with a reference to records_ would destroy isolation. Reading staged.back() without first testing empty would be invalid for the first reading in an empty session.
explain: The comment names the proposed history and its purpose.
Copy the live vector into a separate local vector; auto infers its type.
Borrow each raw element without changing it; the colon means take elements from batch.
Begin defining a constant local normalized sample s.
Call the adapter and use its returned value to initialize s.
First require the candidate history to be nonempty before using its last element.
Begin comparing the new identifier against the most recent candidate identifier.
Complete the comparison with the last candidate identifier and open the rejection branch.
Begin throwing a validation exception for broken ordering.
Finish the exception construction with its explanatory message.

focus.title: Store the intake decision, then commit once
focus.what: The chosen rule produces a boolean, a proposed record stores it, and one vector swap makes the completed batch visible. The flag becomes historical data at this point.
focus.where: This block is the end of ingest. The loop repeats classification and append for each valid sample; swap runs once after the loop ends successfully.
focus.why: Keeping the commit outside the loop gives a late rejection the same effect as an early rejection: no accepted history change. Storing the boolean prevents a later rule replacement from rewriting the past.
focus.invariant: Every staged record has been normalized, ordered, and classified. The live vector changes exactly once on success and never changes on an ordinary pre-commit exception.
focus.risk: Moving swap into the loop produces partial commits. Re-evaluating flags during reporting changes the meaning of history. Side effects inside alert would lie outside the vector rollback guarantee.
explain: The comment records the time at which the decision is made.
Call the currently owned rule and keep its answer in hot; the arrow accesses the pointed-to object.
Append a Record containing the sample value and its intake flag to the candidate history.
Close the loop after this item; further items repeat the same process.
The comment identifies the single point where a fully valid batch becomes accepted.
Swap vector contents so records_ owns the new history and staged owns the old one.

focus.title: A report borrows records and returns owned text
focus.what: The loop formats accepted values and counts their stored flags. It does not ask the current rule to judge old readings, and it does not change monitor state.
focus.where: This is inside ReportFacade::summary after stream formatting has been set. The method adds a final count line and returns the string after this focused block.
focus.why: One reporting entry point keeps unit labels, precision, row order, and alert counts consistent. A short const borrow avoids a full history copy without leaking a reference to report callers.
focus.invariant: Each row reflects a stored normalized sample and its original alert flag. Output order matches history order, and the resulting string owns its characters independently of the monitor.
focus.risk: Retaining an element reference for later use can become unsafe after ingest replaces vector storage. A report must not run concurrently with mutation without a synchronization contract.
explain: The comment explains that reporting reads without taking ownership.
Begin a range loop that borrows each Record without changing it.
Use the monitor history as the range and open the loop body.
Add one for an alert and zero otherwise; the conditional operator chooses between those values.
Write the sample identifier followed by a colon and a space.
Write the normalized temperature followed by its explicit Celsius unit label.
Choose the text ALERT or ok from the stored flag.

Graduate lecture narration
Consider the statement that our program printed 42. It reports an observation, but it does not specify the input domain, the compiler assumptions, or whether an invalid memory access occurred on the way to that output. A stronger argument separates a contract, assumptions, and evidence. The contract says what counts as correct. Assumptions identify the conditions under which the reasoning applies. Evidence is what we inspected or measured.

These categories prevent two common mistakes. First, a useful test result is not a universal proof. Second, a documented guarantee is not a measured performance result. During the lecture, attach each conclusion to its boundary: language, binary interface, operating system, or hardware. If the observation conflicts with the prediction, revise the model or inspect a lower-level artifact rather than inventing a promise that the interface never made. This framework is an instructional elaboration of the original chapter's contract model.

Sixth-grade explanation
Do not stop at “it worked.” Say what you expected, what had to be true, and what you checked.

Discussion / pause
What is missing from the claim “the executable ran successfully”?

Expected response: The success criterion, input domain, environmental assumptions, and evidence beyond that one run.

Transition: Hardware: compute, state, and movement.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.1 · HARDWARE & SOFTWARE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter begins with a deliberately simplified CPU-memory-I/O model. CPU cores execute instructions, registers hold working state, memory holds addressable instructions and data, and controllers connect devices to the rest of the machine. Storage and peripherals have different purposes and access mechanisms from registers. Buses and interconnects carry requests and data among these components.

Use this picture to ask three questions: where does a value currently exist, which component initiates its movement, and what event tells another component that progress occurred? The picture is not a claim that contemporary processors execute one instruction at a time or that all transfers pass through one physical wire. It is a model of responsibilities. The software side supplies instructions and data, while the language, executable format, operating system, and device interface assign meaning to particular encodings. A sequence of bits does not identify its own type or purpose.

Sixth-grade explanation
The processor does the work. Registers and memory hold information. Controllers help the computer talk to storage and other devices.

Discussion / pause
Does a byte sequence tell you whether it is an instruction, an integer, or text?

Expected response: No. Its interpretation depends on the surrounding interface, representation, and execution context.

Transition: Follow the value—not just the statement.

Section: 1.1.1 · CPU, REGISTERS & MEMORY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 18.

Graduate lecture narration
Suppose a source expression adds three to a value. Before discussing the addition, ask how the value became available to the executing instruction. It might arrive in an argument register, come from a prior calculation, or require a load. The result might remain in a register, be used immediately, or be stored. This is why a source variable should not automatically be imagined as a permanently assigned RAM slot.

The instruction stream also has to be fetched. Therefore, saying that an addition needs no data-memory access is not the same as saying that the processor uses no memory-related machinery. The original chapter makes this distinction in its expression example. Our register-workbench analogy explains placement, not exact timing or physical implementation. At this stage, track architectural inputs and outputs and leave detailed cache behavior and processor scheduling to later chapters.

Sixth-grade explanation
Think of registers as a tiny workbench and memory as a larger set of shelves. A value may already be on the workbench when it is needed.

Discussion / pause
Can the addition itself avoid a data-memory load?

Expected response: Yes, when the needed operand is already in a register or the compiler can otherwise supply it without a load.

Transition: Controllers and interrupts coordinate I/O.

Graduate lecture narration
I/O introduces a boundary between requesting work and completing work. A controller supplies a device-facing interface. Systems software translates a higher-level request into actions the device supports. An interrupt is one mechanism by which the system can learn that an event needs attention; it should not be mistaken for the application itself performing the hardware operation.

A useful explanation identifies the requester, the component doing the transfer, and the component reporting completion. Do not silently assume that a library call corresponds to one device command or that returning from a high-level call means durable storage has been achieved. Those are separate contracts. The source deck names controllers and interrupts; this slide makes the request/completion distinction explicit without prescribing one device protocol. We will revisit the same distinction when we discuss buffered output and partial failures.

Sixth-grade explanation
A device does not always finish right away. The program asks for work, the device does it, and the system reports what happened.

Transition: Software role is not execution privilege.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.2–1.1.3 · SOFTWARE CATEGORIES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 4.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter classifies systems software by role: kernels control resources, compilers translate, linkers connect compiled units, runtime libraries supply startup and shared operations, and drivers handle device-specific interactions. Application software performs tasks for users or services. The distinction is useful, but not absolute. A database application may contain its own allocator, scheduler, or storage engine.

Execution privilege is a different axis. A compiler is systems software that normally executes as an ordinary user process. A server may manage important information without becoming kernel code. Conversely, a particular driver architecture can place components on either side of a privilege boundary. Avoid using the labels low-level, systems, and privileged as synonyms. For diagnosis, ask what a component is responsible for and what operations it is authorized to perform. These questions may have different answers.

Sixth-grade explanation
Some programs help the computer run other programs. That does not mean they all get special permission to control the machine.

Discussion / pause
Why does a compiler not need kernel privilege just because it is systems software?

Expected response: Translation is its role; the OS can provide ordinary process permissions sufficient to read inputs and write outputs.

Transition: An abstraction is a smaller contract.

---

topics.title: An abstraction is a smaller contract
topics.summary: The original slide describes an abstraction as hiding detail while preserving a contract. For example, a file descriptor lets a caller request byte-oriented I/O without manipulating a storage controller. A vector presents a sequence while hiding many allocation decisions. Hidden details continue to exist; they are simply not all part of the caller's interface.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.4 · ABSTRACTION LAYERS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 5.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original slide describes an abstraction as hiding detail while preserving a contract. For example, a file descriptor lets a caller request byte-oriented I/O without manipulating a storage controller. A vector presents a sequence while hiding many allocation decisions. Hidden details continue to exist; they are simply not all part of the caller's interface.

At graduate level, describe a contract using preconditions, permitted effects, postconditions, and failure behavior. Preconditions tell the caller what must already hold. Postconditions constrain the result when the operation succeeds. Failure behavior says what may have changed and what remains valid. This is a reasoning framework, not a claim that every real interface documents all of these perfectly. A missing or ambiguous guarantee is something to investigate, not permission to assume convenient behavior. Abstraction succeeds when the smaller contract is sufficient for the caller's reasoning.

Sixth-grade explanation
A button can be easy to use even when the machine behind it is complicated. You still need to know what pressing the button promises.

Transition: Guaranteed, customary, or measured?.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.5 · HARDWARE / SOFTWARE INTERFACES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.

Graduate lecture narration
An API is a source-facing interface: names, operations, argument meanings, and behavioral contracts. An ABI governs compiled interoperability: calling conventions, register use, data layout, and other binary rules. An ISA describes machine operations and software-visible architectural state. These boundaries answer different questions even when one program crosses all three in a few instructions.

Use a function call as the running example. Its source declaration tells the compiler how the call is written and typed. Binary conventions tell caller and callee where to put arguments and results. The selected machine instructions must then be valid for the target architecture. Matching at one boundary does not imply matching at the others. The original chapter's three warnings remain important: identical APIs do not imply binary compatibility; a shared ISA does not imply a shared ABI; and a shared ISA does not imply identical microarchitecture or speed.

Sixth-grade explanation
The API says what you can ask for. The ABI says how compiled parts pass things. The ISA says which machine commands the processor understands.

Transition: One ISA can support different calling conventions.

---

Section: 1.1.5 · ABI CASE STUDY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Here is a concrete graduate extension of the chapter's ABI distinction. For an ordinary function taking two int parameters, a System V AMD64 caller uses the integer argument-register convention associated with RDI and RSI, with the int values in their 32-bit portions. The usual Microsoft x64 convention uses RCX and RDX for those positions instead. For the int return in this example, EAX is used in both conventions.

This is a deliberately narrow example. Real ABIs also define stack rules, preserved registers, alignment, aggregate classification, and other details. Do not extend this two-int table to every type or every function. It is enough to demonstrate the logical point: a machine can implement the x86-64 ISA while binary components disagree about how a function is called. Source-level similarity is not evidence that independently built objects can be combined safely.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two people can speak the same language but use different handoff rules. Compiled functions also need to agree on where each value goes.

Expected response: No. Caller and callee must also agree on argument locations and the rest of the binary contract.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.1.5 · ISA VS. MICROARCHITECTURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 6, 18, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter warns that an ISA and a microarchitecture are not the same thing. The ISA defines the software-visible operations and state that an implementation must honor. Microarchitecture concerns how a particular implementation realizes that behavior. The existence of the same instruction in two systems does not establish the same latency, throughput, cache behavior, or resource contention.

Keep two explanations separate. A functional explanation asks which architectural result an instruction produces under its specified conditions. A performance explanation asks how long a workload takes on a particular implementation and why. A correct functional trace does not provide enough information to derive whole-program timing. Conversely, a favorable benchmark cannot excuse an invalid instruction assumption or a violated language rule. This distinction prepares the performance discussion without turning Chapter 1 into a processor-design course.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two cars can follow the same road rules but have different engines. Two processors can run the same commands at different speeds.

Transition: Locate the boundary before proposing a fix.

---

Source mapping: original slide(s) 6, 11, 12, 21.

Graduate lecture narration
A systems failure is easier to investigate when the symptom is attached to a boundary. A missing source declaration is not the same problem as a missing compiled definition. A binary that requires a different instruction set has a different issue from a program that lacks access to a file. The table gives initial hypotheses, not a complete diagnostic decision tree.

The graduate task is to state the evidence that would discriminate among plausible explanations. For a binary-interface concern, examine build settings and the ABI of both components. When something breaks, first find which handoff went wrong. Fixing the wrong part wastes time.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.2 · FROM SOURCE TO EXECUTION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 7.

Graduate lecture narration
The source chapter presents a seven-stage model: source, preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and execution. The model separates responsibilities; it does not require every implementation to launch a separate operating-system process for every stage. Compiler drivers often orchestrate several stages in a single command.

Each stage changes what kind of evidence is available. Source text exposes the programmer's operations and obligations. Preprocessed text exposes the translation unit after directives and macros. Assembly exposes symbolic target operations. An object file exposes encoded data, symbols, and relocation requirements. A linked executable describes a loadable program, while loading and runtime establish and exercise the process environment. Notice that passing an earlier stage does not guarantee passing later stages. Successful compilation does not supply an omitted definition, and successful loading does not guarantee that a runtime resource will be available.

Sixth-grade explanation
The program goes through several stations before and while it runs. Each station has a different job and can find a different kind of problem.

Transition: Source code describes an abstract computation.

Supporting primary sources
[GCC] GCC manual, Overall Options. Compilation stages and the -E, -S, -c, and -o compiler-driver options. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Overall-Options.html

Section: 1.2.1 · SOURCE-LEVEL CONTRACT
Source mapping: original slide(s) 8.

Graduate lecture narration
Before imagining instructions, identify the source-level semantics. The original chapter lists types, expressions, statements, lifetimes, synchronization rules, and observable behavior. These constrain the abstract computation, but source order is not a literal physical schedule. A correct implementation may transform the computation while preserving the behavior required by the language and the implementation's documented guarantees.

For a pointer access, ask whether the object exists, whether the access is in range, and whether its lifetime and synchronization obligations hold. For arithmetic, ask whether the result is representable under the relevant rules. These are not optional details to check after performance tuning. They define the domain in which the rest of the explanation is valid. The public C committee draft provides a reference for abstract-machine reasoning; the lab retains the source deck's C17 compilation mode.

Code has rules about what values mean and when they may be used. The computer may organize the work differently while keeping the promised result.

Include processing makes header content available to the translation unit; it does not automatically cause an external function implementation to be linked into the final program. Macros operate on preprocessing tokens. They are not typed runtime variables or ordinary function calls. blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.2 · PREPROCESSOR COUNTEREXAMPLE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 9.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This is a deliberately invalid example for analysis, not a program to use as a numerical experiment. The SQUARE macro replaces its parameter in two positions. Giving it i++ expands the increment expression twice. In C, the two modifications shown in the multiplication expression are unsequenced relative to one another, so the example has undefined behavior. There is no correct portable numeric answer to predict.

Parentheses are still useful in macros because they prevent some precedence surprises, but they do not make repeated evaluation safe. A function that receives an already computed value separates the caller's side effect from the body calculation. Even then, arithmetic range requirements remain: replacing the macro with a function does not make arbitrary signed multiplication overflow valid. This extension turns the source deck's warning about duplicated side effects into a concrete contract failure.

Sixth-grade explanation
A macro can copy your instruction more than once. Asking it to “use the number and then increase it” can accidentally copy the increase too.

Discussion / pause
What portable value should we predict for y?

Expected response: None. The shown expanded expression violates C sequencing rules.

Transition: Declarations enable checking; definitions supply entities.

The compiled caller can still depend on a definition that will be supplied later. That is the central reason a program may compile and then fail at the link stage.

The graduate nuance is that a header is not intrinsically declaration-only. Headers can also contain definitions, subject to language and linkage rules. Our teaching layout places this externally linked function's declaration in the header and its definition in one source file. The include guard in the companion lab is an added organizational aid. Distinguish a file's conventional role from a language restriction. Also remember that consistent declarations across translation units are a programmer and build-system responsibility; a conventional linker is not a complete source-level type checker.

Sixth-grade explanation
A declaration says that a function exists and how to call it. A definition contains the actual function body.

Transition: The compiler transforms meaning into a target program.

C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.4 · ASSEMBLY & OBJECT FILES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 10, 11.

Graduate lecture narration
Assembly output is not a uniform list of executable instructions. It can contain labels, directives, data, and symbolic references. Labels identify positions or symbols; directives tell the assembler how to organize material. The assembler encodes instructions and data and emits the additional object-file information required for later stages.

A relocatable object can contain a reference whose final address is not yet known. Keeping that information is not a failure to assemble the file. It is part of separate compilation. The chapter's caller can therefore assemble before the linker sees the definition of add. When reading assembly or disassembly, separate the actual instructions from organizational metadata. When examining an object, ask both what bytes it already contains and what obligations remain unresolved. This is the bridge between compiler output and linking.

Sixth-grade explanation
Assembly uses readable names for machine operations. The assembler makes the bytes and keeps information needed to connect unfinished references later.

Transition: Linking connects separate compiled responsibilities.

Supporting primary sources
[AS] GNU assembler manual, Symbols. Symbolic assembly information retained for later stages. https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/as/Symbols.html
[ELF] System V generic ABI, Relocation. Relocation entries; processor-specific interpretation. The lecture arithmetic is an explicitly illustrative model. https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/elf/gabi4+/ch4.reloc.html

Graduate lecture narration
The source chapter describes linking as combining object files and libraries, resolving symbol references, laying out sections, and applying relocations that can be handled at link time. In our example, main.o refers to add and sum.o provides the corresponding definition. The linker connects the reference using the applicable object format and binary conventions.

An undefined-reference diagnostic points us toward the link inputs, symbol names, and compatible definitions. It is not normally fixed by adding another source declaration to the caller. We will intentionally omit sum.o to create a focused failure whose cause can be explained from the artifact chain.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.5 · GRADUATE WORKED MODEL
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Relocation records preserve information needed to adjust address-dependent content. To make the arithmetic visible, use an illustrative PC-relative relocation model with a symbol address S, an addend A, and a relocation-place address P. Under the chosen model, the stored result is S plus A minus P. For the slide's hexadecimal values, 0x1200 minus 0x1000 gives 0x0200, or 512 decimal.

This is explicitly a teaching model, not the exact encoding of a particular call instruction. Real relocation types define which location P denotes, how an addend is stored, the field width, alignment, and overflow constraints. Some instruction encodings require an addend that accounts for the relationship between the relocation field and the next instruction. The important conceptual result is that assembly can preserve a solvable equation without knowing its final numeric answer. A processor-specific ABI supplies the exact rule.

Sixth-grade explanation
A reference can say “fill in the distance to this function later.” Once the function has a final location, the linker can calculate the distance.

Discussion / pause
Why can the assembler emit a valid object before S is known?

Expected response: It records the unresolved symbol and relocation information so a later stage can compute the needed value.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.5–1.2.6 · LINK-TIME VS. LOAD-TIME WORK
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11, 12.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter mentions both link-time relocation and dynamic loaders that can finish runtime linking. The distinction is timing and packaging, not a choice between having contracts and having none. Static linking selects needed material from object inputs and archives into the output. Dynamic linking leaves shared-object dependencies and associated work for the runtime environment.

A dynamically linked executable can be well formed and still fail to start when a required shared object cannot be found or is incompatible. Likewise, successfully finding a shared library does not establish that the application will handle its later inputs correctly. Do not say that static linking universally means every operating-system dependency disappears, or that every dynamic symbol must always resolve at exactly the same moment. Policies differ. The teaching goal is to identify which obligations remain after the static link stage.

Sixth-grade explanation
Some program pieces are joined before the program runs. Other pieces are found and connected when the program starts or later.

Transition: Loading establishes the executable process image.

Section: 1.2.6 · LOADING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 12.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Loading connects an executable file to the process that will execute it. The source chapter describes mappings and possible dynamic-loader work. For our Linux teaching environment, execve replaces the current process image with a new program image; it should not be described as creating a new process by itself. Process creation and image replacement are distinct operations.

Executable metadata describes what must be mapped and how execution begins. For ELF, program headers describe segments relevant to loading; these should not be confused with the section-oriented view used by many link and inspection operations. blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.6 · DEMAND PAGING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 12.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter explicitly separates mapping from residency. A mapping establishes a relationship in the process's virtual address space. It does not necessarily mean every mapped page already has its contents resident in physical memory. With demand paging, an access may cause the operating system to make a page available before the program continues.

Therefore, a page fault is not automatically evidence of an invalid program. Some faults are part of normal demand handling. An invalid access or a protection violation is a different case and can cause failure. For measurement, a first access can have different costs from a later access, so a benchmark should state whether initialization and first-touch effects are included. That last point is a reasoning consequence of the mapping/residency distinction, not a claim that every page fault requires disk I/O.

Sixth-grade explanation
Having a place on the map does not mean the page is already on your desk. The system may bring it into memory only when you first use it.

Discussion / pause
Does mapping a large file prove that every byte has already been read into RAM?

Expected response: No. Mapping and current physical residency are different properties.

Transition: Runtime begins before main and extends through termination.

Supporting primary sources
[MMAP] Linux man-pages, mmap(2). Virtual mappings and population-related behavior; lecture distinguishes mapping from residency. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html

blocks.text:
Section: 1.2.7 · RUNTIME EXECUTION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 12.

Graduate lecture narration
A hosted program's runtime story does not begin and end with the first and last lines of main. Startup establishes the language and library environment. The program then executes its own code and library code, sometimes requesting kernel services through system calls. Scheduling can interrupt its progress or delay when it resumes. The source deck makes these boundaries part of the chapter rather than treating them as hidden trivia.

Termination also has a contract. Normal library termination and abrupt process termination do not necessarily perform the same user-space cleanup. For the ordinary hosted C case, returning from the initial main is associated with normal termination behavior. Avoid generalizing that all ways to stop a process flush buffers or run cleanup code. When reviewing a design, ask which completion path occurs and what it promises about resources and output. This matters even for small examples.

Sixth-grade explanation
The system prepares things before main starts. While the program runs, it may wait or ask the operating system for help. It also needs to finish properly.

Graduate lecture narration
We now connect the chapter's opening claim to its two-file example. The call to add produces an int result under the function's valid arithmetic domain. printf interprets the format string and supplied value and uses the library's output machinery. That machinery may buffer output before a lower-level operating-system request occurs. The kernel coordinates the relevant output destination and device path.

The diagram is a responsibility trace, not a promise of one system call per printf call or one hardware transaction per output request. The destination might be a terminal, a regular file, or a pipe, and that changes the environment. The original minimal program assumes that its demonstration output succeeds; it is not a complete production error-handling example. Our expected value is 42, but explaining that value and explaining successful delivery of its printed characters are separate parts of the contract.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · ORIGINAL CHAPTER PROGRAM
Source mapping: original slide(s) 16.

Graduate lecture narration
This is the original chapter's worked example, with the same function, operands, and expected result. Read it in terms of responsibilities rather than merely from top to bottom. sum.h introduces the callable interface. sum.c includes that interface and supplies the function body. main.c includes both the standard output declarations and the project declaration, then uses add as an argument to printf.

The mathematical addition of 17 and 25 is representable as int, so the demonstrated arithmetic has no signed-overflow problem. The function itself is not a checked arbitrary-integer addition service; its precondition is that the mathematical sum is representable. The minimal program also assumes successful demonstration output. Our companion header adds an include guard and a precondition comment without changing the example's computation. The build was tested in the creation environment and printed 42. Platform addresses and tool output can differ elsewhere.

Sixth-grade explanation
The header describes add, one file builds add, and another file uses it. The linker joins the two compiled pieces.

Transition: Stop the pipeline at each observable artifact.

Source mapping: original slide(s) 17.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original source deck shows compiler-driver options that stop at preprocessing, assembly text, and object output. This graduate variant explicitly feeds a saved artifact into the next stage so the chain is easy to inspect. main.c becomes main.i, main.i becomes main.s, and main.s becomes main.o. sum.c is compiled separately before both object files are linked.

The distinction between an operation and a driver option matters. The option -S stops after compilation proper and writes assembly text; it does not mean that the assembler has run. The option -c produces an object without linking. Using -c on a C file normally includes its earlier preprocessing and compilation steps. In the companion script, build artifacts live under build/ to keep the source directory organized. The slide omits that directory prefix for readability. The same substantive sequence was executed successfully during preparation.

Sixth-grade explanation
Pause the build after each station so you can inspect what that station made. This makes the hidden steps easier to understand.

Transition: Inspect evidence: symbols, relocations, and segments.

blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · GNU BINARY TOOLS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11, 17.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
An artifact inspection is strongest when it answers a specific question. nm shows symbols, so use it to connect an undefined reference in the caller with a definition in the other object. In the tested GNU nm output, add was marked U in main.o and T in sum.o. U denotes an undefined symbol, while T identifies a text-section symbol in this case. Exact addresses are not needed for the inference.

readelf -r examines relocation entries. objdump -dr combines disassembly with relocation information. readelf -l shows the executable's program headers, which connect back to loading. These commands are GNU/Linux/ELF-oriented extensions of the source deck's artifact exercise, not portable C language operations. Record versions when comparing outputs, and avoid inferring that a compiler must generate one fixed symbol layout or instruction listing. The relevant evidence is the relationship between the artifacts.

Sixth-grade explanation
The build leaves clues. Special tools can show which functions are missing, which are defined, and how the finished program is arranged.

Transition: Break only the link contract.

[AS] GNU assembler manual, Symbols. Symbolic assembly information retained for later stages. https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/as/Symbols.html

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · CONTROLLED FAILURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11, 17, 20.

Graduate lecture narration
A controlled failure is useful because it changes one obligation at a time. The caller was compiled with a visible declaration, so its source-level call can be accepted. Now intentionally omit sum.o from the final command. The missing definition of add prevents the ordinary executable link from completing. This was tested during preparation and failed as expected with a diagnostic mentioning add.

Do not demand identical diagnostic wording across compilers and linkers. The stable prediction is the failed link and its relationship to the omitted definition. Reintroducing sum.o addresses that specific obligation. Adding another header include to main.c does not supply the missing compiled body. Nor does this experiment show that every undefined-reference problem has the same cause: symbol spelling, linkage, and binary compatibility can matter in more complex builds. Here the intentionally omitted object isolates the cause.

Sixth-grade explanation
Leave out the piece that defines add. The caller can still be compiled, but the linker cannot finish the whole program.

Transition: Incremental builds follow dependency information.

Supporting primary sources
[LD] GNU linker manual, Overview. Linker role in combining, relocating, and resolving object inputs. https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Overview.html

---

blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · PREDICT BEFORE REBUILDING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 20.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original guided lab asks students to change one function and predict which artifacts should change. For our ordinary separate-compilation model, changing sum.c requires rebuilding sum.o and relinking the executable. Changing the shared declaration in sum.h can affect both translation units that include it, so both objects need to be reconsidered. A main.c edit similarly affects its own object and the final link.

These are dependency obligations, not guarantees of different output bytes. Recompilation can produce identical bytes when a change does not affect the result, and timestamps or build metadata can change for unrelated reasons. Optimization across translation units can also introduce additional dependencies beyond this simplified model. A good lab report distinguishes “must be rebuilt according to dependencies” from “must have a different hash.” The companion activity uses a no-LTO, separate-object workflow to keep the causal chain visible.

Sixth-grade explanation
When one part changes, rebuild the parts that depend on it. A change to shared instructions can affect more than one source file.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · SOURCE-LEVEL REASONING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 8, 18.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original expression is int y = x + 3. Begin with a valid int value x and a context in which reading it is permitted. For the mathematical result to be representable as int, x must not exceed INT_MAX minus three. Adding a positive three to any representable x cannot cross the lower bound, so the upper bound is the interesting arithmetic condition here.

Under those assumptions, the source-level postcondition is that y has the mathematical value of x plus three. That is the claim the implementation must realize when the result matters. The variable can be optimized away if the surrounding program has no required observable use for it. This sequence of reasoning deliberately precedes instruction selection. It prevents the mistaken argument that a familiar hardware addition or a successful test somehow establishes valid source semantics for every possible input.

Sixth-grade explanation
Before adding three, check that the starting value is allowed and the answer fits. A good-looking answer does not fix a broken rule.

Discussion / pause
Why do we not need a separate lower-bound overflow check for adding positive 3?

Expected response: For a valid int x, adding positive 3 cannot make the mathematical result smaller than INT_MIN.

Transition: Trace the same expression into architectural state.

Supporting primary sources
[LANG] WG14 N1570, Programming languages — C, committee draft (2011). §3.4 behavior categories; §5.1 abstract machine and execution; §6.5 expressions; declarations and external definitions. C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · MACHINE-LEVEL REASONING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 18.

Graduate lecture narration
After establishing the source contract, follow the implementation. The compiler selects a target realization, the assembler encodes the instructions, and the processor executes the resulting machine operations. The source slide notes that an operand already in a register may let the addition itself avoid a data-memory access. That is a conditional statement, not a claim that all additions are memory-free.

Keep architectural effects separate from physical scheduling. We can explain that the appropriate result becomes available in architectural state without asserting a one-to-one relationship between source lines, instruction issue events, and elapsed cycles. The instruction bytes still come through the instruction-fetch path, and the surrounding program may require loads, stores, calls, or no retained calculation at all. The companion add3 example saves -O0 and -O2 assembly so students can observe two real builds while keeping target-dependent output distinct from language guarantees.

Sixth-grade explanation
Once the calculation is valid, the compiler chooses machine commands. The processor follows those commands and updates its working values.

Transition: The six concerns of systems programming.

Supporting primary sources
[OPT] GCC manual, Optimize Options. Optimization controls and target/build dependence; no fixed assembly listing promised. https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Optimize-Options.html

topics.title: The six concerns of systems programming
topics.summary: The original chapter organizes systems programming around six concerns rather than a single language feature or level of privilege. Low-level reasoning addresses representation and machine behavior. Performance distinguishes latency and throughput. Resource management identifies ownership and release responsibilities. Correctness connects behavior to specifications and invariants. Robustness defines controlled behavior under failure. Portability makes environmental assumptions visible.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.3 · SYSTEMS PROGRAMMING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter organizes systems programming around six concerns rather than a single language feature or level of privilege. Low-level reasoning addresses representation and machine behavior. Performance distinguishes latency and throughput. Resource management identifies ownership and release responsibilities. Correctness connects behavior to specifications and invariants. Robustness defines controlled behavior under failure. Portability makes environmental assumptions visible.

These concerns interact without becoming interchangeable. A faster implementation can violate an ownership rule. A memory-safe operation can still produce the wrong specified result. Portable source can have poor performance on a second platform, and a compatible binary can still depend on missing runtime resources. In the following slides, keep asking which concern a proposed change improves and which assumptions it introduces. Graduate reasoning requires identifying those tradeoffs rather than labeling a design simply good or bad.

Sixth-grade explanation
Systems programmers care about what the bits mean, how fast work happens, who owns things, and what happens when something goes wrong.

Transition: Low-level reasoning makes representation explicit.

---

topics.title: Low-level reasoning makes representation explicit
topics.summary: The low-level concern is not merely using assembly syntax. It is recognizing where representation becomes part of the program's obligations. Values have sizes, layouts, alignment requirements, and interpretation rules. Storage contains encodings; an interface supplies the meaning. A pointer value that is useful inside one process is not automatically a useful representation for a file or another process.

Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 13, 15.

Graduate lecture narration
The low-level concern is not merely using assembly syntax. It is recognizing where representation becomes part of the program's obligations. Values have sizes, layouts, alignment requirements, and interpretation rules. Storage contains encodings; an interface supplies the meaning. A pointer value that is useful inside one process is not automatically a useful representation for a file or another process.

The original chapter links representation to machine behavior and later asks for explicit serialization. The graduate consequence is to identify every point where an internal representation becomes an external contract. Writing raw object bytes can accidentally expose padding, platform data layout, or addresses that have no meaning to the reader. This slide presents the design question; the later byte-order example supplies a concrete protocol. Make platform assumptions visible rather than hiding them behind a familiar type name.

Sixth-grade explanation
The same bits can mean different things under different rules. Programs must agree on how to read and store them.

Transition: Performance: latency, throughput, and elapsed time.

topics.title: Performance: latency, throughput, and elapsed time
topics.summary: The chapter names latency and throughput as separate performance concerns. Latency measures a completion interval for a chosen unit of work. Throughput counts completed work per unit time. Improving one does not logically establish an improvement in the other; the workload and measurement boundary matter.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.2 · PERFORMANCE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter names latency and throughput as separate performance concerns. Latency measures a completion interval for a chosen unit of work. Throughput counts completed work per unit time. Improving one does not logically establish an improvement in the other; the workload and measurement boundary matter.

For a simple single-thread observation, partition a chosen elapsed interval into time running on the CPU, time blocked, and time runnable but waiting for CPU service. Under this teaching model, those states are mutually exclusive and account for the interval. The illustrative values total twelve milliseconds. They are not measurements of the companion program. The point is diagnostic: optimizing instructions cannot remove time that the thread spends waiting for a resource or scheduling opportunity. For multiple threads, sums of CPU time and elapsed wall time require more care because work can overlap.

Sixth-grade explanation
Latency is how long one job takes. Throughput is how many jobs finish in a period. A job can also spend time waiting instead of working.

Transition: Derive the limit of a local speedup.

---

topics.title: Derive the limit of a local speedup
topics.summary: This derivation makes the chapter's performance concern quantitative without pretending that a local optimization accelerates the entire system equally. Normalize the original total time to one. Assume that sixty percent belongs to a component we can make three times faster and that the remaining forty percent is unchanged. The new time is 0.60 divided by three plus 0.40, or 0.60 of the original total. Overall speedup is therefore one divided by 0.60, about 1.67.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.2 · GRADUATE PERFORMANCE DERIVATION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This derivation makes the chapter's performance concern quantitative without pretending that a local optimization accelerates the entire system equally. Normalize the original total time to one. Assume that sixty percent belongs to a component we can make three times faster and that the remaining forty percent is unchanged. The new time is 0.60 divided by three plus 0.40, or 0.60 of the original total. Overall speedup is therefore one divided by 0.60, about 1.67.

The assumptions are the substance of the argument: the same work is performed, the fractions come from the same baseline, the portions do not overlap in this simplified account, and no new overhead appears. If a redesign changes concurrency, I/O, or the workload itself, the model needs revision. A graduate explanation should state both the result and the circumstances under which it follows. The numbers are an invented worked example, not a measured claim.

Sixth-grade explanation
Speeding up one part does not speed up the whole job by the same amount. The parts you did not improve still take time.

Discussion / pause
Why is the total speedup not 3×?

Expected response: Forty percent of the original time has not improved.

Transition: Make a performance claim reproducible.
