topics.title: Make a performance claim reproducible
topics.summary: The original chapter states that performance claims require measurement. The graduate extension is to specify what another person would need to reproduce the claim. Define the workload, input sizes, correctness criterion, and unit of work. Record the compiler and relevant options, the platform, and whether initialization and first-touch effects are included. Repeat the measurement and report variability rather than selecting a single favorable number.

Source mapping: original slide(s) 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter states that performance claims require measurement. The graduate extension is to specify what another person would need to reproduce the claim. Define the workload, input sizes, correctness criterion, and unit of work. Record the compiler and relevant options, the platform, and whether initialization and first-touch effects are included. Repeat the measurement and report variability rather than selecting a single favorable number.

This is a proposed experimental protocol, not a claim that all benchmarks require one rigid recipe. For a program with external services, the environment may be difficult to control, so the report must describe those limitations. A fair comparison also separates instrumented correctness builds from performance builds. Sanitizers change the program being measured. Source mapping: original slide(s) 14.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter says every acquisition needs an owner, a validity interval, and a release rule. Think of memory, file descriptors, handles, or other resources as obligations that persist beyond one successful function call. The operation that acquires a resource may differ from the component responsible for releasing it, but that transfer must be explicit.

The original invariant owner(fd) equals exactly one component is a design policy, not an automatic property of the operating system. References can be shared, descriptors can be duplicated, and ownership protocols can vary. What must remain unambiguous is the release responsibility for each owned resource. A borrowed reference should not silently acquire permission to release the underlying resource. Diagram the lifecycle before writing complicated error paths. That often reveals leaks, double release, and use after the agreed validity interval.

Sixth-grade explanation

blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.5 · CONTROLLED FAILURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 15.

Graduate lecture narration
Robustness is not the assertion that nothing can go wrong. The source chapter describes invalid input, unavailable resources, interruptions, and partial failures as conditions that should lead to controlled behavior. A robust specification explains the result, the state that remains, and the obligations still owned by the caller or callee.

For a failed operation, ask three practical questions. What changed before the failure was reported? Which resources are still valid and who owns them? Is retry safe, and from which point? These questions connect robustness to the invariants and ownership model rather than treating error handling as a message printed at the end. Returning an error code while leaving shared state inconsistent is not controlled failure. The next example shows why partial progress and total failure must be distinguished.

Sixth-grade explanation
A strong program plans for bad input and missing resources. When it fails, it should still leave things in a known, safe condition.

Transition: Partial success changes the retry position.

blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.5 · ROBUST I/O REASONING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 15.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Suppose a byte-output interface is asked to write ten bytes and returns a positive count of four. That count records progress. In this illustrative stream or ordinary file-output case, the next attempt to send the remaining data starts at buffer plus four and requests six bytes. Repeating the original request can duplicate the already completed prefix.

The Linux write interface documents partial writes and distinct failure conditions, but this slide is not a universal retry loop. A complete implementation must handle the actual interface's interruption, blocking, signal, and error rules, as well as its own cancellation or retry limits. Message-oriented protocols and non-idempotent operations may require different recovery logic. The arithmetic teaches a broader design principle from the chapter: define what remains true after failure, including partial effects, before deciding whether a retry is safe.

Sixth-grade explanation
If four of ten items were delivered, six are left. Sending all ten again may repeat the first four.

Discussion / pause
Why is retrying all ten bytes potentially wrong?

Expected response: The first four may already have taken effect, so repeating the entire request can duplicate them.

Transition: Portability has at least three separate targets.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: 1.3.6 · PORTABILITY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 15.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter explicitly distinguishes source portability, binary compatibility, and performance portability. Source portability concerns whether the program can be translated appropriately for another supported environment. Binary compatibility concerns whether compiled components can interoperate or execute under the expected machine and runtime conventions. Performance portability concerns whether the implementation still meets the relevant performance goals across platforms.

These are related but independent claims. A portable source program may need rebuilding. A binary can require a particular ABI or shared library. A program that executes correctly may have different bottlenecks on a second implementation. Make each platform assumption visible and testable: representation, interfaces, resource limits, compiler options, and runtime dependencies. Do not call a design portable without specifying the supported environments and the level of portability being claimed.

Sixth-grade explanation
Code that can be rebuilt elsewhere, a file that runs elsewhere, and a program that stays fast elsewhere are three different achievements.

Transition: Serialize a value—not an accidental object layout.

Graduate lecture narration
Take the unsigned value 0x01020304 and assume an environment with eight-bit bytes and a 32-bit unsigned value representation for this example. Its four byte values can be ordered most-significant first or least-significant first. The table defines both sequences explicitly. A protocol that chooses most-significant byte first specifies the bytes independently of the sender's internal order.

This is an illustrative serialization design, not a universal rule that every protocol uses one byte order. A complete format also defines field widths, versioning where needed, and the meaning of the values. Copying an entire in-memory structure can accidentally export padding, alignment-dependent layout, or process-local addresses. Graduate lecture narration
The original deck compares two checksum versions using twelve and eight milliseconds. Those numbers are an illustrative comparison in the supplied teaching material, not benchmark measurements collected for this revision. Version A produces the expected checksum and has no known contract violation under the stated test. Version B appears to produce the checksum but reads beyond its buffer.

The smaller timing does not repair Version B's invalid access. We should also avoid overstating the evidence for Version A: passing the stated check does not by itself prove correctness for every input. The appropriate conclusion is narrower. Version A has passed the specified observation, while Version B has an identified rule violation and cannot be accepted as a valid optimization of the same contract. Repair the semantic issue first, then rerun correctness checks and compare performance under a controlled method.

Sixth-grade explanation
Finishing a race faster does not count if you cut across a forbidden area. A program must obey its rules before speed can make it better.

Graduate lecture narration
This integration exercise asks students to move from a symptom to a justified next observation. A preprocessor problem calls for inspection of included content and macros. A link problem calls for symbols and link inputs. A shared-object loading problem calls for deployment and loader evidence. A buffer violation calls for source-level range and lifetime reasoning even when visible output looks correct.

Treat the entries as starting points. Real failures can cross layers, and a symptom alone may be ambiguous. For example, an apparently missing function can result from build selection, naming, or incompatible conventions. The graduate response is to propose an observation that separates those hypotheses. Do not replace diagnosis with a ritual such as rebuilding everything, ignoring warnings, or retrying indefinitely. The chapter's layered model is useful precisely because it limits what each success or failure can tell us.

Sixth-grade explanation
Each kind of problem leaves a different clue. Look at the clue that matches the stage where the problem happened.

Graduate lecture narration
The original guided lab asks for a second calculation function in its own source file. The supplied companion solution uses multiply, declared in calc.h and defined in calc.c. main_extended.c calls both add and multiply using the same operands, seventeen and twenty-five. The expected combined output is sum equals forty-two and product equals four hundred twenty-five. Both values fit the required int arithmetic for the demonstration.

Before running the build, write down which source file owns each definition and which object should contain each unresolved reference. Keep the new interface in a shared header so the caller and implementation use the same declaration. The companion implementation was tested and produced the predicted output.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: ORIGINAL REVIEW QUESTION · RUNTIME GUARANTEES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 21.

Graduate lecture narration
The original question asks why an executable can load successfully and fail on its first file operation. Answer by assigning guarantees to boundaries. Loading establishes the program image and the required starting conditions. A later file operation has its own pathname, access, resource, and error contract. A required file may not exist in the runtime environment, or the requested access may not be permitted.

Those examples are possible causes, not a diagnosis without evidence. The next observation should be the operation's returned result and the environment relevant to that request. Recompiling a correct executable cannot by itself create a missing runtime file or establish the right access. The graduate answer explicitly separates the loader's completed work from the runtime operation's unfulfilled preconditions. This is the chapter's layered model applied to a realistic first failure.

Sixth-grade explanation
Opening the classroom door does not guarantee that the book you need is inside. Starting a program does not guarantee that every resource is available.

Discussion / pause
What evidence should you inspect next?

Expected response: The file operation result and the environment relevant to its pathname, access requirements, and available resources.

Transition: Review 2: correct output with an out-of-bounds read.

Supporting primary sources
[EXEC] Linux man-pages, execve(2). Image replacement, startup, and executable interpreter behavior. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/execve.2.html

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
Section: ORIGINAL REVIEW QUESTION · DEFINED BEHAVIOR
Source mapping: original slide(s) 21, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
The source deck asks whether a run that prints the right number but reads beyond an array boundary is evidence of language-level correctness. The answer is no. The observation tells us what was printed on that execution, but the invalid access contradicts the relevant language-level obligation. We cannot use the favorable output to establish that the operation was valid.

A graduate answer should also say what to do next. Identify the access, reconstruct the valid range and lifetime, and repair the path so that it satisfies the contract. Add boundary tests and suitable runtime checks where useful, while recognizing their limits. Only then should the revised implementation be compared for performance. This response does not deny the usefulness of tests; it gives them the correct scope. Observed output is evidence about an observation, not a substitute for defined behavior.

Sixth-grade explanation
Getting the right answer once does not prove the steps were allowed. Reading outside an array still breaks the program’s rules.

Discussion / pause
What did the successful-looking output actually establish?

Expected response: Only that the expected value was observed on that run; it did not make the invalid access legal.

Transition: Graduate review: a symbol can link despite incompatible types.

Supporting primary sources
[LANG] WG14 N1570, Programming languages — C, committee draft (2011). §3.4 behavior categories; §5.1 abstract machine and execution; §6.5 expressions; declarations and external definitions. C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf
[ASAN] Clang documentation, AddressSanitizer. Runtime memory-error checking and instrumentation use. https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html

topics.title: Graduate review: a symbol can link despite incompatible types
topics.summary: Imagine two translation units that do not share a consistent header. The caller sees convert declared with a double parameter, while the definition in the other translation unit takes an int. An ordinary symbol-oriented link may match the name without rejecting the incompatible source types. That does not make the resulting call valid. The source-level declarations disagree, and the binary argument conventions can disagree as a result.

blocks.text:
Section: SYNTHESIS · API, ABI & LINKING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6, 9, 11, 16.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Imagine two translation units that do not share a consistent header. The caller sees convert declared with a double parameter, while the definition in the other translation unit takes an int. An ordinary symbol-oriented link may match the name without rejecting the incompatible source types. That does not make the resulting call valid. The source-level declarations disagree, and the binary argument conventions can disagree as a result.

This is an analysis scenario, not an instruction to execute an invalid program and predict its value. A strong answer identifies the missing shared interface discipline and explains why link success is insufficient evidence. The practical repair is to provide one correct shared declaration, rebuild the affected units, and verify that the implementation and callers use it. More diagnostic tooling may help, but the contract must be coherent before tools can validate the intended composition.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two pieces may use the same function name but disagree about what to pass. Matching names alone does not make the pieces fit.

Discussion / pause
Which repair addresses the cause rather than the symptom?

Expected response: Use a correct shared declaration in both translation units, rebuild affected objects, and verify the complete interface contract.

Transition: Defend a systems explanation—not just a result.

Supporting primary sources
[LANG] WG14 N1570, Programming languages — C, committee draft (2011). §3.4 behavior categories; §5.1 abstract machine and execution; §6.5 expressions; declarations and external definitions. C11 draft reference, not the published C17 standard. Lab examples use C17 mode. https://www.open-std.org/jtc1/sc22/wg14/www/docs/n1570.pdf
[LD] GNU linker manual, Overview. Linker role in combining, relocating, and resolving object inputs. https://sourceware.org/binutils/docs/ld/Overview.html

Graduate lecture narration
Use the chapter's two-file program as a short oral defense. First, trace the successful result through declarations, definitions, object references, linking, loading, and output. Second, choose one failure such as an omitted object, unavailable runtime file, or invalid range, and identify the boundary where the relevant guarantee stops. Third, describe the evidence that would support the diagnosis and its limits.

A strong response does not simply recite the seven stage names. It explains a causal connection. For example, a declaration enables the caller to compile while the omitted definition makes the link fail. Or a mapped region can require first-access work even though the executable loaded. Distinguish your measured observations from teaching examples and documented guarantees. This exercise tests whether the mental model is portable to a new symptom rather than memorized only for the exact program shown.

Sixth-grade explanation
Explain your answer so someone else can check it. Name the rule, show the clue, and say what you still do not know.

Transition: Chapter 1: the system is a chain of contracts.

blocks.text:
Section: TAKEAWAYS & CHAPTER 2 PREVIEW
Source mapping: original slide(s) 22.

Graduate lecture narration
Return to the original chapter's takeaways. Computer systems are layered contracts, not one undifferentiated machine. API, ABI, and ISA describe different interfaces. Source passes through preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and runtime execution. Systems work makes representation, ownership, failure, and platform assumptions explicit. Correctness and performance are different properties, and each requires appropriate evidence.

The graduate addition is a method for making these statements operational. State a contract, name assumptions, predict an observation, inspect the relevant artifact, and explain what the result does and does not establish. The lab demonstrates this method with a small enough program that every required source file and link input can be accounted for. Chapter 2 moves into C and C++ as systems-programming languages. The concepts introduced here will guide how their features are interpreted rather than treating syntax as the whole subject.

Sixth-grade explanation
A computer works because its parts follow shared rules. Good programmers check those rules, watch the handoffs, and plan for failures.

Graduate lecture narration
The ABI example is deliberately restricted to ordinary two-int argument passing and an int result. The System V AMD64 reference and Microsoft's x64 documentation support that comparison; neither table in this lecture claims to be a complete ABI specification. Linux manual pages support the Linux-specific image replacement, dynamic loading, mapping, output, and termination discussion. The ELF program-header reference supplies the segment-versus-section distinction used in the loading extension.

The sanitizer references document the scope and use of two complementary diagnostic tools. They do not turn a clean test run into a proof of whole-program correctness. These platform-specific sources are identified as such so that readers do not mistake the Linux/GNU examples for universal C language requirements. The lecture package also records the actual compiler environment used for its companion build test. All reference codes resolve to full primary-source entries in the notes and References.md.

Sixth-grade explanation
Different handoffs have different rulebooks. Check the one that matches the function call, operating-system request, or testing tool.

Supporting primary sources
[ABI] System V AMD64 ABI, draft 0.99.6, §3.2 (2012). Ordinary integer calling conventions, register usage, and processor-specific ABI context. https://refspecs.linuxfoundation.org/elf/x86_64-abi-0.99.pdf

[DYNL] Linux man-pages, ld.so(8). Shared-object discovery and dynamic-loader behavior. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man8/ld.so.8.html
[MMAP] Linux man-pages, mmap(2). Virtual mappings and population-related behavior; lecture distinguishes mapping from residency. https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/mmap.2.html

topics.title: Chapter 2 — C and C++ for Systems Programming
topics.summary: Slide 1: Chapter 2 — C and C++ for Systems Programming. The focus here is representation · types · pointers · lifetime. C and C++ expose representation and lifetime directly. Name ≠ storage  and  pointer ≠ ownership  and  scope ≠ lifetime. Language vocabulary for the systems work that follows. The systems-programming point is to treat these statements as contracts rather than as syntax trivia. When you inspect real code, ask what values are representable, what object is actually alive, who owns it, what bounds apply, and which conversions occur before an operation is evaluated. topics.summary: Slide 46: Guided Lab. The focus here is read-only borrow. Replace the mutating function with a sum function taking std::span<const int>. Return a sufficiently wide integer for a documented input bound. Test an empty sequence and [3, 5, 7]. Acceptance: empty sum = 0 and no element changes. The systems-programming point is to treat these statements as contracts rather than as syntax trivia. topics.title: 3.1 Bits
topics.summary: A bit is a binary digit with two possible values, conventionally zero and one. A group of w bits has 2^w possible patterns. Four bits have 16 patterns; eight bits have 256. The number of patterns follows from independent choices: each new position doubles the number of combinations. Physical devices need not store literal written zeros and ones. They distinguish states that are interpreted as those values. Software normally reasons above that physical level. What matters to the program is the behavior promised by the storage and instruction interfaces, including whether a read or write is atomic for the particular object and access. A bit pattern is an ordered collection of bits. If bits are numbered from the least significant position, bit i contributes a weight of 2^i to an unsigned interpretation. The pattern 10110110 therefore represents 128 + 32 + 16 + 4 + 2 = 182 when treated as an unsigned eight-bit value. The pattern itself has not changed if another interpretation calls it a negative signed number. This distinction explains why a debugger can show the same storage in several formats. A display format is a lens on the stored representation. It does not alter the bytes or prove that the chosen interpretation matches the program’s intended type. Boolean operations combine truth values. AND is true when both inputs are true. OR is true when at least one is true. XOR is true when the inputs differ. NOT reverses a truth value. Applied independently to corresponding bit positions, these operations become bitwise operations on a word. Logical operators such as && and || are not substitutes for bitwise & and | . Logical operators convert operands to truth values and short-circuit evaluation. Bitwise operators operate on integral representations after the applicable promotions. x && y asks whether both are nonzero; x & y preserves positions where both patterns have a one.

topics.title: 3.2 Bytes
topics.summary: In a byte-addressable machine, consecutive addresses identify consecutive bytes. A four-byte integer occupies four such positions. A machine may transfer a wider quantity in one operation, but the address still names its starting byte. The reference x86-64 platform uses eight-bit bytes. Byte addressability does not guarantee that every byte address is valid or equally efficient for every access width. A page may be unmapped, an address may not meet a type’s alignment, or an access may cross a cache-line boundary. Keep addressing granularity separate from access permission, required alignment, and transfer granularity. An address is usually written as a hexadecimal number because hexadecimal groups bits neatly. Increasing an address by one moves one byte in the reference machine. Increasing a typed pointer by one moves one element, which may occupy several bytes. Confusing those two increments is a common source of incorrect offset calculations. Addresses are meaningful within a context. A process address space, a device’s bus address space, and a file offset are not interchangeable even when their numeric values fit in the same integer type. Label the address domain in interfaces and diagnostic output. A correct number in the wrong domain still points to the wrong place. An object’s representation is the sequence of bytes used to store it. Some bits carry value information; others may be padding. Character-type access and suitable byte-copy operations allow representation inspection without pretending that an unrelated typed object exists in that storage. Representation inspection is not serialization. A raw structure dump can include padding, host byte order, pointers, and implementation-specific layouts. It may also disclose bytes the application never intended to publish. Define external formats field by field, with explicit sizes and byte order, and decode into ordinary language objects after validating the input.

topics.title: 3.3 Number Bases
topics.summary: Binary uses base two. Each position has twice the weight of the position to its right. 110101 means 1 × 32 + 1 × 16 + 0 × 8 + 1 × 4 + 0 × 2 + 1 × 1 , giving 53. Leading zeroes change the displayed width but not the unsigned value. Binary notation makes masks and bit fields visible, but it becomes long for addresses and large integers. Use it when the positions themselves are the subject of the explanation. When only the value matters, decimal or hexadecimal may be easier to read. Decimal uses base ten. The number 347 means 3 × 100 + 4 × 10 + 7 . Decimal is convenient for human counts and measurements, but it does not reveal power-of-two boundaries as clearly as binary or hexadecimal. topics.title: 3.4 Bitwise Operations
topics.summary: Bitwise AND, written & , retains a one only where both operands have one. It is commonly used to test or extract fields. If flags & mask is zero, none of the masked bits are set. If the requirement is that all masked bits are set, test (flags & mask) == mask instead. These two predicates are different. With mask 0b1100 and flags 0b0100 , “any” is true but “all” is false. A permission check that confuses them can authorize an operation based on only part of the required state. Name helper functions according to the exact predicate they implement. Bitwise OR, written | , sets a bit when either input has it set. flags |= mask turns on the selected bits while leaving other positions unchanged. It does not toggle them: applying the same OR operation twice has the same result as applying it once. This idempotence is useful for accumulating capabilities or marking completed phases. It is not automatically thread-safe. Two ordinary read-modify-write expressions on a shared word can race even when they set different bits. Use an atomic operation or a lock when multiple threads update the same shared object. Bitwise XOR, written ^ , sets a bit when the input bits differ. flags ^= mask toggles selected positions. XORing with the same mask twice restores the original pattern because each selected bit is flipped twice. XOR can also compare patterns: a ^ b marks their differing positions. It does not provide cryptographic security by itself. A repeated fixed XOR mask is a reversible encoding, not a secure encryption design. In systems code, use XOR for clearly defined bit manipulation rather than as an unexplained clever trick. Bitwise NOT, written ~ , flips every bit in the promoted operand type. That last phrase matters: applying ~ to a small integer type often first promotes it to int . The result may therefore have a wider type than the original byte. To clear selected bits in a word, use word &= ~mask with a mask of a suitable unsigned word type. When displaying or storing a smaller result, perform the intended conversion explicitly. Do not assume that a unary operator preserves the width of an eight-bit input merely because the variable was declared as a byte. A left shift moves bits toward more significant positions and fills low positions with zero. For unsigned values, it corresponds to multiplication by a power of two with reduction to the result type’s width. The shift count must be nonnegative and smaller than the width of the promoted left operand. Use unsigned types for field manipulation. The signed rules differ across language versions, and mathematical multiplication may overflow even when a target instruction happens to discard high bits. A shift by the full width is not a portable way to create zero. Handle full-width masks as an explicit special case. [ R36 ] For unsigned values, right shift fills high positions with zero and corresponds to division by a power of two with the fractional part discarded. It is the natural operation for moving a field down to bit zero before masking it. C17 leaves the right shift of a negative signed integer implementation-defined. C++20 specifies the signed result consistently with rounding division by a power of two toward negative infinity. This differs from signed integer / , which truncates toward zero. To avoid accidental dependence on these distinctions in binary formats, decode fields into unsigned values first. [ R8 , R36 ] A mask is a pattern that selects positions. A single-bit mask at position k can be formed as a correctly typed unsigned one shifted by k , after checking the count. A low- n -bit mask is often written (1u << n) - 1 , but that expression fails when n reaches the type width. Define the allowed field width and position before constructing a mask. For a 32-bit word, require width <= 32 , position <= 32 , and width <= 32 - position . The subtraction form avoids overflow in position + width . Handle width zero and width 32 deliberately. To extract a field of width w beginning at bit p , shift the word right by p , then AND with a low- w -bit mask. In notation, field = (word >> p) & mask . The result is right-justified and independent of unrelated high bits. For word = 0xB6 , p = 2 , and w = 3 , the shifted value is 0x2D ; masking with 0x07 yields 5. The selected bits are positions 4, 3, and 2, read as 101 . Write down the numbering convention before tracing; formats sometimes number bits in a different direction. Insertion has two separate operations: clear the destination field, then OR in the new field value. Merely ORing the new value leaves old one-bits in place. The usual expression is (word & ~shifted_mask) | ((value & mask) << position) for a validated nonempty field. Masking the incoming value truncates it. That may be the intended policy, but protocol encoders often should reject a value that does not fit instead. Silent truncation can hide invalid input. Decide whether the operation is a bit-level replacement or a validated semantic assignment, then make that decision visible in its interface.

A permission check that confuses them can authorize an operation based on only part of the required state. Name helper functions according to the exact predicate they implement. Bitwise OR, written | , sets a bit when either input has it set. flags |= mask turns on the selected bits while leaving other positions unchanged. It does not toggle them: applying the same OR operation twice has the same result as applying it once. This idempotence is useful for accumulating capabilities or marking completed phases. It is not automatically thread-safe. Two ordinary read-modify-write expressions on a shared word can race even when they set different bits. Use an atomic operation or a lock when multiple threads update the same shared object. Bitwise XOR, written ^ , sets a bit when the input bits differ. flags ^= mask toggles selected positions. XORing with the same mask twice restores the original pattern because each selected bit is flipped twice. XOR can also compare patterns: a ^ b marks their differing positions. It does not provide cryptographic security by itself. A repeated fixed XOR mask is a reversible encoding, not a secure encryption design. In systems code, use XOR for clearly defined bit manipulation rather than as an unexplained clever trick. Bitwise NOT, written ~ , flips every bit in the promoted operand type. That last phrase matters: applying ~ to a small integer type often first promotes it to int . The result may therefore have a wider type than the original byte. To clear selected bits in a word, use word &= ~mask with a mask of a suitable unsigned word type. When displaying or storing a smaller result, perform the intended conversion explicitly. Do not assume that a unary operator preserves the width of an eight-bit input merely because the variable was declared as a byte. A left shift moves bits toward more significant positions and fills low positions with zero. For unsigned values, it corresponds to multiplication by a power of two with reduction to the result type’s width. The shift count must be nonnegative and smaller than the width of the promoted left operand. Use unsigned types for field manipulation. The signed rules differ across language versions, and mathematical multiplication may overflow even when a target instruction happens to discard high bits. A shift by the full width is not a portable way to create zero. Handle full-width masks as an explicit special case. [ R36 ] For unsigned values, right shift fills high positions with zero and corresponds to division by a power of two with the fractional part discarded. It is the natural operation for moving a field down to bit zero before masking it. C17 leaves the right shift of a negative signed integer implementation-defined. C++20 specifies the signed result consistently with rounding division by a power of two toward negative infinity. This differs from signed integer / , which truncates toward zero. To avoid accidental dependence on these distinctions in binary formats, decode fields into unsigned values first. [ R8 , R36 ] A mask is a pattern that selects positions. A single-bit mask at position k can be formed as a correctly typed unsigned one shifted by k , after checking the count. A low- n -bit mask is often written (1u << n) - 1 , but that expression fails when n reaches the type width. Define the allowed field width and position before constructing a mask. For a 32-bit word, require width <= 32 , position <= 32 , and width <= 32 - position . The subtraction form avoids overflow in position + width . Handle width zero and width 32 deliberately. To extract a field of width w beginning at bit p , shift the word right by p , then AND with a low- w -bit mask. In notation, field = (word >> p) & mask . The result is right-justified and independent of unrelated high bits. For word = 0xB6 , p = 2 , and w = 3 , the shifted value is 0x2D ; masking with 0x07 yields 5. The selected bits are positions 4, 3, and 2, read as 101 . Write down the numbering convention before tracing; formats sometimes number bits in a different direction. Insertion has two separate operations: clear the destination field, then OR in the new field value. Merely ORing the new value leaves old one-bits in place. The usual expression is (word & ~shifted_mask) | ((value & mask) << position) for a validated nonempty field. Masking the incoming value truncates it. That may be the intended policy, but protocol encoders often should reject a value that does not fit instead. Silent truncation can hide invalid input. Decide whether the operation is a bit-level replacement or a validated semantic assignment, then make that decision visible in its interface.

topics.title: Worked example — Updating one packed field
topics.summary: The requirement is to replace the three-bit field at positions 2 through 4 in 0xB6 with the value 3, while preserving every other bit. Companion listing: ch03/fields.c First, low is 0x07 , and shifting it left twice produces mask = 0x1C . Clearing that mask from 0xB6 produces 0xA2 . Shifting the new field, 3, left twice produces 0x0C . ORing 0xA2 and 0x0C yields 0xAE . The program reports old=5 new=0xAE . Verification should also check preservation: (next & ~mask) == (word & ~mask) . This proves that the example did not change any unselected bit. If the clear step is removed, old ones remain and the result becomes 0xBE , not the requested replacement. That controlled failure shows why “set bits” and “replace a field” are different operations.

topics.title: Worked example — Building and extracting a bit field
topics.summary: Store a 3-bit mode in bits 4 through 6. To insert value 5 ( 101b ), clear the field with word &= ~(0x7u << 4) , then set it with word |= (5u & 0x7u) << 4 . To extract it later, compute (word >> 4) & 0x7u , yielding 5 . Mask before shifting so unrelated high bits cannot leak into the field.

topics.title: Worked example — Converting hexadecimal to binary
topics.summary: Take byte 0xB6 . Each hexadecimal digit represents four bits: B is 1011 and 6 is 0110 , so the byte is 10110110 . The high nibble is 0xB ; the low nibble is 0x6 . This direct nibble mapping is why hexadecimal is convenient for addresses, masks, instruction bytes, and binary protocols.

topics.title: 4.1 Unsigned Integers
topics.summary: An unsigned w -bit value interprets every bit as a nonnegative positional weight. The value is the sum of b_i * 2^i over positions 0 through w-1 . There is no sign bit in this interpretation. Every pattern represents a value. For eight bits, 11111111 is 128+64+32+16+8+4+2+1 = 255 . This direct relationship makes unsigned types useful for masks, counters with explicitly modular behavior, and binary fields. It does not make unsigned the best choice for every ordinary quantity, especially where negative error indicators or differences are meaningful. The minimum unsigned value is zero. topics.title: 4.2 Signed Integers
topics.summary: Two’s complement assigns the high bit a negative weight. A w -bit pattern has value -b_(w-1)*2^(w-1) + sum(b_i*2^i) for the remaining positions. The range is -2^(w-1) through 2^(w-1)-1 . There is one more negative value than positive nonzero values. This is the representation used by the reference platform and required by C++20’s signed integer representation rules. C17 permits additional signed representations, so statements about their byte patterns must be treated as platform assumptions in a C17 program. Representation does not change the rule that overflowing ordinary signed arithmetic is undefined. In two’s complement, the most significant bit distinguishes nonnegative and negative values, but it is not an independent minus-sign flag. Flipping that bit alone does not generally negate the number. It changes the contribution of a power-of-two weight. For an eight-bit value, 00000101 is 5, while 10000101 is -128 + 5 = -123 , not -5. The representation of -5 is 11111011 . This is why sign-magnitude intuition gives incorrect results when interpreting ordinary machine integers. Nonnegative two’s-complement values have a zero high bit and the same low-bit encoding as their unsigned values. Eight-bit 37 is 00100101 . This shared encoding makes many machine operations work naturally for both signed and unsigned data, with the interpretation of flags or comparisons providing the difference. The largest positive eight-bit value is 01111111 , or 127. Incrementing it in a raw eight-bit hardware operation produces the pattern 10000000 . That observation does not license a C or C++ signed expression to overflow. The source-language contract and machine result must remain separate. A negative two’s-complement pattern can be interpreted by subtracting 2^w from its unsigned interpretation. For eight bits, 11110011 is 243 unsigned and 243 - 256 = -13 signed. This is often the quickest way to decode a negative pattern by hand. The minimum value has only the high bit set: 10000000 is -128. There is no positive 128 in the same signed type. This asymmetry is responsible for special cases in negation, absolute value, and division. Boundary tests should include the minimum, not merely small negative values. At the bit-pattern level, two’s-complement negation in a fixed width is obtained by inverting the bits and adding one, with the result reduced to that width. For eight-bit 13, 00001101 becomes 11110010 , then 11110011 , representing -13. The minimum value maps to its own pattern under this modular operation. In signed source arithmetic, negating the minimum is not representable and therefore is not a valid ordinary signed result. An absolute-value routine must check or use a representation that can hold the positive magnitude. Do not assume abs(x) is safe for every value of a signed type.

topics.title: 4.3 Integer Conversion
topics.summary: Conversion to an unsigned type produces the unique value congruent to the original integer modulo 2^w . Thus converting -1 to an eight-bit unsigned type yields 255, and converting -13 yields 243. This is a value-conversion rule, not merely a claim that implementations copy the same bytes. The conversion is useful when modular semantics are intended. It is dangerous when a negative length indicates an error. Check the signed value before converting it to size_t . Once -1 becomes a large positive size, later code can mistake the error for a huge valid allocation or copy request. When the value fits in the destination signed type, the value is preserved. For values outside the destination range, C17 and older C++ rules require special care: C17 permits an implementation-defined result or an implementation-defined signal. C++20 specifies the destination value congruent modulo 2^w , where w is the destination width. [ R8 , R35 ] Portable cross-language code should not depend on an unchecked out-of-range conversion. Validate against the destination’s maximum first when the semantic requirement is a nonnegative signed value. An explicit cast documents that a conversion occurs; it does not establish that losing range is acceptable. Widening a two’s-complement signed value preserves its value by repeating the sign bit in the newly added high positions. Eight-bit -13, 11110011 , becomes 16-bit 11111111 11110011 . Interpreting the widened pattern still gives -13. Sign extension is a representation consequence of value-preserving widening on this platform. A compiler may use a sign-extending instruction, fold the result into another operation, or already hold the value in a wider register. The required result matters more than the presence of one particular mnemonic. Widening an unsigned value preserves its value by filling new high positions with zeros. Eight-bit 243 becomes 00000000 11110011 in 16 bits. The low bits match the sign-extension example, but the high bits and interpreted value differ. When decoding a binary format, select extension based on the field’s declared meaning. A one-byte temperature offset may be signed; a one-byte payload length is normally unsigned. Loading the same byte with the wrong extension can turn a small negative value into a large positive value or the reverse. Narrowing to an unsigned type retains the low-order portion of the value modulo the destination range. For example, converting 0x1234 to an eight-bit unsigned value yields 0x34 . The discarded high bits are lost information. Before narrowing an externally supplied value, ask whether truncation is intended. An encoder that silently narrows 300 to an eight-bit length can produce a header claiming 44 bytes while writing 300 bytes. Rejecting an out-of-range value preserves agreement between the representation and the data it describes.

topics.title: 4.4 Integer Arithmetic
topics.summary: Unsigned addition wraps according to its type. Signed addition requires the mathematical result to be representable. To check nonnegative unsigned addition before performing it, test b <= maximum - a . For signed addition, use separate positive and negative cases or a documented checked-arithmetic facility. Checking after a signed overflow is too late. An expression such as if (a + b < a) cannot reliably detect signed overflow because the addition itself may already violate the language’s requirements. Validate the operation’s precondition, not merely the resulting pattern. Unsigned subtraction also wraps. If an unsigned count is zero, subtracting one produces the maximum value, not -1. This is the classic failure in a reverse loop whose condition is i >= 0 : the condition is always true for an unsigned i . For lengths, subtraction is often safer than addition only after the order is established. To validate a region, first require offset <= total , then require length <= total - offset . This avoids overflow in offset + length while preventing unsigned underflow in the subtraction. Allocation and indexing frequently multiply a count by an element size. The product must fit before it is passed to an allocator. For nonzero s , require count <= SIZE_MAX / s . Then count * s is representable as size_t . A successful allocation of a wrapped, too-small product is more dangerous than a clean allocation failure. The code may later write the original number of elements into the undersized block. Treat multiplication validation as part of memory safety, not merely numerical correctness. Integer division discards a fractional part. For signed division in the language versions used here, truncation is toward zero: -7 / 3 is -2. The remainder satisfies a == (a/b)*b + a%b when the operations are defined, and its sign follows the dividend when nonzero. Division by zero is invalid. Dividing the minimum signed value by -1 is also invalid when the positive quotient cannot be represented. A checked division must handle both cases. Unsigned division does not have the signed-minimum case, but still requires a nonzero divisor. Overflow means the mathematical result exceeds the representable range. The consequence depends on the operation and type. Unsigned modular arithmetic is defined. Ordinary signed overflow is undefined. A machine instruction may set a carry or overflow flag, but an ordinary source expression does not automatically expose or check that flag. Use a tested checked-arithmetic routine when values approach limits. Compiler built-ins can help on supported compilers, but they are not part of the portable C17 or C++20 core interface. A library boundary should report range failure explicitly rather than returning a plausible wrapped size. For integers, “underflow” is often used informally for a result below the minimum representable value. Unsigned 0 - 1 wraps; signed subtraction below the minimum is undefined. Floating-point underflow has a different technical meaning involving tiny results, discussed in Chapter 5. Use precise language in diagnostics. “Negative length rejected” is more useful than “underflow happened” when the actual failure is invalid input. The distinction helps identify whether the fix belongs in input validation, type selection, or arithmetic checking. Wraparound is the cycling of a finite modular value through its range. It can be useful for checksums, sequence counters, and ring indices, but only when the algorithm is designed for it. Comparing modular sequence numbers requires a defined window of ambiguity; ordinary numeric order is not automatically the desired temporal order. For a ring of arbitrary capacity, index = (index + 1) % capacity is conceptually clear but still requires nonzero capacity and a representable increment. If the capacity is a power of two and the index domain is controlled, masking can implement the wrap. The optimization follows from the invariant; it does not replace it.

topics.title: Worked example — Checking a byte-count calculation
topics.summary: Suppose an input requests 1,500 records, each occupying 24 bytes, plus a 64-byte header. The required calculation is header + count*stride . The order of checks must prevent both multiplication and addition overflow. Companion listing: ch04/checked_size.cpp The multiplication produces 36,000. Adding 64 produces 36,064. The first guard ensures that the multiplication is valid in the size domain, while the second guard ensures that the header fits in the remaining range. A zero stride is allowed by this mathematical helper; an application can impose a stricter semantic rule before calling it. Now consider a count larger than maximum / 24 . The function rejects it before multiplying. This is the recovery boundary: no allocation has occurred and no partial object exists. A tempting alternative, multiplying first and checking whether the result looks small, is harder to reason about and easy to get wrong when signed types or additional arithmetic enter the expression.

topics.title: Chapter 5 — Floating-Point Representation
topics.summary: Floating point trades exactness for a wide dynamic range. It stores a sign, a scale, and a finite set of significant bits. The consequences are systematic: nearby representable values become farther apart as magnitude grows, decimal fractions can be rounded on input, and changing operation order can change the final result. These are properties to design around, not random defects.

topics.title: 5.1 Floating-Point Concepts
topics.summary: The sign distinguishes positive and negative values. In common IEEE 754 binary formats, it is stored separately from exponent and fraction fields. Unlike two’s-complement integers, changing only the floating-point sign bit changes the sign of an ordinary finite value without changing its magnitude. The format also contains positive and negative zero. They compare equal in ordinary numerical comparison, but operations such as reciprocal can distinguish them under IEEE arithmetic. A diagnostic that prints only 0 can therefore hide a representational distinction relevant to numerical algorithms or branch-cut conventions. The exponent determines the power-of-two scale. Normal binary floating-point values have the form (-1)^s * (1.f) * 2^e . The stored exponent is biased so the field can represent both negative and positive exponents without a separate exponent sign bit. For binary32, the exponent field has eight bits and the normal-value bias is 127. A stored exponent of 130 therefore corresponds to an exponent of 3. Some exponent field values are reserved for zero, subnormal values, infinity, and NaN, so not every field pattern describes an ordinary normalized scale. The significand carries the significant digits. For a normalized binary value, the leading digit is always one, so common IEEE binary formats omit that leading one from storage. Binary32 stores 23 fraction bits but has 24 bits of normal-value precision. Binary64 stores 52 fraction bits and has 53 bits of normal-value precision. Precision is the number of significant bits, not the number of fixed decimal places. A value near one and a value near one billion do not have the same absolute spacing between representable neighbors. Numerical error requirements should therefore distinguish absolute error from relative error. [ R9 ]

topics.title: 5.2 IEEE 754
topics.summary: For binary32 with exponent field E from 1 through 254 and fraction field F , the represented value is (-1)^s * (1 + F/2^23) * 2^(E-127) . Read this as a signed significand multiplied by a power-of-two scale. Normalization gives a unique leading-one form for ordinary nonzero values. For example, binary 1101.01 becomes 1.10101 * 2^3 . The shift changes the exponent while preserving the value. Format calculations should identify the stored exponent and the mathematical exponent separately to avoid off-by-bias errors. The term subnormal is preferred for values historically called denormalized. When the exponent field is zero and the fraction is nonzero, binary32 uses (-1)^s * (F/2^23) * 2^-126 . There is no implicit leading one. This extends representable values gradually toward zero below the smallest normal magnitude. Subnormals provide gradual underflow but have fewer significant bits relative to their magnitude. Some execution modes flush tiny values to zero for particular operations. Such modes alter numerical behavior and must be treated as explicit configuration, not assumed equivalent to default IEEE-style arithmetic. An all-zero exponent field and zero fraction represent zero, with the sign field distinguishing positive and negative zero. Both compare equal, so a hash or serialization design that uses raw bits must decide whether these representations should remain distinct or be normalized. An exact zero result and a tiny result rounded to zero are not the same computational event. The latter can indicate lost information. Numerical diagnostics may need to examine exception flags or compare against a higher-precision reference rather than looking only at the final printed value. An all-one exponent field with a zero fraction represents infinity. Positive and negative infinity can arise from operations such as an overflowing finite result or division of a nonzero finite value by zero under the relevant floating-point environment. Infinity is not the largest finite number. It participates in comparison and arithmetic as a special value. An application that requires finite measurements should validate with a finite-value predicate rather than testing only that the input lies below one chosen threshold. Infinity can otherwise propagate through an algorithm and obscure the original failure. An all-one exponent field with a nonzero fraction represents a NaN, or “not a number.” NaNs represent invalid or unrepresentable numerical results such as certain indeterminate operations. topics.title: 5.3 Floating-Point Arithmetic
topics.summary: A format’s precision limits how many significant bits can be retained. Near 2^24 , adjacent binary32 values are two units apart. Thus the exact integer 16,777,217 cannot be represented as binary32, even though many much larger powers of two can be represented exactly. Range and precision are different. A type can hold values of enormous magnitude while failing to distinguish two nearby integers. Never use floating point as a general replacement for exact identifiers, byte counts, or unbounded integer counters. Its suitability follows from the numerical error budget of the problem. When an exact result lies between representable values, a rounding mode selects the stored result. A common default is round to nearest, ties to even: choose the nearest representable value, and choose the one with an even low significand bit when exactly halfway. Rounding occurs at operations and conversions according to the language, compiler options, and execution environment. A fused multiply-add computes a product and addition with one final rounding rather than rounding the product separately. This can improve accuracy while changing the last bits compared with two separate operations. Reproducibility requires control over such choices. A decimal fraction such as 0.1 has a repeating binary expansion, so a finite binary format stores a nearby value. Subsequent arithmetic operates on those stored approximations. Printing a short decimal representation can hide the difference; printing more digits can reveal it. Repeated addition, subtraction of nearly equal values, and changes in summation order can amplify or expose error. Use stable algorithms, appropriate precision, and tolerances tied to the problem. A fixed arbitrary epsilon is not a universal equality rule. A useful comparison often combines an absolute tolerance near zero with a relative tolerance at larger magnitudes, while treating NaNs and infinities explicitly. Floating-point overflow occurs when a result’s magnitude exceeds the format’s finite range. The result depends on the rounding mode and environment; infinity is common under round-to-nearest behavior. This is not the same rule as undefined signed integer overflow. Prevent avoidable overflow by reformulating calculations. For example, computing a Euclidean norm as sqrt(x*x + y*y) can overflow intermediate squares even when the final mathematical norm is representable. A suitable hypot implementation scales its inputs to avoid that unnecessary failure. Algorithm selection can therefore matter more than selecting a slightly wider type. Underflow concerns tiny results near zero. A result may become subnormal or round to zero. In IEEE terminology, signaling underflow is tied to tininess and inexactness rather than simply “the value is smaller than the smallest normal.” An exactly representable subnormal does not imply the same exception event as an inexact tiny result. Do not silently treat every tiny result as a defect. Some algorithms naturally produce small probabilities or residuals. The question is whether the retained information meets the application’s needs. Rescaling, logarithmic representations, or a more stable formulation may preserve useful information better than repeatedly widening every variable.

topics.title: Worked example — Encoding 13.25 as binary32
topics.summary: Start with the decimal value 13.25. The integer part 13 is binary 1101 ; the fraction 0.25 is 0.01 , so the complete binary value is 1101.01 . Normalize it to 1.10101 * 2^3 . The sign is zero. The stored exponent is 3 + 127 = 130 , or binary 10000010 . The stored fraction is 10101 followed by zeros to fill 23 positions. Its numeric field is 0x540000 . Combining sign, exponent, and fraction gives the 32-bit pattern 0x41540000 . This value is exactly representable because its binary expansion terminates within the available precision. Companion listing: ch05/float_bits.c The reference platform prints 0x41540000 . The numeric interpretation of a copied representation also assumes the reference platform’s compatible integer and float byte ordering; the format checks alone do not prove every representation detail on every machine. The example inspects a platform representation rather than defining a portable wire encoding. For a second trace, add 1 to binary32 16,777,216. The exact result lies halfway between 16,777,216 and 16,777,218. Under round-to-nearest, ties-to-even, it rounds to 16,777,216. The addition occurred, but the format could not retain that unit difference. This is precision loss, not integer-style wraparound.

topics.title: Worked example — Why 0.1 is approximate
topics.summary: Binary floating point represents fractions whose denominator is a power of two exactly. Decimal 0.1 has a repeating binary expansion, so a finite format stores the nearest representable value rather than exactly one tenth. Repeated arithmetic can therefore accumulate small errors. Equality tests on computed floating-point results should reflect the numerical problem rather than assuming decimal literals are exact.

topics.title: Worked example — Classifying an IEEE 754 value
topics.summary: For a binary32 value with exponent field all ones and a nonzero fraction, the value is NaN. With exponent all ones and fraction zero, it is infinity with the sign bit determining the sign. With exponent all zeros and fraction zero, it is signed zero. The exponent and fraction fields must be interpreted together; the exponent alone does not determine the numerical category.

topics.title: 6.1 Arrays
topics.summary: Array elements occupy adjacent storage with no extra gap between complete elements beyond each element’s own size. If the element type includes padding, that padding is included in the stride. An array of structures therefore repeats the full structure size, not just the sum of useful field bytes. Contiguity supports efficient traversal and simple address calculations. It also means one out-of-bounds write can reach a neighboring element or another object. The fact that a numeric address lies near valid storage does not make it part of the array. Bounds come from the object, not from what the surrounding memory happens to contain. The element size is sizeof(element_type) . In int a[10] on a platform with four-byte int , the array occupies 40 bytes. In struct Record a[10] , each step uses sizeof(struct Record) , including any tail padding needed to align the next record. A pointer alone does not retain the number of elements. Keep count and capacity with the allocation, or use a container or span. When reading a file of fixed-size records, check both that the total byte count fits and that any required record-size divisibility holds. A leftover partial record is a format error, not an invitation to read beyond the buffer. For a one-dimensional array, address(a[i]) = base + i*sizeof(T) . This is a mathematical address model; source-level pointer arithmetic still requires i to identify an element or the permitted one-past position. To access an element, require i < count . Suppose the base is 0x2000 and each element is eight bytes. Element 5 begins at 0x2028 , because 5 × 8 = 40 = 0x28 . This simple calculation recurs in assembly scaled indexing, structure arrays, file offsets, and cache-line analysis. Always state whether the index counts elements or bytes. A built-in C or C++ array such as int a[3][4] is an array of three arrays, each containing four integers. Its rows are contiguous, and elements within a row are contiguous. With four-byte integers, the address of a[r][c] is modeled as base + (r*4 + c)*4 for valid indices. This is not the same representation as int** , which points to pointers and may describe separately allocated rows. Do not cast between them as a shortcut. For generic matrix interfaces, pass dimensions and strides explicitly or use a suitable multidimensional view. A stride describes layout; it does not itself establish ownership or bounds.

topics.title: 6.2 Structures
topics.summary: Structures place members in an implementation-defined layout subject to language constraints. In ordinary C structures, members follow declaration order with possible padding. C++ standard-layout types provide the predictable subset needed for facilities such as offsetof ; inheritance, virtual functions, and other class features add additional rules. Use offsetof and sizeof when inspecting a supported type rather than guessing from field names. A debugger’s display can show logical members without exposing all padding. When interfacing with hardware or a file format, prefer an explicitly decoded representation over assuming that an ordinary structure matches the external bytes. A type’s alignment constrains the addresses at which its objects may be placed. If a four-byte-aligned member follows a one-byte member, the implementation may insert three padding bytes before it. The enclosing structure’s alignment generally accommodates its most demanding member on the reference ABI. Alignment is both a language validity requirement and an implementation consideration. An x86 instruction’s ability to load an unaligned address does not make an improperly aligned C++ T* access valid. Use byte copying to an aligned object when decoding data at arbitrary byte offsets. Internal padding lies between members; tail padding follows the final member so array elements begin at suitable alignments. Padding bytes do not necessarily have stable values. Comparing whole object representations with memcmp can therefore disagree with memberwise equality. Padding also matters at trust boundaries. Sending an uninitialized structure’s full storage can disclose residual bytes even when every named field has been assigned. Zeroing storage is not a substitute for a stable external format, but explicit field encoding avoids both the layout dependency and accidental padding disclosure.

topics.title: 6.3 Unions
topics.summary: Union members overlap. Only enough storage for the largest and most aligned alternative is needed, subject to padding. A tagged union pairs that storage with a discriminator indicating which alternative is active. The discriminator and active object must agree at every interface boundary. Changing the tag without constructing or assigning the appropriate alternative can leave a logically impossible state. In C++, nontrivial member lifetimes make manual unions especially delicate. std::variant packages the tag and lifetime management when its cost and behavior fit the requirement. A union does not create several independent values in the same bytes. It supplies alternative interpretations subject to language rules. Reading a member different from the one most recently established is not a general portable way to reinterpret arbitrary C++ objects. For a representation copy between suitable trivially copyable types of equal size, C++20 provides std::bit_cast ; memcpy is also useful for byte transport. These operations still require valid representations for the intended use. No copying technique can turn arbitrary untrusted bits into a valid pointer or a well-formed complex object merely by avoiding an aliasing violation.

topics.title: 6.4 Endianness
topics.summary: In little-endian storage, the least significant byte of a multi-byte value is at the lowest address. A 32-bit value 0x12345678 appears in increasing addresses as 78 56 34 12 . The reference x86-64 platform uses this ordering for ordinary integer storage. The numeral 0x12345678 itself has not changed. Endianness describes the mapping between the value’s bytes and memory addresses, not the written order of digits in a debugger’s integer display. Inspect bytes explicitly when diagnosing a format mismatch. In big-endian storage, the most significant byte is at the lowest address. The same 32-bit value appears as 12 34 56 78 . Many network protocol fields use a specified big-endian order, often called network byte order. A format can also choose little endian or define fields byte by byte. The important property is agreement, not that one order is inherently more correct. Convert at the boundary and keep internal computation in the language’s ordinary value types whenever possible. A portable decoder assembles a value from explicitly ordered bytes. For a four-byte big-endian field, the value is (b0<<24) | (b1<<16) | (b2<<8) | b3 , with each byte converted to a sufficiently wide unsigned type before shifting. The widening is essential. A small byte can undergo signed integer promotion, and shifting into an unsuitable signed range can be invalid in some language modes. A clear decoder validates that four bytes are present, widens them, combines them, and then checks the resulting semantic value. That sequence keeps bounds, representation, and meaning separate.

topics.title: 6.5 Alignment
topics.summary: “Natural alignment” usually refers to an alignment convenient for a type’s ordinary machine accesses, often related to its width. It is not one universal language rule saying every n -byte type must be aligned to n bytes. Query the implementation with _Alignof in C or alignof in C++. Over-aligned objects require allocation that honors their larger alignment. Ordinary raw byte buffers or a custom allocator may not suffice. A placement construction does not repair an unsuitable address. The storage provider and object constructor must agree on both size and alignment. To round an offset upward to alignment a , a general mathematical expression is ceil(offset/a)*a . For a power-of-two alignment, (offset + a - 1) & ~(a - 1) is a common bitwise form, but the addition must be checked for overflow and a must be nonzero and a power of two. An allocator must account for both the alignment gap and the payload size before returning storage. Rounding first and checking only the payload can miss an overflow or exceed the arena. Chapter 10 develops this as an allocator invariant rather than treating alignment as a cosmetic adjustment. Aligned accesses can reduce the chance of crossing cache-line or page boundaries and may be required by particular instructions. Unaligned accesses on x86-64 are often supported, but their cost depends on width, boundaries, cache state, and instruction choice. “Unaligned is always slow” is too broad, while “x86 allows it, so it is free” is equally misleading. topics.title: Worked example — Accounting for every byte
topics.summary: Consider a reference-platform structure containing a one-byte kind, a four-byte length aligned to four bytes, and a two-byte flags field aligned to two bytes. The kind begins at offset 0. Offsets 1 through 3 are padding. The length begins at 4 and occupies four bytes. Flags begins at 8 and occupies two bytes. Two tail-padding bytes make the total size 12 and keep an array’s next element four-byte aligned. Companion listing: ch06/layout.c On the stated reference layout, the output is size=12 align=4 and kind=0 length=4 flags=8 . The program reports actual implementation values rather than forcing those expectations on every C implementation. Reordering the fields as length, flags, kind commonly reduces the size to eight bytes on this ABI: four bytes, then two, then one, then one tail-padding byte. An array of one million records would then use about four million fewer bytes. That is a derived storage saving, not a measured speedup. The changed member offsets also mean the two structures are not binary-compatible layouts.

topics.title: Worked example — Computing an array address
topics.summary: If an array of 32-bit integers begins at address 0x1000 , element 7 begins at 0x1000 + 7 × 4 = 0x101C . The multiplication by element size is implicit in C and C++ pointer arithmetic: &a[7] equals a + 7 . This scaling is why adding one to an int* advances by sizeof(int) , not one byte.

topics.title: Worked example — Predicting structure padding
topics.summary: Consider fields char c; int x; char d; with 4-byte int alignment. c can occupy offset 0, followed by 3 padding bytes so x begins at offset 4. d occupies offset 8, and trailing padding may extend the structure to 12 bytes so array elements remain aligned. Reordering fields can reduce padding, but only after preserving required semantics and ABI constraints.

blocks.text: Open Scenarios to choose an answer, then compare your reasoning with the explained solution.

scenario.prompt: A structure’s sizeof exceeds the sum of its member sizes. What is a plausible reason?
options: Alignment padding between members or at the end.
All structures have a universal fixed size.
sizeof always counts heap allocations too.
The compiler must be duplicating each field.
scenario.explanation: Alignment can require unused bytes so members and successive array elements meet placement requirements. Layout is not a universal wire format.

topics.title: Chapter 7 — Pointers and Address Arithmetic
topics.summary: Pointer reasoning is object reasoning. topics.title: 7.1 Addresses versus pointers
topics.summary: An address is a location identifier. A pointer is a language value used to designate an object, function, or permitted boundary position. Implementations commonly represent object pointers as virtual addresses, but the language attaches rules that are not captured by the displayed number alone. For example, two allocations may reuse the same numeric address at different times. A stale pointer to the first allocation does not become a valid owner of the second merely because the bits match. Similarly, converting a pointer to an integer for logging does not grant permission to perform arbitrary integer arithmetic and convert the result back. Use pointer-producing operations that preserve the intended object relationship.

topics.title: 7.2 Dereferencing
topics.summary: A dereference is valid only when the designated access is valid. Ask five questions: Is the target alive? Is it within the permitted range? Is it correctly aligned? Does the access type match the object’s allowed interpretation? Is the access properly synchronized with conflicting operations? A hardware page permission check answers only part of this list. A use-after-free can access a page that is still mapped and writable. An out-of-bounds write can remain within the same mapped page. The operating system protects address-space regions, while the language and program design must protect object boundaries and lifetimes inside those regions.

topics.title: 7.3 Pointer arithmetic
topics.summary: For a pointer into an array, adding an integer moves in units of the pointed-to type. If p points to a[2] , then p + 3 points to a[5] when that position is within the permitted array range. Subtracting two pointers into the same array yields an element count, not a byte count, provided the difference is representable in ptrdiff_t . Do not form a wildly out-of-range pointer and then compare it with an end pointer. Validate an index against the remaining element count before computing the pointer. A one-past pointer is permitted as a boundary marker but not as an element. It is a useful sentinel precisely because the traversal stops before dereferencing it.

topics.title: 7.4 Arrays and pointers
topics.summary: An array often converts to a pointer to its first element, but the conversion loses extent information. A function parameter written int values[] is adjusted to an int* parameter; it does not carry the caller’s array length. The callee needs a separate count or a range abstraction. An array of pointers is also different from a pointer to an array. int* rows[3] contains three pointer objects. int (*row)[4] points to a four-integer array. These declarations produce different scaling and memory access. Draw the objects and arrows when syntax becomes confusing: the picture should show actual pointer objects separately from the integer storage they designate.

topics.title: 7.5 Iterators
topics.summary: An iterator generalizes traversal over a sequence. Some iterators are ordinary pointers; others hold more complex state. An iterator and an end sentinel describe a range whose validity depends on the owning container and on operations that may invalidate positions. A vector reallocation invalidates pointers, references, and iterators to its elements. Inserting into other containers has different rules. Do not generalize one container’s behavior to another. A range-based loop can still be invalidated by changes made inside the loop. The abstraction removes repetitive syntax, not the need to respect lifetime and invalidation rules.

topics.title: 7.6 Pointer comparisons
topics.summary: Equality comparisons can test whether pointers designate the same relevant position or are null, subject to language details. Relational ordering and subtraction are much more constrained. Comparing positions within one array is meaningful; using built-in relational operators as a portable ordering for arbitrary unrelated allocations is not a sound general technique. In C++, std::less for pointer types provides a strict total ordering suitable for ordered containers when such ordering is needed. That ordering is not a statement that two objects are adjacent or belong to one allocation. An ordered pointer map does not authorize arithmetic across its keys.

topics.title: 7.7 Pointer validity
topics.summary: Pointer validity is a property maintained by program structure. An owner keeps storage alive; borrowers use it only within an agreed interval. A mutation that reallocates storage ends the validity of old element pointers even if the container itself remains alive. Represent these rules in interfaces. A function that retains a pointer should say so. A returned view should identify the owner whose lifetime supports it. A callback should not outlive its context. Nulling one pointer after release helps avoid accidental reuse through that variable, but it does not update other aliases. Ownership discipline prevents the error earlier than a last-minute null check.

topics.title: 7.8 Aliasing
topics.summary: Aliasing occurs when multiple expressions can access the same storage. Aliasing can be intentional, as when two pointers refer to the same integer. The compiler must preserve required behavior for permitted aliases, but type-based access rules allow it to assume that certain unrelated typed accesses do not designate the same object. Casting an int* to float* and reading through it is not a portable representation conversion. Use byte access or a suitable copy operation. In C++, char , unsigned char , and std::byte have designated representation-inspection roles; do not assume every small integer type has the same privilege. Aliasing also affects optimization: a store through one pointer may force a reload through another unless non-aliasing can be established. [ R7 , R8 ]

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded cursor
topics.summary: The requirement is to read a two-byte big-endian field from a byte sequence without advancing past its end. Model the state as a span of remaining bytes. A successful operation consumes exactly two bytes; failure consumes none. Companion listing: ch07/cursor.cpp Initially the range length is three. The first check passes, and 0x12 × 256 + 0x34 = 4660 . The cursor then becomes a one-byte range. The second check fails before any indexing, leaving that range unchanged. The final output is 4660 1 . The design’s key property is transactional cursor movement: validation and decoding occur before the state change. An alternative that increments the pointer after reading the first byte can leave the parser half-consumed on failure. Keeping the cursor unchanged makes recovery or higher-level error reporting much easier.

topics.title: Worked example — Walking a bounded range
topics.summary: Given int a[4]={10,20,30,40}; , begin with pointers p=a and end=a+4 . While p != end , dereference *p and then increment p . The one-past pointer a+4 may be formed and compared but not dereferenced. This pattern captures the core validity rule behind many iterators and spans.

topics.title: Worked example — Recognizing an aliasing hazard
topics.summary: If two pointers can refer to the same integer, storing through one may change what a later load through the other must observe. A compiler cannot freely reuse an old loaded value unless the language’s aliasing rules prove the pointers independent. When optimization depends on non-aliasing, express that contract using the mechanisms supported by the language and implementation rather than assuming the compiler will infer it.

topics.title: 8.1 Code/text segment
topics.summary: The text region contains executable instructions. In an ELF file, sections organize linking information while loadable segments describe mappings needed at execution time. Several sections can contribute to one segment. Do not confuse a linker section name with a complete runtime mapping. Executable mappings are commonly readable and executable but not writable. This limits accidental modification and supports security policy. A function’s instructions may be shared physically among processes running the same executable while each process retains its own virtual mappings and private writable state. The sharing is below the source-level function abstraction.
