topics.title: 8.2 Read-only data
topics.summary: Read-only regions commonly hold constants, string literals, and tables that need not change. A string literal’s storage must not be modified through an ordinary program operation. In C, historical syntax may allow a pointer assignment that does not itself enforce that rule; the attempted modification is still invalid. A const object is not guaranteed to appear in a particular read-only section. It may be automatic, optimized away, embedded into instructions, or stored elsewhere according to its use. The language’s const qualification and the operating system’s page permissions are related design tools, not identical mechanisms.

topics.title: 8.3 Initialized data
topics.summary: Writable objects with static storage duration and explicit nonzero initial values commonly contribute to an initialized-data region. Their initial bytes are described by the executable or its loading process. Each process can then modify its private copy according to the mapping rules. A global counter initialized to seven is logically initialized before ordinary application use, but the exact startup work can differ for C++ objects requiring dynamic initialization. Separate the initial byte image from constructors and runtime initialization. A complex global object’s readiness may depend on code that runs before main .

topics.title: 8.4 Uninitialized data
topics.summary: The conventional BSS region represents static-duration storage that begins zero-initialized without requiring every zero byte to be stored literally in the executable file. “Uninitialized data” is therefore a misleading everyday label: these objects do receive the language’s required initial state. An automatic local integer without an initializer is different. Its value is not made zero merely because a global integer would be. The storage-duration distinction matters more than whether the source visibly contains = 0 . The loader and runtime can efficiently establish zero-filled pages for large static regions.

topics.title: 8.5 Heap
topics.summary: The heap is a conventional name for dynamically managed storage. A user-space allocator may obtain regions from the operating system through several mechanisms and divide them into allocations. Large allocations may use separate mappings rather than one continuously growing area. Calling malloc does not necessarily trigger a system call, and calling free does not necessarily return pages immediately to the operating system. The allocator can retain free blocks for reuse. Consequently, a process’s resident memory may remain high after application objects are released. Distinguish live allocations, allocator-retained storage, mapped address space, and resident physical pages.

topics.title: 8.6 Stack
topics.summary: A thread’s stack supports call state and automatic storage that the compiler chooses to place there. On the reference ABI it conventionally grows toward lower addresses. Optimized functions can omit frame pointers, keep values in registers, or use other layouts permitted by the ABI. Each thread needs its own execution stack. Stack capacity is finite, and guard mappings can detect some growth beyond its boundary. Large automatic arrays and deep recursion can exhaust it. A stack overflow is not reliably recoverable by ordinary code that needs the same exhausted stack to run its error path.

topics.title: 8.7 Command-line arguments
topics.summary: Program startup provides an argument count and an array of pointers to strings. In the usual main(int argc, char* argv[]) form, valid argument entries are argv[0] through argv[argc-1] , and argv[argc] is a null pointer. The first entry conventionally identifies the program, but applications should not treat it as a trusted executable path. Arguments are input, not authority. Parse numeric strings with range and syntax checks. A string that begins with a valid number but contains trailing junk should not silently become a valid count unless that grammar is intended. Never use an argument length or value directly in allocation arithmetic without validation.

topics.title: 8.8 Environment
topics.summary: The environment supplies named string values such as locale settings, search paths, and configuration. It is inherited and can be replaced when a new program image is executed. Environment values can affect library behavior before the application examines them. Treat environment data as untrusted configuration where appropriate, especially across privilege boundaries. Avoid printing the complete environment in diagnostics because it can contain secrets. Concurrent modification also complicates use: a pointer returned by an environment lookup should not be assumed permanently stable while other code changes the environment. Prefer capturing required configuration during controlled startup.

topics.title: Worked example — Predicting placement without assuming addresses
topics.summary: Consider four objects: a global initialized integer, a global zero-initialized array, an automatic local integer, and an allocated integer. Their storage-duration categories are known from the source. Their exact addresses are runtime observations and may change between executions because of address-space randomization. Companion listing: ch08/regions.c The stable value output is values=7 0 11 13 . The pointer output is intentionally variable. Predict categories first, then compare addresses with a mapping tool such as the process’s Linux maps view. A large gap between two addresses does not prove a corresponding amount of physical memory is resident. The program does not print function pointers by converting them to void* , because that conversion is not a general portable C object-pointer operation. To inspect executable mappings, use binary and process inspection tools. This keeps a language-level demonstration from quietly depending on an unnecessary pointer-conversion extension. [ R4 , R37 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Placing common objects conceptually
topics.summary: A function’s instructions normally belong to executable text; a string literal typically resides in read-only data; an initialized global such as int g=7; belongs to initialized static storage; an uninitialized global such as int h; is represented in a zero-initialized region; dynamically allocated storage comes from the heap; and ordinary local variables commonly use stack storage. Exact addresses are loader and ABI details, but these conceptual regions explain protection and lifetime differences.

topics.title: Worked example — Estimating stack growth
topics.summary: Suppose a recursive function consumes roughly 256 bytes of stack per call and the usable thread stack is 8 MiB. Ignoring guard pages and other frames, the crude upper bound is 8 × 1024 × 1024 / 256 = 32768 frames. Real safe depth is lower because startup frames, alignment, libraries, and variable frame sizes consume space too. The calculation is an estimate, not a recursion guarantee.

topics.title: 9.1 Heap allocation
topics.summary: A heap allocation requests a region large enough and suitably aligned for a purpose. The allocator may satisfy the request from existing free space or obtain more backing storage. Allocation can fail because of size limits, fragmentation, policy, or resource exhaustion. A successful request for raw storage does not necessarily mean every page has already been physically committed or touched. Nor does it initialize arbitrary C++ objects by itself. Separate storage acquisition, object initialization, use, destruction, and storage release. This sequence helps explain both raw allocation APIs and higher-level containers.

topics.title: 9.2 malloc
topics.summary: malloc(n) requests at least n bytes of storage and returns a suitably aligned pointer for the supported ordinary object alignments, or a null pointer on failure. The returned bytes are not initialized. In C, assignment through an appropriately typed pointer can establish the intended object use within the language’s effective-type rules. Compute n safely before calling. Use sizeof *pointer rather than repeating a type name when it reduces maintenance risk. A zero-size request has special behavior that should not be used as an application control signal. Handle an empty collection explicitly so the ownership rules do not depend on a zero-size allocation convention. [ R39 ]

topics.title: 9.3 calloc
topics.summary: calloc(count, size) requests storage for an array and zeroes the allocated bytes. Its separate count and size arguments allow the implementation to detect multiplication overflow. The application still needs semantic bounds, because a representable request may be far larger than policy permits. All-zero bytes are not a universal initializer for every possible object representation. On the reference platform they represent zero for ordinary integer storage, but portable C does not equate zero bytes with every null pointer or floating-point zero representation. In C++, use constructors and value initialization for objects rather than treating calloc as a replacement for object semantics.

topics.title: 9.4 realloc
topics.summary: realloc changes the size of a previously allocated block while preserving the common prefix of the old and new sizes. It may move the block. For a nonzero requested size, failure leaves the original allocation available. Success ends the old allocation’s role and returns the pointer to use afterward. Store the result in a temporary pointer. Assigning directly to the only owning pointer can lose the original allocation on failure. After success, old aliases must not be used, even if the returned numeric address happens to match. Avoid realloc(p, 0) in portable application logic because its historical and language-version semantics are troublesome; use an explicit free-and-empty path instead.

topics.title: 9.5 free
topics.summary: free releases a block obtained through the matching allocation family. Passing a null pointer has no effect. Passing an interior pointer, a pointer to automatic storage, or an already freed pointer violates the contract. The allocator needs the original allocation identity, not merely an address somewhere inside its payload. Freeing storage does not guarantee that its bytes are erased or that the operating system immediately reclaims its pages. Do not use free as a data-sanitization operation. More importantly, do not read the bytes after release merely because a debugger still shows the old contents. The lifetime boundary is semantic, not a visible overwrite event.

topics.title: 9.6 new
topics.summary: A C++ new expression obtains storage and initializes an object. Ordinary allocation failure throws std::bad_alloc ; a nothrow form can return null. If construction throws after storage acquisition, the language arranges the matching cleanup for that failed construction path. Prefer std::make_unique for unique dynamic ownership and containers for collections. A raw new is sometimes needed inside a low-level abstraction, but it should not force every caller to reason about cleanup. The distinction between an allocation function named operator new and a complete new expression also matters: the former obtains storage, while the latter includes object initialization.

topics.title: 9.7 delete
topics.summary: A delete expression destroys the object and releases its storage through the matching mechanism. Scalar new matches scalar delete ; array new[] matches delete[] . Mixing allocation families, such as malloc with delete , is invalid. Deleting through a base-class pointer requires appropriate polymorphic destruction when the dynamic object is derived. A base intended for such ownership generally needs a virtual destructor. Resource ownership through a pointer is therefore a type-design issue as well as an allocator issue. A correct address with the wrong destruction interface is still unsafe.

topics.title: 9.8 Allocation lifetime
topics.summary: An allocation’s lifetime must cover every use of its storage. Borrowed pointers into a resizable allocation have especially fragile lifetimes because growth can move the block. A function that returns an interior pointer should document which operations invalidate it. Group objects with the same lifetime when that simplifies ownership. A request-scoped arena can release many short-lived allocations together. A vector can own a sequence whose elements move as one resource. Avoid creating a separate ownership obligation for every small object unless independent lifetimes are actually needed.

topics.title: 9.9 Ownership
topics.summary: Ownership identifies the component responsible for destruction and release. Unique ownership has one responsible owner. Shared ownership coordinates several owners, commonly with reference counting. Borrowing grants access without release responsibility. Shared ownership is not free and does not automatically make the object thread-safe. A reference count protects lifetime, not arbitrary member updates. Cycles can also prevent reclamation unless broken by weak references or another policy. Choose the simplest ownership model that matches the required lifetime graph; do not use shared ownership merely to avoid deciding who owns a resource.

topics.title: Worked example — Growing a C buffer without losing ownership
topics.summary: The requirement is to grow a four-integer allocation to eight integers. If growth fails, the original allocation must remain releasable. The program uses fixed small sizes so the example can focus on ownership rather than input parsing. Companion listing: ch09/grow.c Before growth, four initialized elements exist. On success, the first four values are preserved, but the new suffix is not initialized by realloc ; the program initializes it before reading. Only after that does it update the logical count. The sum is 1+2+3+4+5+6+7+8 = 36 . The failure branch releases the original pointer. The success branch adopts the returned pointer and never compares or uses stale aliases. A production growable buffer would also check multiplication, enforce a capacity limit, and avoid updating its public state until all required initialization succeeds.

topics.title: Worked example — Growing a dynamic array safely
topics.summary: If p owns a malloc allocation, do not write p = realloc(p,new_size) unless losing the old block on failure is acceptable. Use tmp = realloc(p,new_size) . If tmp is non-null, assign p=tmp ; otherwise p still owns the original allocation. The temporary preserves ownership across the failure path.

topics.summary: An allocator converts larger regions of storage into smaller allocations while tracking which regions are available. topics.title: 10.1 Blocks
topics.summary: A block is a unit of storage managed by the allocator. It may contain a header, a payload returned to the caller, and padding. The caller’s requested size and the allocator’s actual block size can differ. A 13-byte request might occupy a larger block because of alignment or size classes. The fundamental invariant is that live allocation payloads do not overlap and remain valid until release. A custom allocator should state its supported alignments, maximum request size, zero-size policy, and threading model. Without those declarations, callers cannot know whether a returned address is appropriate for their object.

topics.title: 10.2 Metadata
topics.summary: Metadata records information such as block size, allocation state, neighboring blocks, or free-list links. It can be stored next to the payload or in separate tables. Adjacent metadata is convenient but can be corrupted by an out-of-bounds write from the payload. Never treat allocator metadata as trustworthy after detecting memory corruption. Continuing to allocate and free through damaged state can amplify the failure. A teaching allocator can use assertions and validation scans; a production allocator also needs careful hardening, concurrency control, and recovery policy. Implementing an allocator is not just writing a fast search loop.

topics.title: 10.3 Free lists
topics.summary: A free list links blocks available for reuse. An implicit list discovers free blocks by walking every block’s metadata. An explicit list links free blocks directly, often storing links inside the free payload. Segregated lists group blocks by size to reduce search cost. Every insertion and removal must preserve list consistency. A block must not appear twice, and an allocated block must not remain on a free list. In a concurrent allocator, these are shared-state invariants requiring synchronization or a carefully proved lock-free scheme. Thread-local caches reduce contention but can retain memory that another thread could otherwise use.

topics.title: 10.4 First fit
topics.summary: First fit scans candidates and selects the first block large enough. It is simple and can stop early, but its behavior depends on list order. Over time, small leftover regions near the beginning can increase search work or change fragmentation patterns. A first-fit policy is not inherently bad; its suitability depends on request sizes, lifetimes, and workload locality. Measure representative traces rather than judging a policy by one allocation. Search cost, fragmentation, cache behavior, and synchronization overhead can move in different directions.

topics.title: 10.5 Best fit
topics.summary: Best fit selects the smallest available block that can satisfy the request. It tries to minimize the immediate leftover amount, but finding that block can require more search or a more complex index. Small leftovers can also become unusable fragments. The name describes a local choice, not a proof of globally optimal memory use. Future requests are unknown. A slightly larger current remainder might be more useful later than a tiny one. Compare allocator policies using complete traces and explicit metrics rather than assuming that the word “best” guarantees the best outcome.

topics.title: 10.6 Block splitting
topics.summary: When a free block is larger than needed, the allocator can divide it into an allocated block and a remaining free block. The remainder must be large enough to hold required metadata, alignment, and a useful payload. Otherwise it is often better to give the entire block to the request. Splitting changes both physical-neighbor relationships and free-list membership. Update these consistently before exposing the new state. A trace should show old block boundaries, allocated size, remainder size, and every metadata update. This makes off-by-header and alignment mistakes visible.

topics.title: 10.7 Coalescing
topics.summary: Coalescing merges adjacent free blocks into a larger free region. It reduces external fragmentation by restoring space that can satisfy larger requests. Adjacency means neighboring addresses in the managed region, not neighboring nodes in an arbitrary free-list order. Boundary tags or external metadata can help find physical neighbors. Immediate coalescing merges on each release; deferred coalescing postpones work until needed. Either policy must avoid merging across live blocks or unrelated regions. A correct merge removes old list entries before inserting the combined block exactly once.

topics.title: 10.8 Alignment
topics.summary: The allocator must align the payload, not merely the block header. A header whose size is not a multiple of the requested alignment can misalign the returned address. The allocator may add padding before the payload and must retain enough information to find the actual block on release. For an arena, alignment consumes part of the remaining space before the requested bytes are reserved. Check both components. C++ std::align can help find an aligned subregion within a bounded span of storage. It does not allocate more memory or initialize an object; it only adjusts a pointer and available-space description.

topics.title: 10.9 Internal fragmentation
topics.summary: Internal fragmentation is unused space inside an allocated block, such as rounding a 13-byte request to a 16-byte size class. The application owns the block’s payload contract but may not be allowed to use all allocator-internal spare bytes. Measure internal fragmentation as actual reserved bytes minus requested useful bytes under a clearly stated accounting rule. Headers and alignment padding may be reported separately or included; consistency matters. A small per-object waste becomes substantial when millions of objects are live.

topics.title: 10.10 External fragmentation
topics.summary: External fragmentation occurs when free space is divided into regions that cannot satisfy a larger request even though their total size is sufficient. Two free 40-byte regions separated by a live block cannot satisfy one contiguous 64-byte request. Coalescing helps only when free regions are physically adjacent. Compaction could move live objects, but ordinary raw pointers make transparent movement difficult. Handles, indirection, or moving-memory runtimes can support compaction; a conventional C allocator cannot simply relocate an arbitrary live allocation without the program’s cooperation.

topics.title: 10.11 Arena allocation
topics.summary: An arena obtains a region and serves allocations from it, often by advancing a cursor. Individual deallocation may be omitted; all storage is reset together. This makes allocation fast and cleanup simple when objects share a lifetime, such as one parsed document or request. Resetting an arena invalidates every object and view backed by it. Nontrivial C++ objects may need destructors before reset, and retained pointers must not escape the arena’s lifetime. An arena trades flexible reclamation for a stronger lifetime discipline. It is excellent when that discipline matches the problem and dangerous when callers assume independent object lifetimes.

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded bump arena
topics.summary: The requirement is to allocate aligned byte regions from a fixed 128-byte arena and reject requests that do not fit. Individual release is intentionally unsupported. The arena provides storage only; the example does not construct nontrivial objects inside it. Companion listing: ch10/arena.cpp The first request consumes three bytes. On the stated alignment model, the next eight-byte-aligned start is offset 8, so five padding bytes are skipped and the second payload occupies offsets 8 through 15. The cursor becomes 16. The 200-byte request cannot fit and leaves the cursor unchanged. The abstraction has deliberately narrow semantics. Returned regions remain valid only until reset or destruction, and the arena is not thread-safe. A complete object allocator would add construction, destruction, and stronger alignment policy. Keeping the storage-only contract explicit makes this example useful without presenting it as a drop-in replacement for the standard allocator.

topics.title: Worked example — Splitting a free block
topics.summary: Suppose a free-list allocator has a 256-byte free block and receives a 96-byte aligned request plus 16 bytes of metadata. If the allocator rounds the payload to 96 and needs 112 total bytes, it can allocate 112 bytes and leave a 144-byte remainder if that remainder is large enough to represent another valid block. Otherwise it may consume the whole block, creating internal fragmentation.

topics.title: Worked example — Coalescing neighbors
topics.summary: Imagine three consecutive heap blocks: allocated 64, free 80, free 48. When the allocator notices the two free neighbors are physically adjacent, it can merge their payload and metadata representation into one larger free block. Coalescing reduces external fragmentation because future large requests can use space that was previously split into smaller holes.

topics.title: Staged project — A reusable free-list allocator
topics.summary: The bump arena is intentionally retained because it isolates alignment and bounded allocation. The next implementation adds individual deallocation and combines the mechanisms introduced in Sections 10.1 through 10.10. Its contract is deliberately narrower than malloc : it manages one fixed 512-byte region, returns storage aligned to 16 bytes, accepts only pointers returned by its own allocate , uses first fit, splits only when the remainder is at least 32 bytes, and immediately coalesces physically adjacent free blocks. It is single-threaded and does not construct C++ objects. Companion listing: ch10/freelist_allocator.cpp The companion listing contains the complete definitions and executable tests. Keeping block descriptors in a vector rather than inside the managed bytes makes the teaching invariant easier to inspect: descriptors are in increasing address order, their half-open ranges exactly partition [0, 512) , and no two live allocations overlap. A production allocator would normally avoid allocating metadata dynamically while servicing an allocation request. Allocation trace. Begin with [0,512) F . Allocate 64 bytes: [0,64) A [64,512) F . Allocate 80 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,512) F . Allocate 48 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,192) A [192,512) F . Free the middle block: [0,64) A [64,144) F [144,192) A [192,512) F . A 32-byte request reuses the 80-byte hole and splits it because the 48-byte remainder exceeds the minimum split: [0,64) A [64,96) A [96,144) F [144,192) A [192,512) F . Coalescing trace. Free [0,64) , then [64,96) . The allocator first merges left with the newly free block and then merges the adjacent [96,144) remainder, producing [0,144) F . Freeing [144,192) merges on both sides as applicable; the final free of the last live block restores [0,512) F . The test therefore exercises reuse, left coalescing, right coalescing, and restoration of the original region. Statistics distinguish requested bytes from reserved bytes. Their difference is internal fragmentation under this implementation’s rounding rule. External fragmentation can be reported as free_bytes - largest_free : zero means every free byte is currently in one contiguous block. These metrics are policy-dependent descriptions, not universal allocator-quality scores. The implementation rejects zero-sized requests, arithmetic that would overflow during alignment rounding, pointers outside the arena, pointers into the interior of a block, and a second release of a block that is still represented as free. These checks are intentionally limited. After coalescing, stale pointers can coincide with a later allocation start, corrupted metadata can invalidate the reasoning, and address reuse makes perfect temporal error detection impossible without additional generation or quarantine metadata. Sanitizers and hardened allocators use stronger mechanisms; this example does not claim complete invalid-free detection. Allocator project tests. Verify exhaustion without state corruption; reuse of a freed first-fit block; 16-byte alignment for every successful result; refusal to create a remainder smaller than 32 bytes; coalescing with a free predecessor, successor, and both neighbors; invalid and double-free rejection for the cases above; overflow-checked size rounding; and conservation of the 512 managed bytes after every operation.

LECTURE NARRATION
The bump arena is intentionally retained because it isolates alignment and bounded allocation. The next implementation adds individual deallocation and combines the mechanisms introduced in Sections 10.1 through 10.10. Its contract is deliberately narrower than malloc : it manages one fixed 512-byte region, returns storage aligned to 16 bytes, accepts only pointers returned by its own allocate , uses first fit, splits only when the remainder is at least 32 bytes, and immediately coalesces physically adjacent free blocks. It is single-threaded and does not construct C++ objects. Companion listing: ch10/freelist_allocator.cpp The companion listing contains the complete definitions and executable tests. Keeping block descriptors in a vector rather than inside the managed bytes makes the teaching invariant easier to inspect: descriptors are in increasing address order, their half-open ranges exactly partition [0, 512) , and no two live allocations overlap. A production allocator would normally avoid allocating metadata dynamically while servicing an allocation request. Allocation trace. Begin with [0,512) F . Allocate 64 bytes: [0,64) A [64,512) F . Allocate 80 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,512) F . Allocate 48 bytes: [0,64) A [64,144) A [144,192) A [192,512) F . Free the middle block: [0,64) A [64,144) F [144,192) A [192,512) F . A 32-byte request reuses the 80-byte hole and splits it because the 48-byte remainder exceeds the minimum split: [0,64) A [64,96) A [96,144) F [144,192) A [192,512) F . Coalescing trace. Free [0,64) , then [64,96) . The allocator first merges left with the newly free block and then merges the adjacent [96,144) remainder, producing [0,144) F . Freeing [144,192) merges on both sides as applicable; the final free of the last live block restores [0,512) F . The test therefore exercises reuse, left coalescing, right coalescing, and restoration of the original region. Statistics distinguish requested bytes from reserved bytes. Their difference is internal fragmentation under this implementation’s rounding rule. External fragmentation can be reported as free_bytes - largest_free : zero means every free byte is currently in one contiguous block. These metrics are policy-dependent descriptions, not universal allocator-quality scores. The implementation rejects zero-sized requests, arithmetic that would overflow during alignment rounding, pointers outside the arena, pointers into the interior of a block, and a second release of a block that is still represented as free. These checks are intentionally limited. After coalescing, stale pointers can coincide with a later allocation start, corrupted metadata can invalidate the reasoning, and address reuse makes perfect temporal error detection impossible without additional generation or quarantine metadata. Sanitizers and hardened allocators use stronger mechanisms; this example does not claim complete invalid-free detection. Allocator project tests. Verify exhaustion without state corruption; reuse of a freed first-fit block; 16-byte alignment for every successful result; refusal to create a remainder smaller than 32 bytes; coalescing with a free predecessor, successor, and both neighbors; invalid and double-free rejection for the cases above; overflow-checked size rounding; and conservation of the 512 managed bytes after every operation.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, the bump arena is intentionally retained because it isolates alignment and bounded allocation.

topics.title: Chapter 11 — Memory Errors
topics.summary: Memory errors are violations of object boundaries, lifetime, initialization, or ownership. Their visible symptoms can occur far from their cause. A write beyond one buffer may corrupt a pointer that fails minutes later. The most effective debugging approach identifies the first invalid operation rather than explaining only the final crash.

topics.title: 11.1 Buffer overflow
topics.summary: A buffer overflow writes more data than a buffer can hold. The relevant bound is the actual destination capacity, not a claimed input length. A safe copy needs agreement among source availability, destination capacity, and requested count. String operations add another requirement: space for the terminator when the result must be a C string. A ten-character payload needs eleven bytes in that representation. Prefer length-aware interfaces and verify arithmetic before allocation. A bounded function can still be misused if the supplied bound describes the source instead of the destination.

topics.title: 11.2 Out-of-bounds access
topics.summary: An out-of-bounds read or write accesses outside an object’s permitted range. Reads matter as much as writes: they can disclose data, fault, or influence control flow using unrelated bytes. A read that remains within a mapped page can still violate the language’s rules. Check indices before forming an invalid pointer. For a region described by offset and length, use the guarded subtraction pattern from Chapter 4. In multidimensional code, validate every dimension and stride relationship. A valid row index does not rescue an invalid column index that happens to land inside neighboring storage.

topics.title: 11.3 Memory leaks
topics.summary: A leak occurs when storage remains allocated without a reachable ownership path that will release it when required. Losing a pointer is a common cause, but a reachable container that grows forever can also create a practical retention problem even when a leak detector sees it as reachable memory. Distinguish accidental leaks from intentional caches and from unbounded retention. Measure live object counts and ownership paths, not only process resident size. A cache needs a limit and eviction policy. An ownership cycle needs a way to break the cycle. “The operating system frees it at exit” does not justify unbounded growth in a long-running service.

topics.title: 11.4 Double free
topics.summary: A double free releases the same allocation more than once. It often arises when two components both believe they own a raw pointer, or when a cleanup path runs after an earlier release without updating ownership state. The repair is a single ownership protocol, not merely adding scattered null checks. After ownership transfer, the previous owner must no longer release. In C++, move-only resource wrappers make this rule visible in the type system. In C, document transfer and reset the owning state in a disciplined way while remembering that unrelated aliases remain unchanged.

It often arises when two components both believe they own a raw pointer, or when a cleanup path runs after an earlier release without updating ownership state. The repair is a single ownership protocol, not merely adding scattered null checks. After ownership transfer, the previous owner must no longer release. In C++, move-only resource wrappers make this rule visible in the type system. In C, document transfer and reset the owning state in a disciplined way while remembering that unrelated aliases remain unchanged.

topics.title: 11.5 Invalid free
topics.summary: An invalid free passes a pointer that is not a currently releasable allocation from the matching family. Interior pointers, stack addresses, and pointers from a different allocator are common examples. The allocator’s metadata lookup can be corrupted or confused by such inputs. A function returning a borrowed interior pointer should not expose an interface that suggests ownership. Name and document it as a view. Where several allocators exist, keep the release operation with the owner or use a deleter that records the matching mechanism. Allocation provenance is part of the resource contract.

topics.title: 11.6 Use-after-free
topics.summary: Use-after-free accesses storage after its allocation has been released. The storage may retain old bytes, be reused for a different object, or become inaccessible. None of those physical outcomes restores the old access’s validity. Concurrent use-after-free is especially subtle. One thread can validate a pointer while another releases the target before the first dereferences it. Protect the lifetime across the entire access interval with ownership, locking, or a carefully designed reclamation scheme. Atomic pointer loads alone do not keep the pointed-to object alive.

topics.title: 11.7 Dangling pointers
topics.summary: A dangling pointer or reference outlives the object it designates. It can result from returning a local address, destroying an owner, reallocating a vector, or resetting an arena. The pointer variable itself may remain perfectly intact. Track invalidation events in interface documentation and code review. A function that returns a view into a container should specify which mutations invalidate it. Avoid storing borrowed views in long-lived objects unless the owner’s lifetime relationship is explicit and enforceable. Lifetime bugs become easier to prevent when the design limits how far a borrow can travel.

topics.title: 11.8 Uninitialized memory
topics.summary: Raw allocation does not initialize its payload, and many automatic scalar declarations do not establish a usable value. Reading an indeterminate scalar value is generally invalid in the language modes used here, with narrow special rules that are not a basis for ordinary application logic. Initialize before use, but do not confuse initialization with semantic validation. A zeroed length can be a valid default while a zeroed state tag may still be invalid for the protocol. Tools for uninitialized-value tracking complement address sanitizers because staying within allocated storage does not guarantee that the bytes have been meaningfully initialized.

topics.title: 11.9 Undefined behavior
topics.summary: Undefined behavior means the language imposes no requirements on the program’s behavior for the offending execution. It is not a promise to wrap, crash, throw, or continue with a random value. Optimizations can rely on the assumption that valid programs do not perform the invalid operation. This is why an apparently harmless out-of-bounds access can change unrelated-looking code after optimization. The right response is to remove the invalid operation, not to demand that the compiler preserve one observed accident. Debug and release builds are different experiments; both must implement a program whose source-level behavior is defined.

topics.title: 11.10 Sanitizers
topics.summary: AddressSanitizer instruments memory accesses and allocation boundaries to detect classes such as heap and stack out-of-bounds access and use-after-free. UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer targets selected language violations. ThreadSanitizer tracks data races. Their coverage and limitations differ, and some configurations cannot be combined. [ R5 , R6 ] A clean sanitizer run covers only executed paths and the checks enabled in that build. Some lifetime, intra-object, protocol, and logical errors remain outside a tool’s detection. Use sanitizers alongside warnings, tests, fuzzing of parsers, ownership design, and review. Instrumented performance is not production performance.

topics.title: Worked example — Replacing an unchecked copy contract
topics.summary: The requirement is to copy exactly the available source bytes into a destination only when the destination is large enough. Failure must leave the destination unchanged. A bounded range interface makes both extents explicit. Companion listing: ch11/bounded_copy.cpp The three-byte source cannot fit in the two-byte destination. The function rejects the request before writing anything. The exact-size destination succeeds, and every byte is compared against the source. The interface explicitly requires nonoverlapping ranges; supporting overlap would call for a different copy contract, such as an appropriately bounded memmove operation. topics.title: Worked example — Diagnosing use-after-free
topics.summary: After free(p) , the numeric bits stored in p may remain unchanged, but the allocation lifetime has ended. Dereferencing p is invalid even if the allocator has not reused the region yet. Setting p=NULL can prevent some accidental reuse through that variable, but aliases may still exist. Ownership design, not pointer clearing alone, prevents the class of bug.

topics.title: Chapter 12 — Instruction Set Architecture
topics.summary: The instruction set is the boundary between software’s requested operations and a processor’s implementation. It describes registers, instructions, address calculations, and architectural effects. It does not specify that every instruction takes one cycle or that internal work occurs in source order. Reading assembly well requires keeping the architectural result separate from the microarchitectural method.

topics.title: 12.1 Machine instructions
topics.summary: A machine instruction is an encoded operation the processor recognizes. It identifies an operation and, explicitly or implicitly, its operands. Instructions can move data, perform arithmetic, change control flow, or request privileged behavior. On x86-64, instructions have variable-length encodings rather than one fixed size. The visible instruction sequence is not necessarily the processor’s internal execution sequence. A processor may decode instructions into smaller operations, overlap independent work, and speculate past branches. Architectural rules determine what results may become visible. An assembly listing is therefore a semantic description and an input to performance analysis, not a cycle-by-cycle hardware trace.

topics.title: 12.2 Registers
topics.summary: Registers are named architectural storage locations used directly by instructions. General-purpose registers hold integer values and addresses. Other register classes support vector, floating-point, control, and status operations. Keeping a value in a register can avoid a memory access, but the number and use of registers are constrained by the ISA and ABI. Architectural register names need not correspond one-to-one with fixed physical storage inside a modern processor. Register renaming can map successive architectural values to different physical registers. This helps remove false dependencies while preserving the program’s required register behavior. Source-level programmers normally need the architectural model first and the renaming model only for deeper performance work.

topics.title: 12.3 Memory
topics.summary: Instructions access memory through effective addresses computed from available operands. A load brings a value into a register or another destination; a store writes a value to memory. Some x86 instructions combine memory access with arithmetic, but that does not eliminate the underlying data movement. A memory operand can involve address translation, cache lookup, coherence, and fault checks. Two instructions with similar arithmetic can have very different costs if one waits for a cache miss. Count memory traffic and dependencies, not just mnemonics, when estimating performance.

topics.title: 12.4 Program counter
topics.summary: The program counter identifies the instruction position used for control flow. On x86-64 the architectural instruction pointer is %rip . Sequential execution advances to the next instruction; branches, calls, returns, and exceptions change the flow according to their rules. For RIP-relative addressing, the displacement is interpreted relative to the next instruction’s address. This detail matters when manually calculating a target from disassembly. The value displayed beside an instruction is usually its own starting address, not necessarily the base used in that instruction’s relative-address computation.

topics.title: 12.5 Processor state
topics.summary: Processor state includes more than general-purpose registers. It can include condition flags, vector registers, floating-point control state, stack state, privilege state, and address-translation configuration. The exact state relevant to an operation depends on the architecture and execution context. A context switch must preserve enough state for a thread to resume as though its execution had been paused. A normal function call has a narrower contract: the calling convention specifies which registers the caller or callee must preserve. Confusing a context switch with a function call leads to incorrect assumptions about who saves what.

topics.title: 12.6 ISA versus microarchitecture
topics.summary: The ISA specifies architectural behavior. The microarchitecture is the implementation: pipelines, execution units, caches, predictors, queues, and scheduling logic. Different processors can execute the same binary while exhibiting different latency, throughput, and energy behavior. An optimization based on a particular instruction cost may not transfer to another processor implementing the same ISA. The portable part of the reasoning is the algorithm and architectural semantics; the measured part belongs to a specific machine and workload. The Intel architecture manuals separate instruction behavior from implementation-oriented performance guidance. [ R3 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Tracing a tiny abstract machine
topics.summary: Use a deliberately simplified machine with one accumulator, a program counter, and four instructions: load immediate, add immediate, multiply immediate, and halt. This is a teaching model, not x86 assembly. Companion listing: ch12/machine.py The trace is (1,6) , (2,10) , and (3,30) . Each pair records the next instruction index and accumulator after one operation. The halt instruction leaves the final pair unchanged. The model makes control and data state explicit, but it intentionally omits fixed-width overflow, memory, interrupts, and timing. Now imagine an implementation that computes the addition and multiplication through several internal steps. As long as the architectural result at each required boundary is preserved, those internal steps need not resemble this simple interpreter. That is the distinction between an ISA-level explanation and an implementation-level explanation.

topics.title: Worked example — Separating ISA from implementation
topics.summary: Two processors can both implement x86-64 and execute the same architectural instruction stream while using different pipelines, cache sizes, branch predictors, and execution widths internally. The ISA specifies programmer-visible behavior; the microarchitecture determines how a particular implementation achieves it. Performance differences therefore do not imply different source-level semantics.

topics.title: 13.1 General-purpose registers
topics.summary: The baseline x86-64 general-purpose register set includes %rax , %rbx , %rcx , %rdx , %rsi , %rdi , %rsp , %rbp , and %r8 through %r15 . They can hold integer values or addresses, with some instructions imposing implicit operand roles. The ABI distinguishes caller-saved and callee-saved registers. Caller-saved values may be overwritten by a call, so a caller must preserve any such value it needs afterward. Callee-saved registers must be restored by a function that changes them. This division reduces unnecessary saving while allowing separately compiled functions to cooperate. [ R4 ]

topics.title: 13.2 Register widths
topics.summary: A 64-bit register has narrower named views. %rax is the full 64-bit register, %eax its low 32 bits, %ax its low 16 bits, and %al its low eight bits. %ah names another eight-bit portion, but legacy high-byte registers have encoding restrictions with REX prefixes and are best avoided in beginner examples. Writing a 32-bit general-purpose register zeroes the upper 32 bits of the corresponding 64-bit register. Writing a 16-bit or eight-bit subregister generally leaves the other bits unchanged. This is why movl $1, %eax establishes a full %rax value of one, while movb $1, %al does not.

topics.title: 13.3 %rax
topics.summary: %rax commonly carries an integer or pointer return value under the System V ABI. It is caller-saved. Some multiply and divide instructions use %rax implicitly, often together with %rdx for a double-width value. Do not assume a call preserves an unrelated value in %rax ; the callee is allowed to use it for the result and temporary work. The low byte %al also has a special role when calling variadic functions under this ABI: it conveys information about vector-register arguments. Handwritten assembly that calls a variadic library routine must follow that rule rather than only loading the visible integer arguments.

topics.title: 13.4 %rbx
topics.summary: %rbx is callee-saved in the reference calling convention. A function can use it for a long-lived local value across nested calls, but must restore the caller’s original value before returning. The cost of using %rbx may include a save and restore if the function changes it. A compiler weighs that cost against repeatedly saving a caller-saved value around calls. Register allocation is therefore influenced by value lifetimes and call structure, not simply by choosing the shortest register name.

topics.title: 13.5 %rcx
topics.summary: %rcx holds the fourth ordinary integer or pointer argument in the System V convention. It is caller-saved. The low byte %cl is also the implicit count operand for traditional variable-count shift instructions. Implicit roles can constrain instruction scheduling. A compiler may need to move a shift count into %cl even when the count originally resides elsewhere. In Linux’s x86-64 system-call ABI, the fourth argument is not passed in %rcx ; the syscall interface uses %r10 for that position. Function calls and system calls must be learned as separate interfaces.

topics.title: 13.6 %rdx
topics.summary: %rdx carries the third ordinary integer or pointer argument and is caller-saved. It also participates in full-width multiplication and division. For signed 64-bit division, %rdx:%rax forms the signed double-width dividend, and the remainder is returned in %rdx . Before dividing a sign-extended 64-bit value, cqto prepares %rdx from the sign of %rax . Clearing %rdx instead is correct for certain unsigned dividends but wrong for a negative signed dividend. The register pair’s interpretation must match the chosen instruction.

topics.title: 13.7 %rsi
topics.summary: %rsi carries the second ordinary integer or pointer argument. It is caller-saved and also has a source-index role in string instructions. Inside a function it can be reused once the argument is no longer needed. A name’s historical association is not a restriction on ordinary general-purpose use. A compiler may keep a loop bound in %rsi even when no string operation exists. Read the data flow in the current function instead of assuming the register always carries the same kind of value.

topics.title: 13.8 %rdi
topics.summary: %rdi carries the first ordinary integer or pointer argument and is caller-saved. It has a destination-index role in string instructions. In a simple function taking a pointer and a length, %rdi commonly receives the pointer and %rsi the length. The first argument can also be hidden by a language ABI rule, such as a result-storage pointer or a C++ object pointer in particular cases. The simplified six-register rule is a useful starting point for ordinary scalar functions, not a complete classification algorithm for every aggregate or language feature.

topics.title: 13.9 %rsp
topics.summary: %rsp is the stack pointer. Push, pop, call, and return operations use it according to their instruction semantics. The ABI requires suitable alignment at call boundaries and restoration of the caller’s stack position before a normal return. Corrupting %rsp can redirect subsequent stack accesses and returns. Handwritten assembly must account for every push, pop, and explicit adjustment. A balanced count alone is not enough if the adjustments occur on only some control-flow paths. Trace the stack depth along every path to the return instruction.

topics.title: 13.10 %rbp
topics.summary: %rbp is callee-saved and can serve as a frame pointer. A conventional prologue saves the old value and makes %rbp a stable reference point for the current frame. Optimized code often omits this dedicated role and uses the register for other purposes. The absence of %rbp -based accesses does not mean a function lacks local state or cannot be unwound. Debugging and exception unwinding can use metadata that describes stack changes. Conversely, having a frame pointer does not make corrupted stack contents trustworthy.

Optimized code often omits this dedicated role and uses the register for other purposes. The absence of %rbp -based accesses does not mean a function lacks local state or cannot be unwound. Debugging and exception unwinding can use metadata that describes stack changes. Conversely, having a frame pointer does not make corrupted stack contents trustworthy.

Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

In simpler terms, %rbp is callee-saved and can serve as a frame pointer.

topics.title: 13.11 %r8–%r15
topics.summary: %r8 and %r9 carry the fifth and sixth ordinary integer or pointer arguments. %r10 and %r11 are caller-saved temporaries. %r12 through %r15 are callee-saved. The narrower forms use suffixes such as %r8d , %r8w , and %r8b . These registers expand the available working set and reduce some memory spills compared with a smaller register set. They do not eliminate register pressure. Large expressions, vector work, and many simultaneously live values can still require spills to stack storage. A spill is a consequence of allocation constraints, not necessarily a sign of an incompetent compiler.

topics.title: 13.12 Instruction pointer
topics.summary: %rip identifies the instruction stream position. It is not manipulated as an ordinary general-purpose destination in the same way as %rax ; control-transfer instructions and relative-addressing mechanisms provide the relevant operations. RIP-relative addressing supports position-independent access to nearby code and data. The code can refer to a symbol using a displacement that remains useful when the image is relocated. Relocations and linker decisions still matter, especially for symbols outside the current image or with different visibility.

topics.title: 13.13 Condition flags
topics.summary: The flags register includes status bits such as zero, sign, carry, and overflow. Arithmetic and comparison instructions update selected flags. Conditional branches, conditional moves, and set-on-condition instructions then interpret them. Flags do not have one universal “comparison result” meaning. Signed and unsigned order use different combinations. Carry is relevant to unsigned overflow or borrow interpretation; overflow describes signed-range overflow for particular arithmetic operations. An intervening instruction can overwrite flags, so keep the producing instruction and consuming branch connected in the data-flow analysis. [ R3 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Watching partial-register writes
topics.summary: Start %rax with every bit set. A 32-bit write of one clears its high half. A 16-bit write changes only the low 16 bits. An eight-bit write changes only the low byte. Companion listing: ch13/widths.S Companion listing: ch13/main.c Build on the reference platform with cc main.c widths.S -o widths . The successive full-register values are FFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF , 0000000000000001 , 0000000000001234 , and 0000000000001256 . The return value verifies the final state without requiring a debugger.

topics.title: Worked example — Subregister write behavior
topics.summary: On x86-64, writing a 32-bit general-purpose subregister such as eax zero-extends into the full 64-bit register rax . Thus if rax was 0xFFFF000000000001 and an instruction writes eax = 5 , the resulting rax is 0x0000000000000005 . This differs from many 8- and 16-bit partial-register writes.

topics.title: Worked example — Following argument registers
topics.summary: Under the System V AMD64 ABI, the first integer or pointer arguments are commonly passed in rdi , rsi , rdx , rcx , r8 , and r9 , with integer return values in rax . A call f(10,20) therefore places the first two arguments in the first two designated registers before transferring control, unless optimization removes or transforms the call.

topics.title: 14.1 Immediate operands
topics.summary: An immediate operand encodes a constant in the instruction, such as $7 . It is a value, not a request to read memory at address seven. The distinction between $symbol and symbol can similarly distinguish an address-like immediate from a memory reference, subject to relocation and encoding rules. Not every instruction accepts every immediate width. Some encodings sign-extend a smaller immediate, and a full 64-bit constant may require a different encoding or instruction form. Let the assembler diagnose illegal forms, then inspect the actual encoding when code size or exact semantics matter.

topics.title: 14.2 Register operands
topics.summary: A register operand names an architectural register or subregister. movq %rdi, %rax copies the 64-bit value from %rdi to %rax . The source remains unchanged. The q suffix indicates a quadword, or 64-bit operation, in this syntax. Register moves can sometimes be handled efficiently inside a processor through renaming or other mechanisms, but they remain architectural operations. Do not assume a source-level assignment always requires a move instruction; the compiler may keep two names associated with one value or remove an unused assignment.

topics.title: 14.3 Memory operands
topics.summary: A memory operand describes an effective address. (%rdi) refers to memory at the address held in %rdi ; it does not refer to the register’s bits as the final data value. movq (%rdi), %rax loads eight bytes, while movq %rax, (%rdi) stores eight bytes. Most ordinary two-operand x86 data-processing instructions do not allow two explicit memory operands. Moving between two memory locations generally requires a register or a specialized instruction. A memory operand can fault even when its address calculation is simple, because mapping and permission checks occur separately from arithmetic validity.

topics.title: 14.4 mov
topics.summary: The mov family copies data without ordinary arithmetic transformation. Width matters: movb , movw , movl , and movq operate on 8, 16, 32, and 64 bits. The 32-bit register-destination rule zeroes the upper half of the corresponding 64-bit register. Sign-extending and zero-extending moves are separate forms. A byte loaded as unsigned into a larger register needs zero extension; a signed byte may need sign extension. A plain narrow load can leave unrelated upper bits unchanged. Always identify whether later code consumes only the narrow value or the full register.

topics.title: 14.5 Addressing modes
topics.summary: A common x86-64 memory-address form is D(B,I,S) : displacement plus base register plus index register multiplied by scale. In mathematical notation, the effective address is D + B + I*S . Missing components contribute zero or their applicable default. The addressing mode computes a byte address. The source language’s element size has already been translated into a scale or explicit arithmetic. A scale of eight is natural for an array of eight-byte elements, but a structure size of 24 may require an additional multiply or combination of additions. The hardware does not know the source-level array type.

topics.title: 14.6 Displacement
topics.summary: A displacement is a constant offset included in the address expression. 8(%rdi) accesses eight bytes beyond the address in %rdi . It can identify a structure member, a later array element, or a stack-frame location. Displacements are not automatically bounds-checked against a structure definition. The assembler sees an address expression, not the C++ object contract. When reverse-engineering generated code, relate the displacement to known member offsets and widths. A load at offset eight might be one eight-byte field or several smaller fields depending on the instruction and layout.

topics.title: 14.7 Base/index addressing
topics.summary: Base/index addressing combines a starting address with a variable position. (%rdi,%rsi) adds the two register values. If %rdi is a byte-buffer base and %rsi is a byte offset, this directly selects the desired byte position. A valid numerical addition does not prove that the resulting access stays inside an object. High-level bounds checks must precede the load or store when the index is not already trusted. Optimized assembly may move or combine checks, but the programmer’s correctness argument still needs a bounded input domain.

topics.title: 14.8 Scaled indexing
topics.summary: The standard scaled-index factor is 1, 2, 4, or 8. (%rdi,%rsi,8) is convenient for eight-byte elements. A separate displacement can select a field or shift the element index, as in 8(%rdi,%rsi,8) . For an array of 24-byte records, the compiler might compute 3*i with an lea , then use a scale of eight. Several equivalent instruction sequences can implement the same address formula. Choose the interpretation that explains the complete expression rather than assigning one source operation to each instruction mechanically.

topics.title: 14.9 RIP-relative addressing
topics.summary: RIP-relative addressing computes a location from the next instruction’s address plus a displacement. It is widely used for position-independent references to code and data within a reachable range. The assembler and linker supply relocations when the displacement cannot yet be finalized. A RIP-relative reference is not an indirect pointer lookup by itself. It computes an address relative to the instruction stream and then, for a memory instruction, accesses that address. Some dynamic-linking sequences do add another level through a table entry. Distinguish the address of a pointer slot from the pointer value stored in that slot.

topics.title: 14.10 lea
topics.summary: lea , or load effective address, computes an address-form expression and places the resulting value in a register without reading the memory at that address. It is useful for pointers and for arithmetic combinations such as x + 2*x . Unlike an ordinary add instruction, lea does not update the usual arithmetic condition flags. This can preserve a comparison result for a later branch. The name does not imply that the result must be used as a pointer; the instruction computes a numeric expression using address-generation syntax. [ R3 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Translating an indexed load
topics.summary: The requirement is to return values[index + 1] from a valid array of 64-bit unsigned integers. The caller guarantees that the requested element exists. The assembly combines the extra element offset and scaled indexing in one memory operand. Companion listing: ch14/pick.S Companion listing: ch14/main.c With a hypothetical base of 0x3000 , index 2 gives 0x3000 + 8 + 2 × 8 = 0x3018 . That is element 3, whose value is 44. The example’s address is a model; the actual allocation address is not fixed. Replacing movq with leaq would return the computed address instead of reading the value 44.

topics.title: Worked example — Decoding scaled-index addressing
topics.summary: An address such as 8(%rbx,%rcx,4) means base rbx plus index rcx multiplied by 4 plus displacement 8. If rbx=0x1000 and rcx=3 , the effective address is 0x1000 + 12 + 8 = 0x1014 . This form naturally addresses array elements plus a field displacement.

topics.title: 15.1 Addition
topics.summary: addq source, destination adds 64-bit operands and stores the low 64 bits in the destination. It updates condition flags, including carry and signed overflow indicators. A register-memory form also performs the relevant memory access. The low-bit addition result can serve either signed or unsigned interpretation. Carry indicates unsigned overflow beyond the width; overflow indicates that the signed result cannot be represented. These flags answer different questions. An assembly routine exposing checked arithmetic must return or branch on the appropriate condition rather than assuming the caller can inspect flags after an ordinary C call.

topics.title: 15.2 Subtraction
topics.summary: subq source, destination computes destination minus source. This operand order is easy to reverse when switching between AT&T and Intel syntax. The result updates flags used by both arithmetic and comparisons. Subtraction underlies cmp , which computes flags without retaining the result. For unsigned order, carry-related conditions describe borrow behavior. For signed order, the sign and overflow relationship matters. A raw negative-looking high bit is not enough to establish the result of a signed comparison after overflow-sensitive subtraction.

topics.title: 15.3 Multiplication
topics.summary: The imul family supports signed multiplication in several forms. Two-operand forms retain the low-width result, while one-operand forms can produce a double-width result using implicit registers. Unsigned mul also uses implicit accumulator registers for full-width products. The low w bits of a product are the same under signed and unsigned modular interpretations of the input patterns. The high half and overflow interpretation differ. A compiler can therefore use a signed-named multiply instruction for some unsigned low-result calculations. Read the instruction’s actual result width and use, not only its mnemonic’s historical label.

topics.title: 15.5 Increment/decrement
topics.summary: inc and dec add or subtract one. They update several arithmetic flags but do not update the carry flag. This difference can matter when a later instruction consumes carry from an earlier operation. A compiler may choose add $1 or sub $1 instead, depending on code size, dependencies, and target tuning. Do not use instruction spelling as the sole measure of efficiency. The surrounding flag dependencies and pipeline behavior can be more important than the apparent simplicity of “increment.”

topics.title: 15.6 AND
topics.summary: and computes a bitwise intersection and updates status flags based on the result, while clearing carry and overflow in the ordinary instruction semantics. It is useful for masking and alignment calculations. Masking an address down to a boundary is a numeric operation, not a proof that the resulting address is an owned object. In allocator code, the masked or rounded address must still lie inside the managed region. In security-sensitive parsing, masking a length may silently truncate an invalid input rather than reject it.

topics.title: 15.7 OR
topics.summary: or combines set bits and updates flags from the result. It can set selected flag bits in an ordinary data word or combine nonoverlapping fields. Like other non-atomic memory read-modify-write instructions, an ordinary or to shared memory is not automatically a valid language-level synchronization operation. A locked machine instruction can provide particular atomic hardware behavior, but handwritten synchronization also needs compiler and language ordering guarantees. Prefer standard atomic interfaces for application code so the compiler understands the concurrency contract.

topics.title: 15.8 XOR
topics.summary: xor toggles differing bits. A common zeroing idiom is xorl %eax, %eax , which produces a full zero in %rax because a 32-bit register write clears the high half. It also changes flags, so it cannot be inserted between a comparison and a branch without considering that dependency. A zeroing idiom may be recognized specially by the microarchitecture, but its correctness follows from the architectural XOR result. A programmer should first establish that zero is the required value and that flag changes are harmless. Performance tuning follows only after those conditions are satisfied.

topics.title: 15.9 Shifts
topics.summary: Logical shifts move bits and fill with zeros; arithmetic right shift replicates the sign bit. In AT&T syntax, shl or sal names left shift, shr logical right shift, and sar arithmetic right shift. Traditional variable counts use %cl . x86 masks shift counts according to operand width, but C and C++ source shifts with out-of-range counts are not thereby made valid. Hardware behavior is not a substitute for language preconditions. Likewise, arithmetic right shift of a negative value rounds differently from signed division by a positive power of two when the value is not evenly divisible. [ R3 , R36 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Signed division with explicit preparation
topics.summary: The requirement is to divide -29 by 6. The mathematical quotient truncated toward zero is -4, and the remainder is -5 because -29 = (-4)*6 + (-5) . Companion listing: ch15/divide.S Companion listing: ch15/main.c Before idivq , %rax holds the two’s-complement pattern for -29 and %rdx is all ones. This pair represents the sign-extended dividend. Afterward %rax is -4 and %rdx is -5. Clearing %rdx instead would describe a large positive double-width number, not -29, and could cause a quotient-overflow fault.

topics.title: 16.1 cmp
topics.summary: cmp source, destination sets flags as though it computed destination minus source, but discards the arithmetic result. In AT&T syntax, cmpq %rsi, %rdi therefore compares %rdi against %rsi . The following branch determines whether the comparison is interpreted as signed or unsigned. The cmp instruction itself does not carry a high-level signedness tag. A wrong branch condition can make identical input patterns produce an incorrect ordering even though the subtraction flags were generated correctly.

topics.title: 16.2 test
topics.summary: test sets flags from a bitwise AND without storing the AND result. testq %rax, %rax is a common way to test whether a register is zero. test with a mask checks selected bits. Testing a value against itself also exposes its sign bit through the sign flag, but the intended predicate must still be clear. A masked test followed by a zero branch means no selected bit was set. It does not mean all unselected bits were zero or that the entire value equals the mask.

topics.title: 16.3 Condition flags
topics.summary: For common comparisons, zero ( ZF ) indicates equality, sign ( SF ) reflects the result’s sign bit, carry ( CF ) supports unsigned order, and overflow ( OF ) corrects signed-order interpretation when subtraction’s sign alone would mislead. A useful subset is: Keep the comparison and branch adjacent in your reasoning even when scheduling places other instructions between them. An instruction that changes relevant flags changes the branch’s input.

topics.title: 16.4 Conditional branches
topics.summary: A conditional branch transfers control when a flag predicate is true. Otherwise execution continues with the following instruction. The processor may predict the outcome and execute speculatively, but architectural behavior must match the permitted branch result. A misprediction can waste speculative work, yet removing a branch is not automatically faster. A branch may avoid an expensive or invalid operation. A branchless replacement that computes both alternatives can increase work or access memory that the original branch protected. Preserve semantics before comparing speed.

topics.title: 16.5 Unconditional branches
topics.summary: An unconditional jump changes the next instruction without testing flags. It can target a fixed label or an address obtained indirectly. Compilers use jumps to connect basic blocks, implement loop back edges, and skip alternate paths. An indirect jump’s target must be valid for the intended control-flow graph. Table indices and function pointers need bounds and type validation. A control-flow error can redirect execution even when no arithmetic result is wrong. Security mechanisms can constrain some targets, but the program must still maintain valid dispatch state.

topics.title: 16.6 Loops
topics.summary: A loop usually contains initialization, a condition, a body, an update, and a back edge. Compilers may place the condition at the top or bottom, duplicate a test, or transform the induction variable. The resulting assembly can look different from the source while preserving the iteration domain. To understand a loop, identify its invariant and progress measure. A pointer may advance while a count decreases. An index may be compared against an end value. Determine whether the loop handles zero iterations before examining the body; many off-by-one errors arise from assuming at least one element exists.

topics.title: 16.7 Conditional moves
topics.summary: A conditional move selects a value according to flags without a control-flow branch. It can be effective when both candidate values are cheap and valid to compute. It is not a general replacement for a branch guarding unsafe work. In particular, a conditional move with a memory source can require the memory operand to be read even when the condition would leave the destination unchanged. Do not use it to hide an invalid address behind a false condition. High-level conditional expressions also have language evaluation rules that the compiler must preserve for valid programs.

topics.title: 16.8 Jump tables
topics.summary: A jump table stores branch targets or offsets indexed by a selector. It can efficiently dispatch among many dense cases. The compiler normally includes a range check before indexing the table, possibly after subtracting the lowest case value. Sparse selectors may be better served by comparisons or a search structure. A table’s size and locality also matter. The fact that a source switch has many cases does not guarantee a jump table, and the presence of a table does not mean every possible input is a valid index.

topics.title: 16.9 switch translation
topics.summary: A switch can become a jump table, comparison tree, sequence of branches, arithmetic transformation, or data lookup. Cases returning constants may become a value table rather than a table of instruction addresses. Optimization depends on case density and behavior. When inspecting translation, start with the source’s semantic mapping from input values to outcomes. Then identify how the assembly implements that mapping and handles the default case. This avoids mistaking a compact arithmetic transformation for missing cases or assuming a table entry is executable code when it is merely data.

topics.title: Worked example — A count-controlled sum loop
topics.summary: The requirement is to sum a valid array of 64-bit unsigned values, with modular 64-bit addition. A zero-length input must return zero without reading memory. Companion listing: ch16/sum.S Companion listing: ch16/main.c The loop invariant is that %rax contains the sum of consumed elements, %rdi points to the next element, and %rsi is the number remaining. Initially the count is four and the sum zero. After successive iterations, the sums are 10, 30, 60, and 100 while the counts are 3, 2, 1, and 0. The final subq supplies the flags consumed by jne .

cards.question: Explain Worked example — A count-controlled sum loop. What mechanism, rule, or distinction must you remember?
cards.answer: The requirement is to sum a valid array of 64-bit unsigned values, with modular 64-bit addition. A zero-length input must return zero without reading memory. Companion listing: ch16/sum.S Companion listing: ch16/main.c The loop invariant is that %rax contains the sum of consumed elements, %rdi points to the next element, and %rsi is the number remaining. topics.title: 17.1 call
topics.summary: A near call transfers control to a target and places a return address on the stack. The return address identifies where execution should continue after the callee finishes. On the reference 64-bit convention, the pushed return address occupies eight bytes. The instruction itself does not allocate a complete source-level stack frame or save every register. Those are responsibilities handled by the caller and callee according to the ABI. A function can therefore be extremely small if it needs no local stack storage and changes no callee-saved register.

topics.title: 17.2 ret
topics.summary: A normal ret obtains the return address from the stack and transfers control there, advancing the stack pointer accordingly. It assumes the stack state has been restored to the expected return-address position. A mismatched push/pop sequence or corrupted return address can send execution to the wrong location. Stack canaries and other mitigations can detect or constrain some corruption, but they do not make an incorrect frame layout safe. Verify the stack pointer at each return path, especially when a function has early exits.

topics.title: 17.3 Argument registers
topics.summary: For ordinary integer and pointer arguments in the System V AMD64 ABI, the first six use %rdi , %rsi , %rdx , %rcx , %r8 , and %r9 . Additional arguments may use the stack. Floating-point and vector arguments use other rules and register classes, and aggregates require ABI classification. This simplified rule is enough for the scalar examples in this book. It is not sufficient for every structure return, variadic call, or C++ object interface. When interoperating with an unfamiliar signature, consult the full ABI and inspect a compiler-generated reference rather than guessing from the number of parameters. [ R4 ]

topics.title: 17.4 Return registers
topics.summary: Ordinary scalar integer and pointer results commonly return in %rax . Some wider or aggregate results use multiple registers or caller-provided storage. Floating-point results commonly use vector registers such as %xmm0 under the applicable rules. The result type determines how the caller interprets the returned bits. Declaring an assembly function with the wrong C type can produce a mismatch even when the routine returns a sensible machine value. Keep the declaration and assembly contract together, including width, signedness, and any hidden storage assumptions.

topics.title: 17.5 Stack pointer
topics.summary: The stack pointer tracks the active stack region used by calls and local storage. The callee must return with the caller’s expected stack position restored. Adjustments reserve or release space but do not initialize the bytes automatically. A stack allocation can be large enough numerically yet violate alignment or exceed the mapped stack. Dynamic-sized stack objects need careful bounds. Prefer heap or arena storage when input-controlled size could make stack use unbounded. A call chain’s total stack requirement includes every simultaneously active frame.

topics.title: 17.6 Stack frames
topics.summary: A stack frame is the region and saved state associated with one active call. It may hold saved registers, spilled values, local objects, and outgoing arguments. Some leaf functions need no explicit frame allocation. Frame layout is a compiler and ABI matter, not a fixed translation of source declaration order. Optimization can reuse slots for nonoverlapping lifetimes or eliminate objects. Debugger displays reconstruct source concepts from machine state and metadata; an optimized-out variable is not necessarily missing from the computation.

topics.title: 17.7 Stack alignment
topics.summary: For the ordinary scalar calls used here, %rsp is 16-byte aligned immediately before call . The eight-byte return-address push means %rsp is eight modulo sixteen at callee entry, or equivalently %rsp + 8 is aligned. Additional alignment requirements can apply to particular stack-passed vector arguments. A callee that makes another call must account for its pushes and local allocation before doing so. One eight-byte push at entry changes the stack pointer from eight modulo sixteen to zero modulo sixteen, making it ready for a nested ordinary call. A second push would require another adjustment. Count bytes, not just source variables.
