topics.title: 17.8 Caller-saved registers
topics.summary: Caller-saved registers may be overwritten by a callee. If the caller needs one of their values after a call, it must save the value in a preserved register or memory, or recompute it. The choice depends on lifetime and cost. An assembly routine cannot promise preservation accidentally and expect every future implementation to keep doing so unless that stronger promise is part of its interface. Callers should rely on the ABI contract, not on what a current disassembly happens not to modify.

topics.title: 17.9 Callee-saved registers
topics.summary: A callee using %rbx , %rbp , or %r12 through %r15 must restore their incoming values before return. Saving them on entry and restoring them on exit is common, but optimized code can save only on paths that need them if unwind information and control flow remain correct. The saved value belongs to the caller. It is not the callee’s previous invocation state. Recursive calls therefore need independent preservation at each active level. A missing restore can corrupt a caller long after the callee’s own result appears correct.

A callee using %rbx , %rbp , or %r12 through %r15 must restore their incoming values before return. Saving them on entry and restoring them on exit is common, but optimized code can save only on paths that need them if unwind information and control flow remain correct. The saved value belongs to the caller. It is not the callee’s previous invocation state. Recursive calls therefore need independent preservation at each active level. A missing restore can corrupt a caller long after the callee’s own result appears correct.

At graduate level, do not treat this as a term to memorize. Identify the contract being described, the state or representation it constrains, and the assumptions that must remain true. When this topic appears in real systems code, separate what the language guarantees from what a compiler, operating system, ABI, ISA, or particular machine happens to do. Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

SIXTH-GRADE EXPLANATION
In simpler terms, a callee using %rbx , %rbp , or %r12 through %r15 must restore their incoming values before return.

topics.title: 17.10 Local variables
topics.summary: Local source objects may live in registers, stack slots, or no materialized storage at all. Address-taking can require an object to have addressable storage, but even then the compiler may optimize within the language’s observable behavior rules. A local array’s address must remain valid throughout every borrowed use. Passing it to a function that retains the pointer beyond return is unsafe. The calling convention transports the pointer correctly; it cannot extend the pointed-to object’s lifetime. ABI correctness and object-lifetime correctness are separate obligations.

topics.title: 17.11 Recursive calls
topics.summary: Each recursive invocation has its own logical parameters and local state. The machine commonly represents that state with repeated frames. If the recursion depth is d and each active frame requires roughly f bytes, stack use grows approximately with d*f , plus calling and alignment overhead. A base case is necessary but not sufficient for robustness. A valid but deeply nested input can still exceed the stack. Bound input depth, choose an iterative representation, or provide a resource-aware algorithm. Do not depend on tail-call optimization unless the implementation contract explicitly guarantees the needed behavior.

topics.title: 17.12 Function prologue
topics.summary: A prologue establishes any required frame, saves preserved registers, and reserves local storage. A conventional sequence might push %rbp , copy %rsp into it, and subtract space. Many functions use a different or shorter sequence. Handwritten assembly intended to participate in debugging or unwinding should provide appropriate call-frame information directives. Those directives describe how to recover caller state; they are not executed instructions. A correct normal return path does not automatically imply correct exception or debugger unwinding through the routine.

topics.title: 17.13 Function epilogue
topics.summary: An epilogue reverses the frame setup: release local space, restore preserved registers, and return. Every exit path must satisfy the same caller-visible contract. A function with an error return still owes the caller its saved registers and stack alignment state. The epilogue is a useful review boundary. List what the function acquired or changed, then verify that each relevant item has been restored or intentionally returned. This resembles resource cleanup in C and C++ because both problems are about preserving invariants across a boundary.

topics.title: Worked example — Preserving a value across a nested call
topics.summary: The requirement is to compute mix(x, 5) + x , where mix(x, y) returns 3*x + y using unsigned arithmetic. The assembly caller must retain x across the call to mix . It uses the callee-saved %rbx , saving and restoring the caller’s original value. Companion listing: ch17/nested.S Companion listing: ch17/main.c At entry, %rsp is eight modulo sixteen. Pushing %rbx makes it zero modulo sixteen, satisfying the ordinary nested-call alignment. %rbx then holds 9 while mix is free to overwrite caller-saved registers. mix returns 32, the wrapper adds 9, and popping restores the original %rbx before returning 41.

topics.title: Worked example — Tracking a call frame
topics.summary: Suppose a function needs 24 bytes of local storage but the ABI requires stack alignment at call boundaries. The compiler may round the stack adjustment upward, for example to 32 bytes, rather than allocate exactly 24. It also preserves any callee-saved registers it modifies. The frame therefore reflects ABI obligations as well as source locals.

topics.title: Worked example — Caller-saved versus callee-saved
topics.summary: If a caller needs a value currently in a caller-saved register after invoking another function, it must arrange to preserve that value, perhaps by spilling it. A callee that modifies a callee-saved register must restore it before returning. This division lets callers and callees coordinate without knowing each other’s source code.

topics.title: 18.1 Inlining
topics.summary: Inlining replaces a call boundary with the callee’s operations in the caller’s optimization context. It can remove call overhead and expose constants, dead branches, and redundant work. The inline keyword in C++ has important language linkage and definition rules; it is not a command forcing machine-code substitution. Inlining can increase code size and instruction-cache pressure. A small frequently used helper may benefit, while duplicating a large cold path may hurt. Let measurement and compiler diagnostics guide the decision. The best result can be a mixture of inlined hot paths and shared out-of-line slow paths.

topics.title: 18.2 Constant folding
topics.summary: Constant folding evaluates expressions whose values are known during translation. A fixed arithmetic expression can become a literal, and a condition based on a known constant can select one path before runtime. The expression must still be meaningful under the language’s rules. A compiler is not required to preserve a runtime-looking overflow merely because the programmer wrote it as a sequence of constants. Use appropriately typed constants and checked compile-time expressions when limits matter. Compile-time calculation reduces runtime work but does not remove semantic obligations.

topics.title: 18.3 Dead-code elimination
topics.summary: Dead-code elimination removes operations whose results cannot affect required observable behavior. An unused local calculation may disappear completely. A benchmark that computes a value and never uses it can therefore measure almost no intended work. Make benchmark results observable through a legitimate output or comparison outside the timed region. Do not indiscriminately mark all data volatile; that changes the workload and can block useful optimization. The goal is to preserve the operation being measured without introducing a different memory-access contract.

topics.title: 18.4 Common-subexpression elimination
topics.summary: When the compiler can prove that an expression has the same value at several points, it may compute it once and reuse the result. The proof depends on whether intervening operations can change its inputs, including memory reachable through aliases. Two identical-looking loads are not necessarily redundant if another operation can modify the location. Conversely, two differently written expressions may be equivalent after simplification. Help the compiler with clear ownership, const-correct interfaces, and limited aliasing rather than duplicating manual caches whose validity is difficult to maintain.

topics.title: 18.5 Loop unrolling
topics.summary: Unrolling repeats the loop body several times per control iteration. It can reduce branch overhead and expose independent work, but it increases code size and requires a remainder path when the element count is not a multiple of the unroll factor. A correct unrolled loop handles zero elements and the final partial group without reading past the range. Performance can worsen if extra code strains instruction storage or register allocation. Unrolling is a transformation to evaluate, not a universal improvement. Vectorization and memory bandwidth may dominate the outcome.

It can reduce branch overhead and expose independent work, but it increases code size and requires a remainder path when the element count is not a multiple of the unroll factor. A correct unrolled loop handles zero elements and the final partial group without reading past the range. Performance can worsen if extra code strains instruction storage or register allocation. Unrolling is a transformation to evaluate, not a universal improvement. Vectorization and memory bandwidth may dominate the outcome.

topics.title: 18.6 Tail-call optimization
topics.summary: A call in tail position can sometimes reuse the current function’s frame rather than creating another active frame. This can turn some recursion into constant-stack iteration. Language cleanup requirements, ABI constraints, and compiler choices determine whether the transformation is possible. A local object requiring destruction after the call can prevent a simple tail transfer. Debugging options or calling-convention differences can also matter. Do not use a recursive algorithm with unbounded depth on the assumption that a compiler will always optimize it into a loop. Establish the resource bound independently.

topics.title: 18.7 Strength reduction
topics.summary: Strength reduction replaces an operation with an equivalent cheaper sequence in the relevant context. Multiplication by a constant might become shifts and adds, or a loop might update a pointer incrementally instead of recomputing an index product. The “cheaper” operation depends on the target. Modern processors can multiply efficiently, while a longer shift-add sequence may create more dependencies. Signed division transformations also need correct rounding for negative values. Prefer clear source and inspect generated code before manually encoding a transformation whose benefit may have disappeared on the target machine.

topics.title: 18.8 Arithmetic transformations
topics.summary: Integer and floating-point transformations obey different algebraic freedoms. Unsigned arithmetic has modular identities. Signed arithmetic can be transformed under the assumption that defined executions do not overflow. Floating-point addition is generally not associative because rounding depends on evaluation order. Options that permit reassociation or disregard special values change the numerical contract. A faster result under such options is not automatically an equivalent result for every input. Document any relaxed arithmetic assumptions, including finite-only inputs, acceptable error, and reproducibility requirements. [ R2 ]

topics.title: 18.9 Aliasing restrictions
topics.summary: Aliasing limits which memory operations can move past one another or reuse loaded values. C’s restrict qualifier is a promise about access relationships during a particular execution region, not a runtime check. Standard C++20 does not have a directly identical core-language restrict keyword, though compilers provide extensions. An incorrect non-aliasing promise can make an otherwise plausible loop undefined or miscompiled relative to the programmer’s intent. Use it only when the API actually excludes overlapping access patterns. The performance opportunity comes from a true invariant; annotations cannot manufacture that invariant.

topics.title: 18.10 Optimization barriers
topics.summary: A barrier limits particular transformations. Volatile access, compiler-specific assembly constraints, atomic operations, and external calls can impose different restrictions, but they are not interchangeable. A compiler barrier need not be a hardware memory fence, and a hardware fence needs a correct language-level interface. volatile is not a thread-synchronization mechanism. It serves specific observable-access roles, including some device interfaces under implementation rules. For concurrent application state, use atomics and synchronization primitives. For benchmarking, use a narrowly justified technique rather than disabling the optimizer across the entire workload.

topics.title: 18.11 The as-if rule
topics.summary: The as-if principle allows any implementation that preserves the program’s required observable behavior. A variable can disappear, operations can combine, and a loop can become a constant when the result is known. The preserved behavior is defined by the language and relevant options, not by the programmer’s expectation of a one-to-one translation. Undefined behavior undermines the premise on which source-level reasoning depends. Optimization is therefore a reason to be more precise about validity, not a reason to avoid optimization. A well-defined program should remain correct across optimization levels even when its instructions and timing change substantially.

topics.title: Worked example — Optimizing a known-length calculation

topics.title: Worked example — Constant folding and dead code
topics.summary: For int x = 4 × 8; if (0) use(x); , an optimizing compiler can replace the multiplication with constant 32 and remove the unreachable branch entirely. These transformations are legal because no permitted observation changes. Debug builds may retain more structure, so source-to-assembly correspondence depends strongly on optimization settings.

topics.title: Worked example — Aliasing blocks a load elimination
topics.summary: Consider *p = 5; x = *q; . If p and q may alias, the store through p can affect the load through q . The compiler cannot generally replace the load with a previously known value of *q . Proving non-aliasing creates optimization freedom, but the proof must follow language and ABI rules.

topics.title: Chapter 19 — Kernel Fundamentals
topics.summary: A running application can calculate addresses, perform arithmetic, and call functions, but it does not have unrestricted authority over the machine. The kernel establishes the environment in which those actions occur. It manages resources shared by mutually untrusting programs and provides controlled ways to request services that a program cannot perform directly. The important boundary is not between “ordinary code” and “special code.” It is between execution contexts with different permissions. Kernel code is software, but hardware mechanisms give that software the authority to configure mappings, handle devices, and control execution. This chapter describes the Linux/x86-64 model; other architectures and kernels divide these responsibilities differently. [ R3 , R10 ]

topics.title: 19.1 Kernel
topics.summary: The kernel is the privileged core of an operating system. Its responsibilities include scheduling runnable work, maintaining virtual memory, mediating file and device access, and implementing interprocess communication. It also maintains bookkeeping: which descriptors a process owns, which pages may be written, and which operations the process’s credentials permit. Not every operating-system service must execute inside the kernel. A command interpreter, a graphical desktop, and many service managers are user-space programs. The design boundary varies among monolithic kernels, microkernels, and other arrangements. Regardless of architecture, a request must be validated at the point where it crosses a trust boundary. Moving an operation into a service does not eliminate the need for access control.

topics.title: 19.2 User mode
topics.summary: User mode is an execution mode with restricted authority. In the usual x86-64 Linux arrangement, application instructions execute at current privilege level 3. User mode is not synonymous with “untrusted person” or “unimportant program.” A privileged administrator’s ordinary application still runs in user mode. Its credentials may cause the kernel to approve more requests, but those credentials do not turn every application instruction into a ring-0 instruction. topics.title: 19.3 Kernel mode
topics.summary: Kernel mode allows execution of operations needed to control protected machine state. On the reference platform, the kernel normally executes at privilege level 0. Entry into this mode occurs through configured mechanisms rather than by an application choosing an arbitrary destination and declaring itself privileged. Kernel mode does not make software infallible. Invalid pointers, synchronization bugs, and incorrect bounds checks remain possible. Their consequences can be more severe because the kernel has broader authority. Nor does kernel mode imply that every virtual address is mapped or that every memory access succeeds. The currently installed mappings and protection features still matter.

topics.title: 19.4 Privilege levels
topics.summary: A privilege level is a hardware-defined part of execution state. x86 provides four numbered rings, although ordinary Linux application/kernel separation primarily uses rings 3 and 0. Virtualization adds another dimension of control; “hypervisor” is not adequately explained by pretending that x86 simply has a normal ring numbered minus one. Privilege checks apply to particular operations and accesses. Accessing a supervisor-only page and executing a privileged instruction are different checks, although both can prevent user code from performing unauthorized work. Software credentials form an additional policy layer. A successful mode transition therefore does not automatically authorize the requested operation: the kernel still checks arguments, ownership, capabilities, and resource limits.

topics.title: 19.5 Protected resources
topics.summary: Protected resources include physical memory mappings, device registers, scheduling state, privileged processor controls, and objects governed by operating-system policy. A disk block may contain another user’s data. A device command may affect the entire machine. A page-table edit may expose memory that was intended to remain isolated. Applications receive controlled references rather than raw authority whenever possible. A file descriptor identifies an entry in a process’s descriptor table; it is not a physical disk address. The kernel interprets the descriptor in the caller’s context and applies the object’s rules. This indirection makes it possible to share resources selectively while preserving a central place to enforce policy.

topics.title: 19.6 Dangerous instructions
topics.summary: Some instructions alter machine-wide or privileged execution state. Examples include operations involving control registers or interrupt-enable state. Hardware restricts these instructions so that an ordinary process cannot take over the machine by executing a short instruction sequence. An attempted prohibited operation raises an architectural exception rather than granting the requested authority. [ R3 ] Other instructions are not privileged but can still be dangerous when used incorrectly. An ordinary store can corrupt a program’s own heap. Integer division can fault for an invalid divisor. “Unprivileged” means permitted at the current hardware privilege level, not harmless. Labs in this book inspect and model privileged behavior; they do not require running privileged instructions or changing kernel settings.

topics.title: 19.7 Hardware protection
topics.summary: Hardware protection supplies mechanisms such as permission checks on translations and controlled entry points for exceptions and system calls. The kernel configures these mechanisms, and the processor enforces them during execution. Software policy and hardware enforcement are complementary: a policy without enforcement can be bypassed, while a mechanism without correct policy can faithfully enforce the wrong permissions. Protection operates at particular granularities. A writable page normally permits stores throughout the mapped writable region; it does not know that a C++ vector currently contains only five elements. Consequently, process isolation does not provide complete object-level memory safety. Bounds, lifetime, and concurrency correctness remain responsibilities of the language implementation and program design.

topics.title: Worked example — Following a protected request
topics.summary: Suppose a process wants to read bytes from an already-open file. topics.title: Worked example — Protecting kernel memory
topics.summary: Page-table permissions mark kernel mappings inaccessible to ordinary user-mode accesses. A user pointer that numerically resembles a kernel address does not grant permission to read it. If the CPU checks the access in user mode and protection forbids it, control transfers to the kernel’s fault path rather than completing the load.

topics.title: Chapter 20 — Protected Control Transfer
topics.summary: Control flow can leave a program for reasons beyond a source-level function call. A device may need attention, an instruction may encounter an invalid condition, or the program may explicitly request an operating-system service. The processor and kernel cooperate to save enough state, select an appropriate handler, and eventually continue or terminate the interrupted activity. Terminology depends on context. In this chapter, fault and trap use the architectural distinction when discussing x86 exceptions. They are not C++ exceptions, and the informal phrase “trap into the kernel” does not imply that every system call is an x86 trap-class exception. [ R3 ]

topics.title: 20.1 Exceptions
topics.summary: An architectural exception arises in relation to instruction execution. Examples include a page fault, an invalid instruction, or a divide error. The processor identifies the condition and transfers control through a configured mechanism. The saved state allows the handler to determine what happened and decide whether execution can continue. A language exception such as throw std::runtime_error(...) belongs to a different abstraction. Its implementation may unwind call frames entirely in user space. Although both mechanisms redirect control, their causes, handlers, and guarantees differ. Do not infer operating-system privilege changes from the presence of a C++ try statement.

topics.title: 20.2 Interrupts
topics.summary: An interrupt is commonly an externally generated event delivered to a processor, such as a timer or device notification. Its timing is asynchronous with respect to the program’s intended instruction sequence. The interrupted program did not necessarily request the event and may have no direct relationship to the device that generated it. Interrupt handling must preserve the context required by the architecture and kernel. A handler may acknowledge an event, make work runnable, and defer lengthy processing. Interrupts are one reason that elapsed wall time can exceed a program’s own CPU execution time. They are also one reason that a single-core system can exhibit interleavings even without simultaneous application execution.

cards.question: Explain 20.2 Interrupts. What mechanism, rule, or distinction must you remember?
cards.answer: An interrupt is commonly an externally generated event delivered to a processor, such as a timer or device notification. Its timing is asynchronous with respect to the program’s intended instruction sequence. The interrupted program did not necessarily request the event and may have no direct relationship to the device that generated it. Interrupt handling must preserve the context required by the architecture and kernel. A handler may acknowledge an event, make work runnable, and defer lengthy processing. Interrupts are one reason that elapsed wall time can exceed a program’s own CPU execution time. They are also one reason that a single-core system can exhibit interleavings even without simultaneous application execution.

topics.title: 20.3 Traps
topics.summary: In the x86 exception classification, a trap is reported after the instruction associated with it has completed. The saved instruction location generally supports continuation after that instruction. Debugging facilities use trap-like mechanisms to regain control at intentional observation points. The word is also used more broadly in operating-systems discussions for a deliberate transfer into privileged handling. When reading documentation, identify which meaning applies. A precise trace should state whether the current instruction will be retried, whether the next instruction will run, or whether execution will end. Those distinctions matter more than an ambiguous label.

topics.title: 20.4 Faults
topics.summary: A fault is reported in a way that can support restarting the faulting instruction after the underlying condition is corrected. A page fault is the central example: the instruction attempts a memory access, translation or protection checks fail, and the kernel decides whether the access is legitimate and recoverable. Recoverable does not mean automatically recovered. A legitimate demand-paged access may cause the kernel to install a mapping and retry the instruction. An access to an invalid address may instead lead to a signal and process termination. The same architectural entry mechanism can therefore serve both routine resource management and error reporting.

topics.title: 20.5 System calls
topics.summary: A system call is an explicit request for a kernel service through an operating-system ABI. A C library wrapper translates a source-level interface into that ABI and translates the result back into the library’s conventions. Some library operations require several system calls; others require none for a particular invocation. The Linux x86-64 system-call register convention is not identical to the System V function-call convention from Chapter 17. In particular, the fourth integer system-call argument uses %r10 , not %rcx , and syscall has specific effects on %rcx and %r11 . Handwritten wrappers must respect the correct ABI. This book normally uses documented C interfaces instead of embedding raw system-call assembly. [ R46 ]

topics.title: 20.6 User-to-kernel transition
topics.summary: A protected entry transfers control to a destination configured by privileged software. The entry path establishes the kernel’s execution environment and records state needed for a return. Do not picture every entry as an ordinary call instruction that simply pushes a return address on the application’s stack. For example, x86-64 syscall does not itself perform a conventional push of the entire user context onto a kernel stack. The processor provides specified register and control-state changes, and kernel entry code performs additional work, including establishing suitable stack state. The exact entry sequence is architecture- and kernel-dependent. The stable lesson is that user-supplied state must not be trusted merely because execution is now privileged. [ R3 ]

topics.title: 20.7 Kernel-to-user return
topics.summary: Before returning, the kernel prepares a valid user execution context and a result. The return may resume the original user instruction stream, deliver a signal through an arranged user-space path, or select another runnable task before the original one eventually continues. A system call that blocks is not completed by busy-waiting in user code. The kernel can place the caller in a waiting state and schedule other work. When the relevant event occurs, the caller becomes eligible to run again. Becoming runnable and actually receiving CPU time are distinct events; scheduling determines the latter.

topics.title: 20.8 Timer interrupts
topics.summary: Timer facilities let the kernel regain control and account for or schedule work. A runnable process cannot assume that avoiding voluntary system calls grants it indefinite uninterrupted use of a CPU. The hardware timer and scheduling mechanisms provide opportunities to reconsider execution. Modern systems need not use a simplistic fixed periodic tick for every purpose. Exact timing and scheduling policy vary. For reasoning about an application, the important fact is that preemption can occur between operations that appear adjacent in source code. A sequence is not atomic merely because it is short or usually finishes within one timer interval. [ R38 ]

topics.title: Worked example — System-call round trip
topics.summary: A user program calling read eventually enters the kernel through the platform’s system-call mechanism. Hardware changes privilege context and transfers to a registered kernel entry path. The kernel validates the descriptor and user buffer, performs or schedules the operation, places a result in the calling convention’s return location, and returns to user mode. The library wrapper then exposes the result to C code.

topics.title: Worked example — Fault versus interrupt
topics.summary: A page fault is synchronous with the instruction that attempted the access: retrying that instruction may succeed after the mapping is fixed. A timer interrupt is asynchronous with respect to the current instruction stream and is generated by hardware timing. Both transfer control to privileged handlers, but their causes and restart semantics differ.

topics.title: Chapter 21 — Processes
topics.summary: A process is an operating-system-managed execution environment. It combines an address space, references to resources, credentials, and one or more threads of execution. The abstraction gives a program the appearance of its own machine while allowing the kernel to share actual processors, memory, and devices among many programs. Processes are not identical to executable files. Several processes can run the same executable, and one process can replace its program image with another through exec . A process also need not have exactly one thread. These distinctions become important when considering scheduling, resource ownership, and process creation. [ R15 , R16 , R38 ]

topics.title: 21.1 Process abstraction
topics.summary: The process abstraction groups resources and identity. Its virtual address space determines which addresses have meaning; its descriptor table determines what small descriptor numbers refer to; its credentials help determine which requests are allowed. Two processes can use the integer descriptor 3 for entirely different files. A thread is an execution stream within that environment. Threads in one process usually share mappings and many resources while retaining their own register state and stacks. Therefore, “switching processes” and “switching threads” are related but not interchangeable descriptions. The scheduler chooses runnable execution entities, while the process abstraction supplies much of their shared environment.

topics.title: 21.2 Process state
topics.summary: A simple state model includes running, runnable, waiting, stopped, and terminated states. Runnable means eligible for CPU execution; running means currently executing. A process waiting for input is not made faster merely by adding more CPU time if the required input has not arrived. A terminated child may temporarily remain as a zombie until its parent collects the termination information. The zombie is not executing the old program. Its remaining bookkeeping supports the parent’s ability to retrieve status. Real kernels expose more detailed states than this teaching model, but the model is sufficient to separate eligibility, execution, and event waiting.

topics.title: 21.3 CPU context
topics.summary: CPU context includes the register and control state needed to resume an execution stream. It encompasses more than the source-level local variables a programmer can name. The instruction pointer, stack pointer, flags, and other architecture-defined state influence what happens next. Not all context is necessarily saved and restored through one identical path. Kernel implementations optimize context handling, and architecture extensions enlarge the state that may need management. For reasoning, the essential requirement is preservation of the execution semantics promised to the program. A resumed thread must not receive another thread’s live register values as though they were its own.

topics.title: 21.4 Address space
topics.summary: An address space defines the virtual mappings visible to a process. It contains executable code, data, stacks, dynamically allocated regions, shared mappings, and reserved or inaccessible gaps. Two processes can map different physical storage at the same virtual address. Conversely, two processes can map the same physical storage at different virtual addresses. This is how shared mappings can coexist with otherwise distinct address spaces. A pointer stored in shared memory is therefore not automatically meaningful in another process. Use offsets or another explicitly designed representation when the same region may appear at different base addresses.

topics.title: 21.5 Process isolation
topics.summary: Isolation limits the ability of one process to read or modify another process’s private state. Page tables and permissions provide a major hardware-backed mechanism. Kernel policy controls explicit exceptions, such as shared mappings and authorized debugging interfaces. Isolation is a security and reliability boundary, but it is not an absolute statement that processes can never communicate or interfere indirectly. They may share files, services, CPU capacity, and other resources. An application must distinguish intentional communication from accidental sharing and must still validate input received across process boundaries.

topics.title: 21.6 Context switching
topics.summary: A context switch changes which execution stream uses a processor. It requires saving and restoring relevant state and may involve changing the active address-space context. Switching between threads in the same process can avoid some address-space changes, but it still has scheduling and execution-state costs. The effects extend beyond the instructions that perform the switch. A different working set can displace useful cache entries or translations. Conversely, a context switch does not imply that all caches are universally flushed. Actual hardware and kernel mechanisms determine which state remains useful. Avoid reducing context-switch cost to one supposedly universal number.

topics.title: 21.7 Scheduling
topics.summary: Scheduling selects runnable work according to policy and constraints. General-purpose scheduling balances responsiveness, fairness, and throughput; real-time policies make different tradeoffs and require careful system-level design. Application priorities do not create CPU capacity that does not exist. A scheduling trace must include waiting as well as computation. A server may consume little CPU because it is blocked on clients, not because it is efficient. A compute-heavy application may scale until it encounters memory bandwidth or synchronization limits. Measure runnable demand, actual execution, and blocking causes separately before changing priorities or thread counts. [ R38 ]

topics.title: Worked example — A scheduling model with waiting
topics.summary: Assume one CPU, zero switching overhead, and a scheduler that gives a newly runnable job the next available opportunity. Job A needs 2 milliseconds of CPU, then waits 5 milliseconds for I/O, then needs 1 millisecond of CPU. Job B needs 4 milliseconds of CPU and never blocks. Both are ready at time zero, and A starts first. A consumes 3 milliseconds of CPU but finishes after 8 milliseconds of wall time. B consumes 4 milliseconds and finishes at time 6. The CPU performs 7 milliseconds of useful work during an 8-millisecond observation interval, giving modeled utilization of 7 / 8 = 87.5% . This calculation assumes that the I/O wait completes at time 7 independently of B. It excludes kernel work, interrupt overhead, and real scheduling details. The point is not to predict a production trace but to establish the vocabulary and accounting needed to interpret one.

Both are ready at time zero, and A starts first. A consumes 3 milliseconds of CPU but finishes after 8 milliseconds of wall time. B consumes 4 milliseconds and finishes at time 6. The CPU performs 7 milliseconds of useful work during an 8-millisecond observation interval, giving modeled utilization of 7 / 8 = 87.5% . This calculation assumes that the I/O wait completes at time 7 independently of B. It excludes kernel work, interrupt overhead, and real scheduling details. The point is not to predict a production trace but to establish the vocabulary and accounting needed to interpret one.

topics.title: Chapter 22 — Virtual Address Spaces
topics.summary: A pointer used by an ordinary process usually identifies a location in that process’s virtual address space. It is not a direct index into installed DRAM. Translation lets the system place data in physical storage independently of the addresses used by the program, share selected storage, and reject accesses that violate mapping permissions. Virtual memory is not simply “using disk as extra RAM.” Paging to storage is one possible policy built on translation. Isolation, controlled sharing, sparse address spaces, and flexible placement are useful even when every actively used page remains in physical memory. [ R3 , R10 ]

topics.title: 22.1 Virtual addresses
topics.summary: A virtual address is interpreted in an address-space context. The same numeric address in two processes can designate unrelated objects. The meaning of an address also changes over time when a mapping is removed and another mapping occupies the same range. Do not infer usable address-space size from pointer size alone. A 64-bit pointer representation does not imply that all 64 bits are available as independent implemented virtual-address bits. x86-64 configurations support particular address widths and canonical-address rules. The examples here use explicitly stated simplified widths rather than treating one hardware configuration as universal.

topics.title: 22.2 Physical addresses
topics.summary: A physical address identifies a location in the processor’s physical address map. That map can include ordinary memory and regions associated with devices; physical does not mean that every possible address corresponds to an installed DRAM byte. The operating system manages physical frames and establishes mappings that connect them to virtual pages. Applications normally neither choose arbitrary frames nor rely on a mapping remaining attached to one frame forever. Moving or replacing backing storage is possible as long as the required observable behavior is preserved and the translation machinery is updated correctly.

blocks.text:

topics.title: 22.3 Address translation
topics.summary: Translation maps a virtual address to a physical address while checking the requested access. A useful teaching decomposition is virtual address = virtual page number + page offset . The page number selects a mapping; the offset identifies the byte within that page. With equal-sized pages and frames, translation preserves the offset. Translation is therefore not an arbitrary byte-by-byte lookup. Contiguous bytes within one mapped page share the same mapping and permissions at the paging granularity. An access that spans a page boundary can involve more than one translation and can encounter different permissions on the two pages.

topics.title: 22.4 Memory isolation
topics.summary: Separate address-space mappings allow the kernel to keep one process’s private storage inaccessible to another. Permission checks further distinguish reads, writes, instruction fetches, and user versus supervisor access, subject to the architecture and configuration. The word private requires context. A private mapping can initially share physical storage through copy-on-write while preserving logically private modification semantics. Isolation describes what each process is allowed to observe and change, not necessarily whether every byte has a unique physical copy at every instant.

topics.title: 22.5 Shared memory
topics.summary: Shared memory deliberately maps common storage into more than one execution environment. A store through one mapping can become visible through another according to the platform’s memory and synchronization rules. This avoids copying every message through a separate transfer buffer, but it does not remove the need for a communication protocol. Shared-memory programs must define ownership, synchronization, initialization, and recovery from participant failure. They must also avoid assuming equal virtual base addresses. An offset of 128 bytes from the shared region’s base is portable across mappings of that region; an ordinary process-local pointer stored there may not be.

topics.title: Worked example — Equal numbers, different storage
topics.summary: Assume 4-KiB pages. Process A maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 12; process B maps virtual page 4 to physical frame 27. Both load from virtual address 0x4123 . The virtual page number is 0x4 , and the offset is 0x123 . A reaches physical address 0xC123 ; B reaches 0x1B123 . The same pointer bits do not imply shared data. Now suppose A maps virtual page 8 and B maps virtual page 9 to physical frame 30. A’s 0x8080 and B’s 0x9080 both identify physical address 0x1E080 . These calculations illustrate two independent properties: equal virtual addresses can refer to different storage, and different virtual addresses can refer to shared storage. They say nothing by themselves about access permission or synchronization. A correct access requires the mapping and the requested operation to be allowed.

topics.title: Worked example — Same virtual address, different memory
topics.summary: Process A and process B can each map virtual address 0x400000 to different physical frames. Both programs can therefore use the same conventional layout without reading each other’s data. Address translation combines the active process’s mapping state with the virtual address; the numeric virtual address alone does not identify a unique physical byte system-wide.

topics.title: Worked example — Intentional shared mapping
topics.summary: Two processes may map the same shared-memory object into different virtual addresses. A store by one process then changes the underlying physical storage observed by the other, subject to synchronization requirements. Shared memory is therefore created by common backing, not by requiring identical virtual addresses.

topics.title: Chapter 23 — Paging
topics.summary: Paging divides virtual address spaces and physical storage into fixed-size units. This simplifies placement: a virtual page can be backed by any suitable physical frame of the corresponding size. It also makes translation arithmetic systematic. The system trades fine-grained flexibility against page-table overhead, internal waste, and translation-cache coverage. [ R10 ]

topics.title: 23.1 Pages
topics.summary: A page is a fixed-size unit in the virtual address space. A mapping associates a virtual page with backing storage and permissions. Pages should not be confused with C objects: a page can contain many objects, part of one object, or bytes that no live language object currently occupies. A large allocation can span many pages. Crossing its internal page boundaries is valid when the allocation and mappings permit it. Conversely, staying within one page does not prove an array index is valid. Object-level bounds and page-level mapping boundaries solve different problems.

topics.title: 23.2 Frames
topics.summary: A frame is a page-sized unit of physical storage. The kernel tracks which frames are free, in use, shared, or involved in other memory-management activity. A virtual page number and a physical frame number need not be equal. The distinction makes noncontiguous physical placement possible. Three adjacent virtual pages can be backed by frames 5, 200, and 9 while still appearing contiguous to the application. Device operations requiring particular physical arrangements need additional platform mechanisms; virtual contiguity alone is not a guarantee of physical contiguity.

topics.title: 23.3 Page size
topics.summary: For the following calculations, the page size is 4 KiB, or 4096 bytes. This is a teaching assumption, not a claim that every mapping on every system uses that size. Systems can support multiple page sizes, and applications should query the relevant platform interface where a runtime page size matters. Larger pages increase the amount of memory covered by one translation entry and reduce some table overhead. They can also waste more space for small or sparsely touched regions and complicate allocation or migration. The best size depends on workload and system policy, not merely on choosing the largest supported number.

topics.title: 23.4 Page offset
topics.summary: For a page size of 2^p bytes, the low p address bits form the page offset. With 4096-byte pages, p = 12 . The offset is address mod 4096 , or equivalently address & 0xFFF for the nonnegative integer model. Translation preserves these low bits when mapping a page to an equal-sized frame. Only the page-number portion changes. This separation makes the final physical-address calculation straightforward and explains why correctly aligned page bases have zeroes in the offset positions.

topics.title: 23.5 Virtual page number
topics.summary: The virtual page number is the address divided by page size, rounded down. In the bit model, it is address >> p . It identifies which page-table mapping applies, potentially through several levels of indexing. The number of bits available for the virtual page number depends on the virtual-address model. In a 32-bit model with 4-KiB pages, there are 20 virtual-page-number bits and 12 offset bits. Do not transfer those counts unchanged to a different address width or page size.

topics.title: 23.6 Physical page number
topics.summary: The physical page number, also called a frame number in this discussion, identifies the selected frame. If the frame number is f , its base address is f * page_size . Add the original offset to obtain the final physical address. A page-table entry contains more than a frame number, so real software cannot treat every bit of an entry as an address. Flag bits and architecture-specific encodings must be interpreted correctly. The arithmetic below deliberately uses a dictionary of already-decoded frame numbers to isolate the translation concept.

topics.title: Worked example — Counting pages
topics.summary: A 10,000-byte region starting on a page boundary spans ceil(10000/4096)=3 pages. If the region begins 3,000 bytes into a page, it consumes the remaining 1,096 bytes of that page plus enough later pages for the rest, so alignment of the start address can increase the number of pages touched.

topics.title: Chapter 24 — Page Tables
topics.summary: A page table describes mappings and their permissions. Large address spaces make a single fully populated flat table expensive, so many architectures use a hierarchy in which intermediate entries point to lower-level tables. Unused regions can then avoid allocating all possible lower-level structures. [ R3 , R10 ]

topics.title: 24.1 Page-table entries
topics.summary: A page-table entry encodes mapping information and control bits. Depending on its level and configuration, it can point to another table or describe a mapped page. It may include a physical address, presence information, access permissions, and status used by memory-management policy. An entry is not a portable C structure whose bit layout can be guessed from a diagram for another architecture. Kernel code must follow the architecture’s encoding and required update procedures. Ordinary user programs should reason about the behavior exposed by mapping APIs instead of attempting to manipulate active page tables.

topics.title: 24.2 Present bit
topics.summary: A present indicator tells hardware whether an entry is valid for the corresponding translation step. An absent entry can cause a page fault. The kernel may use nonpresent encodings and its own metadata to remember whether the region is demand-paged, swapped, invalid, or associated with another policy. Therefore, “not present” does not automatically mean “read this page from disk.” The handler must first establish that the access is legitimate. A zero-filled anonymous page may require no file read at all. A completely invalid address must not be repaired by granting access merely because a fault occurred.

topics.title: 24.3 Writable bit
topics.summary: A writable permission controls whether stores are allowed under the architecture’s access rules. A mapping can be readable without being writable. Copy-on-write commonly uses a temporarily nonwritable hardware mapping for a region that is logically permitted to become privately writable after a fault. Permission interpretation can involve multiple levels and processor controls. It is unsafe to inspect only one leaf bit and conclude that an access must succeed. The complete translation and protection state determines the result. This chapter’s exercises state a simplified combined-permission rule explicitly.

topics.title: 24.4 User-accessible bit
topics.summary: A user/supervisor permission distinguishes mappings accessible to user-mode code from mappings reserved for privileged access. It helps prevent an application from treating kernel data as ordinary user memory even when some related address range exists in the broader translation structure. This hardware distinction does not replace file permissions, process credentials, or application authorization. A user-accessible buffer may still contain data that an application should not disclose to a particular network client. Memory-access enforcement and application-level information policy operate at different layers.

topics.title: 24.5 Multilevel page tables
topics.summary: A multilevel design divides the virtual page number into several indexes. Each index selects an entry in the current table; that entry leads to the next level until a mapping is found. Large-page entries can terminate a walk earlier when the architecture supports them. A familiar x86-64 example uses four levels with 9 index bits per level and a 12-bit offset, describing a 48-bit virtual-address organization subject to canonical-address rules. Other configurations can add a fifth level and expand the address width. The exact layout is a platform fact, not a consequence of the C++ pointer type alone. [ R3 , R10 ]

topics.title: 24.6 Page-table walks
topics.summary: A page-table walk follows the hierarchy to resolve a translation. Hardware performs walks on the reference architecture, potentially using internal caches for table information. The naive count of one ordinary memory access per level is a useful upper-level teaching model but not a complete performance prediction. A walk can stop because it finds a valid leaf mapping, encounters an absent entry, or detects a protection problem. Once a translation is cached in a TLB, later accesses can avoid repeating the full walk until the entry is evicted or invalidated. The next chapter separates translation caching from data caching.

topics.title: 24.7 Memory protection
topics.summary: Protection checks combine the requested operation with the applicable mapping permissions and architectural state. Reading data, writing data, and fetching instructions are not necessarily governed by identical permissions. Non-executable mappings help separate data storage from executable code. Changing a page-table entry is not enough when processors retain cached translations based on the old state. The system must perform the required invalidation and coordination. On a multicore system, other cores may also hold relevant translations; this is the reason for translation invalidation mechanisms often discussed as TLB shootdowns.

topics.title: Worked example — A two-level address decomposition
topics.summary: Use a 16-bit teaching address space with 256-byte pages and two levels of 16-entry tables. The address fields are: Address 0xABCD yields outer index 0xA , inner index 0xB , and offset 0xCD . Suppose outer entry A points to a valid inner table and inner entry B maps frame 0x34 . The translated address is 0x34CD in a physical model that supports that frame number. Now add permissions. The outer entry allows user reads and writes, but the inner entry allows only user reads. A user load succeeds; a user store fails. For this model, effective permissions are the intersection of the permissions along the path. Giving the outer entry more authority cannot override a restrictive leaf entry. A flat table for all 256 virtual pages needs 256 entries. The two-level arrangement needs one 16-entry outer table plus 16 entries for each allocated inner table. With only one populated inner table, it uses 32 entries; with all 16 inner tables allocated, it uses 272 entries. Hierarchy saves space for sparse mappings but is not automatically smaller for a fully populated tiny address space.

cards.question: Explain Worked example — A two-level address decomposition. What mechanism, rule, or distinction must you remember?
cards.answer: Use a 16-bit teaching address space with 256-byte pages and two levels of 16-entry tables. The address fields are: Address 0xABCD yields outer index 0xA , inner index 0xB , and offset 0xCD . Suppose outer entry A points to a valid inner table and inner entry B maps frame 0x34 . The translated address is 0x34CD in a physical model that supports that frame number. Now add permissions. The outer entry allows user reads and writes, but the inner entry allows only user reads. A user load succeeds; a user store fails. For this model, effective permissions are the intersection of the permissions along the path. Giving the outer entry more authority cannot override a restrictive leaf entry. A flat table for all 256 virtual pages needs 256 entries. The two-level arrangement needs one 16-entry outer table plus 16 entries for each allocated inner table. With only one populated inner table, it uses 32 entries; with all 16 inner tables allocated, it uses 272 entries. Hierarchy saves space for sparse mappings but is not automatically smaller for a fully populated tiny address space.

topics.title: Chapter 25 — Translation Hardware
topics.summary: Virtual memory would be unnecessarily expensive if every load required a full uncached traversal of page tables. Translation hardware therefore caches recently useful mappings. This cache is related to, but distinct from, the caches that hold instruction and data bytes. A program can have excellent data-cache behavior and still suffer from poor translation locality. [ R3 , R10 ]

topics.title: 25.1 MMU
topics.summary: The memory-management unit, or MMU, is the processor machinery involved in translation and access checking. It interprets the configured address-space structures according to architectural rules. Its implementation can include several translation caches and page-walk optimizations. The MMU does not understand a source-level vector or ownership model. It knows translation and permission information at the architecture’s supported granularity. This explains why a legal machine address can still produce undefined behavior in C or C++: the language may forbid an access that hardware page checks permit.

topics.title: 25.2 TLB
topics.summary: A translation lookaside buffer, or TLB, caches translations and associated permission information. A matching entry can supply the physical-frame relationship without a complete new walk. Real processors may have distinct instruction and data TLBs, multiple levels, and different handling for page sizes. TLB entries must be interpreted in the correct address-space context. Hardware and kernels can use address-space identifiers and other mechanisms to retain useful entries across switches without confusing one process’s mapping with another’s. Do not assume either that every switch flushes every translation or that retaining entries requires no context tagging.

topics.title: 25.4 TLB misses
topics.summary: A TLB miss means that the required translation is not available in the consulted translation cache. The processor can search another translation level or perform a page-table walk. If the tables describe a valid permitted mapping, the translation can be installed and the access can continue without a page fault. A page fault occurs when translation or protection rules cannot complete the access as requested. It requires software handling on the reference system. The distinction is essential: TLB miss does not imply page fault , and neither event is synonymous with a data-cache miss.

topics.title: 25.5 Translation caching
topics.summary: Translation caching rewards locality in the set of pages accessed. A rough measure called TLB reach multiplies the number of usable entries by the page size, but associativity, separate structures, mixed page sizes, and access patterns can reduce the usefulness of that simple estimate. For a teaching cache with 64 entries and 4-KiB pages, nominal reach is 256 KiB. A loop touching one byte in each of 1024 different pages can have a small useful-byte working set but a large translation working set. Packing those bytes into fewer pages can improve translation locality without changing the number of logical items.

topics.title: Worked example — Translation and data are separate events
topics.summary: Assume a fully associative, four-entry LRU TLB and a repeating virtual-page trace: The first four accesses miss and install translations. The next four hit, giving 4 hits in 8 accesses, or 50% over the entire cold trace. Repeating the four-page cycle afterward yields hits while no other activity evicts entries. Now use five pages: Every access misses under this particular capacity and replacement model. By the time a page is reused, the other four pages have displaced it. This trace does not establish anything about whether the data bytes are in L1 or DRAM, and it does not require any page fault when all mappings remain valid. An experiment that touches one byte per page should distinguish cold page allocation, first-touch faults, TLB behavior, and data-cache behavior. Timing the first traversal alone mixes several effects. A useful design initializes the mapping, records the access pattern, repeats controlled passes, and uses available counters only when their meaning and permissions are understood.

topics.title: Worked example — TLB speedup intuition
topics.summary: Without a TLB, a multilevel page-table walk can require several memory references before the actual data access. On a TLB hit, the cached translation supplies the frame mapping immediately, avoiding those walk references. The data cache lookup is still a separate concern; a TLB hit does not imply the requested data is in L1.

topics.title: Worked example — Handling a TLB miss
topics.summary: On a hardware-managed design, a TLB miss triggers a page-table walk. If the required PTEs are valid, the translation is inserted into the TLB and the memory access proceeds. If the walk discovers an absent or disallowed mapping, the result becomes a page fault rather than a successful TLB fill.

topics.title: 26.1 Missing pages
topics.summary: A missing translation can correspond to a legitimate region whose physical backing has not yet been installed. Anonymous memory can be provided lazily, and file-backed mappings can bring in pages as needed. Deferring work avoids allocating and reading pages that the application never touches. A missing page can also correspond to no valid mapping at all. The handler must consult the mapping policy rather than assume that any requested address deserves storage. Otherwise, invalid pointers would silently create new memory instead of being rejected.

topics.title: 26.2 Protection faults
topics.summary: A protection fault occurs when a mapping exists or is described, but the attempted operation is not permitted by the active protection state. Writing to a read-only mapping and fetching instructions from a non-executable mapping are examples under the relevant hardware configuration. Some protection faults are intentionally recoverable, notably copy-on-write. Others indicate an error. The handler must distinguish the region’s logical policy from its current hardware permission bits. A read-only code page is not made writable simply because a process attempted a store.

topics.title: 26.3 Demand paging
topics.summary: Demand paging supplies a page when it is actually needed. For a file mapping, the kernel can obtain the corresponding file data; for anonymous memory, it can provide zero-initialized storage consistent with the mapping’s semantics. Existing cached data can avoid a new storage-device read. The performance consequence depends on the work required. Some faults can be satisfied without reading from storage; others wait for I/O. A fault count without classification and workload context is therefore an incomplete performance metric. The same number of faults can represent very different elapsed costs.

topics.title: 26.4 Fault handling
topics.summary: Conceptually, handling involves identifying the faulting address and access, locating the mapping policy, validating the operation, obtaining suitable backing, updating translation structures, and resuming or rejecting the instruction. The kernel must synchronize this work with concurrent mapping changes and other faults. Application error handling usually does not attempt to repair arbitrary invalid pointer faults. Recovering from a corrupted execution state is much harder than catching a normal return-code error. Design programs to prevent invalid access and use operating-system errors for expected resource failures. Signal handling is discussed separately in Chapter 41.

topics.title: 26.5 Copy-on-write
topics.summary: Copy-on-write lets logically independent mappings share backing until a writer requires a private version. After fork , parent and child can initially share many physical pages while observing private-memory semantics. A write fault can cause the kernel to create a private copy for the writer and update its mapping. [ R15 ] A physical copy is not mandatory in every write-fault case. If the kernel determines that the backing is no longer shared in a way requiring separation, it may be able to make the page writable without copying. The semantic guarantee is private modification, not a promise that every store invokes a particular copying algorithm.

topics.title: Worked example — A model of private modification
topics.summary: The following model uses immutable Python bytes as initial shared content and returns a new object when a private writer changes a byte. It demonstrates the observable contract of copy-on-write; it does not claim to implement page tables or reproduce the kernel’s physical allocation decisions. Companion listing: ch26/cow_model.py The expected output is ABCD AXCD . The model copies the entire small object for every store, which is deliberately simpler than a page-based implementation. Its value is that the ownership and visibility contract can be checked without relying on process scheduling or privileged inspection. The model also clarifies a boundary: a shared mapping would require a different contract. Making a private copy is correct for private modification but wrong for a communication region whose purpose is to expose one participant’s writes to another.

topics.title: Worked example — Demand-zero allocation
topics.summary: A process may reserve a new virtual page without immediately receiving a physical frame. The first write faults because no frame is present. The kernel allocates a zeroed frame, installs a writable mapping, and restarts the instruction. The application experiences ordinary memory semantics while physical allocation is deferred until use.

topics.title: Worked example — Copy-on-write after fork
topics.summary: After fork , parent and child can initially map the same physical page read-only. If the child writes it, a protection fault lets the kernel allocate a private copy, copy the original contents, and remap the child’s page writable. The parent’s mapping still references the original frame. Copying is paid only for pages actually modified.

topics.title: Chapter 27 — Memory Hierarchy
topics.summary: A computer does not store every useful byte in one uniformly fast place. It uses a hierarchy of storage technologies and structures with different capacities, access costs, and management rules. Programs perform well when frequently needed information remains in the levels that can serve it efficiently. This chapter uses qualitative relationships rather than a table of supposedly universal nanosecond values. Actual latency and bandwidth depend on the processor, memory configuration, access pattern, contention, power state, and measurement method. Treat hardware specifications and local measurements as evidence for a particular machine, not as constants of the language. [ R3 , R30 ]

topics.title: 27.1 Registers
topics.summary: Registers hold operands and execution state directly used by instructions. The compiler allocates many frequently used values to registers, subject to instruction constraints and calling conventions. Values that cannot remain in registers may be spilled to memory. A source-level local variable is not automatically a stack slot. It can live in a register, be folded into another expression, or disappear when it has no observable effect. Looking at generated assembly is the appropriate way to investigate a particular compiled implementation.

topics.title: 27.2 L1 cache
topics.summary: An L1 cache is a small, fast cache close to an execution core. Processors commonly distinguish instruction and data L1 caches, although exact organizations vary. Its limited capacity favors compact working sets and repeated access to nearby data. The cost of an L1 hit is not simply the cost of a complete source statement. topics.title: 27.3 L2 cache
topics.summary: L2 provides additional capacity beyond L1 at a different access cost. It can satisfy requests for lines absent from L1 without requiring a trip to main memory. Whether an L2 is private to a core or shared is a hardware design choice. A working set too large for L1 can still perform well when it fits in L2 and has predictable access. Performance often changes gradually or in steps as working-set size crosses hierarchy boundaries, rather than following a single universal “memory access” time.

topics.title: 27.4 L3 cache
topics.summary: An L3 or last-level cache often provides larger shared capacity, but names and sharing arrangements are not universal. Shared caches allow data to serve multiple cores while also creating competition for capacity and bandwidth. Cache inclusion policies vary. Do not assume that every line in a private cache must also exist in the last-level cache, or that evicting a line has identical consequences on all processors. For application design, focus first on working-set size, sharing patterns, and measured behavior.

topics.title: 27.5 DRAM
topics.summary: DRAM supplies main-memory capacity beyond the processor caches. Access cost depends on more than a single chip latency: memory controllers, channels, banks, row state, access concurrency, and NUMA placement can all matter. Bandwidth and latency limits are distinct. A workload with many independent sequential accesses may approach a bandwidth limit, while a dependent pointer-chasing workload may be limited by the latency of each next address. The same number of bytes can therefore take different times under different dependency patterns.

topics.title: 27.6 SSD
topics.summary: An SSD is persistent storage accessed through a device and operating-system stack rather than as ordinary CPU cacheable DRAM. Its behavior depends on request size, queue depth, write patterns, device state, and filesystem policy. A file read that returns quickly may have been served from the operating system’s page cache without reaching the SSD. Distinguish cached file-access measurements from device measurements. Similarly, successful buffered writes do not by themselves prove that data has reached durable media.

topics.title: 27.7 Persistent storage
topics.summary: Persistent storage is intended to retain data across power loss or restart under specified guarantees. The complete durability story involves hardware behavior, filesystem semantics, and explicit synchronization operations. Persistence is a property to request and verify at the appropriate layer, not a synonym for “the write function returned.” A robust design distinguishes data in an application buffer, data accepted by the kernel, and data committed according to the required durability contract. Chapters 35 and 59 revisit this distinction when discussing buffering and recovery. [ R33 ]

topics.title: 27.8 Latency
topics.summary: Latency is the time required for one operation or dependency to complete. A dependent chain exposes latency because later work cannot begin until earlier results are available. For example, following linked-list pointers often prevents the next address from being known in advance. Report the operation being measured. Cache-hit load latency, end-to-end request latency, and storage-read latency describe different boundaries. A number without its start event, end event, and conditions is difficult to interpret.

topics.title: 27.9 Throughput
topics.summary: Throughput is completed work per unit time. A system can have high throughput while individual requests experience substantial latency, especially when many operations overlap. Conversely, a fast isolated operation can yield poor aggregate throughput when shared resources serialize it. Useful units include bytes per second, records per second, and requests per second. Choose a unit tied to completed useful work, not merely to internal activity. Counting retries or duplicated work as successful throughput can conceal a broken design.

topics.title: 27.10 Capacity
topics.summary: Capacity is the amount of information a level can hold. Larger capacity can reduce misses, but only for data that remains useful before eviction. A cache filled with streaming data that will never be reused may displace a smaller, more valuable working set. Working-set analysis asks how much data is actively needed over a relevant interval. Total dataset size alone does not answer that question. A terabyte dataset processed in small independent tiles can have a modest active working set.

topics.title: 27.11 Cost
topics.summary: Cost includes hardware expense, energy, area, management overhead, and opportunity cost. Faster storage structures are constrained by more than purchase price. A design that used the fastest possible storage for every byte would face physical and economic limitations. The hierarchy is therefore a resource-allocation strategy. Software participates by making reuse visible, avoiding unnecessary movement, and organizing work so that scarce fast capacity holds valuable information. Optimization is often about moving fewer bytes rather than executing a cleverer arithmetic instruction.

topics.title: Worked example — Why capacity increases down the hierarchy
topics.summary: Registers are fastest but scarce; caches are larger and slower; DRAM is much larger; persistent storage is larger again. If every byte could economically have register latency and SSD capacity, a hierarchy would be unnecessary. Engineering trades latency, cost, power, and capacity at each level.

topics.title: Chapter 28 — Locality
topics.summary: Locality is a pattern of reuse. Temporal locality concerns returning to the same information, while spatial locality concerns accessing nearby information. Hardware caches and software buffers exploit these patterns by retaining recently useful data and moving adjacent bytes together. Locality is not a property of a data structure in isolation. It depends on the traversal and workload. The same matrix can be accessed in a cache-friendly or cache-hostile order, and the same linked structure can behave differently when nodes are allocated compactly rather than scattered.

blocks.text:
LECTURE NARRATION
Locality is a pattern of reuse. Temporal locality concerns returning to the same information, while spatial locality concerns accessing nearby information. Hardware caches and software buffers exploit these patterns by retaining recently useful data and moving adjacent bytes together. Locality is not a property of a data structure in isolation. It depends on the traversal and workload. The same matrix can be accessed in a cache-friendly or cache-hostile order, and the same linked structure can behave differently when nodes are allocated compactly rather than scattered.

Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

topics.title: 28.1 Temporal locality
topics.summary: Temporal locality occurs when an item used now is likely to be used again soon. A loop repeatedly updating a small set of accumulators exhibits it. Retaining those values in registers or cache avoids repeated access to slower levels. “Soon” must be interpreted relative to competing accesses and capacity. Reusing an item after touching millions of unrelated bytes may be too late for a small cache. Reuse distance—the intervening distinct data relevant to a cache model—is often more informative than elapsed time alone.

topics.title: 28.2 Spatial locality
topics.summary: Spatial locality occurs when an access predicts accesses to nearby bytes. A sequential array traversal typically uses several elements from each fetched cache line. Fetching an entire line is valuable when the remaining bytes are consumed before eviction. Spatial proximity is not automatically useful. A structure containing many rarely used fields can force frequently used fields to share lines with irrelevant data. A layout that groups the fields used together may reduce transferred bytes without changing the logical records.

topics.title: 28.3 Working sets
topics.summary: A working set is the collection of data and instructions actively used during a relevant phase or interval. Its size and access order determine pressure on caches, TLBs, and physical memory. Different phases of one program can have different working sets. A useful analysis chooses a time scale: one inner loop, one request, one batch, or a steady-state interval. Counting every allocation in the process may overestimate the hot working set, while counting only explicit input arrays may omit indexes, metadata, code, and thread stacks.

topics.title: 28.4 Sequential access
topics.summary: Sequential access follows adjacent locations in a predictable order. It can use most bytes of each cache line and allow hardware prefetching to anticipate future accesses. It also often reduces translation pressure by consuming many bytes within each page. The benefit depends on actual use. Reading a large array once still incurs compulsory traffic. Sequential order makes that traffic efficient; it does not make the bytes free. Streaming too much unrelated data can also evict useful cached state.

topics.title: 28.5 Strided access
topics.summary: Strided access advances by a fixed distance between elements. Small strides may retain useful spatial locality; large strides may touch a new line or page for every item. Particular stride patterns can also interact poorly with cache-set indexing. When analyzing a stride, express it in bytes. A stride of 16 elements means 64 bytes for four-byte elements but 128 bytes for eight-byte elements. Element count without element size does not determine cache-line use.

topics.title: 28.6 Random access
topics.summary: Random access uses an order that is difficult to predict from recent addresses. It can reduce prefetch usefulness and increase the number of distinct lines or pages needed for a small amount of useful data. Randomness should be defined carefully: a random permutation of a compact array differs from pointers distributed across a much larger heap. A benchmark should generate its access order outside the timed region when the goal is to measure memory traversal rather than random-number generation. It should also preserve dependencies intentionally: independent random loads and dependent pointer chasing test different limits.

topics.title: Worked example — Row-major versus column-major traversal
topics.summary: Assume a row-major 64 × 64 matrix of eight-byte elements and 64-byte cache lines. A row contains 512 bytes, or eight lines. Traversing a row consecutively uses eight elements from each line before moving on. A column traversal advances by 512 bytes between successive elements. It touches one element in each of 64 different rows before returning to the next element of the first row. If the relevant cache cannot retain those lines, much of each fetched line is wasted before reuse. If it can retain them, the difference may be smaller. Capacity and associativity determine the result; “column traversal always misses” is too strong. A blocked traversal processes a smaller rectangle before moving elsewhere. For example, an 8 × 8 tile contains 512 bytes of element data. In a transpose or matrix operation, choosing tiles whose active input and output regions fit the useful cache budget can preserve reuse. Include all simultaneously active arrays and temporary storage when estimating the budget.

topics.title: Worked example — Temporal locality in a counter
topics.summary: A loop that increments count every iteration repeatedly accesses the same small piece of state, demonstrating temporal locality. Once its cache line is loaded, many subsequent updates can hit in cache. If the loop instead touches a fresh random page each iteration, reuse falls dramatically and translation/cache misses become more frequent.

topics.title: Worked example — Stride and cache lines
topics.summary: For 64-byte cache lines and 8-byte elements, sequentially reading doubles uses eight neighboring elements per fetched line. Reading every eighth double touches one element per line. Reading every sixteenth skips a full line between accesses. Larger strides therefore waste more fetched bytes and reduce spatial locality.
