topics.title: Chapter 29 — Cache Organization
topics.summary: A cache stores copies of blocks from a larger addressable space. Its organization determines where a block may reside and how hardware recognizes whether the requested block is present. The following models use byte addresses and power-of-two sizes to make the arithmetic transparent. Real processors add details such as physical or virtual indexing choices, coherence states, replacement approximations, and multiple cache levels. Use the simplified models to understand mapping and conflicts, not to infer every detail of a particular CPU from a virtual address alone. [ R3 ]

topics.title: 29.1 Cache blocks
topics.summary: A block is the fixed-size unit transferred between levels in the model. If blocks contain 64 bytes, addresses 0 through 63 belong to block 0, and addresses 64 through 127 belong to block 1. The block number is address / block_size , rounded down. The within-block offset selects the requested byte after the correct block has been found. Fetching a block can benefit later accesses to any of its bytes.

topics.title: 29.2 Cache lines
topics.summary: A cache line is the cache storage associated with one block’s data and its identifying state. Informal usage often treats “block” and “line” as interchangeable, but distinguishing the transferred block from its cache-resident slot can clarify replacement. A line contains metadata as well as data: a tag, validity information, and potentially dirty and coherence state. Capacity specifications usually refer to data capacity rather than including every metadata bit.

Informal usage often treats “block” and “line” as interchangeable, but distinguishing the transferred block from its cache-resident slot can clarify replacement. A line contains metadata as well as data: a tag, validity information, and potentially dirty and coherence state. Capacity specifications usually refer to data capacity rather than including every metadata bit.

topics.title: 29.3 Cache slots
topics.summary: A slot is a possible resident location for a block. A direct-mapped cache gives each block exactly one eligible slot. More associative organizations give a block several or all slots as candidates. Replacement selects among eligible resident lines, not among arbitrary locations that the indexing rule forbids. This distinction is why unused capacity in one set does not necessarily help a different set that is experiencing conflicts.

topics.title: 29.4 Cache sets
topics.summary: A set groups the eligible slots for a mapping. If a cache has S sets and E ways per set, it has S*E data-line slots. A block maps to one set and can occupy one of that set’s ways. A two-way cache does not mean two sets. It means two eligible line positions within each set. Keep set count, associativity, and line size separate when calculating capacity.

topics.title: 29.5 Tags
topics.summary: A tag identifies which of the many blocks mapping to a set occupies a particular valid line. After selecting the set, the cache compares the requested tag with the valid resident tags. A tag match without a valid line is not a hit. Other state can affect whether a request can proceed, especially for writes in a coherent system. The basic read-only model tracks validity and tag identity.

topics.title: 29.7 Direct-mapped caches
topics.summary: A direct-mapped cache has one way per set. Lookup and replacement are simple because each block has one possible location. Two frequently used blocks that map to the same set can repeatedly evict each other even when other sets are empty. This behavior is a conflict, not a shortage of total line slots alone. Changing layout, padding, or associativity can alter the conflict pattern. Whether such a change helps an actual application must be measured under the real cache organization.

topics.title: 29.8 Set-associative caches
topics.summary: An E -way set-associative cache permits up to E resident blocks in each set. Associativity reduces some conflicts at the cost of more lookup and replacement complexity. It does not eliminate capacity limits or every conflict pattern. For example, a two-way set repeatedly accessed by three mutually conflicting blocks can still thrash under LRU. More ways help only when the increased flexibility retains useful blocks that would otherwise be displaced.

topics.title: 29.9 Fully associative caches
topics.summary: A fully associative cache allows a block to occupy any line slot. In the model, it has one set and as many ways as resident lines. This removes set-index conflicts but leaves finite capacity and replacement decisions. Fully associative models are useful reference points for classifying misses. They are not automatically practical implementations for large, low-latency hardware caches because searching and maintaining many candidate entries has costs.

topics.title: Worked example — Decomposing an address
topics.summary: Assume a 32-KiB data cache, 64-byte lines, and eight ways. The set count is: There are 6 offset bits and 6 set-index bits. For address 0x1234 , the offset is 0x34 (52), the set is 0x08 (8), and the tag is 0x1 . The block number is 0x48 , or 72; 72 mod 64 = 8 . Address 0x2234 has the same offset and set but tag 2. The two addresses can coexist in different ways of the same set. In a direct-mapped cache with the same 64 sets and line size, they would compete for one line position. Notice that holding set count fixed while changing associativity also changes total capacity; fair comparisons must state which dimensions remain fixed.

For address 0x1234 , the offset is 0x34 (52), the set is 0x08 (8), and the tag is 0x1 . The block number is 0x48 , or 72; 72 mod 64 = 8 . Address 0x2234 has the same offset and set but tag 2. The two addresses can coexist in different ways of the same set. In a direct-mapped cache with the same 64 sets and line size, they would compete for one line position. Notice that holding set count fixed while changing associativity also changes total capacity; fair comparisons must state which dimensions remain fixed.

topics.title: Worked example — Finding set and tag bits
topics.summary: For a 32 KiB, 8-way cache with 64-byte lines, there are 32768/(64 × 8)=64 sets. Six offset bits select a byte within a line and six index bits select one of 64 sets. Remaining address bits form the tag. Two addresses with equal set index but different tags may coexist up to the associativity limit.

topics.title: Worked example — Direct-mapped conflict
topics.summary: In a direct-mapped cache, each memory block has exactly one destination set. If two frequently used blocks map to the same set, alternating accesses can evict each other even when the cache has plenty of unused capacity elsewhere. Increasing associativity can remove this conflict without increasing total capacity.

topics.title: Chapter 30 — Cache Behavior
topics.summary: Cache behavior is a sequence-dependent property. A cache starts in some state, each access either finds a usable resident block or requires additional work, and each insertion or update changes the state seen by later accesses. A hit rate without the access trace and initial conditions can be misleading.

topics.title: 30.1 Cache hit
topics.summary: A hit occurs when the requested block is present in a usable cache entry. The model can satisfy the access at that level. A hit does not imply zero cost; lookup, data delivery, dependencies, and other execution constraints remain. For writes in a coherent machine, a resident line may still require permission acquisition or coordination. The simple examples in this chapter use reads so that tag residency is sufficient to classify a hit.

topics.title: 30.2 Cache miss
topics.summary: A miss occurs when the consulted cache cannot satisfy the request from a usable resident entry. The system obtains the block from another source, potentially another cache, another core, or memory, depending on the hierarchy and coherence state. The cost is not necessarily a full trip to DRAM. An L1 miss that hits in L2 differs from a last-level miss. State which cache level is being discussed and whether a miss rate is local to that level or relative to all original accesses.

topics.title: 30.3 Hit rate
topics.summary: Hit rate is hits divided by accesses for the stated cache and interval. If 90 of 100 accesses hit, the rate is 90%. A cold-start interval can have a lower rate than steady state even when the repeated workload is unchanged. Aggregate hit rate can conceal expensive phases or uneven requests. A large number of cheap hits does not necessarily compensate for a small number of extremely costly misses on a critical dependency chain.

A cold-start interval can have a lower rate than steady state even when the repeated workload is unchanged. Aggregate hit rate can conceal expensive phases or uneven requests. A large number of cheap hits does not necessarily compensate for a small number of extremely costly misses on a critical dependency chain.

topics.title: 30.4 Miss rate
topics.summary: Miss rate is misses divided by accesses. In the simple model where each access is exactly one hit or miss, it equals 1 - hit_rate . Multilevel rates require careful denominators: an L2 local miss rate counts misses among requests that reached L2. If L1 misses on 10% of original accesses and L2 misses on 20% of those, then 2% of original accesses miss both levels. Adding 10% and 20% would be the wrong calculation.

topics.title: 30.5 Compulsory misses
topics.summary: A compulsory miss is the first access to a block in a cold-cache reference model. The block has not yet been brought into the cache by a prior access in that model. Larger lines can reduce the number of distinct blocks for a sequential region but can also fetch unused bytes. Prefetching changes when a block is brought in and how demand misses are observed. It does not make data transfer disappear. When classifying misses, state whether the model includes prefetching and what initial cache state is assumed.

topics.title: 30.6 Capacity misses
topics.summary: A capacity miss occurs because the useful working set exceeds the cache’s available storage under the chosen reference model. Even a fully associative cache of the same capacity cannot retain everything needed across the reuse interval. The common three-category classification compares behavior against a fully associative reference cache with a specified replacement policy, often LRU. Classification depends on that reference. It is not a universal label attached permanently to an address.

topics.title: 30.7 Conflict misses
topics.summary: A conflict miss arises from restricted placement in sets when a fully associative reference cache of the same capacity would have retained the block. Repeated collisions can cause misses even when the total active block count is no greater than cache capacity. The compulsory/capacity/conflict model is useful but incomplete for coherent multiprocessors. Invalidations, sharing, prefetch interactions, and other effects can introduce additional causes. Do not force every hardware event into a three-category model that deliberately excludes those mechanisms.

topics.title: Worked example — A small executable cache model
topics.summary: The following direct-mapped model has four lines of 16 bytes each. The trace accesses byte addresses 0, 16, 0, 64, 0, 16 . Blocks 0 and 4 both map to slot 0, while block 1 maps to slot 1. Companion listing: ch30/cache.py The output is M M H M M H , followed by hits=2 misses=4 . First references to blocks 0, 1, and 4 are compulsory misses. The later miss on block 0 is a conflict miss relative to a four-line fully associative LRU cache, which could retain all three blocks. The overall hit rate is 2/6 , approximately 33.3%. No cycle count follows from that percentage alone. A cost model is needed to translate the event sequence into a time estimate.

topics.title: Worked example — Classifying first and repeated misses
topics.summary: The first access to a never-seen cache block is compulsory. If the working set exceeds total cache capacity and a block is evicted because too much distinct data is active, the later miss can be capacity-related. If two blocks collide in the same limited-associativity set despite enough total capacity, the misses are conflicts.

topics.title: Worked example — Computing hit rate
topics.summary: If 9,600 of 10,000 accesses hit, the hit rate is 9600/10000 = 96% and miss rate is 4%. This aggregate alone does not explain performance: where misses go, whether they overlap, and whether they are instruction or data misses also matter.

topics.title: Chapter 31 — Cache Replacement
topics.summary: When a set is full and a new block must be installed, the cache chooses a resident victim. Replacement policy attempts to retain blocks that will be useful again. Because future accesses are usually unknown, practical policies use limited history and inexpensive approximations. The policies in this chapter apply to abstract caches and also illuminate software caches, page replacement, and bounded object stores. Actual processor caches need not implement exact LRU. The best policy depends on the workload, implementation cost, and information available. [ R3 ]

topics.title: 31.1 FIFO
topics.summary: First in, first out evicts the block that entered earliest among the eligible residents. Hits do not refresh its position. FIFO is simple because insertion age, rather than every access, determines replacement order. Insertion age can be a poor predictor of future use. A frequently accessed old block may be evicted while a newer block that will never be reused remains. FIFO also lacks the general stack property associated with exact LRU, so increasing capacity does not guarantee fewer misses for every trace.

topics.title: 31.2 LRU
topics.summary: Least recently used evicts the block whose most recent access is oldest. Hits refresh recency. It exploits the assumption that recently used blocks are more likely to be used again soon. Exact LRU requires tracking access order, which has a cost. Hardware often uses approximations or other policies. LRU can also perform poorly on cyclic scans slightly larger than capacity: every returning block may have just been evicted.

topics.title: 31.3 Optimal replacement
topics.summary: Optimal replacement evicts the block whose next use lies farthest in the future, or that will never be used again. With a fully known trace, it provides a lower bound on misses for the stated cache model. It is not generally implementable online because future accesses are unknown. Its purpose is comparison: it separates unavoidable misses under the model from misses caused by a practical policy’s limited information. Calling a policy “optimal” requires specifying the objective and assumptions.

topics.title: 31.4 Eviction
topics.summary: Eviction removes a resident block to make space or satisfy another policy. Its cost depends on the block’s state. A clean copy can often be discarded; a modified copy may require propagation before its only current contents are lost. Eviction can also disrupt future locality. A streaming workload may evict a small hot set and then immediately require that set again. Software techniques such as separating phases or limiting batch size can sometimes reduce this interference.

topics.title: 31.5 Dirty blocks
topics.summary: A dirty block contains modifications not yet reflected in the next level according to a write-back policy. Evicting it requires preserving those modifications through the appropriate writeback path. Dirty state therefore adds work beyond fetching the incoming block. Dirty does not mean corrupted. It means newer than the backing copy at the relevant level. The term applies similarly to file-cache pages whose updates have not yet been written according to the filesystem’s policy.

topics.title: 31.6 Clean blocks
topics.summary: A clean block matches the relevant backing copy under the cache’s protocol. It can be discarded without losing unique modifications. A later access may fetch it again if needed. topics.title: Worked example — FIFO and LRU choose different victims
topics.summary: Use a fully associative three-line cache and the block trace: After loading A, B, and C, both caches are full. The next A is a hit. FIFO retains insertion order A, B, C ; LRU updates recency to B, C, A , from oldest to newest. When D arrives, FIFO evicts A, while LRU evicts B. The final A therefore misses under FIFO and hits under LRU. FIFO has five misses and one hit; LRU has four misses and two hits. This trace demonstrates a difference, not a proof that LRU wins on every trace. Another workload can favor a different policy. Now mark A dirty before D arrives. FIFO’s eviction requires writeback of A in a write-back model; LRU’s eviction of clean B does not. The event counts alone still do not yield time: the model must say whether writeback overlaps other work and how much each operation costs.

topics.title: Worked example — Dirty versus clean eviction
topics.summary: Evicting a clean cache line can simply discard it because lower memory already has the same data. Evicting a dirty line in a write-back cache requires writing its modified contents to the next level before reuse of the slot. Dirty state therefore changes eviction cost.

topics.title: 32.1 Average memory-access time
topics.summary: A simple one-level model is: The word additional is important. If the penalty already includes the hit lookup, adding hit time again double-counts it. For two levels, a common serial model is L1 hit time + L1 miss rate * (L2 access time + L2 local miss rate * memory penalty) . This model excludes overlap, out-of-order execution, bandwidth saturation, prefetching, and dependencies among requests. It is useful for accounting and comparisons, not a complete predictor of whole-program runtime.

topics.title: 32.2 Prefetching
topics.summary: Prefetching requests data before demand needs it. Hardware may recognize access patterns; software can sometimes provide explicit hints. Effective prefetching hides latency when requests arrive early enough and the data remains useful until consumption. Prefetching too early can evict useful data. Prefetching too much wastes bandwidth and cache capacity. It also cannot remove a true dependency that prevents the future address from being known. Start with an access pattern that naturally exposes locality before adding architecture-specific hints.

topics.title: 32.3 Batching
topics.summary: Batching groups work so that setup and transfer costs are shared. Processing several records together can reuse metadata, amortize system calls, and expose independent memory operations. It can also increase latency for an individual record waiting for the batch to fill. Bound batch size by both resource capacity and service requirements. An unbounded batch can grow the working set beyond cache, delay cancellation, and exhaust memory. A useful batch is large enough to amortize overhead but small enough to preserve locality and responsiveness.

topics.title: 32.4 Write coalescing
topics.summary: Write coalescing combines nearby or repeated updates into fewer larger transfers. Updating several fields while a line is already present can avoid repeatedly acquiring and evicting it. Buffered file output similarly groups small writes before crossing the kernel boundary. Coalescing changes visibility and durability timing when buffering is involved. A program must still honor synchronization and persistence requirements. Do not delay a required publication or commit merely because a larger batch would be faster.

topics.title: 32.5 Cache-friendly data structures
topics.summary: A cache-friendly structure places information used together close together and avoids loading large amounts of irrelevant state. Arrays often provide compact traversal. Pointer-rich structures provide flexible updates but can add indirection, allocation overhead, and unpredictable access. An array of structures is convenient when most fields of each record are used together. A structure of arrays can be better when a loop uses only one field across many records. Neither layout is universally superior. Let the hot operations determine which bytes should travel together.

topics.title: 32.6 Cache-friendly loops
topics.summary: Cache-friendly loops traverse data in an order that preserves spatial and temporal reuse. Loop interchange can align traversal with physical layout. Blocking limits the active region. Hoisting invariant work reduces repeated computation and sometimes repeated loads. Transformations must preserve dependencies and language semantics. Reordering floating-point reductions can change results; reordering updates can break an algorithm with cross-iteration dependencies. Establish correctness constraints before treating the iteration space as freely rearrangeable.

topics.title: 32.7 Locality optimization
topics.summary: Locality optimization is a sequence: identify the hot phase, estimate its active data, inspect access order, propose a change, verify results, and measure under controlled conditions. Keep a baseline so that an appealing theory can be rejected when the data does not support it. Avoid changing several unrelated factors at once. Replacing a linked structure, changing allocation strategy, and altering the algorithm simultaneously makes it difficult to determine which change helped. A sequence of tested transformations produces more reliable conclusions and easier rollback.

topics.title: Worked example — A two-level AMAT calculation
topics.summary: Assume an L1 hit time of 1 ns, an L1 miss rate of 5%, an L2 access time of 8 ns on L1 misses, an L2 local miss rate of 20%, and an additional memory penalty of 80 ns after an L2 miss. These are illustrative values , not measurements of a named processor. Now suppose a layout change reduces the L1 miss rate to 3% without changing other parameters. The modeled AMAT becomes 1 + 0.03 × 24 = 1.72 ns , a reduction of about 21.8% in this modeled access cost. It would be incorrect to promise a 21.8% whole-program speedup. If these accesses account for only half the original execution time and all other time remains unchanged, the new normalized time is 0.5 + 0.5*(1.72/2.2) , approximately 0.891. The implied speedup is about 1.122, or 12.2%, under those additional assumptions. Chapter 56 generalizes this reasoning with Amdahl’s law.

topics.title: Chapter 33 — Files
topics.summary: A file interface presents data through a persistent name, an open handle, or a stream-like endpoint. The operating system hides many device details, but the abstraction does not make every endpoint behave like a seekable array of bytes. Correct I/O code begins by identifying which guarantees the particular object provides. The Linux/POSIX examples distinguish a pathname , an underlying filesystem object, an open file description , and a process’s file descriptor . Those are related objects, not four names for the same thing. The distinction explains shared offsets, inherited descriptors, and why removing a pathname need not immediately invalidate an already-open handle. [ R47 , R13 ]

topics.title: 33.1 Regular files
topics.summary: A regular file provides byte-oriented contents and metadata under filesystem rules. It usually supports seeking to a position and reading or writing there. Its logical size need not equal the amount of physical storage allocated, as sparse regions illustrate. A pathname is a route through a directory namespace, not a permanent guarantee about object identity. Another process can rename or replace an entry between separate pathname operations. When an operation must apply to the object already opened, use the descriptor and descriptor-relative interfaces where appropriate rather than reopening the name and assuming it still denotes the same object.

topics.title: 33.2 Streams
topics.summary: A stream exposes an ordered flow of bytes or records according to its interface. Pipes and TCP sockets are byte streams that do not support arbitrary seeking. Data may arrive gradually, and a read can return fewer bytes than requested. The C standard-I/O concept of a stream adds buffering and library state through FILE* . That is another layer: a FILE* may wrap a regular file or another supported endpoint. Distinguish the endpoint’s capabilities from the library abstraction used to access it.

topics.title: 33.3 Random-access files
topics.summary: Random access means that the program can select positions rather than consume data only in arrival order. A file format can use fixed-size records, an index, or offsets into variable-length data. The format must define byte ordering, field widths, and bounds independently of a compiler’s in-memory structure layout. Seeking past the end does not itself write intervening bytes. Subsequent writes can extend the file according to filesystem semantics. A robust parser checks offsets and lengths against the actual file size before accessing a region, using subtraction-based bounds checks that avoid overflowing offset + length .

topics.title: 33.4 File position
topics.summary: An open file description maintains a current file offset for interfaces such as read , write , and lseek on seekable objects. Descriptors created by dup or inherited through fork can refer to the same open file description and therefore share that offset. Separate open calls generally create separate open file descriptions, even when the pathname identifies the same file. Their current offsets are independent. Positional I/O such as pread and pwrite specifies an offset for an operation without using the shared current position in the same way, making it useful for independent random access.

topics.title: 33.5 Metadata
topics.summary: Metadata describes properties such as type, size, permissions, ownership, and timestamps. Descriptor-based inspection identifies the already-open object. A metadata result is a snapshot, not a lock that prevents later changes by another process. Security-sensitive code should avoid checking a pathname and then assuming the checked property remains true during a later open. This is a time-of-check/time-of-use problem. Use interfaces and ownership rules that bind validation to the actual object being used, and account for concurrent modification when the application permits it.

topics.title: Worked example — Record boundaries without overflow
topics.summary: Suppose a file format begins with a 16-byte header followed by fixed 24-byte records. A file of 160 bytes contains (160 - 16) / 24 = 6 complete records, with no trailing bytes. Record 4, using zero-based indexing, begins at 16 + 4 × 24 = 112 and occupies bytes 112 through 135. A safe validation sequence first requires file_size >= header_size . It then computes payload_size = file_size - header_size , verifies that payload_size % record_size == 0 , and derives the record count. Only after checking index < record_count should it form the selected record’s offset. For an arbitrary byte range with offset o and length n , prefer: This avoids computing an unchecked sum that could wrap. The checks establish a valid range in the observed file size; they do not prevent another process from truncating the file afterward. The application needs an immutability or coordination policy when concurrent modification is possible.

topics.title: Worked example — Sequential versus random file access
topics.summary: Reading a 1 MiB file from beginning to end advances the file offset naturally after each read. To revisit byte 100 without rereading earlier bytes, a seekable regular file can use lseek to reposition before reading. Pipes and terminals are streams and generally do not support arbitrary seek semantics.

topics.title: Chapter 34 — File Descriptors
topics.summary: A file descriptor is a small nonnegative integer that indexes a process’s descriptor table. It can refer to a regular file, pipe, socket, or other supported object. The descriptor number is meaningful only while that table entry remains open; after closure, the same number can be reused for an unrelated object. The central programming rule is simple: interpret the documented return value of every operation. A request for a certain byte count is not a guarantee that exactly that many bytes moved. Error handling, partial progress, and cleanup are part of the operation’s semantics, not optional additions. [ R11 , R12 , R13 , R47 ]

topics.title: 34.1 Descriptor tables
topics.summary: A descriptor-table entry refers to an open file description or another kernel-managed open object. Descriptor flags such as close-on-exec belong to the descriptor, while file status flags and the current offset have their own sharing rules. Treat ownership explicitly. A function that borrows a descriptor must not close it unless the contract transfers ownership. A function that returns a newly opened descriptor must document who closes it. Copying the integer does not create a new kernel reference; dup does.

topics.title: 34.2 Standard input
topics.summary: Descriptor 0 conventionally represents standard input, accessed through STDIN_FILENO . It may be a terminal, file, pipe, or another redirected source. A program should not assume keyboard input merely because it reads descriptor 0. Reading standard input until end of file makes a utility composable. The same implementation can then process an interactive stream, a redirected file, or a pipeline without knowing which source supplied the bytes.

topics.title: 34.3 Standard output
topics.summary: Descriptor 1 conventionally represents standard output. Machine-readable results should normally go there, while diagnostics go elsewhere. Mixing progress messages into a binary or structured output stream can corrupt downstream processing. A write to standard output can fail or complete partially. Redirection to a full filesystem, a broken pipe, or another failing endpoint changes the result even when the program’s internal calculation succeeded. Output completion is part of overall success.

topics.title: 34.4 Standard error
topics.summary: Descriptor 2 conventionally represents standard error. It gives diagnostics a separate destination from normal output, allowing users to redirect or capture them independently. Separation is a convention supported by descriptor setup, not a guarantee of distinct physical devices. A shell can redirect both descriptors to one file. Diagnostic code should also avoid overwriting the original error information before reporting it.

topics.title: 34.5 open
topics.summary: open resolves a pathname and requests access with specified flags. It returns a descriptor on success and -1 on failure. Creation flags require a permission mode, which is affected by the process’s file-creation mask and other applicable policy. [ R47 ] Choose destructive behavior deliberately. O_TRUNC can discard existing contents; O_EXCL with creation can require that a new name be created. O_CLOEXEC establishes close-on-exec atomically with opening on the reference platform, avoiding a separate setup window in multithreaded code.

topics.title: 34.7 write
topics.summary: write can transfer fewer bytes than requested. A complete-transfer helper advances the pointer and reduces the remaining count after each positive result. A failure after earlier progress does not roll those bytes back. [ R12 ] Keep individual request sizes within the interface’s supported range. The helper below is used only with small bounded buffers on blocking descriptors. It treats a zero-byte result for a positive remaining request as a failure to make progress. Broken-pipe signal behavior is a separate policy discussed in Chapter 40.

topics.title: 34.8 close
topics.summary: close releases a descriptor reference and can report errors associated with outstanding I/O. On Linux, do not blindly retry close after an error: the descriptor number may already have been released and reused. A retry could close an unrelated resource. [ R13 ] This is a documented portability boundary. POSIX.1-2024 specifies different EINTR behavior from Linux’s established behavior. The examples in this book use the Linux rule explicitly rather than presenting one retry pattern as universal. Closing also does not by itself establish durable storage.

topics.title: 34.9 lseek
topics.summary: lseek changes or queries the current offset of a seekable open file description. Its return type is off_t , and failure is indicated by (off_t)-1 . Pipes and sockets are not ordinary seekable files. Changing a shared offset affects other descriptors referring to the same open file description. When independent operations must not interfere through the current position, consider positional I/O or separate open descriptions instead of surrounding every operation with fragile seek/read sequences.

topics.title: Worked example — A complete-transfer copy loop
topics.summary: This utility copies standard input to standard output without assuming that a read fills its buffer or that a write consumes the entire request. It does not promise durable output, nonblocking support, or custom broken-pipe handling. Companion listing: ch34/copy.c For input bytes systems\n , the output must be exactly the same eight bytes. For an empty input, the program emits nothing and succeeds. A binary test should include zero bytes and data larger than 4096 bytes to verify that the implementation does not accidentally treat input as a C string or stop after one iteration.

topics.title: Worked example — Robust read loop
topics.summary: A call to read(fd,buf,4096) may legally return fewer than 4096 bytes even before end of file. A robust loop advances by the number returned, retries when appropriate after interruption, stops on zero for EOF, and handles negative results as errors. One successful call is not a contract for full-buffer delivery.

topics.title: 35.1 System-call overhead
topics.summary: A system call involves an ABI transition, validation, and kernel work. Performing one call for every character can make that overhead significant compared with the useful transfer. Grouping bytes amortizes the fixed portion of the cost. The exact cost is workload- and platform-dependent. A benchmark comparing one-byte writes with block writes should control the destination, total bytes, buffering mode, and error handling. Sending output to a terminal can measure rendering and terminal behavior as much as syscall overhead.

topics.title: 35.2 User-space buffering
topics.summary: A user-space buffer accumulates output or retains input already fetched from the kernel. The library can satisfy several application operations without another system call. That improves efficiency but means an application operation may complete before the underlying descriptor has seen all corresponding output. The buffer has ownership and lifetime requirements. When supplying storage to an interface such as setvbuf , keep that storage alive for the required duration and configure buffering before performing other stream operations as required by the interface. Do not use a short-lived local array as a long-lived stream buffer.

topics.title: 35.3 Standard I/O
topics.summary: The C standard-I/O library provides formatted and block-oriented operations such as fprintf , fread , and fwrite . It tracks buffering, position-related state, end-of-file state, and error state. These are library operations, not one-to-one aliases for system calls. [ R8 ] Check the return values appropriate to each interface. fread and fwrite count complete elements, not always raw bytes unless the element size is one. A short input result requires distinguishing end of file from an error using stream state.

topics.title: 35.4 FILE*
topics.summary: A FILE* refers to a library-managed stream object. It is not an integer descriptor and must not be passed where an int fd is expected. On POSIX systems, fileno obtains the associated descriptor for supported streams, but mixing raw descriptor operations with buffered stream operations requires careful coordination. The library may have read ahead or retained unwritten output. A raw read , write , or lseek can therefore interact with a different logical position than the programmer expects. Prefer one I/O abstraction for a given workflow unless there is a clear synchronization plan.

topics.title: 35.5 Read buffering
topics.summary: Read buffering obtains a block from the underlying endpoint and serves smaller application reads from that block. The descriptor offset may advance beyond the next byte the application will receive from the library buffer. This explains why duplicating a descriptor does not duplicate a FILE* ’s user-space buffer state. It also explains why switching abruptly between buffered and unbuffered reads can appear to skip data. The bytes may already be inside the library’s buffer rather than waiting at the kernel offset.

topics.title: 35.6 Write buffering
topics.summary: Write buffering delays or groups output until the buffer fills, a flush occurs, or another defined event requires transfer. fflush requests that buffered output be sent through the stream’s underlying write path and reports failure if that cannot be completed. fflush does not provide the same durability guarantee as fsync on an appropriate descriptor. It moves data out of the library buffer; the kernel and device may still retain it. Likewise, fclose must be checked because buffered output can fail during final flushing. [ R33 ]

topics.title: 35.7 Buffer cache
topics.summary: The kernel’s file cache retains file data in memory to avoid repeated device access and to batch writes. On Linux, discussion of ordinary file data commonly centers on the page cache. This cache is distinct from CPU caches and from user-space standard-I/O buffers. A warm-cache benchmark may primarily measure memory copying and kernel paths, while a cold-device benchmark includes storage access. Do not label both simply “disk speed.” State whether the relevant data was cached and avoid globally disruptive cache-manipulation commands in ordinary application labs.

topics.title: Worked example — Why buffering reduces calls
topics.summary: Writing 1 byte at a time for 4,096 bytes can require 4,096 system calls if unbuffered. Accumulating those bytes in a 4 KiB user-space buffer can reduce the transfer to roughly one write call. The total data is unchanged, but fixed per-call overhead is amortized across more bytes.

topics.title: Chapter 36 — Memory-Mapped Files
topics.summary: A memory mapping exposes a file region through virtual addresses. The program accesses bytes with ordinary loads and stores, while the kernel supplies backing pages and enforces mapping permissions. This can simplify random access, but it does not remove I/O, faults, concurrency, or lifetime concerns. [ R14 ]

topics.title: 36.1 mmap
topics.summary: mmap requests a mapping with a length, protection flags, sharing mode, descriptor, and offset. Failure is reported as MAP_FAILED , not as a null pointer. A zero-length mapping is not a valid substitute for handling an empty file. The offset must satisfy the platform’s alignment requirements, normally a multiple of the relevant page size. Mapping an arbitrary record offset often requires rounding the mapping base down to a page boundary and retaining an internal displacement, with overflow checks on the total mapped length.

topics.title: 36.2 Address mappings
topics.summary: The returned address identifies the beginning of the mapping in the process’s virtual space. Its validity lasts until the mapping is removed or otherwise changed. Closing the original descriptor does not by itself remove an established mapping on Linux. Pointers into the region become invalid after munmap . A function borrowing the mapping must not retain those pointers beyond the owner’s lifetime. Mapping ownership deserves the same discipline as allocation ownership: one clear owner, explicit extent, and structured cleanup.

topics.title: 36.3 File-backed pages
topics.summary: File-backed pages associate virtual regions with file contents. A shared writable mapping can propagate modifications to the underlying file according to synchronization and filesystem rules. A private mapping provides private modification semantics instead of updating the file with those writes. Mapping flags are not a complete interprocess synchronization protocol. Multiple writers need an agreed layout and synchronization mechanism. Data-race rules still apply to threads in one process, and process-shared synchronization requires facilities designed for that purpose.

topics.title: 36.4 Page faults
topics.summary: The first access to a mapped page may fault so that the kernel can establish backing. Later accesses can still fault under memory-management activity. A mapping therefore does not promise that every load has register-like or even DRAM-like cost. Concurrent file truncation is a serious hazard. Accessing a mapped region whose backing has been removed can generate SIGBUS on Linux. Checking file size before mapping is not enough when another actor can shrink the file afterward. The example below requires a stable regular file throughout the mapping’s lifetime.

topics.title: 36.5 Mapping permissions
topics.summary: Protection flags specify permitted reads, writes, and instruction execution. They must be compatible with the mapping and descriptor’s access rights. A read-only mapping is appropriate for a checksum or parser that does not need to modify the file. Use the least authority required. Do not request writable executable memory merely because it seems convenient. For writable shared file mappings, msync can request synchronization under its documented semantics, while a complete durable-update protocol may require additional filesystem operations. [ R31 , R32 , R33 ]

topics.title: 36.6 Memory-mapped I/O
topics.summary: The phrase memory-mapped I/O also describes device registers placed in an address map. Device mappings are not ordinary file-data mappings: accesses can have side effects, supported widths, ordering requirements, and cacheability constraints. A volatile pointer alone does not provide every device-ordering or synchronization guarantee. Device access must follow the operating system’s driver interfaces and architecture-specific requirements. This book’s user-space file-mapping labs do not access physical device registers.

topics.title: Worked example — A read-only mapped byte sum
topics.summary: This Linux/POSIX utility accepts a regular-file path, handles the empty-file case, checks that the length fits size_t , maps read-only, and computes an unsigned 64-bit byte sum. The sum is a teaching checksum, not a cryptographic integrity mechanism. Companion listing: ch36/mapped_sum.c A file containing exactly ABC produces 198 because 65 + 66 + 67 = 198 on the stated ASCII-compatible reference environment. A binary fixture containing bytes 0, 1, 127, 128, and 255 produces 511. The test suite supplies controlled temporary files; it does not mutate an existing user document.

Unmapping ends the virtual mapping, not the file’s existence.

topics.title: Chapter 37 — Process Creation
topics.summary: Process creation separates an execution environment into independently scheduled participants. On POSIX systems, fork creates a child whose initial state resembles the parent’s at the call boundary, but the two processes receive different return values and can immediately follow different paths. The resemblance must be interpreted carefully. Private memory has independent modification semantics, while inherited descriptors can reference the same underlying open objects. Treating everything as either “fully copied” or “fully shared” produces errors. [ R15 ]

topics.title: 37.1 fork
topics.summary: fork returns once in the parent and once in the child after successful creation. In the parent it returns the child’s process ID; in the child it returns zero. On failure, the parent receives -1 and no child is created. The child begins after the call, not at the beginning of main . Every branch must therefore be explicit about which process owns which cleanup and continuation responsibilities. A child intended to execute a new program should not accidentally fall through into the parent’s main loop when execution fails.

topics.title: 37.2 Parent process
topics.summary: The parent retains its identity and receives a handle-like process ID for the child. It must decide whether to wait immediately, continue concurrently, or supervise several children. It also remains responsible for closing inherited communication endpoints it does not use. A parent cannot assume that it executes first after the fork. Scheduling can run the child before the parent reaches its next statement. Any ordering requirement must be established through waiting or communication, not inferred from source order in the parent’s branch.

topics.title: 37.3 Child process
topics.summary: The child has its own process identity and private execution state. It can modify ordinary private variables without changing the parent’s copies. It may execute a new program, perform bounded work, or participate in a pipeline. After a fork from a multithreaded process, only the calling thread appears in the child, while copied library and mutex state can reflect locks held by threads that no longer exist there. Until a successful exec, the child must obey the applicable async-signal-safe restrictions. The examples here create children from single-threaded programs. [ R15 , R20 ]

topics.title: 37.4 Return values
topics.summary: The three-way return distinction is fundamental: Do not collapse failure and parent behavior into one generic nonzero branch. A failed fork gives no child to wait for. Preserve the error information before cleanup operations that could change errno .

topics.title: 37.5 Address-space duplication
topics.summary: The child receives an address space with corresponding mappings according to the interface’s rules. Ordinary private memory initially contains the same values, but later modifications are logically independent. Shared mappings remain shared according to their mapping semantics. User-space I/O buffers are also memory. If buffered output exists before a fork and both processes later perform normal stream flushing, the same buffered bytes can be emitted twice. Flush deliberately before forking when appropriate, or ensure that an exec-bound child’s failure path uses _exit rather than normal buffered cleanup.

topics.title: 37.6 File-descriptor inheritance
topics.summary: The child’s inherited descriptors refer to the same open file descriptions as the corresponding parent descriptors. They can share current offsets and file status flags. Closing the child’s descriptor releases its reference without closing the parent’s separate descriptor-table entry. This sharing is useful for pipelines and redirection but can also cause surprises. A child’s read can advance the offset subsequently observed by the parent. An accidentally retained pipe write end can prevent another process from seeing end of file.

topics.title: 37.7 Copy-on-write
topics.summary: Copy-on-write can avoid physically copying all private pages immediately. Parent and child initially share backing while hardware permissions trigger separation when a private write requires it. The interface promises the observable private-memory behavior, not an eager byte-for-byte copy at the instant of creation. The amount of memory actually duplicated depends on later writes, mappings, allocator activity, and kernel policy. Forking a large process is therefore not automatically equivalent to immediately allocating another complete physical copy, but it is also not free.

topics.title: Worked example — Private values after fork
topics.summary: This program starts with value 7. The child changes its private value to 12 and reports correctness through its exit status. The parent waits and verifies that its own value remains 7. Companion listing: ch37/private_values.c The output is deterministic because only the parent prints and it waits for the child’s check. This does not prove which process ran first or which physical pages were copied. It verifies the private-value contract visible to the program.

topics.title: Worked example — Interpreting fork returns
topics.summary: After a successful fork , the parent receives the child’s positive PID while the child receives zero. Both continue from the instruction after the call. Code commonly branches on the return value to assign parent and child responsibilities. A negative return in the parent-side call indicates failure and no child was created.

topics.title: Worked example — Inherited descriptor example
topics.summary: If a process opens a file and then forks, parent and child inherit descriptors referring to the same open file description. Writes can therefore interact through a shared offset unless the program coordinates them or opens separate descriptions. The address spaces are logically separate, but kernel objects can remain shared.

topics.title: 38.1 exec
topics.summary: The exec family provides interfaces with different argument and environment conventions. Some accept an argument vector; some accept a variable-length argument list. Interfaces with a p variant search according to documented path rules, while execve takes an explicit pathname and environment vector. Choosing an interface is also a security decision. Searching a mutable or attacker-influenced path can execute an unintended program. Supplying an explicit known path and a controlled environment makes the selection easier to reason about, although executable identity and filesystem permissions still matter.

topics.title: 38.2 execve
topics.summary: execve(path, argv, envp) requests replacement using a pathname, a null-terminated argument-vector array, and a null-terminated environment-vector array. A successful call does not return to the old program. Failure returns -1 with errno describing the error. The strings and pointer arrays must remain valid until the call completes. The kernel constructs the new program’s initial state; the old address space is not retained as ordinary live C objects after success. Do not place essential parent-only cleanup after exec and expect it to run on success.

topics.title: 38.3 Program replacement
topics.summary: Replacement installs new code, data, stack, and related execution state while preserving the process’s identity and selected attributes according to the interface. It is not a normal function call into another executable. Open descriptors generally remain unless marked close-on-exec or affected by a documented rule. This is how a shell arranges standard input and output before executing a command. It is also why accidentally inherited descriptors can leak access into a program that never requested it.

topics.title: 38.4 Arguments
topics.summary: argv is an array of pointers to strings ending with a null pointer. Conventionally argv[0] identifies the program name, while later entries contain arguments. An argument containing spaces remains one argument when represented as one array element; no shell parsing is performed by execve itself. Avoid constructing a shell command string when direct argument passing is sufficient. Direct vectors preserve argument boundaries and avoid interpreting metacharacters as shell syntax. Validation is still required for the target program’s own option and input semantics.

topics.title: 38.5 Environment
topics.summary: The environment is a collection of strings conventionally formatted as NAME=value . Programs and libraries can use it to select paths, locale behavior, configuration, and other settings. Inheriting every variable is convenient but can make behavior depend on the launching context. A controlled launcher should decide which variables to preserve, replace, or omit. Never treat environment variables as automatically trustworthy merely because they came from the parent. Security-sensitive execution requires a deliberate environment and privilege policy.

cards.question: Explain 38.5 Environment. What mechanism, rule, or distinction must you remember?
cards.answer: The environment is a collection of strings conventionally formatted as NAME=value . Programs and libraries can use it to select paths, locale behavior, configuration, and other settings. Inheriting every variable is convenient but can make behavior depend on the launching context. A controlled launcher should decide which variables to preserve, replace, or omit. Never treat environment variables as automatically trustworthy merely because they came from the parent. Security-sensitive execution requires a deliberate environment and privilege policy.

topics.title: 38.6 Process images
topics.summary: A process image includes the executable mappings and initialized runtime environment needed to begin the new program. The loader and dynamic linker perform work beyond the source-level function call used to request replacement. Some signal-related state changes across exec while other state persists according to the documented rules. For example, caught signal dispositions are reset in the ordinary case, while the signal mask is preserved. A launcher that blocks signals during setup must restore the intended mask before executing a program that expects normal delivery. [ R16 , R21 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Exec does not create a second process

On success, the old code, stack, and most mappings are gone, and execution begins in the new program’s startup path.

topics.title: Chapter 39 — Process Termination
topics.summary: Termination ends execution, but it does not erase every trace of a process immediately. The operating system retains enough information for a parent to learn how a child finished. A robust parent separates ordinary exit, signal termination, and temporary state changes rather than interpreting a raw status integer directly. [ R17 ]

topics.title: 39.1 exit
topics.summary: The C library’s exit performs normal termination processing, including registered exit handlers and standard-I/O cleanup. Returning from main has the corresponding normal-termination effect. _exit bypasses that user-space cleanup and is appropriate for many child failure paths after fork. Neither interface returns to the caller. Choose based on the process’s lifecycle, not merely on spelling. Using normal cleanup in an exec-bound child can flush copied buffers or invoke handlers intended for the original parent program.

Returning from main has the corresponding normal-termination effect. _exit bypasses that user-space cleanup and is appropriate for many child failure paths after fork. Neither interface returns to the caller. Choose based on the process’s lifecycle, not merely on spelling. Using normal cleanup in an exec-bound child can flush copied buffers or invoke handlers intended for the original parent program.

topics.title: 39.2 Exit status
topics.summary: An exit status communicates a small result to the parent. Conventionally zero indicates success and nonzero indicates failure, but applications define the meaning of particular nonzero values. On the POSIX wait interfaces used here, ordinary exit status is retrieved from the appropriate encoded status through macros. Do not attempt to return a large integer or arbitrary data structure through exit status. Use a pipe, file, socket, or another explicit channel for richer results. Exit status should summarize completion, not replace a data protocol.

topics.title: 39.3 wait
topics.summary: wait waits for an eligible child and returns its process ID together with status information. It is useful when any child’s completion can be handled next. The parent must still inspect the status classification before extracting a particular result. A parent with several children should not assume that completion order matches creation order. Scheduling and workload determine which finishes first. Waiting for one specific slow child can delay handling other already-finished children, although it remains correct when the program deliberately chooses that policy.

topics.title: 39.4 waitpid
topics.summary: waitpid provides more control over which child or group is considered and whether the call blocks. With WNOHANG , a return of zero means that no matching status is currently available; it is not a child’s process ID and not an error. Retry an interrupted wait when appropriate. Check WIFEXITED before using WEXITSTATUS , and check WIFSIGNALED before using WTERMSIG . Options for stopped and continued children matter for job control, which requires a broader state machine than a simple run-and-wait launcher.

topics.title: 39.5 Zombie processes
topics.summary: A zombie is a terminated process whose parent has not yet collected the retained termination information. It is not executing instructions or holding its former address space as a normal live process. It does occupy bookkeeping that should eventually be released. A long-running supervisor that never reaps children can accumulate zombies. The solution is lifecycle management, not treating zombies as ordinary running tasks to be killed again. The parent must arrange to collect child status according to the applicable process and signal rules.

topics.title: 39.6 Reaping children
topics.summary: Reaping collects a child’s status and releases the retained termination bookkeeping. A parent should have one clear ownership policy for child status, especially when multiple threads or signal-driven code could attempt to wait for the same child. A common event-driven pattern treats SIGCHLD as a notification to check for available statuses and then repeatedly uses nonblocking waits until none remain. Standard signals can coalesce, so one notification must not be assumed to represent exactly one child event.

topics.title: Chapter 40 — Pipes and Redirection
topics.summary: A pipe connects a byte-producing endpoint to a byte-consuming endpoint. Descriptors and duplication let a shell attach those endpoints to a program’s standard input or output without changing the program’s own source. The difficult part is not creating the pipe; it is closing every unused reference and coordinating concurrent execution. [ R18 , R19 , R48 ]

topics.title: 40.1 Pipes
topics.summary: pipe returns two descriptors: one for reading and one for writing. Bytes written to the write end become available at the read end in order. The pipe does not preserve arbitrary application message boundaries as a record protocol. A reader sees end of file only after all write-end references are closed and buffered bytes have been consumed. “The original writer exited” is insufficient when another process accidentally retains a write descriptor.

topics.title: 40.2 Pipe buffers
topics.summary: The kernel stores a bounded amount of pending pipe data. Buffer capacity is not the same as PIPE_BUF , which concerns atomicity guarantees for appropriately sized writes under the documented conditions. Large writes from several writers can interleave. A multiwriter protocol must define record sizes and synchronization rather than assume that one source-level write always becomes one indivisible record. Capacity can vary with system configuration and policy.

topics.title: 40.3 Blocking
topics.summary: A blocking read waits when the pipe is empty but writers still exist. A blocking write can wait when capacity is unavailable. If all read ends are closed, writing can cause SIGPIPE or report EPIPE when signal policy permits the error to be observed. These rules make lifecycle mistakes visible as hangs or unexpected termination. Waiting for a producer before starting its consumer can deadlock when the producer fills the pipe. Start communicating participants before waiting for their completion.

topics.title: 40.4 File-descriptor duplication
topics.summary: Duplication creates another descriptor referring to the same open file description. Both descriptors keep the underlying open object referenced until each is closed. The new descriptor is a new ownership obligation even though it refers to the same object. Duplication shares the underlying offset and status where applicable; it does not copy file contents or create an independent seek position. Descriptor-specific flags have separate rules and should be set deliberately.

topics.title: 40.6 dup2
topics.summary: dup2(oldfd, newfd) makes a specific descriptor number refer to the source object, atomically replacing an existing target reference when appropriate. This avoids the race in a separate close(newfd) followed by dup(oldfd) sequence. When oldfd == newfd and the descriptor is valid, the operation leaves it as that descriptor. Cleanup code must not then blindly close the source number if doing so would close the newly intended standard stream. The example below tests this case before closing the source reference.

topics.title: 40.7 Input redirection
topics.summary: Input redirection opens or obtains a source descriptor and duplicates it onto descriptor 0 before exec. The executed program reads standard input normally and need not know that a file or pipe supplied it. Apply redirections in the defined order. Shell constructs that duplicate descriptors can produce different results depending on whether an earlier redirection has already changed the source descriptor. A shell implementation must preserve syntax order rather than sort redirections arbitrarily.

topics.title: 40.8 Output redirection
topics.summary: Output redirection duplicates a destination onto descriptor 1. File creation, append behavior, and truncation must be requested explicitly. Diagnostics should remain on descriptor 2 unless the command syntax redirects them as well. Opening a destination can fail before exec. The child should report the setup failure and terminate rather than execute the requested program with an unintended output destination. Resource setup is part of launch correctness.

topics.title: 40.9 Pipelines
topics.summary: A pipeline connects several processes so that one process’s output feeds the next process’s input. The parent creates pipes, launches all stages, closes its unused ends, and then waits according to its policy. Every child must close pipe ends it does not need. In a longer pipeline, this includes descriptors for other stages, not only its immediate neighbor. A descriptor ownership table is often the clearest way to design and review the launch sequence.

topics.title: Worked example — Two concurrently started stages
topics.summary: This program runs a fixed, harmless pipeline equivalent to producing two lines and counting them. It assumes the reference environment provides printf and wc in the controlled system path. It is not a general shell. Companion listing: ch40/pipeline.c The output contains the line count 2, with formatting determined by wc . Both processes are launched before either is waited for. On second-fork failure, the parent closes both ends and reaps the already-created producer; the fixed producer exits when its output cannot be delivered under the ordinary broken-pipe policy.

topics.title: Worked example — Constructing producer | consumer
topics.summary: Create a pipe, fork both children, connect the producer’s standard output to the pipe’s write end with dup2 , and connect the consumer’s standard input to the read end. Close unused pipe ends in every process. If the parent accidentally keeps a write end open, the consumer may never observe EOF after the producer exits.

topics.title: 41.1 Asynchronous events
topics.summary: An asynchronous signal can arrive independently of the interrupted statement’s purpose. The program may be halfway through updating a data structure or holding a library’s internal lock. Handler code must not assume a clean application boundary. Synchronous fault signals have a different relationship to execution: they result from an instruction’s behavior. Catching such a signal does not automatically make corrupted state recoverable. Treat routine notifications and invalid-memory faults as different design problems.

topics.title: 41.2 Signal delivery
topics.summary: Signal disposition defines whether a signal is handled, ignored, or given its default action, subject to signals that cannot be caught or ignored. Signal masks control which signals are blocked for a thread. In a multithreaded process, dispositions and per-thread masks have different scopes. Process-directed signals can be delivered to an eligible thread under the platform’s rules. A design that depends on one particular worker receiving a signal should use a deliberate masking and signal-consumption strategy instead of leaving delivery accidental.

topics.title: 41.3 kill
topics.summary: Despite its name, kill sends a signal; the chosen signal’s disposition determines the effect. It can request termination, notify, or test certain existence/permission conditions with signal number zero under documented rules. A PID is a reusable identifier, not an eternal object reference. Long-lived supervisors must account for lifecycle and identity races. This book’s simple examples use freshly created children or the current process rather than treating an old stored PID as permanently trustworthy.

topics.title: 41.4 sigaction
topics.summary: sigaction installs a handler and associated mask and flags. It provides explicit control that is preferable to relying on historically varying signal semantics. Initialize the structure and signal set before installing it. Flags such as SA_RESTART affect some interrupted operations, not every possible wait or system call. Correct I/O code still needs to interpret its own interface’s results. A blanket assumption that signals can never interrupt operations is unsafe.

topics.title: 41.5 Signal handlers
topics.summary: A minimal handler records that an event occurred and leaves substantial work to ordinary control flow. A volatile sig_atomic_t flag supports the limited communication pattern used here. It is not a general atomic counter or a substitute for C++ inter-thread synchronization. Do not call printf , allocate memory, acquire arbitrary mutexes, or use ordinary C++ stream operations from an asynchronous handler. They may rely on state that the interrupted code was modifying. Use only operations guaranteed async-signal-safe for the relevant environment. [ R20 ]

topics.title: 41.6 Blocking signals
topics.summary: Blocking delays delivery; it does not necessarily discard the event. A critical setup sequence can block a signal, install state, and then unblock it at a controlled point. In multithreaded programs, use the appropriate thread-aware mask interfaces and establish masks before creating workers when that is part of the design. Blocking is also needed to close a check-then-sleep race. The signal must not slip between observing a flag and entering a wait that would then have no future notification to wake it.

topics.title: 41.7 Pending signals
topics.summary: A blocked signal can become pending. Standard signals generally do not queue one distinct instance for every repeated occurrence; multiple occurrences can coalesce. Real-time signals provide different queuing semantics under their documented limits. Consequently, a handler flag is usually a request to inspect state, not an exact count of events. A SIGCHLD notification should trigger collection of all available child statuses, not one wait per presumed signal instance.

topics.title: 41.8 Signal safety
topics.summary: Signal safety concerns reentrancy and permitted operations at an asynchronous interruption point. It is not the same as ordinary thread safety. A function protected by an internal mutex can be thread-safe yet deadlock when called from a handler that interrupted a thread holding that mutex. A handler using an async-signal-safe function that can affect errno should save and restore errno when necessary. A self-pipe pattern can notify an event loop with a small write, but it must handle a full nonblocking pipe without blocking inside the handler.

topics.title: 41.9 Signal races
topics.summary: A race occurs when correctness depends on the timing of delivery relative to ordinary state changes. Installing a handler after enabling an event source can miss the intended handling window. Updating shared bookkeeping without a masking plan can expose inconsistent state. Design the state transition and notification together. The signal says that something may have changed; protected ordinary code determines exactly what changed and performs the required work. This parallels condition-variable design in Part XI.

topics.title: 41.10 Sleep/wakeup races
topics.summary: The broken pattern is if (!flag) pause(); : a signal can set the flag after the check but before pause , leaving the program asleep after the only notification. Making the flag volatile does not make those two operations atomic. sigsuspend temporarily installs a signal mask and waits as one coordinated operation. Block the relevant signal while checking the predicate, then use a mask that permits it during the wait. On return, recheck the predicate in a loop. [ R40 ]

topics.title: Worked example — Pending delivery without a lost wakeup
topics.summary: This deterministic demonstration blocks SIGUSR1 , raises it while blocked, and then uses sigsuspend to permit delivery. The handler only sets a flag. It does not require another process or rely on a sleep duration. Companion listing: ch41/signals.c The expected output is signal observed . The signal is already pending before the wait, yet delivery cannot be lost between the predicate check and the temporary unblocking. The example intentionally exits after demonstrating one notification; a reusable component would also restore dispositions and define a broader shutdown policy.

topics.title: Worked example — Safe signal notification
topics.summary: A signal handler should do minimal async-signal-safe work. A common pattern sets a volatile sig_atomic_t flag or writes a byte to a self-pipe, then returns. Normal code observes the flag or file descriptor and performs complex processing outside the handler. Calling arbitrary allocation or I/O library functions inside the handler can violate reentrancy requirements.

Normal code observes the flag or file descriptor and performs complex processing outside the handler. Calling arbitrary allocation or I/O library functions inside the handler can violate reentrancy requirements.

topics.title: Worked example — Closing a sleep/wakeup race
topics.summary: If code checks ready == false and then separately goes to sleep, a signal arriving between those steps can be lost. Correct designs use an atomic blocking primitive such as sigsuspend with a carefully managed signal mask so the state check and sleep transition cannot miss the event window.

topics.title: Chapter 42 — Shell Architecture
topics.summary: A shell is a process-control program with a language front end. It turns command syntax into a plan for programs, arguments, descriptors, process groups, and waiting. A small shell can demonstrate systems concepts, but a complete interactive shell also needs careful syntax, signal, terminal, and lifecycle handling. Separate parsing from execution. Parsing should produce a structured description without opening files or launching programs. Execution should consume that structure according to a documented policy. This separation makes malformed input testable without causing side effects.

topics.title: 42.1 Parsing commands
topics.summary: Parsing begins with lexical rules for words, quoting, escapes, and operators. A space inside quotes is data, while an unquoted pipe character may be syntax. A quoted "|" must not become a pipeline operator merely because its final text is a vertical bar. Represent token kind separately from token text. Then build an abstract command structure containing argument vectors, ordered redirections, pipeline stages, and background status. Reject incomplete constructs before launch, including unterminated quotes and a redirection without a destination.

topics.title: 42.2 Creating processes
topics.summary: The executor creates the required children and tracks each successful creation. Failure halfway through a pipeline requires cleanup of descriptors and already-created children. The plan must define what happens to partially started work. Built-in commands complicate the model. A command such as changing the shell’s current directory must affect the shell process itself in the appropriate context; executing it only in a child would leave the parent unchanged. Decide which operations are built-ins before applying a blanket fork-everything rule.

topics.title: 42.3 Executing programs
topics.summary: Each child prepares descriptors, signal state, process-group membership, and other required context before exec. The argument vector should preserve parsed word boundaries. Exec failure must end the child branch with an appropriate status rather than return to the interactive shell loop. A secure launcher also defines executable lookup and environment handling. A general shell intentionally supports broad user-controlled behavior; an application that merely needs to run one helper should prefer direct argument-vector execution instead of implementing or invoking unnecessary shell syntax.

topics.title: 42.4 Redirection
topics.summary: Redirection modifies a command’s descriptor relationships in the order specified by the language. Input files, output truncation, append mode, and descriptor duplication require distinct operations. Do not postpone error checking until after exec. If opening a required input fails, the command cannot run as requested. The shell should report the setup error and avoid silently falling back to its own input stream.

topics.title: 42.5 Pipelines
topics.summary: A pipeline is a group of connected stages, not a sequence of complete programs run one after another. Its data flow requires overlap when bounded pipes connect producers and consumers. Track pipe-end ownership explicitly. For an N-stage pipeline, there are N−1 connecting pipes, but each child needs only its relevant input and output roles. Extra inherited ends must be closed so that EOF and broken-pipe behavior reflect the intended graph.

topics.title: 42.6 Foreground jobs
topics.summary: A foreground job receives the terminal relationship intended for interactive input and terminal-generated signals. The shell normally waits for the job’s completion or stop state before resuming its prompt. Waiting for one PID is insufficient for a pipeline treated as one job. The shell must track all member processes and determine when the job as a whole is complete or stopped. Status reporting is therefore a job-level state machine.

topics.title: 42.7 Background jobs
topics.summary: A background job allows the shell to continue accepting commands while the job runs. The shell still owns bookkeeping and must reap child statuses. “Do not wait immediately” is not the same as “forget the child forever.” Background terminal access has special behavior under job-control rules. A robust interactive shell must manage notifications, stopped jobs, and later foregrounding rather than assume every background process can freely read from the terminal.

topics.title: 42.8 Process groups
topics.summary: A process group collects related processes, such as all stages of one pipeline, under a group identifier. It lets the shell and terminal mechanisms direct signals to the job as a unit. Group setup has races between parent and child execution. A carefully designed shell establishes membership on both relevant sides as appropriate and checks the documented errors. The exact implementation deserves dedicated testing; it is not replaced by storing several PIDs in a vector.

topics.title: 42.9 Job control
topics.summary: Job control combines process groups, terminal foreground ownership, signal dispositions, and wait-status tracking. Interfaces such as setpgid and tcsetpgrp participate in the POSIX model. The shell must regain the terminal after a foreground job stops or finishes and restore the appropriate state. [ R51 , R52 ] The fixed pipeline from Chapter 40 is not a job-control shell. It has no interactive terminal handoff, stopped-job management, expansion language, or background-job table. Those omissions are intentional so that its descriptor and process behavior remain inspectable. [ R17 , R21 ]

topics.title: Worked example — A typed lexer for a small command language
topics.summary: This lexer supports spaces, single and double quotes, simple backslash escaping, and the operators | , < , > , and & . Its double-quote escape rules are deliberately simpler than a full POSIX shell. It performs no expansion, substitution, execution, or redirection. Companion listing: ch42/lexer.py The explicit active flag preserves an empty quoted argument. Without it, echo "" could be reduced incorrectly to a one-word command. Typed tokens likewise preserve the difference between a quoted vertical bar and an actual pipeline operator. The next stage would validate token sequences and produce a command tree. Only after that validation should an executor allocate pipes or create children. This is an example of a broader systems principle: make invalid plans fail before acquiring external resources whenever practical.

topics.title: Worked example — Parsing before executing
topics.summary: For cat input.txt | grep error > out.txt , the shell must identify two pipeline commands, one input argument, and one output redirection before spawning processes. Redirection operators are syntax for the shell; they are not passed as ordinary arguments to grep . Parsing establishes the execution graph that process creation later realizes.

topics.title: Chapter 43 — Concurrent Execution
topics.summary: Concurrent execution means that multiple activities can be in progress over overlapping intervals. Parallel execution means that work actually proceeds simultaneously on multiple execution resources. A single-core system can run concurrent activities by interleaving them, while a multicore system can combine interleaving with true parallelism. Concurrency adds possible execution orders. Correctness must hold for every execution permitted by the program’s synchronization and platform model, not only for the order observed during one successful run. Timing-based confidence is not a replacement for a state and ownership argument. [ R22 , R34 ]

topics.title: 43.1 Concurrency
topics.summary: Concurrency is useful when activities wait independently, respond to separate events, or need to overlap work. A server can handle another request while one request waits for data. A user interface can remain responsive while a background task computes. Concurrency also adds lifecycle obligations: cancellation, completion, resource ownership, and communication. Creating another thread is only one implementation choice. Processes, event loops, asynchronous operations, and task systems can provide different concurrency structures.
