topics.title: 43.2 Parallelism
topics.summary: Parallelism uses multiple execution resources at the same time. It can reduce elapsed time when work can be divided and shared bottlenecks do not dominate. Adding threads does not guarantee parallel execution or useful speedup. The available parallelism depends on dependencies. Four cores cannot execute the next step of a strictly dependent chain before the current step supplies its input. Parallel design often begins by changing task decomposition or data organization rather than increasing thread count.

topics.title: 43.3 Processes
topics.summary: Processes provide separate address spaces and stronger default isolation than threads within one process. They communicate through explicit mechanisms such as pipes, sockets, or shared mappings. This can make failure containment and ownership clearer. Isolation has costs and exceptions. Communication may require copying or synchronization, and intentionally shared resources still need a protocol. A process boundary does not automatically make an unvalidated message safe or a shared file update atomic.

topics.title: 43.4 Threads
topics.summary: Threads share an address space and many process resources while retaining their own execution state. Sharing makes communication convenient but permits accidental conflicting access to ordinary objects. The central design question is which thread owns each mutable object and when ownership changes. An immutable object safely published to readers has a simpler contract than an object that every thread may update at any time.

cards.question: Explain 43.4 Threads. What mechanism, rule, or distinction must you remember?
cards.answer: Threads share an address space and many process resources while retaining their own execution state. Sharing makes communication convenient but permits accidental conflicting access to ordinary objects. The central design question is which thread owns each mutable object and when ownership changes. An immutable object safely published to readers has a simpler contract than an object that every thread may update at any time.

topics.title: 43.5 Interleavings
topics.summary: An interleaving is one ordering of steps from several activities that preserves required within-activity order. Even a small example can have many interleavings. Source statements may correspond to several machine operations, so treating each line as an atomic step can hide failures. Use interleaving diagrams as models with explicitly defined atomic steps. They explain logical hazards but do not override language memory rules. An unsynchronized C++ data race is undefined behavior; it cannot be justified by saying that a particular hand-drawn interleaving seems harmless.

topics.title: 43.6 Nondeterminism
topics.summary: Nondeterminism means that the same apparent inputs can lead to different permitted execution orders or timing. Output order, completion order, and which thread obtains a lock first may vary. A concurrent program can still have deterministic results when synchronization and algorithm design make those ordering differences irrelevant. For example, independent partial sums combined after all workers finish can produce a fixed integer result when the arithmetic and partitioning are defined.

topics.title: 43.7 Multicore execution
topics.summary: Multicore hardware allows simultaneous instruction execution and maintains coherence for supported shared-memory accesses. Coherence does not make every multi-step operation atomic or provide all ordering needed by a language-level communication protocol. False sharing, cache-line movement, memory bandwidth, and scheduler placement can limit scaling. A correct design is the prerequisite; performance then depends on reducing unnecessary communication and contention while preserving the required synchronization.

topics.title: Worked example — Enumerating an abstract lost update
topics.summary: Model each of two activities as three steps: read a shared counter into a private temporary, add one to that temporary, and write it back. The model treats each step as atomic and enumerates all order-preserving interleavings. It is a mathematical state machine, not an execution of racy C++ code. Companion listing: ch43/interleavings.py The final value can be 1 when both activities read zero before either writes. It can be 2 when one complete increment precedes the other’s read. The lost update occurs because the intended read-modify-write operation was divided into separate steps without a coordination rule. The number of schedules is 6 choose 3 = 20 . Enumerating this tiny state space is feasible; real programs have vastly larger spaces. The scalable response is to establish invariants and synchronization rather than hope to test every timing arrangement.

topics.title: Worked example — Enumerating interleavings
topics.summary: Two threads each execute two operations: A1,A2 and B1,B2. Preserving each thread’s internal order yields six possible interleavings: A1 A2 B1 B2; A1 B1 A2 B2; A1 B1 B2 A2; B1 B2 A1 A2; B1 A1 B2 A2; and B1 A1 A2 B2. Concurrency introduces multiple legal orderings even before true simultaneous execution is considered.

topics.title: Worked example — Concurrency without parallelism
topics.summary: A single-core system can run many threads concurrently by time-slicing: one runs, is preempted or blocks, then another runs. Their executions overlap in time conceptually but not physically at the same instant. Parallelism requires multiple execution resources; concurrency requires overlapping progress and interleavings.

topics.title: 44.1 Thread creation
topics.summary: Creating a thread starts a new execution stream with a callable and arguments. Creation can fail because resources are unavailable. The new thread may begin executing before the constructor’s caller reaches its next statement. Prepare shared state before launching the worker. Capture references only to objects whose lifetimes extend through completion. Capturing a loop variable by reference can accidentally make several workers observe the same changing variable instead of distinct task indexes; capture each intended index by value.

topics.title: 44.2 Thread termination
topics.summary: A thread normally terminates by returning from its callable. An uncaught exception escaping a C++ thread function causes termination of the program under the standard thread interface; it is not automatically delivered to the creating thread. Catch worker failures inside the callable when recovery or reporting is required, and communicate them through an explicit channel such as an exception pointer protected by synchronization. Cooperative cancellation also requires the worker to check or wait on a supported stop condition; a stop request does not forcibly interrupt arbitrary blocking work.

topics.title: 44.3 Joining
topics.summary: Joining waits for a thread to finish and establishes the synchronization needed to observe its completed work. A std::thread must be joined or detached before its joinable destructor runs; otherwise the program terminates. std::jthread requests stop and joins during destruction when appropriate. Automatic joining is ownership help, not a deadlock cure. Destroying a joining thread object while holding a mutex the worker needs can block forever. Scope objects so that locks are released and shutdown conditions are established before joining.

topics.title: 44.4 Shared address spaces
topics.summary: Threads can access the same globals, heap objects, and explicitly shared stack objects. Shared addressability does not imply permission to perform unsynchronized conflicting operations. Ordinary mutable state needs ownership or synchronization. Read-only data is simpler, but its initialization must be safely published and its lifetime maintained. A pointer to immutable bytes is still unsafe after the owner destroys or reallocates the storage.

topics.title: 44.5 Thread-local state
topics.summary: Thread-local state gives each thread a distinct instance, reducing accidental sharing. C++ thread_local variables have thread storage duration and initialization/destruction rules that differ from automatic locals. Thread-local counters can reduce contention, but an aggregate result still requires a collection phase. Thread-local storage also consumes resources per thread, so a design with enormous thread counts can multiply memory costs.

topics.title: 44.6 Thread stacks
topics.summary: Each thread has a stack for its calls and automatic storage under the usual implementation model. A pointer into another thread’s stack can be shared, but the designated object must remain alive and accesses must be synchronized. Large automatic arrays and deep recursion multiply stack pressure across threads. A thread-per-connection server can consume substantial virtual and committed resources even when each worker appears simple. Resource budgeting should include stack and scheduler overhead, not only application payload buffers.

topics.title: 44.7 Thread scheduling
topics.summary: The scheduler decides when runnable threads execute. Thread creation order does not determine completion order. A blocked thread may not resume immediately when its condition becomes true because it must also obtain CPU time and any required lock. Avoid using sleeps to establish correctness. A delay that appears sufficient on one machine can fail under load, debugging, or different scheduling. Use joins, mutexes, condition variables, or explicit atomic protocols to express the required relationship.

topics.title: Worked example — Independent partial sums
topics.summary: Four workers sum disjoint ranges of the integers 1 through 100. Each writes a distinct array element. The parent combines results only after the worker owners leave scope and join. Companion listing: ch44/partial_sums.cpp The expected result is 5050. There is no conflicting access to the same array element during worker execution, and joining completes before the parent’s reads. Adjacent elements may still share a cache line, so the design can exhibit false sharing in a more write-intensive workload without containing a language-level data race. This example demonstrates correctness, not useful speedup for 100 additions. Thread creation overhead is likely to dominate such a small workload. A performance experiment should reuse workers or use sufficiently large tasks while preserving the same partitioning argument.

topics.title: Worked example — Joining a worker
topics.summary: A main thread launches a worker to compute a partial result. If main reads the result before synchronizing, it may observe incomplete state. Calling join waits for the worker to terminate and establishes the required completion relationship for the thread abstraction. After joining, resources associated with a joinable thread can be reclaimed according to the API.

topics.title: Worked example — Thread-local versus shared state
topics.summary: An automatic local variable inside a thread function typically resides in that thread’s stack, while a global variable is in the process address space shared by all threads. Two threads can each have distinct local counters but race on the shared global counter. Storage placement affects sharing semantics.

topics.title: Chapter 45 — Race Conditions
topics.summary: A race condition is a logical dependence on timing that violates the intended result. A data race has a specific C++ memory-model meaning involving conflicting accesses without the required ordering, with at least one access non-atomic. Data races cause undefined behavior; logical races can also occur in programs that use atomics and contain no data race. [ R22 ]

topics.summary: Shared state is information accessible to multiple activities. Mutable shared state requires a policy: one owner, a lock, atomic operations, or another proven protocol. Give each worker a private accumulator, use immutable messages, or transfer ownership through a queue. Eliminating a shared write is often simpler than coordinating it correctly.

topics.title: 45.2 Conflicting accesses
topics.summary: Two accesses conflict when they target overlapping memory in a way relevant to the language rules and at least one modifies state or affects object lifetime. Two ordinary reads can coexist when the object is safely initialized and remains alive. Different source-level variables can still interact through aliasing or overlapping storage. Conversely, distinct non-bit-field array elements are separate memory locations for ordinary concurrent-access reasoning. Hardware cache-line sharing is a performance concern distinct from language-level location identity.

topics.title: 45.3 Race conditions
topics.summary: A check-then-act sequence can race even when each individual check and update is atomic. Two customers may both observe the last item as available and each reserve it unless the combined transaction is coordinated. Define the intended indivisible operation. Is it one counter increment, a transfer between two accounts, or removal of one queue item together with count adjustment? Synchronization must protect that semantic unit, not merely surround an arbitrary convenient statement.

topics.title: 45.4 Data races
topics.summary: In C++, conflicting accesses in different threads require the appropriate happens-before relationship unless the accesses are covered by the atomic rules. A non-atomic shared counter increment without synchronization is not merely allowed to lose updates; the program has undefined behavior. Do not use a run that “usually prints the expected number” as evidence of correctness. Compiler transformations and hardware execution are constrained by the language’s defined programs, not by a programmer’s preferred interleaving of an undefined one. ThreadSanitizer can help detect observed races but cannot prove their absence on every path. [ R6 ]

topics.title: 45.5 Atomicity
topics.summary: Atomicity means that an operation is indivisible with respect to the relevant observers and model. An atomic load and an atomic store are individually indivisible, but the pair is not automatically one atomic read-modify-write transaction. Atomicity also has scope. An atomic integer operation does not make a neighboring ordinary structure update safe. A transaction spanning several objects generally needs a broader synchronization protocol or carefully designed multi-object algorithm.

topics.title: 45.6 Critical sections
topics.summary: A critical section is code that accesses state under an exclusion or coordination rule. Its boundaries should preserve the state invariant: acquire the protection, inspect and update related fields, restore a consistent state, then release. Keep blocking I/O and unknown callbacks outside a lock when possible, but do not shorten the section by moving required validation outside and reintroducing a race. Performance changes must preserve the same indivisible logical operation.

topics.title: Worked example — A data-race-free lost update
topics.summary: The first phase below deliberately separates atomic load and store. A barrier ensures that both participants read zero before either stores one. The second phase uses fetch_add , which performs one atomic read-modify-write per increment. Companion listing: ch45/logical_race.cpp The expected output is load/store=1 fetch_add=2 . Every counter access is atomic, so the first phase has no C++ data race. It is still the wrong implementation of “count two increments.” Strong default memory ordering does not combine separate operations into a transaction. The barrier makes the failure deterministic and inspectable. This is preferable to a demonstration that runs undefined code repeatedly and hopes to display a surprising number.

topics.title: Worked example — Lost update race
topics.summary: Two threads both execute counter++ on an ordinary shared integer initially zero. Each increment conceptually reads, adds one, and writes. If both read zero before either writes, both can store one, so the final value is one rather than two. The operation is not atomic merely because it appears as one source expression.

topics.title: Worked example — Critical-section repair
topics.summary: Protecting the increment with the same mutex makes the read-modify-write sequence mutually exclusive. Thread A locks, reads zero, stores one, unlocks; only then can thread B enter and produce two. The lock protects the invariant that no two threads update the counter simultaneously.

topics.title: Chapter 46 — Atomic Operations

topics.title: 46.1 Atomic loads
topics.summary: An atomic load reads an atomic object’s value according to the selected memory order. It avoids a non-atomic conflicting access to that object. It does not automatically make unrelated ordinary memory safe to read. An acquire load can participate in publication when it observes the appropriate release operation or release sequence under the language rules. Without that relationship, attaching the word acquire to a load is not a general promise that every other thread’s latest writes become available.

topics.title: 46.2 Atomic stores
topics.summary: An atomic store updates one atomic object. A release store can publish earlier ordinary writes to a reader that acquires the corresponding publication. The order applies to the protocol, not to a physical instruction named “flush all memory.” A reusable flag needs more care than a one-shot flag. If a producer overwrites payload data while a consumer still reads it, a correct first publication does not prevent a later race. Reuse requires ownership transfer, acknowledgments, sequence numbers, or another complete protocol.

topics.title: 46.3 Read-modify-write
topics.summary: An atomic read-modify-write operation reads and updates an object as one indivisible operation. Examples include fetch_add , exchange, and compare-and-swap. This avoids the lost-update problem of a separate load followed by store. The returned value and update rule matter. fetch_add returns the previous value, making it useful for allocating unique sequence positions within a bounded, overflow-aware design. It does not make the data stored at those positions automatically initialized or published.

topics.title: 46.4 Atomic variables
topics.summary: std::atomic<T> provides atomic operations for supported types. topics.title: 46.5 Compare-and-swap
topics.summary: Compare-and-swap compares the atomic value with an expected value and conditionally replaces it with a desired value. In the C++ interface, failure updates the expected argument with the observed value. Weak forms can fail spuriously and are commonly used in retry loops. A bounded increment can repeatedly load a value, reject it when at the limit, and attempt to replace it with value plus one. The addition is safe only after proving the bound. CAS does not solve memory reclamation or the ABA problem by itself: a pointer can change away and back while the referenced object’s identity or lifetime changes. A simple default-order loop has this shape: The test expected < limit ensures expected + 1 cannot exceed the unsigned maximum when limit is representable. Explicit weaker memory orders require a separate proof, including valid success and failure order combinations.

topics.title: 46.6 Memory ordering
topics.summary: Relaxed ordering provides atomicity and the atomic object’s modification-order guarantees without using that operation to publish unrelated ordinary data. It is appropriate for some independent statistics and counters when no additional ordering is required. Release/acquire ordering supports directed publication. Sequential consistency adds a single total order for the relevant sequentially consistent operations, consistent with the standard’s constraints. It is a useful starting point but still does not repair an algorithm with the wrong atomic operation boundaries. Do not translate memory orders into folklore such as “always use relaxed on x86” or “a compiler barrier is enough.” The C++ abstract machine, compiler transformations, and hardware ordering all participate. Begin with a simple correct protocol and weaken ordering only when the proof and measured need justify the complexity.

topics.title: Worked example — One-shot publication
topics.summary: A producer initializes a three-element payload and then publishes readiness with release ordering. The consumer waits with acquire ordering and reads the payload before joining the producer. That ordering relationship, not the later join, protects the payload read. Companion listing: ch46/publication.cpp The expected result is 21. The acquire load that observes true synchronizes with the release publication, making the prior payload initialization available to the consumer under the language model. The payload is never modified again, and all objects remain alive through the join. The spin/yield loop is deliberately simple. For long waits, a blocking facility can avoid repeated polling. Do not generalize this one-shot example into a reusable producer–consumer queue by merely resetting the flag; reuse introduces new ownership and ordering requirements.

topics.title: Worked example — Compare-and-swap loop
topics.summary: To increment an atomic value with compare-and-swap, load the expected old value, compute desired = old+1 , then attempt to replace old with desired only if the atomic still equals old. If another thread changed it first, retry using the newly observed value. CAS turns a conditional read-modify-write into one indivisible atomic operation.

topics.title: Worked example — Release/acquire publication
topics.summary: A producer initializes ordinary data, then performs a release store to an atomic ready flag. A consumer spins or waits until an acquire load observes the published ready value. The release/acquire pair establishes visibility of the producer’s earlier writes to the consumer, provided the program obeys the memory-model requirements.

topics.title: Chapter 47 — Mutual Exclusion
topics.summary: Mutual exclusion gives one participant at a time access to a protected region. A mutex is useful not because it makes code “thread-safe” by proximity, but because every relevant access follows the same ownership rule and preserves a defined invariant. The invariant should be stated in ordinary language before the lock operations are written. [ R25 , R34 ]

topics.title: 47.1 Mutexes
topics.summary: A mutex coordinates exclusive ownership. A thread acquires it before accessing protected mutable state and releases it afterward. Correct use establishes both exclusion and the ordering needed to observe prior protected updates. A mutex protects a rule about state , not a particular memory address by magic. If another function accesses the same state without the mutex, the rule is broken. Keep the state private behind an interface where practical so that callers cannot bypass the protection accidentally.

topics.title: 47.2 Lock
topics.summary: Locking obtains exclusive ownership, potentially waiting while another thread owns the mutex. A lock acquisition is therefore a possible blocking point. Avoid assuming that a short critical section always makes acquisition immediate. Use RAII ownership such as std::lock_guard or std::unique_lock in C++ to tie release to scope. Manual lock/unlock pairs are vulnerable to early returns and exceptions. unique_lock is appropriate when the code needs controlled unlocking or condition-variable waiting.

topics.title: 47.3 Unlock
topics.summary: Unlocking releases ownership and permits another participant to acquire the mutex. All protected invariants should hold at this boundary. An exception that leaves partially updated state must either restore the invariant or make failure state explicit before release. Do not unlock a mutex from a thread that does not own it under the ordinary mutex contract. Do not retain references to mutable internal data and then access them after unlocking unless a separate lifetime and synchronization rule permits it.

topics.title: 47.4 Critical sections
topics.summary: The critical section contains the operations that must be observed together. For an account transfer, checking funds and updating both balances belong to one logical transaction. Protecting only the final store leaves a check-then-act race. Keep sections focused. Expensive computation can often be performed on a snapshot outside the lock, but the result may need validation when applied. Releasing the lock does not freeze the state that was inspected earlier.

topics.title: 47.5 Protected state
topics.summary: Related fields should be grouped under a clear protection policy. A queue’s storage, head, tail, count, and closure flag may form one invariant. Protecting each field with an unrelated lock can expose combinations that never represented a valid queue state. Document the policy near the data definition. For example: “All reads and writes of these balances require mutex_ ; their sum remains constant.” Such a statement is more useful than a vague comment saying “thread-safe class.”

topics.title: 47.6 Lock invariants
topics.summary: A lock invariant describes what is true whenever protected state is available to another owner. Temporary internal states can exist while the lock is held, but they must not escape through callbacks, unlocked references, or exceptions. An invariant also guides tests. Verify conservation laws, bounds, and relationships, not only whether threads finish. A program that never crashes can still lose items, duplicate work, or violate accounting constraints.

topics.title: 47.7 Coarse-grained locking
topics.summary: Coarse-grained locking uses one lock for a broad region or related state group. It is often easier to prove correct and avoids many lock-order problems. For modest contention, its simplicity can outweigh theoretical parallelism lost inside the critical section. The cost appears when unrelated operations serialize behind the same mutex. Measure contention before splitting the design. A clear coarse-grained implementation provides a valuable correctness baseline for later optimization.

topics.title: 47.8 Fine-grained locking
topics.summary: Fine-grained locking divides protection among smaller state regions. It can allow independent operations to proceed concurrently but adds ownership, ordering, and lifecycle complexity. Operations spanning regions may need several locks. A finer design must define a consistent acquisition order or use a deadlock-avoiding multi-lock facility. More locks can also increase memory use, cache traffic, and maintenance cost. Fine-grained is a tradeoff, not a synonym for faster.

topics.title: Worked example — Preserve a conservation invariant
topics.summary: The ledger below starts with 1000 units on the left and zero on the right. Four workers each move 100 units, one at a time. One mutex protects both balances, and every transfer preserves their sum. Companion listing: ch47/ledger.cpp The expected output is left=600 right=400 . No transfer can observe the half-updated pair because all protected access uses the same mutex. Returning a copied snapshot keeps callers from retaining a reference that would bypass the lock after the function returns. The arithmetic is bounded by the initial total, so the example’s unsigned additions cannot exceed 1000. A general financial or inventory system would need explicit numeric range and domain rules rather than assuming those bounds remain true for arbitrary inputs.

topics.title: Worked example — Protecting a bank balance
topics.summary: Suppose balance must never be observed halfway through an update. Every operation that reads or modifies the invariant acquires the same mutex. A transfer locks before checking funds and updating the balance, then unlocks after the invariant is restored. The mutex is useful because the protected-state rule is consistent across all access paths.

topics.title: Worked example — Coarse versus fine locking
topics.summary: One global mutex around an entire table is easy to reason about but serializes unrelated operations. One mutex per bucket can allow independent buckets to proceed concurrently but complicates operations touching multiple buckets. Fine-grained locking trades simpler contention behavior for more complicated ordering and invariant management.

topics.title: 48.1 Waiting
topics.summary: Waiting should mean “sleep until it is worth checking the predicate again,” not “assume the event must have happened because I woke up.” A waiter holds the mutex while inspecting state and uses the condition variable to release ownership while blocked. This avoids wasting CPU in a polling loop and allows the producer of the condition to acquire the mutex. Waiting while continuing to hold the needed mutex would prevent the state change that could satisfy the predicate.

topics.title: 48.2 Notification
topics.summary: Notification makes one or more waiters eligible to reconsider their predicates. It does not transfer the mutex directly into a guarantee that the predicate remains true until the awakened thread runs. Another thread may acquire the mutex first and consume the resource. The waiter must therefore recheck under the lock. Notification is a scheduling hint within a state protocol, not the protocol’s authoritative record.

topics.title: 48.3 wait
topics.summary: wait atomically releases the associated lock and enters the waiting operation, then reacquires the lock before returning to the caller. The predicate overload expresses the required loop directly. Use the same mutex discipline for the predicate’s shared state. Updating the predicate without its required protection can introduce a data race or lose the relationship between state change and sleeping. The mutex and condition variable must remain alive while waiters can use them.

topics.title: 48.4 notify_one
topics.summary: notify_one wakes one eligible waiter. It is appropriate when one newly available unit of work can satisfy one interchangeable consumer. The awakened thread still competes for the mutex and checks the predicate. When different waiter classes use different predicates, waking an arbitrary one may not produce progress. Separate condition variables or broader notification may be needed. Choose based on the state machine, not solely on a desire to minimize wakeups.

topics.title: 48.5 notify_all
topics.summary: notify_all wakes all current waiters so that each can check its condition. It is useful for closure, shutdown, or state changes that may satisfy several different predicates. Waking many threads can create contention, sometimes called a thundering herd. That cost does not justify omitting required wakeups. First ensure all affected waiters can make progress or terminate; then refine the notification policy if measurement shows a problem.

topics.title: 48.6 Predicate loops
topics.summary: A predicate loop handles spurious wakeups and state changes consumed by another participant. The canonical form is condition.wait(lock, [&]{ return predicate; }); . After it returns, the predicate is true while the caller still owns the mutex. Do not move the predicate check outside the lock to save a few instructions. The check and decision to wait must be coordinated with the state updates. An atomic flag alone does not automatically repair a poorly designed condition-variable protocol.

topics.title: 48.7 Sleep/wakeup races
topics.summary: A sleep/wakeup race occurs when a thread checks state, another thread changes it and notifies, and the first thread then sleeps without seeing a future notification. The condition-variable wait operation closes this gap when used with the shared mutex and predicate discipline. The structure resembles the signal-mask solution in Chapter 41, although the mechanisms differ. In both cases, the program needs an atomic relationship between checking whether to sleep and making itself eligible for notification.

topics.title: 48.8 Lost wakeups
topics.summary: A notification sent when no thread is waiting is not retained as a future wakeup token. This is harmless when the state predicate remains true: a later waiter sees it and does not sleep. It is a bug only when the design incorrectly relies on notification history instead of persistent state. For example, set ready = true under the mutex, then notify. A worker that starts after the notification still observes ready and proceeds. Omitting the state variable and waiting for an imagined remembered notification is the broken design.

topics.title: Worked example — Notification before waiting is safe with a predicate
topics.summary: The main thread publishes value 42 and marks it ready. The worker may begin waiting before or after publication; either schedule is correct because it tests the protected predicate. Companion listing: ch48/gate.cpp The result is 42 without any sleep-based timing assumption. Notification occurs after unlocking, which is valid for this protocol and can avoid waking a thread only to make it immediately wait for the same mutex. The correctness argument depends on the protected state, not on that performance-oriented placement.

topics.title: Worked example — Correct wait loop
topics.summary: A consumer locks the mutex and evaluates while (queue.empty()) cv.wait(lock); . The wait operation atomically releases the mutex and sleeps, then reacquires the mutex before returning. The loop rechecks the predicate because wakeups can be spurious or another consumer may consume the item first. Notification is a hint to reevaluate shared state, not a transfer of ownership.

topics.title: Worked example — notify_one versus notify_all
topics.summary: If adding one queue item can satisfy at most one waiting consumer, notify_one often avoids waking threads that cannot make progress. topics.title: Chapter 49 — Producer–Consumer Systems
topics.summary: A producer–consumer system separates creation of work from processing of work. A bounded queue connects the two rates and applies backpressure when producers get ahead. Its correctness requires more than a mutex around a container: it needs predicates, closure semantics, ownership rules, and a way for every waiter to terminate. The queue in this chapter stores integers in preallocated slots. That keeps allocation and throwing element moves out of push and pop , making the synchronization argument visible. A generic production queue must additionally define exception guarantees for its element type.

topics.title: 49.1 Producers
topics.summary: Producers create items and attempt to transfer them into the queue. A successful push transfers responsibility to the queue. A rejected push after closure leaves the caller responsible for whatever resource the item represents. Production rate should not be assumed lower than consumption rate. Bursts, slow downstream services, and failures can make the queue fill. Bounded capacity converts that condition into an explicit wait or rejection instead of unbounded memory growth.

A rejected push after closure leaves the caller responsible for whatever resource the item represents. Production rate should not be assumed lower than consumption rate. Bursts, slow downstream services, and failures can make the queue fill. Bounded capacity converts that condition into an explicit wait or rejection instead of unbounded memory growth.

topics.title: 49.2 Consumers
topics.summary: Consumers wait for an available item, remove it under the queue’s protection, and process it outside the queue lock. Processing outside the lock lets other participants enqueue and dequeue while the current item is being handled. A consumer must distinguish temporarily empty from permanently closed-and-drained. Returning an empty result merely because no item is available at one instant would incorrectly terminate a worker while producers are still active.

topics.title: 49.3 Shared buffers
topics.summary: The shared buffer stores items not yet transferred to consumers. A ring buffer uses a fixed array with head and tail indexes. Count distinguishes empty from full when indexes alone are ambiguous. The invariant includes 0 <= count <= capacity , valid head and tail indexes, and a relationship between occupied slots and logical order. All fields that participate in that invariant use the same mutex in this implementation.

topics.title: 49.4 Bounded buffers
topics.summary: A bounded buffer has a fixed maximum number of queued items. It limits queue storage and provides a natural point for backpressure. It does not by itself limit all system resources: producers may hold items before pushing, and consumers may hold items while processing. Budget the complete pipeline. If each of 100 workers can retain a large item, a small queue does not imply a small total memory footprint. Capacity controls one ownership stage, not every live object in the process.

topics.title: 49.5 Buffer-full condition
topics.summary: A producer waits while the queue is full and still open. Its predicate is closed || count < capacity . Including closure ensures that shutdown can release producers that would otherwise wait forever for capacity. After waking, the producer checks closure before inserting. A notification does not reserve a slot for a particular producer; another producer may acquire the mutex first. The predicate loop handles that competition.

topics.title: 49.6 Buffer-empty condition
topics.summary: A consumer waits while the queue is empty and open. Its predicate is closed || count > 0 . If the queue is closed but still contains items, the consumer drains them under the policy used here. When closed and empty, pop returns no item, signaling normal completion. This is drain-on-close , not immediate cancellation. An aborting queue would need a different contract for queued and in-flight items.

topics.title: 49.7 Mutex synchronization
topics.summary: One mutex protects slots, indexes, count, and closure. The queue does not expose references to occupied slots after unlocking. Instead it copies an integer out while protected, then returns ownership of that value. The mutex also supplies visibility between the producer’s slot write and the consumer’s slot read. No extra atomic count is needed in this locked implementation. Adding atomics to already-protected fields can complicate the design without improving correctness.

topics.title: 49.8 Condition-variable synchronization
topics.summary: One condition variable represents the possibility of items becoming available; another represents capacity becoming available. Push notifies a consumer after insertion, and pop notifies a producer after removal. Closure notifies both groups. The predicates remain authoritative. Notifications happen after unlocking in this implementation, but state changes occur under the mutex. Queue destruction is permitted only after all producers and consumers have stopped using it; close is not an automatic join operation.

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded, drainable integer queue
topics.summary: Companion listing: ch49/bounded_queue.hpp Companion listing: ch49/main.cpp The expected sum is 5050. Capacity eight forces the implementation to support reuse of ring slots during the 100-item transfer. Scheduling determines exactly when participants wait; the correctness result does not depend on a particular waiting count. For arbitrary capacity values near size_t limits, even index increment needs range analysis. Here a successfully allocated vector<int> has a practical and implementation-constrained maximum well below a wrapping index increment. A more general storage abstraction should state and enforce its own maximum capacity explicitly.

topics.summary: A bounded queue has at least two logically distinct conditions: not-empty for consumers and not-full for producers. topics.title: Guided lab and review
topics.summary: Lab 49. Test capacity one, immediate closure, closure with queued items, push after closure, and several consumers with per-consumer sums. Then extend the same queue to multiple producers and consumers. Force shutdown while a producer is blocked on a full queue and while a consumer is blocked on an empty queue. Give every attempted item a unique identity and track attempted, accepted, consumed, and rejected-after-close counts. Under the chapter’s drain-on-close contract, verify at quiescence that accepted = consumed and that each accepted identity appears exactly once. All workers must finish before queue destruction. Review 1. Why notify both producer and consumer waiters on close? Review 2. Does bounded queue capacity bound all in-flight memory?

topics.title: Chapter 50 — Deadlock
topics.summary: Deadlock is a state in which participants cannot progress because each waits for resources or actions that the others cannot provide without first progressing themselves. It differs from slow execution, starvation, and livelock. A system can be busy while making no useful progress, or idle while permanently blocked. Preventing deadlock requires a resource-acquisition policy and lifecycle design. Adding timeouts can reveal or limit a wait, but it does not automatically restore a consistent state or release every dependent resource.

topics.title: 50.1 Deadlock conditions
topics.summary: The classical resource model identifies four conditions associated with deadlock: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Together they describe how a closed dependency cycle can become permanent under that model. The conditions are an analysis tool, not a claim that every concurrent failure is a lock cycle. Waiting for a notification that will never be sent, joining a thread while preventing its shutdown, or blocking a pipeline before starting its consumer can create related progress failures that deserve explicit dependency analysis.

topics.title: 50.2 Mutual exclusion
topics.summary: Mutual exclusion means some resource cannot be used by all participants simultaneously. A mutex is the obvious example, but a single-capacity communication slot or exclusive external transaction can also play a role. Removing unnecessary exclusivity can eliminate a dependency. Immutable shared data and independent per-thread state often need no exclusive lock. Where exclusivity is required for correctness, the design must address the other conditions instead of simply removing protection.

Immutable shared data and independent per-thread state often need no exclusive lock. Where exclusivity is required for correctness, the design must address the other conditions instead of simply removing protection.

Then identify the evidence you would inspect to test the claim without overgeneralizing from a single successful run.

In simpler terms, mutual exclusion means some resource cannot be used by all participants simultaneously.

topics.title: 50.3 Hold and wait
topics.summary: Hold and wait occurs when a participant retains one resource while requesting another. A thread holding lock A while waiting for lock B creates an edge from its current ownership to its next dependency. Acquiring all required locks through a coordinated operation or releasing held resources before a retry can break this condition in suitable designs. Releasing and retrying requires care: state may change, so validation must be repeated and partial updates must not escape.

topics.title: 50.4 No preemption
topics.summary: No preemption means the resource cannot simply be taken away from its owner safely. An ordinary mutex cannot be forcibly unlocked by an unrelated thread without violating its contract. The owner may be halfway through an invariant-changing operation. This is why “kill the stuck thread” is not a general recovery strategy. The thread may leave shared state inconsistent and locks permanently unavailable. Process isolation and transactional recovery can provide stronger failure boundaries when forced termination is a requirement.

topics.title: 50.5 Circular wait
topics.summary: Circular wait exists when participants form a dependency cycle. Thread A holds lock X and waits for Y, while thread B holds Y and waits for X. Neither can reach the unlock that the other requires. A global lock order prevents this pattern when every participant follows it. The order must cover all relevant locks, including library callbacks and less obvious resources, or the apparent proof can omit an edge.

topics.title: 50.6 Wait-for graphs
topics.summary: A wait-for graph draws an edge from a waiting participant to the participant whose action or resource release it needs. A cycle indicates a potential or actual deadlock under the graph’s resource assumptions. For locks with one owner, the graph is straightforward. Multiple-instance resources, timeouts, and alternative progress paths require more careful interpretation. Record what each edge means and whether an external event can break it before declaring a permanent deadlock.

topics.title: 50.7 Lock ordering
topics.summary: Lock ordering assigns a consistent order and requires acquisition in that order. Two-account transfers can order accounts by a stable application identifier, or use a facility such as std::scoped_lock that applies a deadlock-avoiding multi-lock algorithm. Do not use built-in relational comparison of unrelated object pointers as a portable general ordering rule. Use stable identifiers or the appropriate library total-order facility when pointer ordering is genuinely needed. Also handle the same-object case before attempting to lock one nonrecursive mutex twice.

topics.title: 50.8 Deadlock prevention
topics.summary: Prevention structurally breaks at least one condition. Examples include avoiding nested locks, using a global order, making state immutable, or acquiring a required set with a coordinated locking algorithm. Prevention can reduce concurrency or require redesign, but it gives a strong argument before deployment. A simple lock hierarchy documented and enforced in code is often more reliable than a collection of ad hoc timeouts added after hangs appear.

topics.title: 50.9 Deadlock avoidance
topics.summary: Avoidance examines current allocations and future needs to reject requests that could enter an unsafe state. Classical banker’s-algorithm reasoning requires known resource limits and maximum claims, which many general software workloads do not provide accurately. An unsafe state is not necessarily already deadlocked; it lacks a guaranteed completion sequence under the stated maximum-need assumptions. Distinguish admission control based on known budgets from prevention through a fixed lock order.

topics.title: Worked example — Opposite-direction transfers without opposite lock order
topics.summary: Two workers transfer one unit in opposite directions 200 times. The transfer operation locks both account mutexes with std::scoped_lock , checks available funds, and updates both balances while protected. The same-account case returns before locking. Companion listing: ch50/transfers.cpp The expected output is 1000 1000 . Initial funds are sufficient even when all 200 transfers in one direction happen first, so no operation should be rejected. The final check verifies the intended balanced workload, while the conserved-total argument bounds arithmetic throughout execution. Now consider an avoidance model with three identical resources. A holds one and may need two more; B holds one and may need two more; one remains available. Neither maximum claim can currently be satisfied to completion, so the state is unsafe under that claim model. It is not necessarily already deadlocked if neither has yet made a blocking request, but an avoidance policy would reject entering such a state when its guarantees require a safe completion sequence.

topics.title: Worked example — Detecting a circular wait
topics.summary: Thread A holds lock X and waits for Y, while thread B holds Y and waits for X. The wait-for graph contains A -> B and B -> A, a cycle. If neither lock can be preempted, the two threads cannot progress. Enforcing a global order such as always acquire X before Y removes this two-lock cycle.

topics.title: Chapter 51 — Network Programming
topics.summary: Network programming extends resource and protocol reasoning across independently scheduled peers. A successful connection does not make the peer’s input valid, and a successful send does not mean that an entire application transaction has completed. Programs must define framing, bounds, byte ordering, completion, and failure behavior explicitly. The examples use local loopback TCP only. They do not provide authentication, encryption, internet deployment, or a production security policy. The goal is to understand socket lifecycle and byte-stream handling without exposing a public service. [ R26 , R27 ]

topics.title: 51.1 Sockets
topics.summary: A socket is an endpoint managed through a descriptor. Its address family and type determine the communication model. Internet stream sockets typically use TCP, while local-domain sockets and datagram sockets provide different addressing or delivery semantics. A socket descriptor follows the same ownership rules as other descriptors: one owner closes it, borrowed uses must finish before closure, and the integer can be reused afterward. Closing a descriptor from another thread is not a universal cancellation mechanism for an in-progress operation.

topics.title: 51.2 socket
topics.summary: socket creates an endpoint with a selected family, type, and protocol. It returns a descriptor or -1 . Creation does not by itself bind a listening address or establish a connection. Set required descriptor and status flags deliberately. On Linux, creation flags can establish close-on-exec or nonblocking behavior atomically. Do not assume that a later accepted socket automatically inherits every desired flag from its listener.

topics.title: 51.3 bind
topics.summary: bind associates a socket with a local address. For an IPv4 loopback service, bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than all interfaces when external access is not required. Using port zero asks the operating system to choose an available ephemeral port. Address structures contain fields with specified byte order. Use conversion functions such as htons and htonl for network-order integer fields. Do not serialize a host-native structure by dumping its memory representation and hoping another machine interprets it identically.

topics.title: 51.4 listen
topics.summary: listen places a suitable socket into a listening state. Its backlog parameter relates to pending connection handling under the platform’s rules; it is not a complete application limit on active clients, memory, or work queues. A server still needs admission control after accepting connections. Increasing backlog does not create more worker capacity or solve resource exhaustion. It changes one stage of a larger queueing system.

topics.title: 51.5 accept
topics.summary: accept obtains a new connected socket from the listener’s pending connections. The listening socket remains available for further accepts. The returned socket, not the listener, carries the client’s byte stream. [ R43 ] A nonblocking listener can return EAGAIN when no connection is currently available, including after a readiness indication whose state changed. Configure accepted-socket flags explicitly. A service that forgets to close rejected or completed client sockets leaks descriptors over time.

topics.title: 51.6 connect
topics.summary: connect requests establishment of a connection to a peer address. Blocking and nonblocking forms have different completion handling. A nonblocking connect that reports in-progress is not yet a successful usable connection; readiness and the socket error state must be checked according to the interface. [ R44 ] Connection failure is normal: the service may not exist, policy may reject access, or the network may be unavailable. Retry policy needs limits and backoff. Repeatedly reconnecting without a budget can turn a remote failure into local resource exhaustion.

topics.title: 51.7 Client/server architecture
topics.summary: A server offers a service through a known or discovered endpoint; a client initiates a request. Once connected, both sides can send and receive according to the application protocol. Roles do not change the need to validate all incoming data. Define request and response formats before writing the main loop. Specify maximum lengths, supported versions, how errors are represented, and whether a connection carries one message or many. Ambiguous framing produces bugs that cannot be repaired merely by enlarging a receive buffer.

topics.title: 51.8 TCP connections
topics.summary: TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream under its protocol, not application-message boundaries. One send can be received through several reads, and several sends can be combined in one read. A positive receive result reports bytes currently obtained, not necessarily a complete request. [ R27 , R49 , R50 ] A common framing scheme uses a fixed-width length prefix followed by exactly that many payload bytes. Decode the prefix in a defined byte order, reject lengths above a configured maximum before allocating, and treat EOF in the middle of a frame as truncation. A normal EOF between frames has a different protocol meaning from a truncated frame.

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded framed loopback exchange
topics.summary: The reusable header below owns descriptors, bounds frames to 1024 bytes, handles partial transfers and EINTR , and treats premature EOF as failure. It uses Linux’s MSG_NOSIGNAL for sends so that a broken connection becomes an error instead of terminating the process through SIGPIPE . The small socket timeouts are per-operation limits, not a complete whole-request deadline policy. Companion listing: ch51/net.hpp The driver binds only loopback, obtains the chosen port, and establishes the client connection before starting the accepting worker. This avoids leaving an accept worker waiting forever if the test’s initial connect fails. The server worker catches its own exceptions; the parent checks its result after joining. Companion listing: ch51/main.cpp The expected output is loopback frame checks passed . The protocol consists of a four-byte big-endian length and payload. The test transfers one five-byte payload, but the helpers also permit an empty frame. A complete service would need repeated-frame handling, whole-request deadlines, admission control, graceful shutdown, and a security layer appropriate to its deployment.

topics.summary: TCP preserves byte order but not application message boundaries. It must first accumulate exactly the framing header, decode the length safely, then accumulate exactly that many payload bytes subject to a configured maximum.

topics.summary: A concurrent server handles overlapping client lifecycles while sharing finite resources. topics.title: 52.1 Thread-per-connection
topics.summary: A thread-per-connection design assigns a worker to each accepted client. Blocking I/O becomes straightforward because one slow connection blocks its own worker rather than the entire server loop. The control flow resembles a sequential protocol handler. The cost grows with active connections: thread stacks, scheduler state, per-connection buffers, and synchronization overhead accumulate. An unbounded thread-per-connection loop can exhaust resources before useful work completes. Bound admission and ensure every thread is joined or otherwise owned through shutdown.

topics.title: 52.2 Connection state
topics.summary: Connection state includes protocol progress, input and output buffers, authentication or session information, deadlines, and lifecycle status. A connection may be reading a prefix, reading a body, computing a response, writing a partial response, or closing. Make state transitions explicit. “Socket exists” is not enough to determine which operation is valid next. A half-closed connection can still have data to drain or a response to send, depending on the protocol. Cleanup should occur only when no worker or event handler can still reference the connection object.

topics.title: 52.3 Shared resources
topics.summary: Connections compete for descriptors, memory, CPU, downstream services, caches, and application data. Per-connection limits do not replace global limits. A thousand individually acceptable requests can collectively overwhelm a shared database or work queue. Define budgets at each stage. An accepted socket may count against a connection limit, a parsed request against a queued-work limit, and an executing task against a worker limit. Transfer the corresponding ownership credits when work moves between stages, and release them on every failure path.

A thousand individually acceptable requests can collectively overwhelm a shared database or work queue. Define budgets at each stage. An accepted socket may count against a connection limit, a parsed request against a queued-work limit, and an executing task against a worker limit. Transfer the corresponding ownership credits when work moves between stages, and release them on every failure path.

topics.title: 52.4 Synchronization
topics.summary: Shared application state requires the same synchronization rules developed in Parts X and XI. A server should avoid holding global locks while waiting for a client or downstream service. Slow external activity inside a critical section can stall otherwise independent clients. Use snapshots, immutable request objects, and bounded queues to separate I/O from protected updates. A worker pool limits simultaneously executing handlers, but an unbounded queue in front of it can still consume unlimited memory and produce extreme waiting times.

topics.title: 52.5 Resource exhaustion
topics.summary: Exhaustion occurs when demand exceeds a resource limit. Symptoms include failed thread creation, descriptor exhaustion, allocation failure, long queues, and timeout cascades. Rejecting or deferring work deliberately is often safer than accepting everything and failing unpredictably later. A robust policy specifies admission limits, maximum frame sizes, idle and whole-request deadlines, output-buffer limits, and shutdown behavior. Per-operation socket timeouts alone do not defeat a client that makes tiny amounts of progress just before each timeout; a whole-request deadline bounds the complete transaction.

topics.title: Worked example — Derive an admission budget
topics.summary: Assume a hypothetical service budget , not a measurement of the host system: The descriptor bound is 1024 - 64 = 960 clients when each client uses one descriptor. The modeled per-client memory is 72 KiB. The remaining memory is 96 MiB, which permits floor(96 × 1024 / 72) = 1365 clients under those assumptions. The combined arithmetic ceiling is therefore 960. Choosing an operational cap of 256 leaves headroom. Its modeled client memory is 256 × 72 KiB = 18 MiB ; adding the 32-MiB base gives 50 MiB. This does not include every possible kernel buffer or thread reservation. The assumptions must be replaced with measurements and explicit accounting before using the number as a deployment limit. Companion listing: ch52/budget.py The output is ceiling=960 cap=256 modeled_MiB=50 . The code verifies the budget calculation, not a claim that 960 live threads or clients are safe on the current machine. Real thread stack reservation and committed use are distinct quantities, and downstream capacity may impose a much lower cap.

topics.title: Worked example — Thread-per-connection budget
topics.summary: If each connection thread reserves an 8 MiB stack, 1,000 concurrent connections can imply roughly 8 GiB of virtual stack reservation before application buffers and kernel state. Even when pages are demand allocated, this architecture has scaling costs. Admission limits and smaller controlled stacks can matter as much as CPU throughput.

topics.title: Worked example — Shared cache synchronization
topics.summary: A concurrent server may let every connection consult a shared in-memory cache. Reads and updates need a synchronization strategy: a mutex, reader-writer scheme, sharding, or another concurrency-safe design. Per-connection threading does not make shared application state private.

topics.title: Chapter 53 — Event-Driven I/O
topics.summary: An event-driven server keeps many connection state machines in a smaller number of execution threads. Instead of blocking one thread per idle connection, it waits for readiness and advances the corresponding state only as far as current I/O permits. This trades simple sequential control flow for explicit state, buffers, and scheduling policy. Readiness is not completion. A readable socket may provide only part of a frame, and a writable socket may accept only part of a response. A correct event loop records partial progress and resumes later without losing ownership or duplicating bytes. [ R28 , R29 ]

topics.title: 53.1 Blocking
topics.summary: A blocking operation can suspend the calling thread until progress or failure occurs. In a one-thread event loop, an unexpected blocking call can stall every connection managed by that loop. Set nonblocking mode on all endpoints whose operations must never stall the reactor. On Linux, accepted sockets need their flags established explicitly; inheriting the listener’s intended behavior is not a portable assumption. Potentially blocking computation and filesystem operations also require architectural attention.

topics.title: 53.2 Polling
topics.summary: Polling can mean repeatedly checking state without sleeping, or using an interface named poll that waits for readiness. Distinguish the two. A tight loop around EAGAIN is busy polling; it consumes CPU without creating data or capacity. A readiness wait lets the kernel block the event-loop thread until an event or timeout is relevant. Some low-latency systems deliberately busy-poll under controlled budgets, but that is a specialized tradeoff, not a default error-handling loop.

topics.title: 53.3 select
topics.summary: select monitors descriptor sets for readiness. The caller prepares sets and a descriptor-range bound, then inspects the modified sets after return. The interface’s set representation imposes limits, including the fixed FD_SETSIZE constraint in common libc implementations. Do not place an arbitrary large descriptor into a fixed-size set. The highest descriptor number, not merely the count of active descriptors, matters. For larger or more dynamic sets, other interfaces often provide a more suitable representation. [ R41 ]

topics.title: 53.4 poll
topics.summary: poll uses an array of descriptor-event entries rather than fixed descriptor bit sets. It reports readiness and error conditions per entry. The array must still be scanned and maintained by the application. A readiness event can coexist with hangup or error indicators. Read buffered data before treating a hangup as proof that no data remains. The operation’s return value remains authoritative when attempted after readiness. [ R28 ]

topics.title: 53.5 epoll
topics.summary: Linux epoll maintains an interest set and returns ready events. It supports level-triggered and edge-triggered modes. Level-triggered behavior continues to report readiness while the condition remains; edge-triggered use requires carefully draining nonblocking operations until they would block. [ R29 ] Do not describe epoll as making every network operation universally constant-time. Registration changes, event delivery, application state lookup, and actual I/O still cost work. Its usefulness comes from avoiding repeated handling of large inactive descriptor sets in suitable workloads.

topics.title: 53.6 Event loops
topics.summary: An event loop waits, dispatches ready connections, performs bounded work, updates interest masks, and handles timers and shutdown. Each connection retains input progress, output progress, and protocol state between dispatches. Register write readiness only when output remains pending; an idle socket is often writable and can otherwise wake the loop continuously. For edge-triggered operation, stopping before EAGAIN for fairness requires an explicit rescheduling strategy so that remaining work is not forgotten while waiting for a new edge.

topics.title: 53.7 Active connections
topics.summary: Connection lifetime must outlast every queued event and task that refers to it. Descriptor numbers can be reused, so identifying a connection solely by an old integer in delayed work can target a new connection accidentally. Use ownership-aware objects, generation identifiers, or another strategy that validates event identity. Closing and deleting a connection is a state transition coordinated with the reactor, not an arbitrary action another thread should perform while callbacks still hold raw pointers.

topics.title: 53.8 Scaling large numbers of connections
topics.summary: Event-driven designs reduce thread-per-idle-connection overhead, but active work still consumes CPU, memory, and bandwidth. Bound input, output, queued tasks, and per-dispatch work. Backpressure is as important in an event loop as in a threaded server. A common architecture combines a small set of I/O reactors with a bounded worker pool for heavier computation. The handoff must preserve connection lifetime and return results through a safe queue. More architectural layers create more ownership transitions to test.

topics.title: Worked example — Drain an edge-triggered stream through EOF
topics.summary: This Linux-only test uses a local nonblocking socket pair rather than a public listener. One endpoint sends ping and half-closes its write direction. The epoll-managed endpoint drains two-byte chunks until EOF, demonstrating that the final data must be read even when closure is also observable. Companion listing: ch53/epoll_read.cpp The expected output is epoll received: ping . The tiny fixed send is performed on an empty local socket buffer; the shared send_all helper treats EAGAIN as failure rather than implementing an output reactor. This test therefore demonstrates the receive-side edge-triggered state machine, not a complete nonblocking server.

topics.title: Worked example — Readiness loop with epoll
topics.summary: Register nonblocking client descriptors with an epoll instance. The event loop waits for readiness, then services whichever descriptors are reported. In edge-triggered mode, a read handler typically continues until EAGAIN so all currently available bytes are drained; otherwise no new edge may arrive for already-buffered data.

topics.title: Worked example — Why nonblocking matters
topics.summary: If an event-loop thread performs a blocking read on one client that has no complete request, the entire loop can stall and stop servicing other ready clients. Nonblocking descriptors let the loop attempt work, detect that an operation would block, and return to multiplexing other connections.

topics.title: Chapter 54 — Measuring Performance
topics.summary: Performance engineering begins by defining the work and the measurement boundary. A number is meaningful only when it identifies what completed, under which conditions, and how the observation was made. Correctness checks belong in the experiment: a program that skips work can appear extraordinarily fast. This chapter distinguishes measured observations , analytical models , and illustrative assumptions . The companion benchmark reports local timings when run, but the book does not convert one container run into a universal hardware claim. Reproduce measurements on the machine and workload that matter. [ R30 , R42 ]

A number is meaningful only when it identifies what completed, under which conditions, and how the observation was made. Correctness checks belong in the experiment: a program that skips work can appear extraordinarily fast. This chapter distinguishes measured observations , analytical models , and illustrative assumptions . The companion benchmark reports local timings when run, but the book does not convert one container run into a universal hardware claim. Reproduce measurements on the machine and workload that matter. [ R30 , R42 ]

topics.title: 54.1 Latency
topics.summary: Latency measures elapsed time from a defined start event to a defined completion event. For a request, the boundary might include queueing, parsing, computation, and response delivery. For a kernel, it might include only the computation after inputs are prepared. Report a distribution when requests vary. A mean can hide a long tail, and a percentile requires enough samples and a clearly defined population. Do not compare one system’s median service time with another system’s end-to-end 99th percentile as though they were the same metric.

topics.title: 54.2 Throughput
topics.summary: Throughput measures completed useful work per unit time. It can be expressed as records, requests, or bytes per second. Define whether failed requests, retries, warmup work, and partial completions count. Throughput and latency interact through queueing. A system can increase completed work by admitting more concurrent requests while making each request wait longer. Evaluate the service objective rather than maximizing a single number without constraints.

topics.title: 54.3 CPU time
topics.summary: CPU time measures processor execution charged to a process or thread under the operating system’s accounting rules. It excludes many periods spent blocked or not scheduled. A multithreaded process can accumulate more total CPU time than elapsed wall time when several threads execute concurrently. CPU time helps distinguish computation from waiting, but it is not a complete explanation. Kernel activity, helper processes, and accounting boundaries may contribute differently. State whether the measurement covers one thread, the whole process, or a larger job.

topics.title: 54.4 Wall-clock time
topics.summary: Wall-clock elapsed time includes waiting, scheduling delays, and other activity between the chosen start and end. For duration measurements, use a monotonic clock such as std::chrono::steady_clock rather than a civil-time clock that can be adjusted. Clock resolution and call overhead matter for very small operations. Batch enough work to make the measured interval meaningful, while ensuring that the batch still represents the workload and does not change cache behavior beyond the intended experiment.

topics.title: 54.5 Utilization
topics.summary: Utilization describes the fraction of a resource’s capacity in use under a stated definition. CPU utilization, memory bandwidth utilization, and device busy time are different metrics. High CPU utilization does not prove that useful work is progressing efficiently; a spin loop can consume an entire core. Low utilization does not automatically mean spare end-to-end capacity. The bottleneck may be a serialized dependency, a lock, a downstream service, or a limit in another resource. Identify the constrained stage before adding more work.

topics.title: 54.6 Benchmarking
topics.summary: A benchmark should state input size and distribution, build configuration, machine context, warmup policy, repetition count, and correctness criteria. Keep setup outside the timed region when the goal excludes setup, and include it when evaluating end-to-end behavior. Preserve observable results so the compiler cannot legally discard the intended work as unused. Inspect generated code when a result seems implausible. Avoid volatile as a blanket benchmarking technique because it can change the workload being measured rather than merely prevent elimination.

topics.title: 54.7 Measurement error
topics.summary: Measurements vary because of scheduling, frequency changes, contention, cache state, page faults, thermal behavior, and instrumentation overhead. Repeated samples reveal variation but do not automatically remove bias. Change one factor at a time where practical and alternate comparison order to reduce drift effects. Report uncertainty honestly. A difference smaller than the experiment’s noise is not strong evidence of improvement, and a statistically clear difference may still be too small to matter operationally.

ENGINEERING IMPLICATIONS
Change one factor at a time where practical and alternate comparison order to reduce drift effects.
Report uncertainty honestly.
A difference smaller than the experiment’s noise is not strong evidence of improvement, and a statistically clear difference may still be too small to matter operationally.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
LECTURE NARRATION
Measurements vary because of scheduling, frequency changes, contention, cache state, page faults, thermal behavior, and instrumentation overhead. Repeated samples reveal variation but do not automatically remove bias. Change one factor at a time where practical and alternate comparison order to reduce drift effects. Report uncertainty honestly. A difference smaller than the experiment’s noise is not strong evidence of improvement, and a statistically clear difference may still be too small to matter operationally.

topics.title: Worked example — A checksum-protected timing boundary
topics.summary: This program constructs a bounded runtime-sized vector, times one summation, and verifies the sum against an independent formula. Setup and verification are outside the timed interval. The output timing is an observation on the machine where it is run, not a fixed expected value. Companion listing: ch54/benchmark.cpp For count 1000, there are three complete groups of values 0 through 250 and a remainder of 247 values, 0 through 246. The expected sum is 3 × 31375 + 247 × 246/2 = 124506 . The elapsed nanoseconds vary. A zero or very small reported duration for a tiny input can reflect clock granularity or overhead dominance rather than infinite throughput. The program is a measurement-mechanics example, not a complete microbenchmark framework. Repeat separate runs, record build flags, inspect the loop, and compare like conditions before interpreting a performance difference. Allocation failure is reported by the C++ runtime unless a surrounding application adds a more specific recovery policy.

topics.title: Worked example — Throughput and latency
topics.summary: If a service completes 12,000 requests in 60 seconds, average throughput is 200 requests/s. That fact does not reveal individual latency: one request may complete in 2 ms while another waits 500 ms. Report throughput and latency distributions separately because batching and queueing can improve one while harming the other.

topics.title: Worked example — CPU time versus wall time
topics.summary: A task reports 2.0 s wall-clock time but only 0.6 s CPU time. The remaining elapsed time may include waiting for I/O, scheduling delays, or sleeps. Optimizing arithmetic cannot remove time spent blocked on a slow dependency unless the design changes that dependency or overlaps it with other work.

topics.title: Chapter 55 — Program Optimization
topics.summary: Optimization changes an implementation while preserving its required behavior. The largest improvements often come from doing less work, moving fewer bytes, or avoiding repeated setup. Low-level instruction tuning is valuable only when the relevant instructions materially contribute to the measured bottleneck. Use a sequence of verified changes. Keep the original implementation as a reference when possible, compare outputs on normal and boundary cases, and measure each candidate under the same workload. A performance improvement that changes the result has not met the same specification. [ R2 ]

topics.title: 55.1 Algorithmic optimization
topics.summary: Algorithmic optimization changes the amount or organization of required work. Replacing repeated scans with an index, using a better asymptotic algorithm, or precomputing reusable summaries can dominate instruction-level changes. Account for construction and update costs. An index that makes queries fast may be inappropriate when the dataset changes constantly and only one query is performed. Optimize the complete workload, including the frequency of preprocessing and maintenance.

topics.title: 55.2 Compiler optimization
topics.summary: Compiler options enable transformations such as inlining, vectorization, and dead-code elimination. The compiler relies on language rules, available definitions, aliasing information, and target architecture. More aggressive flags can change assumptions or numerical behavior. Distinguish ordinary optimization levels from options that relax floating-point semantics or target instructions unavailable on another machine. topics.title: 55.3 Memory optimization
topics.summary: Memory optimization reduces allocation overhead, footprint, copying, and unnecessary lifetime extension. Reusing buffers can help when ownership is clear and retained capacity remains bounded. Do not trade a modest allocation reduction for dangling references or uncontrolled memory retention. A cache of reusable objects needs an eviction and size policy. Peak memory includes temporarily duplicated data during transformations, not merely the final representation.

topics.title: 55.4 Cache optimization
topics.summary: Cache optimization improves useful reuse and reduces transferred irrelevant bytes. Blocking, compact indexes, and traversal changes can help. The working set includes all simultaneously active data, not just the main input array. Measure the effect on total runtime and verify that a cache-focused change does not increase computation or synchronization enough to offset its benefit. Counter changes are evidence about mechanisms, not a replacement for the application’s completion metric.

topics.title: 55.5 Reducing allocations
topics.summary: Repeated small allocations can add allocator work, fragmentation, and cache misses. Reserving known capacity, using stack storage for bounded small objects, or allocating from a scoped arena can reduce those costs. Each technique changes lifetime or memory-use tradeoffs. Reserving too much wastes capacity; stack storage has size limits; arenas often reclaim everything together. Choose a mechanism whose ownership model matches the data’s actual lifetime.

topics.title: 55.6 Batching
topics.summary: Batching amortizes setup, synchronization, and I/O overhead across several items. A batch can also expose vectorization or parallel work. It is especially useful when one operation has a large fixed cost relative to each item’s incremental cost. Batch size is a tuning parameter constrained by latency and memory. A service that waits indefinitely to fill a batch can harm low-volume clients. Use a maximum size and a maximum waiting policy when responsiveness matters.

topics.title: 55.7 Data-layout optimization
topics.summary: Layout determines which fields share cache lines and how many pointers or bytes are traversed. If a hot loop reads only one eight-byte field from a 32-byte record, a separate field array can reduce the relevant data footprint from 256 KiB to 64 KiB for 8192 records in the stated layout model. That arithmetic is not a guaranteed fourfold speedup. The original layout may already be cached, other fields may be needed soon, or reconstruction costs may dominate. A layout serves operations; evaluate the complete access pattern before splitting every structure into separate arrays.
