topics.title: 55.8 Branch behavior
topics.summary: Branches can be inexpensive when predictable and costly when they disrupt useful execution. Replacing a branch with arithmetic or a conditional move can help some distributions and hurt others by forcing work on both paths or creating dependencies. Benchmark representative input distributions. A test with always-true conditions does not predict behavior for irregular production data. Compiler-generated branchless code must still obey access validity; evaluating both candidate memory accesses can be unsafe when one address is invalid.

topics.title: Worked example — Prefix sums replace repeated scans
topics.summary: Suppose a fixed array must answer many sum queries over half-open ranges [begin, end) . A direct scan costs work proportional to each range length. A prefix array stores prefix[k] = sum of elements before k , allowing a query to return prefix[end] - prefix[begin] after validation. For nonnegative bounded values whose total fits uint64_t , prefix construction is linear and each query is constant-time. Signed or floating-point data require additional numeric analysis: overflow and subtraction behavior must match the intended specification. Companion listing: ch55/range_sums.cpp The three query results are 45, 45, and 4500, for a combined 4590. The optimization changes repeated work from scanning every queried element to one preprocessing pass plus constant work per query. It uses extra memory and becomes less attractive when updates invalidate the prefix array frequently.

A prefix array stores prefix[k] = sum of elements before k , allowing a query to return prefix[end] - prefix[begin] after validation. For nonnegative bounded values whose total fits uint64_t , prefix construction is linear and each query is constant-time. Signed or floating-point data require additional numeric analysis: overflow and subtraction behavior must match the intended specification. Companion listing: ch55/range_sums.cpp The three query results are 45, 45, and 4500, for a combined 4590. The optimization changes repeated work from scanning every queried element to one preprocessing pass plus constant work per query. It uses extra memory and becomes less attractive when updates invalidate the prefix array frequently.

topics.title: Worked example — Reducing algorithmic work
topics.summary: Searching 1,000 queries by rescanning a 1,000,000-element array performs on the order of a billion comparisons. Building an index once can reduce each later lookup dramatically. Changing the algorithm often dominates instruction-level tuning because it removes whole classes of work rather than making each iteration slightly cheaper.

topics.title: Worked example — Structure-of-arrays example
topics.summary: If a loop processes only x coordinates from records containing x,y,z,color,metadata , an array-of-structures layout fetches unused neighboring fields into cache lines. Separating frequently processed x values into their own dense array can increase useful bytes per cache line, at the cost of more complex organization for operations that need complete records.

topics.title: 56.1 Identifying bottlenecks
topics.summary: A bottleneck is a stage or resource that constrains the chosen performance objective. Removing one bottleneck can expose another. The limiting factor can also change with input size, concurrency, and cache state. Form a testable hypothesis: “This phase is limited by repeated allocation,” or “These workers wait on one mutex.” Then collect evidence that could disprove it. A profile showing time inside a function does not by itself identify whether the cause is computation, cache misses, or waiting inside that function.

topics.title: 56.2 CPU-bound workloads
topics.summary: A CPU-bound workload spends its critical time performing computation rather than waiting on external I/O. It may still be limited by instruction dependencies, branch behavior, vectorization, or execution-resource throughput. Reducing instruction count can help, but not every instruction has equal cost and not every removed instruction lies on the critical path. Independent work can overlap, while a short dependency chain can dominate latency. Inspect the hot generated code only after establishing that it matters.

topics.title: 56.3 Memory-bound workloads
topics.summary: A memory-bound workload is constrained by data access, such as bandwidth or dependent-load latency. Reducing arithmetic may have little effect when the processor already waits for data. Improving locality or reducing transferred bytes can be more valuable. A simple bandwidth roof illustrates the limit. At arithmetic intensity 0.125 operations per byte and available bandwidth 40 GB/s, the bandwidth-limited rate is 5 billion operations per second under the model. A processor capable of much more arithmetic cannot exceed that rate for the same required traffic without changing the access pattern or reuse.

topics.title: 56.4 I/O-bound workloads
topics.summary: An I/O-bound workload waits on storage, network, or another external service. Useful changes include batching, caching, reducing requests, overlapping independent operations, and improving the protocol. Adding threads can hide some waits but can also overload the downstream system and increase queueing. Distinguish service time from waiting time. When the dependency is saturated, more concurrent demand may worsen latency without increasing completed throughput.

topics.title: 56.5 Profiling
topics.summary: Profiling attributes time or events to code paths. Sampling profiles estimate where execution spends time; instrumentation records chosen events more directly but can perturb behavior. Hardware counters provide additional evidence subject to event definitions and access permissions. A Linux starting point can be perf stat with a small set of understood events, followed by a sampling profile when available. Container, kernel, and administrative policy may restrict access. Record those limitations instead of inventing missing counter data. [ R30 ] The executable path is illustrative; use the actual path produced by the companion build script. A missing tool or denied counter is not a program correctness failure.

topics.title: 56.6 Scaling
topics.summary: Strong scaling holds total problem size fixed while increasing resources. Weak scaling grows the problem with the resource count. They answer different questions and should not be compared without stating which workload changed. Synchronization, communication, memory bandwidth, load imbalance, and serial setup limit scaling. Measure useful throughput and latency alongside CPU use. A program using all cores at high utilization can still scale poorly if much of that activity is contention or redundant work.

topics.title: Worked example — Quantify the improvement ceiling
topics.summary: With serial fraction 0.20 and four workers, the normalized time is 0.20 + 0.80/4 = 0.40 , so speedup is 2.5. With infinitely many ideal workers, speedup cannot exceed 5 unless the serial portion is changed. Now add overhead equal to 0.05 of the original runtime at four workers. Normalized time becomes 0.45 and speedup falls to approximately 2.222. This explains why “80% parallelizable” is not a sufficient performance forecast without a communication and synchronization model. Companion listing: ch56/amdahl.py The output is ideal=2.500 with_overhead=2.222 . A model can also guide priorities: reducing the serial fraction from 0.20 to 0.10 may be more valuable than adding workers beyond the point of diminishing returns. Confirm that the measured serial component is truly independent of worker count before applying the formula mechanically.

topics.title: Worked example — Amdahl calculation
topics.summary: If 80% of a program can be accelerated by a factor of 4 while 20% is unchanged, total speedup is 1 / (0.20 + 0.80/4) = 2.5 . Infinite acceleration of the parallel part would still cap speedup at 1/0.20 = 5 . The unchanged fraction sets a hard upper bound.

topics.title: Worked example — Distinguishing CPU- and memory-bound behavior
topics.summary: If profiling shows execution units frequently idle while the program waits on last-level cache misses, optimizing arithmetic instructions may have little effect. Improving locality, reducing the working set, or prefetching may matter more. A CPU-bound loop with high cache hit rates suggests a different optimization path. Profiling should classify the bottleneck before changes are chosen.

topics.title: Chapter 57 — Memory-Safety Vulnerabilities
topics.summary: A memory-safety vulnerability arises when a program permits access outside the intended bounds, lifetime, type, or ownership of an object in a way that can affect security. The underlying mistake may begin as an ordinary correctness bug, but untrusted input can make its consequences repeatable and externally controllable. The defensive objective is to prevent invalid operations before they occur. Page permissions and hardening features are valuable secondary barriers, but they do not replace length validation, checked arithmetic, lifetime management, and synchronization. This chapter uses safe rejection tests rather than exploitation exercises. [ R5 , R8 , R34 ]

topics.title: 57.1 Buffer overflows
topics.summary: A buffer overflow writes beyond a buffer’s valid extent. The immediate cause can be an unchecked length, a missing terminator allowance, a wrong element-size calculation, or a parser that trusts a field before validating it. Tie every byte operation to an explicit extent. For a destination of capacity c and requested copy length n , prove n <= c before copying. For a string requiring a terminator, include that byte in the contract without computing an overflowing n + 1 . A length-aware interface helps, but its supplied lengths must still be correct.

topics.title: 57.2 Stack corruption
topics.summary: Stack corruption damages automatic storage or implementation-managed call state. A write beyond a local array can affect nearby objects, saved registers, or other control information depending on layout and optimization. Do not rely on a particular stack arrangement to decide whether an overflow is harmless. Compilers can reorder, eliminate, or place objects differently. Prevent the out-of-bounds write itself; a test that happens to modify only padding on one build does not establish safety.

topics.title: 57.3 Heap corruption
topics.summary: Heap corruption damages dynamically allocated objects or allocator bookkeeping. A write can remain inside a mapped writable page and still cross an allocation boundary. The operating system’s page checks may therefore permit the machine access while the language program has already violated its contract. Allocator crashes often occur later than the original bad write. A failure during allocation or deallocation may be a symptom of earlier corruption, not proof that the allocator is the root cause. Instrumented testing and minimizing the first invalid operation are more useful than patching the eventual crash site blindly.

topics.title: 57.4 Use-after-free
topics.summary: Use-after-free accesses an object after its lifetime and ownership have ended. The address may still be mapped and may even contain plausible data. Reuse by another allocation can turn the stale access into corruption of an unrelated object. Ownership abstractions reduce the risk, but raw observers still need lifetime rules. A unique_ptr prevents duplicate ownership but does not make every raw pointer derived from it safe after reset. Shared ownership can extend lifetime, but it does not automatically synchronize mutable contents.

topics.title: 57.5 Integer errors
topics.summary: Integer errors can create memory vulnerabilities indirectly. A negative length converted to an unsigned size can become very large. A wrapped multiplication can allocate too little storage for a later copy. A truncating conversion can make validation inspect a different value from the one subsequently used. Validate in a representation that can express the required range, then convert. For allocation size count * element_size , require count <= maximum / element_size when the element size is nonzero. Use the same validated value for the actual operation; re-parsing or recomputing with different types can reintroduce the defect.

topics.title: Worked example — Validate one complete bounded frame
topics.summary: This parser accepts a two-byte big-endian length followed by exactly that many payload bytes, with a maximum payload of 16 bytes. It returns a borrowed view, so the input owner must remain alive while the result is used. No allocation depends on the untrusted length. Companion listing: ch57/parse_frame.cpp The validation order is deliberate. First prove that the prefix bytes exist. Then decode into a type wide enough for the field. Next enforce the application maximum. Finally compare the remaining input length without an unchecked addition. Only after all checks does the parser create the payload view. The strict equality rejects trailing bytes because this function parses exactly one complete frame. A streaming parser would instead retain unconsumed bytes and return a consumed-length result. Changing that contract requires a deliberate interface change, not silently ignoring extra data.

topics.title: Worked example — Length-field integer bug
topics.summary: A protocol contains a 32-bit length. Code computes length + 4 in 32 bits before allocating. If length is near UINT32_MAX , the addition wraps to a small number, the allocation succeeds, and a later copy uses the large logical length. Validate the bound before addition or promote to a wider checked type so allocation and copy use the same safe size.

topics.title: Worked example — Stack overwrite boundary
topics.summary: A local buffer of 32 bytes cannot safely receive 40 unchecked input bytes. The extra writes can corrupt adjacent stack data such as saved state or other locals. Mitigations may detect or complicate exploitation, but the primary fix is enforcing a correct length contract before writing.

topics.title: Chapter 58 — Exploit Mitigations
topics.summary: Mitigations reduce the consequences or feasibility of exploiting certain bugs. They are defense in depth, not substitutes for memory safety. A program can contain a serious vulnerability even when it is compiled with hardening flags, uses randomized addresses, and has non-executable data pages. Treat mitigation status as a property to inspect in the actual build and deployment. A flag written in a document is not evidence that the final executable or runtime environment enforces the intended protection. [ R3 , R31 , R45 ]

topics.title: 58.1 Stack canaries
topics.summary: Stack-protector instrumentation places a check value in selected stack frames and verifies it before returning through the protected path. Some overwrites can then be detected before corrupted state is used in a normal return sequence. Coverage depends on compiler options and generated code. A canary does not prevent the original out-of-bounds write, protect every object, or guarantee detection of every corruption pattern. It is a detection barrier for a subset of consequences.

topics.title: 58.2 Non-executable memory
topics.summary: Non-executable permissions prevent instruction fetches from designated data regions. Separating executable code from writable data reduces one class of attack opportunity. The processor and operating system must support and enforce the mapping policy. Non-executable data does not prevent all control-flow misuse or data-only corruption. An attacker does not necessarily need to introduce new executable bytes to cause harm. The underlying invalid write, stale pointer, or authorization error still requires repair.

topics.title: 58.3 Address-space randomization
topics.summary: Address-space randomization varies locations of mapped regions to make useful addresses less predictable. Position-independent executables and libraries support relocation under the relevant loader model. Randomization is not confidentiality by itself. Information disclosure can reveal addresses, and entropy varies with architecture and configuration. Do not disable randomization to make an application appear more stable; investigate invalid address assumptions instead.

topics.title: 58.4 Memory permissions
topics.summary: Memory permissions restrict reading, writing, and execution at mapping granularity. A least-permission design avoids writable executable regions and removes unneeded access. Read-only mappings can protect immutable tables from accidental modification. Changing permissions is a privileged service request and may require translation invalidation. Permissions still do not distinguish two objects inside one writable page. They reinforce region-level boundaries while language and application rules govern object-level behavior.

topics.title: 58.5 Privilege separation
topics.summary: Privilege separation divides a system so that components handling untrusted input possess only the authority they need. A small privileged component can perform narrow validated operations for a less-privileged parser or worker. The communication interface becomes a security boundary and must validate message type, size, identity, and requested action. Splitting into processes without reducing authority or validating requests merely relocates the same risk. Failure recovery should also specify what happens when one component exits midway through an operation.

topics.title: Worked example — Build and inspect a hardened parser
topics.summary: The following script compiles the safe Chapter 57 parser with a representative GNU/Linux hardening configuration. It uses the installed compiler and standard library; it does not download software, change kernel settings, or disable any protection. Support for individual options depends on the toolchain. Companion listing: ch58/harden.sh Inspection should distinguish evidence from inference. A position-independent executable normally appears as ELF type DYN with executable context; a GNU_STACK program header should not request execute permission; GNU_RELRO and immediate-binding metadata provide evidence for the requested relocation protections. These observations do not prove that every mitigation is effective on every path, nor that the program has no vulnerabilities. [ R37 , R45 ] _FORTIFY_SOURCE=3 requires a supporting compiler and libc environment and useful optimization. A build failure should be reported and the supported configuration selected deliberately, not hidden by silently dropping flags while continuing to label the output hardened. Sanitizer builds serve a different testing purpose and should be documented separately.

topics.title: Worked example — What a stack canary checks
topics.summary: A compiler can place a random guard value between vulnerable local data and control-sensitive stack state. Before returning, generated code verifies that the guard is unchanged. A sequential overflow that crosses the canary is likely detected, but the mechanism does not prevent every memory error and is not a substitute for bounds safety.

topics.title: Chapter 59 — System Robustness
topics.summary: Robustness is the ability to behave predictably when inputs are invalid, resources are unavailable, operations make partial progress, or dependencies fail. It requires explicit failure contracts and cleanup paths. A robust system does not have to succeed at every request; it must avoid turning a failed request into corruption, leakage, or an unexplained hang. Correctness on the normal path is only the beginning. Examine each resource acquisition and each externally visible update: what can fail before it, what can fail after it, and what state remains when that happens?

topics.title: 59.1 Defensive programming
topics.summary: Defensive programming validates assumptions at trust boundaries and makes internal invariants explicit. Validate external lengths, indexes, versions, and resource requests before using them. Keep validated values in a representation that will not silently change during later conversion. Avoid indiscriminate checks that conceal programming errors or continue with fabricated defaults. A failed invariant inside a component may require stopping that operation rather than proceeding with a “best guess” pointer or size. The response should preserve safety and make diagnosis possible.

topics.title: 59.2 Error handling
topics.summary: Error handling must define the operation’s postcondition after failure. Did nothing happen, did some bytes transfer, or did the update commit but its acknowledgment fail? These are different states with different retry rules. Design for idempotence where retries are expected. Repeating a read is different from repeating a money transfer or appending a record. An error does not necessarily mean that the remote side performed no work. Protocols need identifiers, transactions, or explicit reconciliation when duplicate effects would be harmful.

topics.title: 59.3 Return values
topics.summary: Use each interface’s documented failure indicator. A negative descriptor result, a null allocation result, MAP_FAILED , a short element count, and a C++ exception are not interchangeable conventions. Some APIs return an error number directly rather than storing it in errno , notably many POSIX thread interfaces. Reading errno after such a call can report an unrelated value. Wrap interfaces only after preserving their distinct contracts.

topics.title: 59.4 errno
topics.summary: errno is meaningful when an interface documents that its failure result sets it. A successful call need not clear an old error value. Inspecting errno after success can therefore diagnose a failure that never occurred. Save the error code before cleanup or logging that could change it. Report the failed operation and relevant safe context, not just an unexplained number. In multithreaded POSIX environments, errno access is thread-specific, but that does not make stale values meaningful. [ R54 ]

topics.title: 59.5 Assertions
topics.summary: Assertions document and test internal invariants. They are not a substitute for validating untrusted input because ordinary C/C++ assertion checks can be disabled in builds defining NDEBUG . Do not place required side effects inside an assertion. assert(close(fd) == 0) can remove the close operation when assertions are disabled. Perform the operation explicitly, handle its result, and use assertions only for checks whose removal does not change required behavior.

topics.title: 59.6 Sanitizers
topics.summary: AddressSanitizer, UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer, and ThreadSanitizer instrument different classes of behavior. Their availability, compatible combinations, and runtime requirements differ. Address and undefined-behavior checks are commonly combined; thread-race checking should normally use a separate build. [ R5 , R6 , R53 ] A clean run means that the enabled instrumentation reported no covered failure during that execution. It does not prove memory safety, race freedom, or correct recovery on unexecuted paths. Keep compiler warnings, static analysis, boundary tests, and design review alongside instrumentation.

topics.title: 59.7 Resource cleanup
topics.summary: Cleanup releases every owned resource exactly once: memory, descriptors, mappings, threads, temporary files, and permits. RAII in C++ and structured cleanup paths in C make the ownership visible during both normal returns and failures. Destructors should not casually throw during stack unwinding. Operations whose completion can fail meaningfully, such as flushing durable output, often need an explicit checked completion method before fallback destruction. Cleanup that merely prevents leaks is not the same as successful commit.

topics.title: 59.8 Failure recovery
topics.summary: Recovery establishes a known consistent state after failure. Common techniques include constructing a new result before replacing the old one, writing temporary files before rename, logging transactions, and restarting isolated workers. Atomic visibility and durable persistence are different guarantees. A rename can make a new pathname visible atomically under filesystem rules, while durable recovery after power loss can require synchronizing the file and containing directory. The exact guarantee also depends on filesystem and hardware behavior. [ R33 ]

topics.title: Worked example — A checked snapshot protocol in a private temporary directory
topics.summary: The program below creates its own temporary directory, writes a new snapshot, synchronizes it, closes it, renames it into place, and synchronizes the directory. It then verifies the bytes and removes only its own test artifacts. It does not operate on an existing user file. Companion listing: ch59/snapshot.c The expected output is snapshot checks passed on a filesystem supporting the requested synchronization. The test verifies successful API sequencing and byte contents. It does not simulate power loss, prove a storage device’s behavior, or establish crash consistency on every filesystem. The commit point also matters for real recovery. If rename succeeds but directory synchronization fails, the new file may already be visible even though the requested durability was not confirmed. A production API should report that distinction instead of promising that failure means “nothing changed.” This private test removes its own artifacts after either path, which is appropriate for a lab but not a replacement for an application’s recovery policy.

topics.title: Worked example — errno handling
topics.summary: A function such as open indicates failure through its documented return value. Only after detecting failure should code inspect errno , because unrelated successful library calls may leave old errno values unchanged. Save the error code if subsequent operations could overwrite it before reporting or cleanup.

topics.title: Worked example — Cleanup on partial failure
topics.summary: Suppose initialization opens a file, allocates a buffer, then fails to create a thread. RAII in C++ or structured cleanup paths in C make ownership states explicit so every exit path restores a valid resource state.

options: Only the success-path return value.
Ownership and cleanup rules, plus the documented state guarantee.
Every partially acquired resource indefinitely.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: Chapter 60 — From Source Code to Running Program
topics.summary: The previous chapters examined individual layers. This chapter follows one small program through the complete path: source text becomes instructions, the executable becomes mappings, instructions access translated memory, and I/O requests cross into the kernel. Each layer contributes a different kind of correctness and a different class of failure. The example computes a byte count and an unsigned 64-bit byte sum from standard input. The sum is intentionally simple and wraps modulo 2^64 ; the count rejects overflow rather than wrapping. Neither result is a cryptographic integrity guarantee. The simple operation makes the surrounding system behavior easy to inspect.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.1 Source Code → Compiler
topics.summary: Source code describes behavior under a language standard. Declarations establish types and interfaces; definitions provide objects and function bodies. The preprocessor handles includes and macros before the compiler’s language analysis. The compiler must reason about the program’s allowed behavior, including integer rules, object lifetime, aliasing, and observable effects. A pointer-and-length interface carries preconditions even when its machine representation is only two integer-like values. Invalid source-level behavior is not repaired by the fact that the target CPU can execute some corresponding instruction sequence. [ R1 , R8 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.2 Compiler → Assembly
topics.summary: The compiler lowers the program into target instructions and chooses registers, branches, addressing modes, and transformations. The source loop need not survive as one literal assembly loop; optimization may unroll or vectorize it while preserving required behavior. The unsigned byte sum permits reassociation under modular arithmetic in ways that a strict floating-point sum might not. Numeric semantics therefore influence available machine implementations. Compare generated assembly only after identifying which transformations the source contract permits. [ R2 , R3 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.3 Assembly → Object Code
topics.summary: The assembler encodes instructions and data into a relocatable object file. Symbols identify definitions and references, while relocation records describe locations that need adjustment when final addresses are determined. An object file is not yet necessarily a runnable executable. A call to checksum_update can refer to a symbol whose final location is unresolved until linking. Debug information and symbol tables help tools explain the relationship between source and machine code without being the code’s runtime semantics themselves.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.4 Object Code → Linker
topics.summary: The linker combines object files and resolves symbols against other objects and libraries. It lays out the resulting program according to the executable format and link options. Missing definitions, incompatible interfaces, and duplicate definitions appear at this boundary. The C declaration and definition must agree. A successful link does not prove that a mismatched manually declared ABI is correct, and linking a library does not prove that its runtime dependencies will be available. Build correctness includes the intended headers, object versions, options, and target architecture. [ R1 , R37 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.5 Executable → Loader
topics.summary: Execution asks the operating system to replace a process image with the executable. The kernel validates and interprets the executable format and establishes the initial execution environment. Dynamically linked programs also involve a runtime linker or loader according to the platform’s format and configuration. main is not normally the very first instruction executed. Startup code establishes language-runtime state before calling it. Understanding this explains why a program can fail before reaching the first source line of main , for example when a required dynamic library cannot be loaded. [ R16 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.6 Loader → Virtual Address Space
topics.summary: The executable’s loadable segments become virtual mappings with appropriate permissions and backing. Code, initialized data, zero-filled storage, stack, and libraries occupy regions of the process’s address space. The loader need not eagerly copy every executable byte into physical memory before execution begins. File-backed demand paging and shared mappings allow work to occur as pages are used. The address-space layout is therefore a mapping plan, not simply a complete physical-memory photograph. [ R10 , R14 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.7 Instructions → CPU
topics.summary: The processor fetches and executes instructions according to the ISA. Its microarchitecture can decode, schedule, speculate, and overlap operations while preserving the architectural behavior required for correct execution. The instruction pointer and registers describe the architectural stream, while internal execution details determine performance. A branch, cache miss, or dependency can change how quickly the next useful result becomes available without changing the program’s specified output. [ R3 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.8 CPU → Registers and Caches
topics.summary: The byte-sum loop uses registers for pointers, counters, and partial results where the compiler chooses. Loads obtain input bytes through the cache hierarchy. Several adjacent bytes can share a fetched line, giving spatial locality. Calling the update function may require arguments in the ABI’s designated registers and preservation of callee-saved state. Inlining can remove that call boundary but not the source-level requirement to read only valid input bytes. Machine optimization and memory safety remain separate obligations.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.9 Cache → Main Memory
topics.summary: A cache miss obtains data from another level. Main memory backs the buffer’s resident pages, while translation hardware supplies the virtual-to-physical relationship. TLB misses, data-cache misses, and page faults remain distinct events even within this one loop. The loop’s sequential traversal can use cache lines efficiently, but the total throughput also depends on how input reaches the buffer. If the producer or storage source is slow, arithmetic optimization may have little effect on end-to-end completion time.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.10 Program → System Call
topics.summary: The program calls read to obtain input and write to emit its result. Library wrappers marshal arguments into the operating-system ABI and translate return conventions into the documented C interface. Every positive read result supplies an exact valid extent for the next checksum update. The program must not process the entire 4096-byte buffer when only 100 bytes were returned. This is where an I/O return value becomes a memory-safety boundary. [ R11 , R12 , R46 ]

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.11 System Call → Kernel
topics.summary: The kernel resolves the descriptor, checks the request, and performs or waits for the relevant operation. Standard input may be a regular file, pipe, terminal, or another endpoint, so the same user code can trigger different kernel paths. A blocking read may let another task run, while a read satisfied from available data may return without switching processes. Kernel entry, blocking, and context switching are separate events. Error and short-progress results return responsibility to the program’s control flow.

blocks.text:

The kernel resolves the descriptor, checks the request, and performs or waits for the relevant operation. Standard input may be a regular file, pipe, terminal, or another endpoint, so the same user code can trigger different kernel paths. A blocking read may let another task run, while a read satisfied from available data may return without switching processes. Kernel entry, blocking, and context switching are separate events. Error and short-progress results return responsibility to the program’s control flow.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: 60.12 Kernel → Hardware
topics.summary: When necessary, kernel subsystems and drivers coordinate with storage or network hardware. Interrupts, DMA, device queues, and memory-management policy can participate below the user-visible read interface. A cached read need not reach a device at all. Conversely, a device operation can complete before the waiting application is scheduled again. The end-to-end result is produced by several cooperating layers whose internal timings differ. Measure at the boundary relevant to the application’s requirement rather than attributing every delay to the CPU instruction loop.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: Worked example — Build and trace a complete byte-summary utility
topics.summary: The public interface states that data designates at least length valid bytes whenever length is nonzero. The function borrows the bytes and retains no pointer. Companion listing: ch60/checksum.h Companion listing: ch60/checksum.c Companion listing: ch60/main.c From the chapter’s source directory, the following commands expose separate stages. They write only local build products; use a copy or dedicated build directory for experimentation. The final output is bytes=4 sum=208 . The shell starts a producer and connects it to the utility through a pipe. The utility’s read returns valid bytes, the checksum function processes that exact extent, and a complete-transfer write emits the formatted result. A failure at any stage has a different meaning. Preprocessing can fail to find a header. Compilation can reject a type error. Linking can miss a definition. Loading can fail to locate a runtime dependency. Reading can fail on an invalid descriptor. The checksum itself can remain logically correct while the overall program fails to receive or deliver data. An integrated diagnosis identifies the failed boundary before changing unrelated code.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: Worked example — Following one global variable
topics.summary: A source file defines int g=7; . The compiler emits code that refers to g and object-file data containing its initial value. The assembler encodes instructions and relocation records. The linker assigns g a location in the executable image. The loader maps the appropriate segment, and machine instructions later access the mapped bytes through virtual-memory translation and caches.

topics.chapterTitle: From Source Code to Running Program
topics.title: Worked example — Following one write system call
topics.summary: Source code calls write(fd,p,n) . A library wrapper arranges arguments according to the ABI and executes the system-call entry instruction. The CPU transfers to kernel mode, where the kernel validates the descriptor and user buffer, updates kernel/device state, and returns a byte count or error. User-mode code resumes with the result. This single operation crosses language, ABI, ISA, kernel, and hardware boundaries.

topics.title: Chapter 61 — Putting the System Together
topics.summary: A systems program is correct only when its layers agree. The parser’s length must match the memory operation’s extent. The ownership model must match thread lifetime. The compiler’s numeric assumptions must match the algorithm. The kernel-facing error handling must match the interface. Performance changes must preserve those relationships rather than optimize one layer by violating another. This final chapter develops a bounded concurrent version of the byte-summary utility. It reuses the integer queue from Chapter 49 as an ownership-transfer channel for a fixed set of buffer slots. The program is a batch-processing capstone, not a production service or an asynchronous cancellation framework.

topics.title: 61.1 Data Representation → Machine Instructions
topics.summary: The input is an uninterpreted sequence of bytes. Each byte contributes a value from 0 through 255 to an unsigned 64-bit sum. The count is separately checked against overflow. These representation choices make the required operations explicit and avoid accidental sign extension of char values. Unsigned modular addition is associative, so partial sums can be combined in any worker-completion order. A floating-point reduction or an order-sensitive hash would require a different argument. Choosing a simple additive checksum is what makes the parallel combination straightforward; it is not evidence of cryptographic strength.

topics.title: 61.2 Machine Instructions → Processor Execution
topics.summary: Each worker repeatedly loads valid bytes and updates a private accumulator. The compiler can choose scalar or vector instructions consistent with the source semantics. Independent workers can execute on different cores when scheduling and hardware permit. The program does not assume simultaneous execution. It remains correct if one core interleaves every worker. Parallel hardware affects possible performance, while the ownership and synchronization rules establish correctness across all permitted schedules.

topics.title: 61.3 Processor Execution → Memory Hierarchy
topics.summary: Fixed-size sequential buffers provide spatial locality. Reusing eight slots bounds the payload working set to 32 KiB of byte storage, excluding metadata, stacks, queues, and other runtime state. This is a concrete budget, not a claim that the entire program fits in one cache. Worker-private results reduce shared updates. Adjacent result objects can still share a cache line, so a performance extension might investigate padding or batching result publication. Such changes should follow measurement and preserve the same ownership rules.

topics.title: 61.4 Virtual Memory → Process Isolation
topics.summary: All threads run inside one process and share its virtual address space. Page permissions protect the process from unrelated private mappings, but they do not prevent one worker from accidentally indexing another slot incorrectly. The queue carries validated slot indexes, and the program creates those indexes internally from a fixed bounded range. No untrusted input becomes a pointer or slot identifier. This shows how process isolation and object-level validation work together rather than substitute for one another.

topics.title: 61.5 Processes → Files and I/O
topics.summary: The producer reads from standard input using the descriptor interface. It checks the returned extent and publishes only the bytes actually obtained. Input can come from a file or finite pipeline without changing the processing logic. The example uses blocking input. Queue closure cannot forcibly interrupt a producer already blocked in an external read. A production application needing responsive asynchronous cancellation would integrate readiness waiting and a cancellation event or use another explicitly cancellable I/O design. This limitation is part of the capstone’s stated scope.

topics.title: 61.6 Processes → Interprocess Communication
topics.summary: A shell pipeline can feed data into the capstone through a pipe, creating communication between processes. Inside the capstone, queues coordinate threads through shared memory. These are different mechanisms with different ownership and failure boundaries. The external producer must eventually close its pipe write references for the capstone to observe EOF. An accidentally retained writer can make a correct internal worker system wait indefinitely for input completion. End-to-end diagnosis must include the upstream process graph.

topics.summary: The fixed slot array is shared, but access ownership changes over time. A slot is either free, owned by the producer, queued as ready, or owned by one worker. The worker does not read a slot before obtaining its index from the ready queue. This protocol eliminates simultaneous producer writes and worker reads of the same slot.

topics.title: 61.8 Shared Memory → Synchronization
topics.summary: Queue push and pop operations use mutexes and condition variables. The producer’s byte writes occur before publication into the ready queue; the worker’s successful dequeue establishes the visibility needed before reading those bytes. The reverse handoff through the free queue ensures that the producer reuses a slot only after the previous worker has finished with it. No extra atomic flag is needed per slot because the queue handoff supplies the ordering and exclusive ownership relationship.

topics.title: 61.9 Synchronization → Correct Concurrent Programs
topics.summary: Correct synchronization includes completion and failure. Normal EOF closes the ready queue, allowing workers to drain and finish. Failure records an exception and closes both queues so queue waiters can stop. Every created thread is joined before the slots and queue objects are destroyed. The failure flag is only a stop hint; protected exception storage and joins govern access to the actual failure object. A relaxed atomic is sufficient for that hint because it does not publish the slot data or exception contents. Those use separate synchronization relationships.

topics.title: 61.10 Architecture → Performance
topics.summary: The architecture separates one input producer from several compute workers. It can overlap input handling and checksum work, but the checksum is so lightweight that queue and thread overhead may exceed any benefit. A correct concurrent design is not automatically a faster design. Compare against Chapter 60 on representative files and finite streams. Measure end-to-end time, CPU time, and scaling. Varying slot size, slot count, and worker count changes locality, buffering, and synchronization costs; change one parameter at a time and retain the sequential reference result.

topics.title: 61.11 Operating System → Resource Management
topics.summary: The operating system supplies threads, virtual memory, descriptors, scheduling, and I/O. The application adds its own budgets: four workers, eight buffers, and bounded queue capacity. These limits make resource demand explicit rather than allowing input size to determine allocation growth. Operating-system allocation or thread-creation failure can still occur. The setup path tracks already-created threads and closes queues before joining them on failure. Resource limits reduce risk but do not eliminate the need to handle unavailable resources.

topics.title: 61.12 Correctness + Performance + Security + Robustness
topics.summary: The capstone combines four requirements. Correctness preserves byte counts, modular sums, and exactly-once ownership transfer. Performance is measured against a sequential baseline. Security keeps untrusted bytes separate from lengths, indexes, and authority. Robustness handles partial reads, setup failures, and cleanup within the stated batch-processing scope. These requirements constrain one another. Removing bounds checks can make a microbenchmark faster while violating the input contract. Unbounded buffering can increase short-term throughput while exhausting memory. A sound systems design treats the requirements as one specification rather than four optional features added in sequence.

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded concurrent byte-summary pipeline
topics.summary: The capstone imports the Chapter 49 queue rather than duplicating its synchronization implementation. Eight slot indexes circulate through a free queue and a ready queue. Each worker owns one private result element, combined only after joining. Companion listing: ch61/pipeline.cpp For ABC\n , the result is bytes=4 sum=208 workers=4 . For 100,000 generated bytes where byte i is i mod 256 , the result is bytes=100000 sum=12742320 workers=4 . The worker assignments can differ between runs while these totals remain fixed. The ownership invariant also explains why returning a slot to the free queue cannot block forever during normal completion. There are exactly eight slot identities. A worker holding one identity implies that at most seven others can already be in the free queue. The return therefore has room, assuming no identity was duplicated or lost. This is a progress proof derived from the resource model, not a timing assumption. On failure, no successful summary is printed. Some work may already have been processed, but the operation reports failure instead of presenting a partial aggregate as complete. The program does not implement a resumable checkpoint, input authentication, cryptographic hashing, or cancellation of a currently blocked external read. Those would be separate extensions with new contracts and tests.

topics.title: Worked example — End-to-end array sum
topics.summary: A C++ loop sums an integer array. Integer representation defines each element’s bits; compiler translation produces load/add/control instructions; virtual memory translates addresses; caches exploit sequential locality; the scheduler gives the thread CPU time; and the OS originally supplied the process’s mappings. Correct bounds and integer rules establish validity, while cache behavior and compilation determine performance.

chapters.title: C and C++ for Systems Programming
From Source Code to Running Program

1.title: Understanding Computer Systems
1.transcript:
Systems Programming and Machine Organization
Chapter 1 — Understanding Computer Systems
Charles Dorner | Graduate lecture with sixth-grade explanations

This script corresponds to the 64-slide PowerPoint. The full narration is also embedded in PowerPoint speaker notes. The visible explanations are repeated here so the script can be used without Presenter View.

Source basis: the supplied 22-slide Chapter 1 deck. Graduate elaborations are identified; the lecture does not claim to cover unseen material elsewhere in the book.

Suggested delivery: approximately 90–120 minutes including demonstrations and discussion. This is a planning estimate, not a recorded duration. Slides 61–64 are appendices.

Teaching environment: hosted C17 on Linux/ELF with a GCC-compatible compiler and GNU Binutils. Examples are educational, and their stated preconditions matter. The 12 ms / 8 ms comparison and other timing-model numbers are illustrative, not measurements of the included program.

Slide-by-slide lecture

01. Understanding Computer Systems
Section: CHAPTER 1 · GRADUATE LECTURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 1.

Graduate lecture narration
A useful systems explanation is more precise than saying that the computer runs the code. We want to identify which component translates a representation, which component owns a resource, and which interface guarantees a particular result. Chapter 1 gives us the mental model for doing that. We will follow a small C program from source files to observable output, then ask what build success, a successful launch, and a successful test actually establish. These are different claims.

The supplied 22-slide chapter is our coverage baseline. This expanded lecture retains its organization and examples. Graduate elaborations add explicit assumptions, counterexamples, artifact inspection, and short derivations. The simplified explanation at the bottom of every slide restates the same idea without replacing the technical account. Our recurring question is: what is promised at this boundary, and what evidence would show that the promise was kept?

Sixth-grade explanation
A program is not just a list of commands. Many parts work together, and each part has rules the others must follow.

Transition: The complete Chapter 1 route.

---

02. The complete Chapter 1 route
Section: SCOPE & LEARNING OUTCOMES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 2, 7, 13, 20, 21, 22.

Graduate lecture narration
The first section distinguishes hardware, systems software, and application software, then separates API, ABI, and ISA contracts. The second section follows every stage named in the original chapter: source, preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and runtime execution. The third section develops the six concerns that make systems programming distinctive: representation, performance, resources, correctness, robustness, and portability.

We will retain the two-file addition program, the build-stage experiment, the expression trace, the correctness-versus-performance comparison, the guided lab, and both original review questions. The standard for graduate work is explanation with evidence. You should be able to predict which artifact contains a missing symbol, distinguish a mapping from physical residency, and state an invariant that survives an error path. The lab platform is a hosted C17 program on Linux with a GCC-compatible compiler and GNU binary tools. Other environments require corresponding tools and conventions.

Sixth-grade explanation
We will learn what the computer contains, how code becomes a running program, and how to check that the program behaves safely.

Transition: Turn a claim into a testable argument.

---

03. Turn a claim into a testable argument
Section: GRADUATE METHOD
Source mapping: original slide(s) 2, 5, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Consider the statement that our program printed 42. It reports an observation, but it does not specify the input domain, the compiler assumptions, or whether an invalid memory access occurred on the way to that output. A stronger argument separates a contract, assumptions, and evidence. The contract says what counts as correct. Assumptions identify the conditions under which the reasoning applies. Evidence is what we inspected or measured.

These categories prevent two common mistakes. First, a useful test result is not a universal proof. Second, a documented guarantee is not a measured performance result. During the lecture, attach each conclusion to its boundary: language, binary interface, operating system, or hardware. If the observation conflicts with the prediction, revise the model or inspect a lower-level artifact rather than inventing a promise that the interface never made. This framework is an instructional elaboration of the original chapter's contract model.

Sixth-grade explanation
Do not stop at “it worked.” Say what you expected, what had to be true, and what you checked.

Discussion / pause
What is missing from the claim “the executable ran successfully”?

Expected response: The success criterion, input domain, environmental assumptions, and evidence beyond that one run.

Transition: Hardware: compute, state, and movement.

---

04. Hardware: compute, state, and movement
Section: 1.1.1 · HARDWARE & SOFTWARE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter begins with a deliberately simplified CPU-memory-I/O model. CPU cores execute instructions, registers hold working state, memory holds addressable instructions and data, and controllers connect devices to the rest of the machine. Storage and peripherals have different purposes and access mechanisms from registers. Buses and interconnects carry requests and data among these components.

Use this picture to ask three questions: where does a value currently exist, which component initiates its movement, and what event tells another component that progress occurred? The picture is not a claim that contemporary processors execute one instruction at a time or that all transfers pass through one physical wire. It is a model of responsibilities. The software side supplies instructions and data, while the language, executable format, operating system, and device interface assign meaning to particular encodings. A sequence of bits does not identify its own type or purpose.

Sixth-grade explanation
The processor does the work. Registers and memory hold information. Controllers help the computer talk to storage and other devices.

Discussion / pause
Does a byte sequence tell you whether it is an instruction, an integer, or text?

Expected response: No. Its interpretation depends on the surrounding interface, representation, and execution context.

Transition: Follow the value—not just the statement.

---

05. Follow the value—not just the statement
Section: 1.1.1 · CPU, REGISTERS & MEMORY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 18.

Graduate lecture narration
Suppose a source expression adds three to a value. Before discussing the addition, ask how the value became available to the executing instruction. It might arrive in an argument register, come from a prior calculation, or require a load. The result might remain in a register, be used immediately, or be stored. This is why a source variable should not automatically be imagined as a permanently assigned RAM slot.

The instruction stream also has to be fetched. Therefore, saying that an addition needs no data-memory access is not the same as saying that the processor uses no memory-related machinery. The original chapter makes this distinction in its expression example. Our register-workbench analogy explains placement, not exact timing or physical implementation. At this stage, track architectural inputs and outputs and leave detailed cache behavior and processor scheduling to later chapters.

Sixth-grade explanation
Think of registers as a tiny workbench and memory as a larger set of shelves. A value may already be on the workbench when it is needed.

Discussion / pause
Can the addition itself avoid a data-memory load?

Expected response: Yes, when the needed operand is already in a register or the compiler can otherwise supply it without a load.

Transition: Controllers and interrupts coordinate I/O.

---

06. Controllers and interrupts coordinate I/O
Section: 1.1.1 · STORAGE & PERIPHERALS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 12.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
I/O introduces a boundary between requesting work and completing work. A controller supplies a device-facing interface. Systems software translates a higher-level request into actions the device supports. An interrupt is one mechanism by which the system can learn that an event needs attention; it should not be mistaken for the application itself performing the hardware operation.

A useful explanation identifies the requester, the component doing the transfer, and the component reporting completion. Do not silently assume that a library call corresponds to one device command or that returning from a high-level call means durable storage has been achieved. Those are separate contracts. The source deck names controllers and interrupts; this slide makes the request/completion distinction explicit without prescribing one device protocol. We will revisit the same distinction when we discuss buffered output and partial failures.

Sixth-grade explanation
A device does not always finish right away. The program asks for work, the device does it, and the system reports what happened.

Transition: Software role is not execution privilege.

---

07. Software role is not execution privilege
Section: 1.1.2–1.1.3 · SOFTWARE CATEGORIES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 4.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter classifies systems software by role: kernels control resources, compilers translate, linkers connect compiled units, runtime libraries supply startup and shared operations, and drivers handle device-specific interactions. Application software performs tasks for users or services. The distinction is useful, but not absolute. A database application may contain its own allocator, scheduler, or storage engine.

Execution privilege is a different axis. A compiler is systems software that normally executes as an ordinary user process. A server may manage important information without becoming kernel code. Conversely, a particular driver architecture can place components on either side of a privilege boundary. Avoid using the labels low-level, systems, and privileged as synonyms. For diagnosis, ask what a component is responsible for and what operations it is authorized to perform. These questions may have different answers.

Sixth-grade explanation
Some programs help the computer run other programs. That does not mean they all get special permission to control the machine.

Discussion / pause
Why does a compiler not need kernel privilege just because it is systems software?

Expected response: Translation is its role; the OS can provide ordinary process permissions sufficient to read inputs and write outputs.

Transition: An abstraction is a smaller contract.

---

08. An abstraction is a smaller contract
Section: 1.1.4 · ABSTRACTION LAYERS
Source mapping: original slide(s) 5.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The original slide describes an abstraction as hiding detail while preserving a contract. For example, a file descriptor lets a caller request byte-oriented I/O without manipulating a storage controller. A vector presents a sequence while hiding many allocation decisions. Hidden details continue to exist; they are simply not all part of the caller's interface.

At graduate level, describe a contract using preconditions, permitted effects, postconditions, and failure behavior. Preconditions tell the caller what must already hold. Postconditions constrain the result when the operation succeeds. Failure behavior says what may have changed and what remains valid. This is a reasoning framework, not a claim that every real interface documents all of these perfectly. A missing or ambiguous guarantee is something to investigate, not permission to assume convenient behavior. Abstraction succeeds when the smaller contract is sufficient for the caller's reasoning.

Sixth-grade explanation
A button can be easy to use even when the machine behind it is complicated. You still need to know what pressing the button promises.

Transition: Guaranteed, customary, or measured?.

---

09. Guaranteed, customary, or measured?
Section: 1.1.4 · DO NOT INVENT GUARANTEES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 5, 15, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
Separate what an interface promises from what an implementation commonly does and from what you observed on a particular run. This distinction appears explicitly in the source chapter. Suppose an output operation reports that it accepted some number of bytes. The count is part of that operation's result. Whether all bytes were accepted at once, when physical storage was updated, and how long the operation took are different questions.

The vector example has the same structure: a sequence interface need not expose every allocation decision. A caller who relies on an undocumented growth choice turns an implementation detail into a hidden dependency. When presenting evidence, use precise wording. Say that a run took a measured amount of time under a stated setup, not that the API promises that latency. Say that a platform documents a behavior when it actually does. The method is to classify a claim before relying on it.

Sixth-grade explanation
A rule, a habit, and something you saw once are different. A program should not treat them as the same thing.

Transition: API, ABI, and ISA answer different questions.

10. API, ABI, and ISA answer different questions
Section: 1.1.5 · HARDWARE / SOFTWARE INTERFACES
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.

Graduate lecture narration
An API is a source-facing interface: names, operations, argument meanings, and behavioral contracts. An ABI governs compiled interoperability: calling conventions, register use, data layout, and other binary rules. An ISA describes machine operations and software-visible architectural state. These boundaries answer different questions even when one program crosses all three in a few instructions.

Use a function call as the running example. Its source declaration tells the compiler how the call is written and typed. Binary conventions tell caller and callee where to put arguments and results. The selected machine instructions must then be valid for the target architecture. Matching at one boundary does not imply matching at the others. The original chapter's three warnings remain important: identical APIs do not imply binary compatibility; a shared ISA does not imply a shared ABI; and a shared ISA does not imply identical microarchitecture or speed.

Sixth-grade explanation
The API says what you can ask for. The ABI says how compiled parts pass things. The ISA says which machine commands the processor understands.

Transition: One ISA can support different calling conventions.

11. One ISA can support different calling conventions
Section: 1.1.5 · ABI CASE STUDY
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Here is a concrete graduate extension of the chapter's ABI distinction. For an ordinary function taking two int parameters, a System V AMD64 caller uses the integer argument-register convention associated with RDI and RSI, with the int values in their 32-bit portions. The usual Microsoft x64 convention uses RCX and RDX for those positions instead. For the int return in this example, EAX is used in both conventions.

This is a deliberately narrow example. Real ABIs also define stack rules, preserved registers, alignment, aggregate classification, and other details. Do not extend this two-int table to every type or every function. It is enough to demonstrate the logical point: a machine can implement the x86-64 ISA while binary components disagree about how a function is called. Source-level similarity is not evidence that independently built objects can be combined safely.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two people can speak the same language but use different handoff rules. Compiled functions also need to agree on where each value goes.

Discussion / pause
Would matching instruction sets make these two calling conventions interchangeable?

Expected response: No. Caller and callee must also agree on argument locations and the rest of the binary contract.

Transition: Architecture is a promise; implementation is a choice.

12. Architecture is a promise; implementation is a choice
Section: 1.1.5 · ISA VS. MICROARCHITECTURE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 6, 18, 19.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter warns that an ISA and a microarchitecture are not the same thing. The ISA defines the software-visible operations and state that an implementation must honor. Microarchitecture concerns how a particular implementation realizes that behavior. The existence of the same instruction in two systems does not establish the same latency, throughput, cache behavior, or resource contention.

Keep two explanations separate. A functional explanation asks which architectural result an instruction produces under its specified conditions. A performance explanation asks how long a workload takes on a particular implementation and why. A correct functional trace does not provide enough information to derive whole-program timing. Conversely, a favorable benchmark cannot excuse an invalid instruction assumption or a violated language rule. This distinction prepares the performance discussion without turning Chapter 1 into a processor-design course.

Sixth-grade explanation
Two cars can follow the same road rules but have different engines. Two processors can run the same commands at different speeds.

Transition: Locate the boundary before proposing a fix.

13. Locate the boundary before proposing a fix
Section: 1.1 · INTERFACE REASONING CHECK
Source mapping: original slide(s) 6, 11, 12, 21.

Graduate lecture narration
A systems failure is easier to investigate when the symptom is attached to a boundary. A missing source declaration is not the same problem as a missing compiled definition. A binary that requires a different instruction set has a different issue from a program that lacks access to a file. The table gives initial hypotheses, not a complete diagnostic decision tree.

The graduate task is to state the evidence that would discriminate among plausible explanations. For a binary-interface concern, examine build settings and the ABI of both components. For a runtime file error, inspect the operation's returned status and the relevant environment. For a performance discrepancy, record the workload and implementation. 14. Seven stages, seven different questions
Section: 1.2 · FROM SOURCE TO EXECUTION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 7.

Graduate lecture narration
The source chapter presents a seven-stage model: source, preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking, loading, and execution. The model separates responsibilities; it does not require every implementation to launch a separate operating-system process for every stage. Compiler drivers often orchestrate several stages in a single command.

Each stage changes what kind of evidence is available. Source text exposes the programmer's operations and obligations. Preprocessed text exposes the translation unit after directives and macros. Assembly exposes symbolic target operations. An object file exposes encoded data, symbols, and relocation requirements. A linked executable describes a loadable program, while loading and runtime establish and exercise the process environment. Notice that passing an earlier stage does not guarantee passing later stages. Successful compilation does not supply an omitted definition, and successful loading does not guarantee that a runtime resource will be available.

Sixth-grade explanation
The program goes through several stations before and while it runs. Each station has a different job and can find a different kind of problem.

Transition: Source code describes an abstract computation.

18. A macro can duplicate an operation
Section: 1.2.2 · PREPROCESSOR COUNTEREXAMPLE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 9.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This is a deliberately invalid example for analysis, not a program to use as a numerical experiment. The SQUARE macro replaces its parameter in two positions. Giving it i++ expands the increment expression twice. In C, the two modifications shown in the multiplication expression are unsequenced relative to one another, so the example has undefined behavior. There is no correct portable numeric answer to predict.

Parentheses are still useful in macros because they prevent some precedence surprises, but they do not make repeated evaluation safe. A function that receives an already computed value separates the caller's side effect from the body calculation. Even then, arithmetic range requirements remain: replacing the macro with a function does not make arbitrary signed multiplication overflow valid. This extension turns the source deck's warning about duplicated side effects into a concrete contract failure.

Sixth-grade explanation
A macro can copy your instruction more than once. Asking it to “use the number and then increase it” can accidentally copy the increase too.

Expected response: None. The shown expanded expression violates C sequencing rules.

24. Relocation: finish an address-dependent calculation
Section: 1.2.5 · GRADUATE WORKED MODEL
Source mapping: original slide(s) 11.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
Relocation records preserve information needed to adjust address-dependent content. To make the arithmetic visible, use an illustrative PC-relative relocation model with a symbol address S, an addend A, and a relocation-place address P. Under the chosen model, the stored result is S plus A minus P. For the slide's hexadecimal values, 0x1200 minus 0x1000 gives 0x0200, or 512 decimal.

This is explicitly a teaching model, not the exact encoding of a particular call instruction. Real relocation types define which location P denotes, how an addend is stored, the field width, alignment, and overflow constraints. Some instruction encodings require an addend that accounts for the relationship between the relocation field and the next instruction. The important conceptual result is that assembly can preserve a solvable equation without knowing its final numeric answer. A processor-specific ABI supplies the exact rule.

Sixth-grade explanation
A reference can say “fill in the distance to this function later.” Once the function has a final location, the linker can calculate the distance.

35. Trace x + 3 from a valid source state
Section: WORKED EXAMPLE · SOURCE-LEVEL REASONING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 8, 18.

Graduate lecture narration
The original expression is int y = x + 3. Begin with a valid int value x and a context in which reading it is permitted. For the mathematical result to be representable as int, x must not exceed INT_MAX minus three. Adding a positive three to any representable x cannot cross the lower bound, so the upper bound is the interesting arithmetic condition here.

Under those assumptions, the source-level postcondition is that y has the mathematical value of x plus three. That is the claim the implementation must realize when the result matters. The variable can be optimized away if the surrounding program has no required observable use for it. This sequence of reasoning deliberately precedes instruction selection. It prevents the mistaken argument that a familiar hardware addition or a successful test somehow establishes valid source semantics for every possible input.

Sixth-grade explanation
Before adding three, check that the starting value is allowed and the answer fits. A good-looking answer does not fix a broken rule.

37. The six concerns of systems programming
Section: 1.3 · SYSTEMS PROGRAMMING
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13.

Graduate lecture narration
The original chapter organizes systems programming around six concerns rather than a single language feature or level of privilege. Low-level reasoning addresses representation and machine behavior. Performance distinguishes latency and throughput. Resource management identifies ownership and release responsibilities. Correctness connects behavior to specifications and invariants. Robustness defines controlled behavior under failure. Portability makes environmental assumptions visible.

These concerns interact without becoming interchangeable. A faster implementation can violate an ownership rule. A memory-safe operation can still produce the wrong specified result. Portable source can have poor performance on a second platform, and a compatible binary can still depend on missing runtime resources. In the following slides, keep asking which concern a proposed change improves and which assumptions it introduces. Graduate reasoning requires identifying those tradeoffs rather than labeling a design simply good or bad.

Sixth-grade explanation
Systems programmers care about what the bits mean, how fast work happens, who owns things, and what happens when something goes wrong.

Transition: Low-level reasoning makes representation explicit.

38. Low-level reasoning makes representation explicit
Section: 1.3.1 · REPRESENTATION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 3, 13, 15.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The low-level concern is not merely using assembly syntax. It is recognizing where representation becomes part of the program's obligations. Values have sizes, layouts, alignment requirements, and interpretation rules. Storage contains encodings; an interface supplies the meaning. A pointer value that is useful inside one process is not automatically a useful representation for a file or another process.

The original chapter links representation to machine behavior and later asks for explicit serialization. The graduate consequence is to identify every point where an internal representation becomes an external contract. Writing raw object bytes can accidentally expose padding, platform data layout, or addresses that have no meaning to the reader. This slide presents the design question; the later byte-order example supplies a concrete protocol. Make platform assumptions visible rather than hiding them behind a familiar type name.

Sixth-grade explanation
The same bits can mean different things under different rules. Programs must agree on how to read and store them.

39. Performance: latency, throughput, and elapsed time
Section: 1.3.2 · PERFORMANCE
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter names latency and throughput as separate performance concerns. Latency measures a completion interval for a chosen unit of work. Throughput counts completed work per unit time. Improving one does not logically establish an improvement in the other; the workload and measurement boundary matter.

For a simple single-thread observation, partition a chosen elapsed interval into time running on the CPU, time blocked, and time runnable but waiting for CPU service. Under this teaching model, those states are mutually exclusive and account for the interval. The illustrative values total twelve milliseconds. They are not measurements of the companion program. The point is diagnostic: optimizing instructions cannot remove time that the thread spends waiting for a resource or scheduling opportunity. For multiple threads, sums of CPU time and elapsed wall time require more care because work can overlap.

Sixth-grade explanation
Latency is how long one job takes. Throughput is how many jobs finish in a period. A job can also spend time waiting instead of working.

40. Derive the limit of a local speedup
Section: 1.3.2 · GRADUATE PERFORMANCE DERIVATION
Source mapping: original slide(s) 13, 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
This derivation makes the chapter's performance concern quantitative without pretending that a local optimization accelerates the entire system equally. Normalize the original total time to one. Assume that sixty percent belongs to a component we can make three times faster and that the remaining forty percent is unchanged. The new time is 0.60 divided by three plus 0.40, or 0.60 of the original total. Overall speedup is therefore one divided by 0.60, about 1.67.

The assumptions are the substance of the argument: the same work is performed, the fractions come from the same baseline, the portions do not overlap in this simplified account, and no new overhead appears. If a redesign changes concurrency, I/O, or the workload itself, the model needs revision. A graduate explanation should state both the result and the circumstances under which it follows. The numbers are an invented worked example, not a measured claim.

Sixth-grade explanation
Speeding up one part does not speed up the whole job by the same amount. The parts you did not improve still take time.

Discussion / pause

Expected response: Forty percent of the original time has not improved.

41. Make a performance claim reproducible
Section: 1.3.2 · MEASUREMENT DESIGN
Source mapping: original slide(s) 19.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration

42. Ownership turns resources into explicit obligations
Section: 1.3.3 · RESOURCE MANAGEMENT
Source mapping: original slide(s) 14.
Graduate extension: added analysis, teaching model, diagnostic method, or exercise.

Graduate lecture narration
The chapter says every acquisition needs an owner, a validity interval, and a release rule. Think of memory, file descriptors, handles, or other resources as obligations that persist beyond one successful function call. The operation that acquires a resource may differ from the component responsible for releasing it, but that transfer must be explicit.

The original invariant owner(fd) equals exactly one component is a design policy, not an automatic property of the operating system. References can be shared, descriptors can be duplicated, and ownership protocols can vary. What must remain unambiguous is the release responsibility for each owned resource. A borrowed reference should not silently acquire permission to release the underlying resource. Diagram the lifecycle before writing complicated error paths. That often reveals leaks, double release, and use after the agreed validity interval.

Sixth-grade explanation
When a program borrows something, someone must be responsible for returning it. Passing it to another part must pass that responsibility clearly.
